body: Né chi phí re-embed: Drift-Adapter (arXiv 2509.23471, Harshil Vejendla, nộp 2025-09-27) — Học một transform nhẹ ánh xạ embedding của query mới vào không gian embedding cũ, huấn luyện trên một mẫu nhỏ các cặp (old, new) embedding — thay vì re-embed toàn bộ corpus. Ba biến thể: Orthogonal Procrustes, Low-Rank Affine, Residual MLP. Kết quả tác giả báo cáo: phục hồi 95–99% Recall@10 và MRR so với một lần re-embed đầy đủ, thêm dưới 10 microsecond latency mỗi query, giảm chi phí recompute hơn 100 lần.

AWQ: tìm salient weights (high activation magnitude), scale trước INT4 rounding. Acc > GPTQ cùng bits. NF4 (bitsandbytes): 4-bit NormalFloat, optimal cho normal-distributed weights. Double quant: constants FP32 FP8. GGUF k-quant: Q4_K_M = mixed Q4/Q6 per tensor (attn vs FFN). k=better quant, m=medium size.

body: Caching · appears on: Semantic Caching: The Stack Is 3 Caches Deep - What: The layered caching architecture in a production LLM serving system: Layer 1 (Semantic/response cache) → Layer 2 (KV prefix cache) → Layer 3 (Full inference), with each layer providing a different granularity of reuse. - How it works: A request first hits the semantic cache (100% compute saved on hit via vector similarity). On miss, it hits the KV prefix cache (saves prefill compute for the shared prefix portion). On full miss, it runs complete inference. The semantic cache catches paraphrase-level repeats; the KV cache catches shared context/system-prompt repeats; full inference handles novel queries. - Why it matters: Layering caches at different granularities maximizes cost savings across the query distribution. Each layer handles a different class of repeat: exact/paraphrase (semantic), shared context (prefix KV), novel (full compute). - Gotcha: The three layers must be managed consistently for security: a semantic cache hit bypasses KV cache entirely, so per-tenant salting must be applied at the semantic cache layer too. Cache poisoning at Layer 1 is as dangerous as at Layer 2.
title: 3-Cache Stack

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Expert Parallelism: MoE Scaling - What: A collective communication operation where every GPU sends a distinct portion of its data to every other GPU simultaneously—used in MoE expert dispatch (token routing) and combine (result aggregation). - How it works: In MoE EP, after routing selects experts per token, tokens must move to the GPUs hosting those experts (dispatch A2A), be processed, then results return to the originating GPU (combine A2A). The A2A volume scales as (tokens × hidden_dim × 2) per layer, over NVLink or InfiniBand. DeepEP, nixl, and mooncake provide optimized A2A backends. - Why it matters: A2A is the dominant communication bottleneck in MoE serving; its latency sets the floor for EP-scale throughput. TBO is specifically designed to hide A2A latency. Choosing the right A2A backend (NVLink vs IB) is critical for production MoE deployment. - Gotcha: A2A is NOT the same as the agentic Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol—these are completely different concepts sharing the same acronym. In a serving context, A2A always refers to the MoE collective communication operation.
title: A2A

body: Concept · appears on: Attention Architecture (Long-Context Stack box): 'Jamba (AI21 Labs)' - What: An Israeli AI company that developed Jamba, a hybrid SSM (State Space Model) and Transformer architecture capable of 256K-token context windows with lower KV-cache memory than pure-transformer models. - How it works: Jamba interleaves Mamba SSM layers (which process context in O(1) recurrent state without KV cache) with standard transformer attention layers (which do build KV cache). This allows the model to maintain very long-range context via the SSM state while still using attention for local precise token interactions, achieving 256K context at significantly lower KV memory than GQA at the same parameter count. - Why it matters: Demonstrates that the KV-cache memory wall for long context can be addressed at the architecture level rather than solely via engineering workarounds like MLA or quantization. As a commercial model, Jamba's hybrid design influenced subsequent 2025–26 SSM-Transformer hybrid research (Marconi, Mamba-2). - Gotcha: SSM layers do not support KV-cache prefix sharing (RadixAttention / APC) because their context is encoded in a fixed-dimensional recurrent state, not in explicit per-token key-value vectors. Prefix caching infrastructure built for pure-transformer serving does not apply to the SSM layers.
title: AI21 Labs

body: Decoding · appears on: Drafting Ladder: EAGLE-3 → Parallel Drafting (2026) - What: The mean number of draft tokens accepted per verification round — the honest comparison metric between speculative-decoding methods, in place of a headline “N×”. - How it works: Each round the drafter proposes γ tokens and the target verifies them in one forward pass; AL counts how many survive rejection sampling on average. End-to-end speedup is roughly AL divided by the cost of producing the draft, so AL alone does not determine speed. - Why it matters: AL separates draft quality from draft cost, which is exactly where the 2026 methods differ. DFlash reaches an AL close to EAGLE-3's yet is ~1.5× faster end-to-end, because its drafting is cheaper — not because it drafts better. DSpark instead raises AL itself. - Gotcha: A speedup quoted without AL, block size and batch size is not comparable across papers. AL is also workload-dependent: low-entropy domains (code, math) accept far longer runs than open-ended chat.
title: AL

body: Parallelism · appears on: Parallelism Strategy Guide table (TP tradeoff 'All-reduce sync mỗi layer') and Placement Rules - What: A collective communication operation where all GPUs participating in a group each contribute a tensor, the tensors are element-wise summed (or reduced with another operation) across all devices, and every device receives the complete result — used in tensor parallelism to synchronise partial attention and FFN outputs after each layer. - How it works: In tensor parallelism, each GPU holds a horizontal shard of the weight matrices. A linear layer's output is computed as a partial sum on each GPU; the all-reduce sums these partial results across all TP-group GPUs so every GPU has the full layer output before the next layer runs. NCCL implements all-reduce via ring-reduce (optimal for bandwidth-bound transfers) or tree-reduce (lower latency for small messages). On NVLink-connected GPUs, all-reduce achieves ~900 GB/s; over InfiniBand it falls to ~200 GB/s. - Why it matters: All-reduce is the fundamental latency bottleneck of tensor parallelism: it occurs synchronously every layer, meaning TP latency = compute_time + all-reduce_time per layer. This is why the deck's placement rules specify 'TP within node' (NVLink) — crossing nodes with TP introduces multi-ms all-reduce latency per layer that accumulates over 32–80 layers. - Gotcha: All-reduce does not appear in expert parallelism — EP uses All-to-All instead (tokens routed to specific experts rather than broadcast to all). Pipeline parallelism uses point-to-point activation transfers, not all-reduce. The TP tradeoff row in the parallelism table ('All-reduce sync mỗi layer') is the key reason TP beyond 8 GPUs is rarely beneficial: all-reduce latency grows with group size.
title: All-reduce

body: Parallelism · appears on: Two-Batch Overlap defbox: 'TBO xen kẽ A2A communication và GEMM computation'; Placement Rules 'A2A routing on-demand' - What: A collective communication pattern where each GPU sends a distinct message to each other GPU in the group simultaneously — used in expert parallelism to dispatch tokens from routers to their assigned expert GPUs and to gather expert outputs back to origin GPUs. - How it works: After the MoE router assigns each token to its top-K experts (which may reside on different GPUs), an All-to-All operation simultaneously sends each GPU's outgoing tokens to their target expert GPUs. Post-computation, a second A2A gathers expert outputs back to their origin GPUs for combination. Unlike all-reduce (which communicates the same data to all), A2A routes different data to different destinations, requiring full-mesh connectivity. DeepEP implements A2A over NVLink (726–740 GB/s) with optional FP8 dispatch to halve traffic. - Why it matters: A2A is unavoidable in expert parallelism: the router's dynamic token assignment necessitates non-uniform inter-GPU data movement. Its latency is the primary motivation for Two-Batch Overlap (TBO/DBO): if A2A takes 5ms and GEMM takes 5ms, overlapping them halves the effective per-step time. - Gotcha: A2A is distinct from all-reduce and all-gather. All-to-All bandwidth scales with EP group size: at EP=32 with 32 GPUs each receiving 1/32 of the token stream, individual link utilisation is 1/32 of peak NVLink bandwidth during A2A. FP8 dispatch (halving the data per token) is therefore a significant optimisation at high EP counts.
title: All-to-All

body: Caching · appears on: Inference Engine Evolution: 2020 → 2025; PagedAttention: vLLM v0 → v1 Deep Dive; Prefix Caching: RadixAttention, APC, HiCache & Pricing - What: vLLM's automatic KV cache reuse for common prompt prefixes — enabled by default in V1 (v0.8.0+) — that skips re-computing prefill for any token sequence already in cache. - How it works: When a request arrives, vLLM hashes each 16-token block of the prompt; any block whose hash matches a block already in the physical page pool is mapped directly (no prefill needed). On a cache hit, the prefill phase is reduced to only the new tokens not in cache. In V1, APC adds near-zero overhead (<1% at 0% hit rate) and extends to multimodal content (image hashing). - Why it matters: Reduces TTFT by up to 70% on repeated system prompts (RAG, agent scaffolding, multi-turn); effectively free when hit rate is high since cached blocks cost no compute, only VRAM space. - Gotcha: In vLLM v0, APC required an explicit --enable-prefix-caching flag. V1 made it the default (v0.8.0, Mar 2025, not Jan 2025). Cache misses still compute full prefill and incur full API pricing on hosted services — monitor cache-hit rate in production dashboards.
title: APC

body: Hardware · appears on: Edge Deployment Flow - What: Apple's low-level GPU programming API for macOS and iOS, used by llama.cpp as its GPU backend on Apple Silicon (M-series) Macs, enabling GPU-accelerated LLM inference without CUDA. - How it works: llama.cpp compiles a Metal backend (enabled at build time with LLAMA_METAL=1 or cmake -DGGML_METAL=ON) that dispatches matrix multiply and attention kernels to the Apple GPU via Metal shaders. On Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3/M4), the GPU shares unified memory with the CPU, so GGUF models can be fully loaded into GPU memory without copying. - Why it matters: Metal is the primary GPU acceleration path for llama.cpp on macOS; it provides significant speedup over CPU-only inference and is the default for Ollama on Mac. It makes local development with GPU acceleration available on non-NVIDIA hardware. - Gotcha: Metal performance for LLM inference is limited by Apple Silicon's GPU architecture, which is narrower than discrete GPUs for large matrix operations. Mixed CPU+GPU offload on M-series (where some layers run on ANE, some CPU, some GPU) requires careful -ngl (number of GPU layers) tuning.
title: Apple Metal

Optimized specifically for the short-sequence, high-volume embedding workload. - Why it matters: Embedding throughput is often the bottleneck in production RAG pipelines; at 16x vLLM throughput, Arctic Inference can serve the same workload with 16x fewer GPUs, dramatically reducing the cost of the retrieval half of an AI pipeline. - Gotcha: The 16x figure applies specifically to short-sequence workloads (the dominant RAG use case); gains at long sequences are smaller. This is a Snowflake-proprietary system, not open-source as of 2026.

body: Hardware · appears on: Attention Backend Selection: 'ROCm / Ascend / CPU → triton (cross-platform fallback)' - What: Huawei's AI accelerator chip series (Ascend 910A/B/C, Ascend 310) and its associated CANN (Compute Architecture for Neural Networks) software stack — used primarily in Chinese domestic AI deployments and listed in the deck as a supported non-NVIDIA backend via the Triton attention kernel fallback. - How it works: vLLM and SGLang support Ascend via a community plugin that wraps Huawei's CANN operators through a Triton or PyTorch Inductor compilation path. The '--attention-backend triton' flag enables this path. LMDeploy has historically had stronger Ascend support (Huawei is a primary contributor). EPD disaggregation for VLM on Ascend was demonstrated in EPD-Serve (arXiv:2601.11590) showing +57–69% throughput over collocated PD-disaggregated serving. - Why it matters: US export controls on NVIDIA GPUs to China have made Ascend the primary domestic AI accelerator for Chinese companies. Many Chinese enterprises building LLM serving infrastructure (including those using open-weight models like DeepSeek) must run on Ascend, making Triton fallback support strategically important for open-source engine adoption in that market. - Gotcha: Ascend performance on LLM serving benchmarks is rarely published in peer-reviewed venues and difficult to verify independently. The Triton fallback on Ascend uses PyTorch-level operators rather than hardware-optimised fused kernels, resulting in significantly lower throughput than equivalent NVIDIA hardware with FA3/FA4. CANN versions and compatibility with specific vLLM/SGLang releases can be a significant source of deployment friction.

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Attention Backend Selection: FA3 / FA4 / FlashInfer / FlashMLA - What: A vLLM CLI flag to manually override the auto-selected attention kernel backend, accepting values: fa3, fa4, flashinfer, trtllm_mha, flashmla, triton. - How it works: vLLM's hardware auto-detection normally selects the optimal backend (H100→fa3, B200→fa4/trtllm_mha, A100→flashinfer, DeepSeek→flashmla, others→triton). This flag overrides that selection. Example: --attention-backend flashinfer on an H100 forces FlashInfer instead of FA3, useful for debugging or when FA3 has correctness issues at a specific context length. - Why it matters: Essential for debugging attention correctness bugs (kernel-specific numerical differences), benchmarking kernel performance, or working around hardware/driver-specific issues without rebuilding the engine. - Gotcha: Not all backends support all features: FA3 lacks MLA, flashmla requires block_size=64, trtllm_mha requires extra package installation. Overriding auto-selection can silently disable features like speculative decode — always verify the full feature set after manual override.
title: --attention-backend

body: Attention / KV · appears on: Attention Architecture (Long-Context Stack box): 'StreamingLLM: attention sinks, infinity context' - What: A small set of initial tokens (typically the first 4) in a sequence that receive disproportionately high attention scores and must be retained in the KV cache to prevent catastrophic perplexity spikes when using a sliding-window KV cache. - How it works: StreamingLLM (ICLR 2024) observed that attention weights concentrate heavily on the first few tokens (the 'sink' tokens) regardless of their semantic content — likely because the softmax denominator uses them as a normalisation pivot. If these tokens are evicted when the sliding window advances, perplexity collapses. The fix is to always retain the first 4 token positions in the KV cache while evicting the rest, enabling effectively infinite streaming context within a fixed KV budget. - Why it matters: Enables long-context inference with constant KV memory rather than O(N) memory — critical for streaming chat and real-time applications where generation length is unbounded. vLLM V1 incorporates attention-sink-aware KV eviction logic for hybrid models. - Gotcha: Attention sinks are an inference-time workaround, not a model property: the model must have been trained with a window-compatible positional scheme (RoPE, ALiBi) for the approach to be semantically coherent. It does not preserve long-range semantic coherence — tokens outside the window + sink positions are forgotten.
title: Attention sinks

body: Hardware · appears on: Edge Deployment Flow - What: x86 SIMD instruction set extensions that allow CPUs to process 256-bit (AVX2) or 512-bit (AVX-512) vectors of integers or floats per instruction, providing 4–8x speedup over scalar code for llama.cpp matrix multiply on Intel/AMD CPUs. - How it works: llama.cpp detects and compiles support for AVX2 or AVX-512 at build time (via CMake flags or make LLAMA_AVX2=1). At runtime, matrix multiply kernels use 256-bit or 512-bit SIMD intrinsics to process 8 or 16 float32 values (or 32/64 INT8 values) per instruction. AVX-512 requires Skylake-SP or later Intel CPUs and Zen 4 AMD CPUs. - Why it matters: On CPU-only or mixed CPU+GPU edge deployments, SIMD support is the primary factor in tokens/second; a build without AVX2 runs approximately 2–4x slower than an optimized AVX2 build. The Day 20 lab explicitly includes a 'thread sweep' and 'build flags' bonus track for this reason. - Gotcha: AVX-512 is not universally available: early AMD Zen 3 and Apple Silicon (ARM) do not support it. On Apple Silicon, NEON (ARM SIMD) replaces AVX. Building with AVX-512 on a system without it causes an illegal instruction crash.

aliases: Advanced Vector Extensions 2 / Advanced Vector Extensions 512

title: AVX2 / AVX-512

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization: Precision vs Performance; Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ - What: A 4-bit post-training quantization method that identifies and protects weights with high activation magnitude (salient weights) before rounding to INT4. - How it works: AWQ runs a small calibration set (typically hundreds of samples) through the full-precision model to measure per-channel activation magnitudes. Channels with large activations are rescaled upward so that their corresponding weights survive INT4 rounding with lower error. Only the scale factors are stored; no extra bits are used. The deck gives AWQ 4-bit a BPW of 4.5 (storing the scales), 4.5 GB for an 8B model, and ~1 MMLU-point drop. - Why it matters: AWQ consistently outperforms GPTQ at the same bit-width for the W4A16 regime (~95% quality retained) and is the recommended 4-bit format for GPU cloud deployments where FP8 hardware is unavailable. vLLM, SGLang, and TRT-LLM all support AWQ natively. - Gotcha: Despite AWQ leading on common leaderboards, ACL 2025 found GPTQ W4A16 beats AWQ on several real-world tasks. Always evaluate on your specific task, not just MMLU. AWQ accuracy degrades more on sub-7B models than on 8B+.
title: AWQ

body: Concept · appears on: Semantic Caching frame: 'AWS ElastiCache+Bedrock' - What: Amazon's managed foundation model service that provides API access to third-party and Amazon-developed LLMs; cited in the deck as one of the platforms where semantic caching (via AWS ElastiCache as the vector store) has been demonstrated at 90.3% hit rate with 86% cost and 88% latency reduction. - How it works: In the AWS semantic caching pattern, incoming prompts are embedded and their vector compared against a Redis-based (ElastiCache) vector index of previously seen prompts. If cosine similarity exceeds a threshold, the cached response is returned without forwarding to the Bedrock LLM API. The Nov 2025 AWS demonstration showed 90.3% hit rate and 86% cost reduction on a high-overlap customer-service dataset. - Why it matters: AWS Bedrock serves as the production LLM API target in the semantic cache stack, illustrating that semantic caching is a standard architectural pattern above the LLM serving layer — applicable to both self-hosted and managed LLM deployments. The AWS implementation validates the 3-cache-deep architecture taught in the deck. - Gotcha: The 90.3% hit rate was measured on a deliberately high-overlap dataset (paraphrased customer-service FAQs); realistic production hit rates are 30–68% for FAQ/support and 10–25% for open-ended queries. The '95%' marketing figure cited in some AWS promotional materials requires extreme query repetition and should not be used as a planning assumption.
title: AWS Bedrock

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Semantic Caching: The Stack Is 3 Caches Deep - What: AWS's managed semantic caching integration that uses ElastiCache (Redis/Valkey vector search) to cache and retrieve LLM responses from Amazon Bedrock based on semantic prompt similarity. - How it works: Prompts are embedded and stored in ElastiCache with their corresponding LLM responses. Incoming requests are embedded and compared against stored embeddings; if similarity exceeds a threshold, the cached response is returned without invoking Bedrock. AWS demonstrated 90.3% hit rates and 86% cost reduction in controlled evaluations (Nov 2025), though on high-overlap datasets. - Why it matters: Managed semantic caching eliminates the need for self-hosted vector store + embedding infrastructure for AWS Bedrock users. It sits above the Bedrock API and is transparent to downstream consumers. - Gotcha: The 90.3% hit rate was measured on a high-overlap benchmark dataset — realistic production hit rates for general-purpose applications are 30–68%. The cache backend (ElastiCache) must be sized appropriately and incurs additional AWS costs.
title: AWS ElastiCache Semantic Cache

Large deployments use the UltraServer configuration (16 chips interconnected via Neuron Colosseum at high bandwidth). vLLM and SGLang have Trainium/Neuron backends, though feature parity with CUDA is lagging. - Why it matters: Trainium3 provides AWS-native cost-effective inference at scale, particularly attractive for AWS customers who want to avoid GPU supply constraints. Anthropic running Claude on both Ironwood and Trainium demonstrates frontier labs actively diversifying away from NVIDIA supply dependence. - Gotcha: Trainium3's 2.52 PFLOPS FP8 is significantly below B200's 9 PFLOPS; the cost advantage comes from lower chip price and AWS-internal economies of scale, not raw performance. Neuron SDK compile times and debugging experience lag behind CUDA.

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Model Routing & Cascades: Cross-Model Cost - What: Microsoft Azure's generally available (GA May 2025) model routing service that automatically selects the most cost-effective model from 28+ cross-vendor models for each incoming query based on quality, cost, or balanced optimization modes. - How it works: The Azure AI Foundry Model Router accepts requests in OpenAI-compatible format and applies learned routing policies to dispatch each query to the optimal model from its portfolio of 28+ models (including OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, and others). Three operating modes: Quality (maximize response quality), Cost (minimize token cost), and Balanced. Routing adds <5% latency overhead. - Why it matters: Provides managed infrastructure for the 3-tier model stack pattern without requiring teams to build and maintain their own routing classifiers. The cross-vendor model portfolio means routing can span proprietary and open models based on cost-quality tradeoffs. - Gotcha: The router's routing decisions are opaque (no published classifier architecture); users cannot inspect why a specific query was routed to a specific model. Model availability in the portfolio changes with Azure's partnerships and may not include the most recent model releases.

Incoming requests have their prompts embedded by a configured embedding model; the resulting vector is compared against a vector store (Azure Cache for Redis or Azure Cosmos DB) for similarity matches above a threshold. On hit, the cached response is returned without backend invocation. - Why it matters: Provides enterprise-grade, Azure-native semantic caching without custom development. Integrates with Azure's security model (managed identities, network policies) and usage monitoring, making it suitable for regulated enterprise deployments. - Gotcha: APIM semantic caching is GA as of 2025. The effectiveness depends heavily on the embedding model quality and threshold tuning. Cache hit rates in production may differ significantly from internal benchmarks.

All three can be combined for hybrid retrieval. - Why it matters: Consolidating dense, sparse, and ColBERT representations in one model reduces deployment complexity and allows hybrid retrieval strategies without running multiple models. Widely used as a strong retrieval baseline in RAG pipelines. - Gotcha: Using all three representation types simultaneously triples the memory and compute at query time. In most production deployments, only dense or dense+sparse is used; full ColBERT late-interaction is expensive at scale.

body: Concept · appears on: Embedding & Reranker Serving: The Retrieval Half - What: An embedding architecture that encodes queries and documents independently into dense vectors; similarity is computed as cosine or dot product between the resulting embeddings. - How it works: Query and document are each processed by a transformer encoder (which may share weights or be separate) without attending to each other. The resulting fixed-size vectors are indexed in a vector database. At retrieval time, the query vector is compared against all stored document vectors via approximate nearest neighbor search. - Why it matters: Bi-encoders enable fast retrieval at scale because document vectors are precomputed and indexed; only the query requires online compute. They form the first stage of a two-stage retrieve-then-rerank pipeline. - Gotcha: Bi-encoders sacrifice some accuracy for speed — the query and document never directly attend to each other. For precision-critical applications, a cross-encoder reranker is used in the second stage to rescore top candidates.

The bnb.nn.Linear4bit module stores weights in NF4 with double quantization and dequantizes on the fly during forward passes. - Why it matters: bitsandbytes is the enabling library for QLoRA fine-tuning — it is the only widely available implementation of NF4 + double quantization with gradient support. Hugging Face Transformers integrates it via the load_in_4bit=True flag. - Gotcha: bitsandbytes is primarily optimized for training-time quantization (QLoRA). Blackwell Ultra (B300/GB300) further increases HBM3e bandwidth. TensorRT-LLM v1.3.x, vLLM, and SGLang all support NVFP4 on Blackwell. The deck notes NVFP4 as 'Production Blackwell: default'. - Why it matters: Blackwell shifts the production quantization default from FP8 to NVFP4, delivering 3.5× memory reduction vs FP16 and 1.8× vs FP8. It is the target for FlashAttention-4 and the new frontier for serving throughput. - Gotcha: Blackwell Ultra (B300/GB300) and Vera Rubin (50 PFLOPS NVFP4, 288 GB HBM4, announced CES 2026) are distinct products. Rubin ships H2 2026; B300 is current. Do not conflate 'Rubin' with an 'R100' — there is no official NVIDIA R100 product name.

body: Security · appears on: Confidential Inference: TEE & the Attack Surface - What: NVIDIA Blackwell's hardware feature that encrypts NVLink inter-GPU communication, enabling confidential multi-GPU inference for the first time by closing the plaintext NVLink gap present in Hopper. - How it works: Blackwell GPUs (B200/GB200) extend the confidential computing trust domain across NVLink by encrypting all GPU-to-GPU tensor transfers. Combined with TEE-I/O (which provides TEE attestation for the I/O path), this allows a multi-GPU pod to operate as a single, verifiable confidential enclave. The trust boundary now encompasses the full TP/EP group. - Why it matters: Frontier models (70B+) require tensor parallelism across 4–8 GPUs to serve efficiently. Hopper's plaintext NVLink meant TP-serving could never be fully confidential. Blackwell's NVLink encryption enables confidential deployment of frontier models in regulated industries for the first time. - Gotcha: NVLink encryption overhead on Blackwell has not been publicly benchmarked separately from PPCIE overhead. The <9% total overhead figure encompasses both PPCIE and NVLink encryption combined for large models.
title: Blackwell NVLink Encryption

body: Hardware · appears on: Hardware Landscape 2026 table: 'NVIDIA B300/GB300 ... Blackwell Ultra — current gold standard' - What: NVIDIA's second-generation Blackwell GPU architecture (B300 chip, GB300 system) featuring 288 GB HBM3e memory, 15 PFLOPS dense FP4 throughput, 1,400W TDP, and ConnectX-8 networking — designated the 'current gold standard' for production GPU serving as of mid-2026. - How it works: Blackwell Ultra (B300) doubles the HBM capacity of the original B200 (288 GB vs 192 GB), enabling larger models (e.g., DeepSeek-V3.1 full precision in fewer nodes) and larger KV caches for long-context serving. The 15 PFLOPS FP4 figure is exactly 5/3× the B200's 9 PFLOPS, reflecting improved die area allocation to compute. GB300 NVL72 retains the 72-GPU NVLink domain (130 TB/s) of NVL72 but with Blackwell Ultra chips and ConnectX-8 (200 Gb/s InfiniBand) inter-node fabric. - Why it matters: Blackwell Ultra is the deployment target for NVFP4 KV cache (Blackwell-only feature) and FlashAttention-4 (Blackwell SM100 native). Its '15 PFLOPS FP4' enables 3.5× the FP16 throughput per GPU over H100, changing the economics of both training and inference. The 288 GB memory capacity means Llama-3.1-405B fits in a single GB300 at FP8 without tensor parallelism. - Gotcha: Blackwell Ultra (B300/GB300) shipped in 2025–26 with 135–150 kW/rack power requirements, necessitating direct liquid cooling infrastructure that most existing data centres cannot support without facility upgrades. 'Current gold standard' reflects mid-2026 availability; Vera Rubin NVL144 (~190 kW, 50 PFLOPS NVFP4) is the next generation entering production H2 2026.

body: Decoding · appears on: DFlash: Block Diffusion Drafting + KV Injection - What: A drafting objective in which a diffusion language model denoises a whole block of masked positions at once, rather than generating left to right. - How it works: Masked positions are filled in parallel conditioned on context; the non-causal mask lets every position see every other. Applied to speculation, one denoising pass yields the entire candidate block, which the target then verifies normally. - Why it matters: It converts sequential drafting into block-parallel GPU work while leaving the verification step — and therefore the output distribution — untouched, so the result stays lossless. - Gotcha: Diffusion here is the drafter, not the served model. The same idea appearing as the target model is a separate development (see dLLM).
title: Block diffusion

body: Attention / KV · appears on: PagedAttention vLLM v0 box: 'Block size: 16 tokens/page (default)' - What: The granularity at which vLLM allocates and tracks KV-cache memory: each 'page' or 'block' holds the key and value tensors for exactly 16 consecutive tokens by default. - How it works: Rather than allocating a contiguous array for the entire maximum-length KV cache upfront, vLLM maintains a pool of fixed-size blocks (16 tokens × num_heads × head_dim × 2 × dtype_bytes per block). A logical-to-physical page table maps each sequence's logical block indices to non-contiguous physical blocks. When a request grows beyond its currently allocated blocks, new blocks are allocated on demand from the free pool. This eliminates internal fragmentation (wasted pre-allocated space) — fragmentation drops below 4% in v1. - Why it matters: The 16-token block size balances internal fragmentation (smaller blocks waste less on partially-filled last blocks) against page-table overhead and kernel efficiency (larger blocks reduce indirection). This is why vLLM achieves near-full KV utilisation versus the 60–80% waste of pre-LLM static-allocation schemes. - Gotcha: The block size is a compile-time constant affecting CUDA kernel tiling; changing it requires recompilation of attention kernels. SGLang's RadixAttention uses token-level granularity (block size = 1 for prefix matching purposes), which enables finer-grained prefix sharing but has different kernel implications.
title: Block size

body: Attention / KV · appears on: FlashAttention: IO-Aware Attention (FA1→FA4) - What: The FlexAttention API object that specifies which (query_block, key_block) tile pairs participate in attention computation, enabling sparse attention patterns to skip entire tiles without compute. - How it works: A BlockMask is a 2D boolean mask at block granularity (not token granularity). FlexAttention's compiler uses BlockMask to skip tiles where all entries are masked out, reducing compute for sparse patterns like sliding window attention (where far-away Q-K pairs are zero). Expressed via `create_block_mask()` with a mask-generating function. - Why it matters: Block-level sparsity avoids the O(N²) compute for patterns where most tiles are empty (e.g., document-boundary attention that doesn't cross documents). FlexAttention + BlockMask enables these speedups without custom CUDA. - Gotcha: Block-level masking means the smallest addressable unit is a tile (typically 128 tokens); fine-grained token-level sparsity within a block still requires computing the full tile. Patterns with high intra-block density do not benefit from BlockMask skipping.

body: Metric · appears on: Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ - What: The average number of bits used to store each model weight parameter, accounting for scale factors and quantization overhead. Used to compare quantization schemes at a unified cost basis. - How it works: Calculated as (total bits for weight storage including scales) / (number of parameters). For a pure INT4 scheme with no scales: 4.0 BPW. For AWQ 4-bit with per-group FP16 scales stored per 128 weights: effectively ~4.5 BPW. The deck's comparison table uses BPW as the primary axis. - Why it matters: BPW enables apples-to-apples comparison across formats. A scheme with lower BPW is not automatically better — Q2_K at 2.6 BPW has far more accuracy loss than AWQ at 4.5 BPW. The trade-off between BPW and quality (perplexity) determines which format to choose. - Gotcha: Reported BPW can be misleading if scale storage is omitted. AWQ's 4.5 BPW vs GPTQ's 4.0 BPW looks like AWQ uses more memory, but AWQ achieves better accuracy — so the fair comparison must include quality alongside BPW.

body: Metric · appears on: Pipeline Parallelism: Ultra-Long Context - What: The idle GPU time in Pipeline Parallelism caused by pipeline fill and drain phases, where some stages have no active micro-batch to process. - How it works: At the start of a PP forward pass, stage 0 processes micro-batch 1 while stages 1..P-1 are idle (pipeline fill bubble). Conversely, at the end, stage P-1 processes the last micro-batch while stages 0..P-2 drain. Bubble fraction = (P-1)/(M + P-1) where M is the number of micro-batches and P is the number of stages. More micro-batches reduce bubble fraction. - Why it matters: Bubble latency directly reduces effective throughput compared to fully-utilized TP on a single node. For production PP deployments, minimizing bubble latency (via more micro-batches, dynamic chunking) is critical to maintaining acceptable throughput. - Gotcha: Bubble latency is fundamental to pipeline parallelism—it cannot be eliminated, only amortized. Two-Batch Overlap (TBO) in MoE EP is a related concept but is not the same as pipeline bubble reduction; TBO hides A2A communication, not pipeline idle time.
title: Bubble Latency

body: Caching · appears on: Data Parallelism: DP, DPA & Cache-Aware Router - What: A load-balancing policy that directs requests to the serving instance whose KV prefix cache best matches the incoming request's prefix, trading load balance for cache locality. - How it works: The router hashes the incoming prompt's prefix tokens and compares against each worker's cached prefix tree. The worker with the highest prefix match fraction above a threshold is selected. If all workers are below threshold, routing reverts to least-loaded. This creates a 'sticky' effect where requests sharing a system prompt or document context cluster on the same worker. - Why it matters: Transforms cache hit rate from ~20% (random routing) to ~75% on shared-prefix workloads, which translates directly to higher throughput (less prefill recomputation) and lower TTFT for cached requests. - Gotcha: Cache-aware routing can cause load imbalance if a subset of prefixes (e.g., a very popular system prompt) generates disproportionate traffic, overloading one worker. The threshold parameter controls the tradeoff between cache-hit rate and load balance.
title: Cache-Aware Routing

body: Security · appears on: Semantic Caching: The Stack Is 3 Caches Deep - What: An attack where a malicious actor crafts prompts that cause incorrect or harmful responses to be stored in a shared semantic or KV cache, which are then returned to legitimate users. - How it works: The attacker sends a crafted query designed to be semantically similar (above the cache hit threshold) to common legitimate queries, but paired with a malicious or incorrect response that gets cached. Subsequent legitimate users asking the real question receive the poisoned cached answer. NDSS 2026 demonstrated ~90.6% attack success rates against AWS/Azure/Alibaba/GPTCache implementations. - Why it matters: Shared caches across tenants or users create a supply-chain-like attack surface; a single poisoned entry can affect many downstream users. This is particularly dangerous for high-trust, factual workloads (medical, legal, financial). - Gotcha: The standard mitigation is per-tenant cache salting — prefixing cache keys with a tenant-specific salt so one tenant's cache entries cannot match another's. vLLM implements this via Issue #16016. An untested single global cache is unsafe for multi-tenant deployments.
title: Cache Poisoning

body: Security · appears on: Semantic Caching: The Stack Is 3 Caches Deep - What: A cache isolation technique that prefixes cache keys (for both semantic and KV caches) with a per-tenant or per-user unique token (salt), preventing cross-tenant cache sharing. - How it works: Before hashing a prompt or prefix for cache lookup, the serving engine prepends a tenant-specific identifier to the key material. This ensures that tenant A's cached entries cannot be retrieved by tenant B even if their prompts are semantically identical. vLLM implements this for KV cache (Issue #16016); semantic cache layers require analogous salting. - Why it matters: Without salting, shared prefix caches expose a KV-timing side-channel (PROMPTPEEK) and cache-poisoning attack surface. With salting, tenants are isolated: cross-tenant cache hits are impossible, eliminating both the side-channel and poisoning vector. - Gotcha: Cache salting eliminates cross-tenant prefix reuse as a side effect — if multiple tenants share the same system prompt, each tenant computes its own KV cache copy. This trades security for cache efficiency; system-prompt deduplication must be done explicitly within a tenant's salt namespace.
title: Cache Salting

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Data Parallelism (sgl-router): 'Flags: --router-policy cache_aware --cache-threshold 0.5' - What: An sgl-router CLI flag that sets the minimum cache-hit ratio threshold below which a request is routed to any instance (load-balanced) rather than the instance with the best prefix cache match. - How it works: SGLang's Rust-based sgl-router implements cache-aware load balancing: for each incoming request, it queries each worker instance's RadixAttention trie (via a lightweight RPC) to estimate what fraction of the request's prefix is already cached. If the best-matching instance exceeds the '--cache-threshold' (default 0.5 = 50% prefix overlap), the request is routed there to maximise cache hit; if no instance exceeds the threshold, the request falls back to least-busy routing to avoid overloading a single cache-warm instance. On 8×A100, this strategy improved cache hit rate from 20% to 75% (+275%) and throughput by 92%. - Why it matters: Naive round-robin routing scatters identical-prefix requests across all instances, defeating prefix caching. Cache-aware routing concentrates shared-prefix traffic onto the same instance, converting expensive prefill operations into cheap cache hits. The threshold prevents degenerate cases where all traffic piles onto one instance. - Gotcha: The threshold is sensitive to the prefix distribution of the workload: FAQ/chatbot workloads with many shared system prompts benefit from a high threshold (0.7–0.9); diverse-prefix workloads (code generation) benefit from a lower threshold (0.3–0.5). The 92%/+275% figures are for a specific benchmark and will not generalise to all workloads.
title: --cache-threshold

The system estimates available carbon slack and shifts workloads by hours to take advantage of renewable generation peaks. - Why it matters: Carbon-aware temporal shifting can offset up to ~70% of inference-related carbon emissions for deferrable workloads. As sustainability reporting becomes regulated (EU AI Act, SEC climate disclosure), carbon-aware scheduling is becoming an operational requirement for large-scale AI deployments. - Gotcha: Carbon-aware shifting only applies to batch or async workloads — real-time interactive inference cannot be deferred. Geographic flexibility (shifting workloads to lower-carbon datacenters) is often more powerful than temporal shifting within a single region.

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Model Routing & Cascades: Cross-Model Cost - What: A serving pattern where a sequence of progressively capable (and expensive) models handles a query, with each model deciding whether to return its answer or defer to the next tier based on its confidence score. - How it works: Request arrives → cheap nano model generates a response and computes a confidence score → if confidence > threshold, return immediately; otherwise pass the query (and optionally the nano response) to the mid-tier model → repeat up the chain to the frontier model as needed. Each deferral incurs the full generation cost of the cheaper model. - Why it matters: Cascades can match frontier quality at a fraction of the cost by routing the majority of simple queries to cheap models. However, unlike pre-generation routing, cascades pay generation cost at every tier before deferral. - Gotcha: In 2026, pre-generation routing is preferred over pure cascades for most benchmarks because cascades waste compute generating tokens with the cheap model even when deferral is inevitable. Cascades are better when reliable per-query confidence scores are available.

body: Serving pattern · appears on: PagedAttention: vLLM v0 → v1 Deep Dive; Production Tuning: Memory, Scheduling & Observability - What: A scheduling technique that splits long prompt prefill computations into fixed-size chunks and interleaves them with decode steps to avoid decode stalls and reduce TTFT variance. - How it works: Instead of computing all N prompt tokens at once (monopolizing the GPU for seconds on long contexts), the engine breaks the prefill into chunks of `--chunked-prefill-size` tokens (default 8192 in vLLM V1) and interleaves each chunk with one decode step. This prevents prefill from starving active decode requests. Sarathi-Serve (OSDI 2024) formalized this as 'stall-free chunked prefill' (2.6–3.7x capacity improvement). - Why it matters: Critical for mixed-traffic serving: without chunking, a single 128k-token prompt would block all decode requests for seconds, causing latency spikes. V1 makes chunked prefill the default and prefix-aware. - Gotcha: Reduce --chunked-prefill-size to 2048–4096 when prefill OOM occurs; the default 8192 may be too large for memory-constrained deployments. In vLLM V1, chunked prefill is not hard-disabled by any CLI flag (PR #21645 adding that enforcement was never merged).
title: Chunked prefill

body: Splitting long prefill into chunks to protect inter-token latency; chunk size is a $/token knob (chunk 512 → +25% overhead).
title: Chunked prefill

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Production Tuning: Memory, Scheduling & Observability - What: A CLI flag (both vLLM and SGLang) setting the maximum number of prefill tokens processed per scheduling step, controlling the trade-off between prefill throughput and decode latency smoothness. - How it works: Default is 8192 in vLLM V1. Each scheduling step processes at most this many prefill tokens before yielding to decode requests. Smaller values (2048–4096) reduce GPU memory pressure during prefill and smooth decode latency at the cost of longer absolute prefill time. Larger values maximize prefill throughput for batch processing workloads. - Why it matters: The primary knob for preventing prefill OOM and controlling TTFT/TPOT trade-offs under mixed-traffic conditions; critical for long-context workloads where a single request may have 128k+ prefill tokens. - Gotcha: Reducing this value below 2048 can cause very slow prefill for long prompts and may not be compatible with all attention kernel backends. CUDA graph capture for prefill is disabled (piecewise graphs only) for chunked prefill, which slightly reduces throughput vs full-graph decode.
title: --chunked-prefill-size

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Multi-LoRA Serving - What: SGLang's optimized variant of the SGMV kernel that partitions segmented adapter computations into chunks, reducing latency 20–80% at high concurrency compared to basic Triton-based SGMV. - How it works: Instead of computing all segment GEMMs in one large fused operation (which can cause uneven warp occupancy at high adapter-count), csgmv divides the computation into smaller chunks that better fill the GPU's warp scheduler, especially when batch size and number of distinct adapters are large. - Why it matters: At production concurrency levels with many distinct adapters active simultaneously, basic SGMV leaves GPU threads under-utilized. Chunked SGMV recovers this, making multi-LoRA latency acceptable at scale. - Gotcha: csgmv is SGLang-specific (introduced v0.5.3, Oct 2025). vLLM uses its own SGMV implementation. The 20–80% range is concurrency-dependent; at low concurrency the difference is minimal.
title: Chunked SGMV

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Production SLA: Best Practices - What: A fault-tolerance pattern that monitors error rate or latency on downstream calls and 'opens' (stops forwarding requests) when a threshold is breached, preventing cascading failures. The deck describes it as 'fallback when overloaded'. - How it works: The circuit breaker sits in the request path (API gateway or service mesh like Envoy/Istio). It tracks a sliding window of error rate or latency P99. When errors exceed a threshold (e.g., 50% in 10 s), it opens: new requests immediately receive the fallback response without hitting the inference backend. After a configurable cool-down period, it enters half-open state: one probe request is forwarded; if it succeeds, the circuit closes. - Why it matters: LLM inference backends can fail slowly (GPU OOM, KV cache exhaustion, CUDA deadlock) rather than fast. Without a circuit breaker, the gateway keeps forwarding requests that pile up in the server queue, exhausting all resources and increasing blast radius. The circuit breaker bounds time-to-error for downstream callers. - Gotcha: Circuit breakers in LLM serving need to be tuned for the slower time-scale of LLM failures (responses that take 30–60 s) versus microservice failures (100 ms). A standard 5-second window may falsely open on normal high-TTFT requests.
title: Circuit Breaker

body: Concept · appears on: Embedding & Reranker Serving (Stack 2026): 'BGE-M3 (dense+sparse+ColBERT)' - What: A multi-vector retrieval architecture where both query and document are encoded into token-level embeddings (not a single pooled vector), and similarity is computed as a sum of maximum inner products (MaxSim) between query tokens and document tokens — enabling finer-grained semantic matching than single-vector dense retrieval. - How it works: ColBERT encodes a query into L_q vectors (one per query token) and a document into L_d vectors. Retrieval score = Σ_{i=1}^{L_q} max_{j=1}^{L_d} (q_i · d_j). This late-interaction pattern allows each query token to attend to its best-matching document token independently. BGE-M3 implements ColBERT as one of three retrieval modes (alongside dense single-vector and SPLADE-style sparse), allowing a single model to serve all three paradigms. ColBERT retrieval requires storing L_d vectors per document (much larger than a single dense vector), making it storage-intensive. - Why it matters: ColBERT outperforms single-vector dense retrieval on queries requiring multi-hop reasoning or precise phrase matching. In RAG pipelines, ColBERT-style re-ranking can close the quality gap between bi-encoder first-stage retrieval and expensive cross-encoder reranking. BGE-M3's unified dense+sparse+ColBERT serving reduces the deployment footprint for multi-stage retrieval. - Gotcha: ColBERT's multi-vector storage requirement makes it impractical for large corpora without specialised MIPS (maximum inner product search) infrastructure. BGE-M3's ColBERT mode is slower at retrieval than its dense mode; in production, ColBERT is typically used only for re-ranking a dense-retrieved top-K shortlist, not for full corpus search.
title: ColBERT

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Scaling Strategies - What: The latency penalty incurred when a new GPU replica must be provisioned from zero before it can serve the first request. - How it works: A cold start involves: (1) Kubernetes pod scheduling, (2) container image pull (if not cached), (3) GPU driver and CUDA context initialization, (4) model weight loading from storage to GPU HBM. Steps 3 and 4 dominate for large models — loading a 70B model at ~3 TB/s NVMe speed takes tens of seconds. During this window, an activator buffers incoming requests. - Why it matters: Cold start is the key cost of scale-to-zero: every spike in traffic after a zero-replica period incurs it. The warm-pool pattern is the direct mitigation — keeping N pre-warmed replicas avoids cold starts at the expense of idle GPU cost. - Gotcha: Cold-start latency is highly model-size-dependent and often understated. Quantized smaller models (e.g. 8B Q4) can cold-start in a few seconds; unquantized 70B+ models can take 30–120 seconds. As of mid-2026 there are no published end-to-end GPU-provision-to-first-token benchmarks for llm-d's activator.

body: Decoding · appears on: DSpark: Semi-Autoregressive + Confidence Scheduling - What: A lightweight linear+sigmoid head, trained end-to-end with the drafter and then calibrated, that predicts the probability each drafted position will be accepted. - How it works: It reads the drafter's backbone representation (optionally with the previous-token embedding when paired with the Markov head) and emits a per-position acceptance probability, trained with a binary cross-entropy term. - Why it matters: It converts acceptance from something you discover after paying for verification into something you can estimate before — which is what makes scheduling verification possible. - Gotcha: Predicted confidence needs calibration to be usable as a scheduling signal; raw sigmoid outputs are not probabilities you can threshold safely.

body: Decoding · appears on: DSpark: Semi-Autoregressive + Confidence Scheduling - What: DSpark's system-level contribution: choosing the verification length per request from estimated prefix-survival probability and the engine's throughput profile. - How it works: Using the confidence head's per-position estimates, the scheduler computes how far into the block it is worth verifying for this request under current load, then truncates verification there instead of verifying every block to full length. - Why it matters: Verifying long blocks for every request wastes batch capacity on tokens likely to be rejected — and under high concurrency that waste is what degrades throughput. This is the first time speculative decoding treats batch capacity as a resource to be scheduled rather than a constant. - Gotcha: The benefit is load-dependent: at low concurrency there is little capacity to waste and the gain is small. Its value shows up exactly where the old “turn spec decoding off at high batch” rule used to apply.

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Pre-LLM Era: Serving Infrastructure 2017–2022 - What: A scheduling strategy where finished sequences are immediately evicted from the running batch and new requests are inserted on a per-decode-step basis, keeping GPU utilization near 100% without waiting for the entire batch to finish. - How it works: After each decode step (each token generation iteration), the scheduler checks for completed sequences (those that hit EOS or max length). Completed sequences are removed, their KV-cache pages are freed, and new queued requests are added to fill the slots — all within the same decode step cycle. This is sometimes called 'iteration-level scheduling' (Orca paper, OSDI 2022, which first formalized it). - Why it matters: Continuous batching eliminates head-of-line blocking and dramatically increases GPU utilization for LLM serving. vLLM's 24x throughput improvement over naive HuggingFace Transformers serving (cited in the deck) is primarily due to combining continuous batching with PagedAttention. All modern LLM engines (vLLM, SGLang, TRT-LLM) use continuous batching as their default. - Gotcha: Continuous batching interacts with chunked prefill in important ways: without chunked prefill, a large incoming prefill can block decode steps for existing requests, spiking their TPOT. Chunked prefill slices prefill into fixed-token chunks interleaved with decode steps to prevent this stall (see Sarathi-Serve).
title: Continuous Batching

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Speculative Decoding & Continuous Batching - What: A serving scheduling strategy where requests join and leave the active batch at every decode step, so new requests can be inserted as slots free without waiting for other requests to finish. - How it works: At each decode iteration, the scheduler checks for completed sequences (those that hit EOS or max length) and evicts them, then immediately fills their slots with new requests from the queue. No padding is needed because each sequence occupies exactly as many KV slots as it has generated. The batch size fluctuates dynamically each step. - Why it matters: Eliminates the 200–500 ms wait of static batching and the compute waste from padding. The deck cites 5× latency reduction. Called 'in-flight batching' in TensorRT-LLM and 'continuous batching' in vLLM; they are equivalent concepts. - Gotcha: Continuous batching and chunked prefill are complementary but distinct: continuous batching governs when requests join/leave the batch; chunked prefill (Sarathi-Serve) governs how prefill tokens are interleaved with decode tokens to avoid head-of-line blocking. vLLM V1 uses both simultaneously.
title: Continuous Batching

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Inference Engine Evolution: 2020 → 2025; PagedAttention: vLLM v0 → v1 Deep Dive - What: A serving strategy where new requests join and completed requests leave the active batch mid-generation, rather than waiting for all requests to finish before starting the next batch. - How it works: At each decode step, the scheduler checks for newly completed sequences and immediately fills the freed KV page slots with queued waiting requests. PagedAttention makes this efficient because freeing pages is O(1). The GPU processes a variable-size batch at each step, maximizing utilization. Orca (OSDI 2022) first described this; vLLM operationalized it with PagedAttention. - Why it matters: Without continuous batching, a slow long-output request blocks all subsequent short requests; with it, short requests complete quickly regardless of concurrent long requests, improving p50 latency significantly. - Gotcha: Continuous batching improves throughput at medium concurrency but can increase p99 TTFT at very high load if the queue backs up. The --max-num-seqs (vLLM) or --max-running-requests (SGLang) caps help control this.
title: Continuous batching

body: Metric · appears on: Production SLA: Best Practices - What: The fully-loaded dollar cost to generate one million output tokens, including GPU compute, memory bandwidth, networking, and operational overhead. A primary business KPI for LLM serving economics. - How it works: Calculated as (GPU_hour_cost x hours_to_generate_1M_tokens). If throughput is T tok/s per GPU, then 1M tokens takes 1,000,000/T seconds = 1,000,000/(T x 3600) GPU-hours. At T=1,800 tok/s on an H100 (~$3.50/hr spot), cost per 1M tokens ≈ $0.54. Quantization (FP8, AWQ 4-bit), batching efficiency, and prefix caching all reduce effective T cost. - Why it matters: Cost per 1M tokens is the unit economics metric that determines whether self-hosting beats API pricing (e.g., GPT-4o at $15/1M output tokens vs self-hosted at $0.50-2.00/1M). It drives decisions on quantization depth, hardware selection, and cache strategy. The deck frames it as a continuously optimizable metric. - Gotcha: Published API costs are per token (output tokens charged separately from input). Self-hosted cost per 1M tokens must include idle GPU time (low-traffic periods), not just peak throughput. The break-even vs API typically occurs around 50–100M tokens/month for self-hosted infrastructure.

body: Hardware · appears on: Multimodal (VLM) Serving: Encode–Prefill–Decode - What: Intel Xeon instruction-set extensions for accelerating matrix multiply operations, used to offload ViT encoder compute onto CPU while GPUs handle LLM prefill and decode in parallel. - How it works: Intel Xeon CPUs with AMX can run the vision encoder (ViT) concurrently with GPU prefill/decode operations. The LMSYS team demonstrated (May 2026) that with a capability ratio R=12 (GPU-to-CPU compute ratio), this offloads enough encoder work to reduce P99 TPOT by up to 30x at lower GPU cost. - Why it matters: For large VLM deployments, running the ViT encoder on underutilized CPUs (which exist in every GPU server) instead of consuming GPU compute enables better GPU utilization for the decode-heavy LLM path. - Gotcha: Only beneficial when the server has Xeon CPUs with AMX support and sufficient CPU-GPU bandwidth for embedding transfers. The capability ratio R must be evaluated per deployment to determine if CPU AMX offload is net positive.
title: CPU AMX

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Production Tuning (Observability): 'crash dump: rolling 5-phút buffer' - What: SGLang's '--log-requests' crash dump feature that maintains a rolling 5-minute buffer of recent inference request logs on disk, enabling reproduction and root-cause analysis of server crashes or anomalous outputs. - How it works: When '--log-requests' (basic or full mode) is enabled, SGLang serialises each request's prompt, parameters, and response to a log file in a circular-buffer manner covering the most recent 5 minutes. On an unexpected crash or OOM event, the buffer file persists on disk. Engineers can then invoke 'replay_request_dump.py' to replay the exact request sequence against a fresh engine instance, reproducing the failure in a controlled environment. - Why it matters: LLM servers are notoriously difficult to debug post-hoc because failures are often caused by specific prompt+parameter combinations that are hard to reconstruct from high-level error logs. The rolling buffer captures the exact input state without requiring always-on full logging (which adds I/O overhead). - Gotcha: The 5-minute rolling window means a crash caused by a slow-building memory leak may not capture the first requests that initiated the leak. Full request logging ('--log-requests full') includes prompt text, which may contain PII and should be encrypted or filtered before retention. The replay utility reproduces compute behaviour but not GPU memory state or thermal conditions.

body: Concept · appears on: Embedding & Reranker Serving: The Retrieval Half - What: A reranker architecture that jointly encodes a (query, document) pair in a single forward pass, producing a relevance score by attending across both inputs simultaneously. - How it works: The query and document are concatenated and fed together into a transformer encoder; the model's [CLS] or pooled token output is scored by a linear head. Because query tokens attend to document tokens and vice versa, cross-encoders capture fine-grained relevance signals unavailable to bi-encoders. - Why it matters: Cross-encoders are more accurate than bi-encoders but cannot be precomputed — they must score each candidate pair at query time. They are used in the second stage of retrieval pipelines to rerank the top-K candidates from the bi-encoder. - Gotcha: Cross-encoder latency scales linearly with the number of candidates reranked; typically limited to top 20–100 candidates from bi-encoder retrieval. Running cross-encoders at bi-encoder scale would be prohibitively expensive.

body: Hardware · appears on: Edge Deployment Flow - What: NVIDIA's proprietary parallel computing platform and programming model for GPU compute, required for llama.cpp GPU acceleration on NVIDIA GPUs and for all production NVIDIA serving engines (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM). - How it works: llama.cpp's CUDA backend (cmake -DGGML_CUDA=ON) compiles CUDA kernels for matrix multiply, attention, and quantization dequantize operations. CUDA 12.3+ is required for Hopper FP8 features; CUDA 12.8 for Blackwell FlashMLA. Production engines like vLLM use CUDA graphs to eliminate kernel launch overhead. - Why it matters: CUDA is the dominant GPU compute platform in 2026; nearly all optimized serving kernels (FlashAttention 3, FlashInfer, custom FUSED ops) are CUDA-first, with ROCm/Triton ports following. For NVIDIA GPU servers, CUDA is not optional. - Gotcha: CUDA is NVIDIA-only; ROCm (AMD), OneAPI (Intel), and Triton (cross-platform) are alternatives but lag in feature parity. CUDA version must match the driver version and the target GPU's compute capability (SM level); mismatches cause silent performance degradation or crashes.
title: CUDA

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Model Compilation: torch.compile + CUDA Graphs + TensorRT - What: The two-phase CUDA graph workflow: Record captures a GPU computation sequence into a replayable graph object; Replay submits the pre-recorded command stream cheaply on each subsequent call. - How it works: During record, tensors are bound to graph nodes by address; replay reuses the same memory addresses. Input data for each step is updated via `cudaMemcpy` into the pre-allocated input buffer before calling `replay()`, so the graph sees fresh inputs without re-recording. In vLLM V1, decode graphs are recorded at startup for each batch-size bucket. - Why it matters: Eliminates per-step Python overhead (kernel launch scheduling, argument marshalling) that accumulates over thousands of decode steps. For a 1000-token generation, 0.5 ms/step saved = 0.5 seconds saved — significant at batch=1 interactive latency. - Gotcha: Graph memory is allocated at record time and cannot be freed while the graph exists. For large models, maintaining graphs for many batch-size buckets adds GPU memory overhead at serving startup.
title: CUDA Graph Record/Replay

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Model Compilation: torch.compile + CUDA Graphs + TensorRT - What: A CUDA mechanism that records an entire sequence of GPU operations (a forward pass) as a static graph, then replays that graph on subsequent calls by resubmitting the pre-built command stream without re-launching kernels from Python. - How it works: Record phase: run one forward pass with `cuda.graph.capture_begin/end`; the GPU driver records every kernel launch, memory copy, and synchronization event in a graph object. Replay phase: `graph.replay()` resubmits the same command stream in microseconds, bypassing Python's per-operation overhead (0.5–2 ms/step for LLM decode). - Why it matters: LLM decode executes the same operations (same kernel sizes, same order) for every generated token — exactly the pattern CUDA graphs are designed for. The 10–20% additional throughput on top of all other optimizations comes entirely from eliminating Python dispatch overhead. - Gotcha: CUDA graphs require static shapes: the graph is recorded with specific tensor shapes, so it can only be replayed with the same shapes. Variable sequence lengths (prefill) cannot use full CUDA graphs without shape bucketing or the piecewise variant. vLLM V1 uses full CUDA graphs for decode but eager execution for prefill.

body: Parallelism · appears on: Data Parallelism: DP, DPA & Cache-Aware Router; Distributed Inference: Parallelism Strategy Guide - What: A parallelism strategy that replicates the entire model (weights + KV cache) across multiple GPUs, with each replica handling an independent subset of incoming requests. - How it works: Each GPU runs an identical copy of the model; a load balancer distributes requests across replicas. No inter-GPU communication is required during inference—each replica is fully self-contained. Scales throughput linearly with GPU count for CPU/memory-bound workloads. - Why it matters: Simplest and most reliable parallelism for multi-user serving where the model fits on a single GPU. Throughput scales linearly, and GPU failures only affect one replica. Used as the baseline against which DP-Attention's benefits are measured. - Gotcha: Standard DP duplicates the KV cache on every replica, wasting VRAM proportional to N replicas. For MoE models with MLA, this KV duplication is the primary memory cost—motivating DPA. DP also means no KV cache sharing across replicas for the same user session.

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Disaggregated Prefill/Decode Serving - What: In a disaggregated architecture, the set of GPUs dedicated exclusively to autoregressive token generation (the decode phase), optimized for high HBM memory bandwidth. - How it works: Decode pools receive KV tensors from the prefill pool via NIXL/NVLink/IB and run autoregressive generation (one token per forward pass). Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound: each decode step reads the full KV cache from HBM and performs one attention operation. Decode GPUs benefit most from high-HBM-bandwidth hardware (H200, B200) and large batches to amortize the fixed read cost. - Why it matters: Allows deploying decode capacity proportional to desired output throughput independently from prefill capacity proportional to prompt ingestion rate — the correct resource match for production traffic with varying prompt/output length ratios. - Gotcha: Decode pools must maintain KV caches for all active sequences simultaneously — VRAM for the decode pool = num_active_sequences × avg_context_length × KV_bytes_per_token. At 100k average context with DeepSeek MLA (~70 KB/token), 128 active sequences = ~900 GB needed, requiring a GB200 NVL72 shared pool.

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Expert Parallelism: MoE Scaling - What: DeepSeek's open-source high-performance All-to-All communication library for MoE expert dispatch and combine, designed for NVLink and InfiniBand interconnects. - How it works: Uses JIT-compiled kernels for all-to-all dispatch/combine operations; NVLink bandwidth 726–740 GB/s measured. FP8 dispatch mode halves A2A traffic (vs BF16) by quantizing tokens before sending. V2 adds ElasticBuffer for dynamic token-count adjustment. Exposed via `--moe-a2a-backend deepep` in SGLang. - Why it matters: Replacing NCCL's general A2A with a specialized MoE dispatch kernel cuts communication overhead and enables the dual-batch overlap (TBO) optimization. Used in DeepSeek's own production system (EP32/EP144) and reproduced by LMSYS on 96×H100. - Gotcha: DeepEP v1.2.1 (Sep 16 2025) is the production version. Alternative A2A backends include mooncake and nixl (for IB/RoCE transport). FP8 dispatch requires FP8 dispatch support in the expert runner.
title: DeepEP

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Expert Parallelism (Key Optimizations): 'DeepEP mode: --deepep-mode auto / normal / low_latency' - What: An SGLang CLI flag that selects the operating mode of the DeepEP All-to-All dispatch/combine kernel: 'auto' (engine picks based on batch size), 'normal' (high-throughput mode, favours large batches), or 'low_latency' (optimised for small batch, single-digit-millisecond A2A). - How it works: DeepEP (v1.2.1, Sep 2025) implements two kernel variants: the normal mode uses large NVLink transfers optimised for saturating bandwidth at batch sizes typical of prefill; the low_latency mode uses finer-grained dispatch with reduced synchronisation overhead, trading peak bandwidth for lower latency at small decode batches. 'auto' selects between them per-step based on the current batch size, equivalent to DeepSeek's production dual-phase EP (prefill EP32 uses normal mode; decode EP144 uses low_latency). - Why it matters: Prefill and decode have fundamentally different A2A requirements: prefill processes large token batches (hundreds to thousands of tokens simultaneously) and needs maximum bandwidth; decode processes one token per sequence per step and needs minimum latency. A single mode cannot optimise both; '--deepep-mode auto' enables the engine to switch dynamically. - Gotcha: The 'low_latency' mode achieves its latency gains partly by using fewer NVLink lanes simultaneously, which means its effective bandwidth is lower than 'normal' mode. On NVL72 clusters where all GPUs share a single NVLink domain, the low_latency kernel's reduced lane usage may not be necessary; benchmarking both modes is recommended before production deployment.
title: --deepep-mode

body: Decoding · appears on: Speculative Decoding & Continuous Batching - What: DeepSeek's built-in speculative decoding mechanism in DeepSeek-V3, where extra prediction heads trained during pre-training predict the next 1–2 tokens ahead, achieving ~1.8× throughput with 85–90% acceptance rate. - How it works: Rather than a separate draft model, MTP adds lightweight heads directly to the target model during training. At inference, these heads propose draft tokens that the base model verifies in the same forward pass, eliminating draft-model memory overhead. SGLang reports +60% throughput; the official DeepSeek evaluation cites 85–90% acceptance. - Why it matters: Because MTP heads are trained jointly with the model, they generalize better to the model's own distribution. No separate draft model is needed, reducing deployment complexity and VRAM overhead versus external draft models. - Gotcha: The 85–90% acceptance and 1.8× figure is DeepSeek's own evaluation, not independently production-verified. AMD ROCm reports a separate 1.2–2.1× range. MTP requires models trained with MTP heads; it cannot be retroactively added to existing checkpoints.

Production serving uses EP32/4-node prefill and EP144/18-node decode, DeepEP A2A, EPLB, FP8 matmul, BF16 MLA, and dual-batch overlap. LMSYS reproduced ~$0.20/1M output tokens on 96×H100. - Why it matters: DeepSeek-V3 is the reference deployment for every MoE serving optimization in §4 (TBO, EPLB, DPA, sgl-router). Its open infrastructure index is the most cited MoE serving blueprint in 2025–26. - Gotcha: The LMSYS 96×H100 benchmark is DeepSeek-V3 (not R1). DeepSeek-V3.1 (a later iteration) uses 4K fixed or 12K dynamic chunk sizes for Pipeline Parallelism. Do not conflate V3, V3.1, R1, and V4 Flash pricing/benchmarks.
title: DeepSeek-V3

body: Concept · appears on: Pipeline Parallelism (Optimal Chunk Size): 'DeepSeek-V3.1: 4K fixed hoặc 12K dynamic'; PP vs TP defbox - What: A frontier open-weight MoE model from DeepSeek (671B total parameters, trained in FP8) whose full-precision serving requires multi-node pipeline parallelism, making it the primary motivating example for PP chunk-size tuning in the deck. - How it works: At full FP16/BF16 precision, DeepSeek-V3.1's 671B parameters require ~1.3 TB VRAM, exceeding single-node capacity even on 8×H100 (640 GB) or 8×H200 (1.1 TB). Pipeline parallelism splits its 61 transformer layers across 2–4 nodes. The optimal chunked-prefill chunk size for DeepSeek-V3.1 is 4K tokens fixed or 12K dynamic (smooth factor 0.65) — smaller than Qwen3-235B because larger per-layer activations fill pipeline bubble slots faster. - Why it matters: DeepSeek-V3.1 is the production reference for open frontier MoE serving: it established the EP32-prefill/EP144-decode blueprint, the FP8 training standard, and the DeepGEMM/DeepEP open-source kernel stack. Its PP chunk-size figures are empirically validated tuning parameters that practitioners serving it should use as starting points. - Gotcha: Piecewise CUDA Graph (PCG) automatically disables when PP is active, falling back to eager mode for prefill. The 'V3.1' designation refers to the updated weights release; the architecture is identical to V3. 'Full precision' serving of DeepSeek-V3.1 on open infrastructure is rare — most deployments use FP8 quantisation which fits in fewer nodes.
title: DeepSeek-V3.1

body: Tooling · appears on: DSpark: Semi-Autoregressive + Confidence Scheduling - What: DeepSeek's open, MIT-licensed full-stack codebase for training and evaluating speculative-decoding drafters — DSpark, DFlash and Eagle3 in one harness. - How it works: It covers data preparation (which needs an inference engine to serve the target model and is storage-hungry — roughly 38 TB for the default Qwen3-4B setting), training, and evaluation across gsm8k, math500, aime25, humaneval, mbpp, livecodebench, mt-bench, alpaca and arena-hard-v2. Checkpoints are published for Qwen3-4B/8B/14B and Gemma-4-12B. - Why it matters: It makes the DSpark-vs-DFlash-vs-EAGLE3 comparison reproducible on identical data and targets, which is rare in this literature. - Gotcha: The 38 TB data-generation footprint makes a from-scratch reproduction impractical for a classroom; use the published checkpoints. Adapted from SpecForge (Apache-2.0) and DFlash (MIT).

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Inference Engine Evolution: 2020 → 2025 - What: Microsoft's 2021 GPU-distributed inference library, introducing tensor parallelism and ZeRO-Inference for serving large models across multiple GPUs before specialized LLM engines existed. - How it works: DeepSpeed Inference partitions model weights across GPUs using tensor parallelism (splitting attention heads and FFN layers) and ZeRO-Inference (partitioning optimizer/activation state). It provided INT8 quantization via SmoothQuant and mixed-precision. Did not implement continuous batching or KV cache virtualization. - Why it matters: Enabled multi-GPU serving of GPT-scale models in 2021 before vLLM existed; established tensor parallelism (TP) as a standard serving primitive that all modern engines inherit. - Gotcha: DeepSpeed Inference is now largely superseded for serving by vLLM/SGLang/TRT-LLM but remains relevant for fine-tuning (ZeRO-3) and is still used in ZeRO-Inference for models that don't fit on a single node.

body: Concept · appears on: Milestone 1: 'Lakehouse: Delta Lake + Medallion' - What: Delta Lake is an open-source lakehouse storage layer (ACID transactions, schema enforcement, time travel on top of Parquet files in object storage); Medallion Architecture is a data organisation pattern (Bronze/Silver/Gold tiers) used together in Milestone 1 as the data storage layer for the AI infrastructure platform. - How it works: In the Milestone 1 stack, Delta Lake stores raw ingested data in Bronze tables (append-only, schema-on-read), validated/cleaned data in Silver (schema enforced, duplicates removed), and feature-engineered/aggregated data in Gold (queryable by models and dashboards). Delta's ACID transaction log enables time-travel queries and rollback — critical for ML reproducibility (re-training with data from a specific timestamp). In the serving context, Gold tables feed the vector store and feature store used by the LLM serving endpoint. - Why it matters: Medallion + Delta Lake is the industry-standard data architecture for ML pipelines as of 2025–26: it is the default stack in Databricks Lakehouse Platform and is directly relevant to Day 17 (Data Pipeline) and Day 18 (Lakehouse) content. Understanding it as a serving prerequisite (clean, versioned data → vector store → RAG endpoint) completes the N16–N20 infrastructure arc. - Gotcha: Delta Lake is a storage-format/transaction layer, not a compute engine; querying Delta tables requires a Spark, DuckDB, or Polars reader. In small-scale Milestone 1 deployments, DuckDB+Delta is often substituted for Spark for resource reasons. The Medallion pattern is a convention, not a Delta Lake technical requirement — any layered table structure achieves the same result.

body: Parallelism · appears on: Distributed Inference: Parallelism Strategy Guide - What: A logical N-dimensional array structure that maps parallelism dimensions (TP, PP, DP, EP) to physical GPUs, defining which GPUs communicate via which collective operations. - How it works: In vLLM/Ray, the device mesh is constructed as a 2D or higher array where one axis is TP (intra-node) and another is PP (inter-node). Each parallelism strategy operates on its mesh sub-dimension: TP ranks share a NCCL communicator for All-Reduce; PP stages share P2P communicators. EP adds a third dimension for expert routing. - Why it matters: Properly defining the device mesh ensures that NCCL and NVLink routes are used efficiently—TP on NVLink, PP/EP on IB. Incorrect mesh assignments (e.g., TP across nodes) cause performance collapses. - Gotcha: Ray 'automatically manages' the device mesh but this auto-detection is heuristic. For complex topologies (multi-NIC, multi-rail IB), manual mesh specification or NCCL tuning is required. EP adds a third mesh dimension that current frameworks (mid-2026) are still maturing.
title: Device Mesh

body: Decoding · appears on: DFlash: Block Diffusion Drafting + KV Injection - What: A speculative-decoding drafter (arXiv 2602.06036) that uses a lightweight block diffusion language model to produce an entire draft block in one forward pass, reporting >6× lossless acceleration and up to 2.5× over EAGLE-3. - How it works: The drafter receives γ mask tokens and uses a non-causal attention mask so every query attends to the verifier's hidden states and the mask-token embeddings at once, emitting all draft tokens simultaneously. Target hidden states are additionally injected into the drafter's KV cache (see KV injection). The drafter is 5 layers (vs EAGLE-3's 1) but runs once instead of K times. - Why it matters: It is the clearest demonstration that drafting latency, not drafting quality, was the binding constraint: on Qwen3-4B its AL matches EAGLE-3's (GSM8K 4.2 vs 4.2) while delivering ~1.5× more speedup. NVIDIA measured >15× throughput vs autoregressive decoding on gpt-oss-120b (8× DGX B300, TensorRT-LLM) at the 500–600 tok/s/user interactivity band. - Gotcha: Swapping EAGLE-3 → DFlash in vLLM is a config-only change through the Speculators library, but it still needs a DFlash checkpoint trained against your target model. Open checkpoints exist for Qwen3-4B/8B/14B and Gemma-4-12B.
