body: Serving pattern · appears on: Distributed Inference: Parallelism Strategy Guide - What: A serving architecture that routes prefill (prompt processing) and decode (token generation) phases to physically separate GPU pools, each optimized for its phase's different compute/memory characteristics. - How it works: Prefill is compute-bound (large GEMM on full prompt); decode is memory-bandwidth-bound (KV cache access, batch=1 per step). By separating them, prefill nodes use TP for throughput and decode nodes use smaller replicas for latency. KV cache is transferred between stages via NIXL/Mooncake transport over InfiniBand/NVLink after prefill completes. - Why it matters: Eliminates the fundamental tension where collocated P/D must compromise between throughput (needs big batches) and latency (needs low queuing). NVIDIA Dynamo 1.0 reports up to 30x throughput on DeepSeek-R1/GB200 vs non-disaggregated. Best for long RAG and prefill-heavy workloads. - Gotcha: Disaggregation is NOT universally beneficial—gains are workload-conditional (NVIDIA 'Beyond the Buzz', arXiv:2506.05508). KV transfer bandwidth is the cost: over IB at 200 GB/s, transferring 10GB KV takes ~50ms. FlowKV reports 96% KV-transfer latency reduction, but end-to-end speedup is only 15–49%.
title: Disaggregated Prefill/Decode

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Disaggregated Prefill/Decode Serving - What: An architecture that runs the prefill (prompt processing) and decode (token generation) phases on separate GPU pools, decoupling their distinct resource requirements — prefill is compute-bound, decode is memory-bandwidth-bound. - How it works: Requests arrive at a router; the router sends the prompt to a prefill GPU pool, which computes the full KV cache. The KV cache is then transferred to a decode GPU pool (via NVLink or InfiniBand/RDMA) that generates tokens autoregressively. Prefill GPUs can be high-compute (H100 for compute throughput) while decode GPUs can be cost-optimized (more GPUs for bandwidth). DistServe (OSDI'24) and Splitwise (ISCA'24) defined the research foundations; NVIDIA Dynamo, llm-d, and Mooncake operationalize it in production. - Why it matters: In monolithic serving, prefill and decode compete for the same GPU resources: long prefills stall decode (spiking TTFT), while large decode batches reduce prefill throughput. Disaggregation allows each phase to be scaled and optimized independently, improving TTFT-TPOT SLO attainment simultaneously. - Gotcha: KV transfer overhead (~10 GB/s over typical IB) is significant — disaggregation only pays off for prefill-heavy traffic (long contexts, RAG) where per-request KV transfer cost is amortized. For short unique prompts, disaggregation adds latency without benefit. NVIDIA 'Beyond the Buzz' paper (arXiv:2506.05508) confirms: gains are workload-conditional, not universal.
title: Disaggregated Prefill/Decode serving

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Disaggregated Prefill/Decode Serving - What: The foundational academic paper (arXiv:2401.09670, OSDI'24) establishing disaggregated prefill/decode as a production architecture, demonstrating up to 7.4x more requests meeting SLO vs monolithic serving. - How it works: DistServe formalized the observation that prefill and decode have different resource profiles (prefill: high FLOP/s, decode: high HBM bandwidth) and showed that placing them on separate GPU groups with optimized intra-group parallelism and KV migration between groups outperforms monolithic scheduling. Introduced the concept of goodput (requests per second meeting joint TTFT+TPOT SLOs) as the correct optimization target. - Why it matters: Provided the theoretical and empirical foundation for all production disaggregated serving systems (Dynamo, llm-d, Mooncake, Splitwise); the 7.4x goodput improvement motivated the industry-wide shift to P/D disaggregation. - Gotcha: DistServe's 7.4x is under specific SLO requirements (tight TTFT + tight TPOT simultaneously) on Llama-2-class models — gains vary by model size, context length, and traffic mix. Short-prompt workloads may see <1.5x benefit.
title: DistServe

body: Concept · appears on: Disaggregated Prefill/Decode (Systems 2026): 'DistServe (OSDI'24) / Splitwise (ISCA'24): foundational papers' - What: Two concurrent 2024 research papers that independently proposed and validated prefill/decode disaggregation — the architectural separation of LLM prefill and decode into distinct, independently scalable GPU pools — now the production default for hyperscale LLM serving. - How it works: DistServe (arXiv:2401.09670, OSDI 2024) formalised the prefill-decode interference problem: when collocated, long prefill operations delay decode steps, spiking TPOT for all in-flight sequences. DistServe showed that routing prefill requests to prefill-optimised GPUs (high compute utilisation) and decode requests to decode-optimised GPUs (high memory bandwidth) and transferring KV caches between pools via NVLink/InfiniBand enables up to 7.4x more requests within SLO. Splitwise (ISCA 2024) independently demonstrated that using heterogeneous GPU tiers (H100 for prefill, cheaper A10 for decode) achieves 1.4x per-dollar throughput. These papers provided the theoretical and empirical foundation for NVIDIA Dynamo 1.0, llm-d, and Mooncake. - Why it matters: Understanding DistServe and Splitwise is essential for interpreting why Dynamo 1.0 / llm-d exist and what problem they solve. The core insight — that prefill is compute-bound (benefits from high TFLOPS) while decode is memory-bandwidth-bound (benefits from high HBM bandwidth) — is the first principle behind all P/D disaggregation serving systems. Students who understand these papers can reason about when disaggregation is beneficial (prefill-heavy, long RAG) vs harmful (short unique prompts, KV transfer overhead dominates). - Gotcha: DistServe's 7.4x improvement is measured in 'more requests within SLO' (goodput), not raw throughput — at saturation, disaggregation adds KV transfer overhead that can hurt throughput for short prompts. The NVIDIA 'Beyond the Buzz' paper (arXiv:2506.05508) explicitly warns that disaggregation needs dynamic rate matching and is not universally beneficial. Neither paper addresses the cost of the KV transfer network fabric, which is a significant real-world deployment cost.
title: DistServe / Splitwise

body: Model architecture · appears on: Diffusion LLM: Khi Model Đích Không Còn Autoregressive - What: A language model that generates by denoising a block of positions in parallel rather than emitting one token per forward pass — now shipping commercially, not just a research curiosity. - How it works: Production dLLMs use block diffusion: the sequence is generated block by block, each block denoised over several steps. The dominant 2026 recipe converts an existing autoregressive checkpoint rather than training from scratch — LLaDA 2.0 (arXiv 2512.15745) does this with a three-phase block-level WSD schedule (progressively larger blocks → full-sequence diffusion → back to compact blocks), yielding open 16B mini and 100B flash instruction-tuned MoE variants. - Why it matters: It breaks the assumption underneath most of this day's material. “TPOT” stops being a natural unit, and the quality/latency knob becomes the number of denoising steps — a parameter autoregressive serving has no analogue for. Diffusion reached your stack as a drafter (DFlash) before arriving as the model. - Gotcha: PagedAttention and continuous batching assume the KV cache grows by exactly one token per step; dLLMs violate that, so the §9 capacity arithmetic does not transfer. Also treat vendor throughput numbers as vendor-reported — Inception's own Mercury 2 post gives no tokens/sec figure at all, despite the ~1,009 tok/s number circulating on aggregator sites.

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ - What: A technique introduced in QLoRA where the quantization constants (scale factors) stored per group are themselves quantized from FP32 to FP8, saving an additional ~0.37 bits per parameter. - How it works: In standard 4-bit quantization, each group of 64 weights stores a 32-bit float scale, adding 32/64 = 0.5 bits per weight overhead. Double quantization quantizes those 32-bit scales to 8-bit floats per group of 256 scales, reducing the scale overhead from 0.5 to ~0.127 bits per weight. The deck notation is 'constants FP32 → FP8'. - Why it matters: For a 65B-parameter model, double quantization saves ~3.6 GB of VRAM versus single quantization, making the difference between fitting or not on a single 80 GB A100. - Gotcha: Double quantization is a QLoRA fine-tuning optimization; it applies to the bitsandbytes NF4 path. It is not the same as quantizing both weights and activations (W4A8), which is a different technique.
title: Double Quantization

body: Quantizing the quantization constants themselves for additional savings.
title: Double quantization

body: Parallelism · appears on: Data Parallelism: DP, DPA & Cache-Aware Router - What: A hybrid parallelism mode that replicates only the attention layers (and their KV caches) across DP replicas while sharing MoE/FFN expert weights via Expert Parallelism, eliminating KV cache duplication. - How it works: Attention computation and KV cache are local to each DP rank (no inter-replica A2A for attention). MoE expert weights are distributed via EP and shared across all DP ranks (A2A for expert dispatch/combine still occurs). Enabled via `--dp-size N --enable-dp-attention` in SGLang. - Why it matters: For MoE models with MLA (like DeepSeek-V3/R1), standard DP duplicates the already-compressed MLA KV cache N times. DPA avoids this: larger effective batch sizes and significant VRAM savings. Combined with sgl-router, DeepSeek config `--tp 8 --dp-size 8 --ep 8 --enable-dp-attention` achieves +92% throughput. - Gotcha: DPA requires MLA (or similarly compressed KV) to be meaningful—for standard MHA, the KV cache is too large anyway and DPA alone doesn't help much. DPA is a DeepSeek-V3/R1 specific optimization in practice. The MLA benefit (DPA + MLA = bigger batch, less VRAM) is the compound effect.
title: DP-Attention

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Data Parallelism: DP, DPA & Cache-Aware Router - What: The reference production configuration for DeepSeek-V3 multi-GPU serving: `--tp 8 --dp-size 8 --ep 8 --enable-dp-attention`, combining Tensor Parallelism, Data Parallelism Attention, Expert Parallelism, and cache-aware routing. - How it works: tp=8 shards attention/dense weights across 8 GPUs per DP replica; dp-size=8 creates 8 DP replicas; ep=8 shards expert weights 8-way across EP group (satisfying ep_size=tp_size); enable-dp-attention prevents KV cache duplication across DP replicas. sgl-router with cache-aware routing routes to the replica with the best KV prefix hit. - Why it matters: This configuration achieved +92% throughput in the deck's 8×A100 80GB benchmark. It is the most cited practical recipe for serving DeepSeek-scale MoE models efficiently. - Gotcha: This config requires 64 GPUs (8 TP × 8 DP) for one logical serving cluster plus the sgl-router process. The 92% gain is specifically for a workload with significant KV prefix sharing; gains are lower for diverse-prefix or single-turn workloads.
title: DP+EP Config

body: Differentially-private stochastic gradient descent -- clipping and adding noise to gradients during training to bound any single record's influence.
title: DP-SGD

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Data Parallelism frame: 'Flags: --dp-size N --enable-dp-attention'; DeepSeek-V3 DP+EP config - What: An SGLang CLI flag that sets the data parallelism degree — how many replicas of the attention computation (when combined with '--enable-dp-attention') or the full model (in pure DP mode) are deployed across GPUs. - How it works: In pure DP, '--dp-size N' creates N identical full-model replicas; each handles an independent slice of incoming requests. In DP-Attention mode ('--dp-size N --enable-dp-attention'), only the attention layers are replicated N times while MoE/FC layers are shared via Expert Parallelism — eliminating KV-cache duplication for MLA-based models like DeepSeek-V3. The production DeepSeek-V3 config shown in the deck is '--tp 8 --dp-size 8 --ep 8 --enable-dp-attention', achieving 92% throughput uplift on 8×A100 80GB. - Why it matters: Data parallelism is the simplest throughput scaling strategy; DPA extends it to MoE models without the KV-cache memory cost of full replication. Combined with cache-aware routing ('--router-policy cache_aware'), DPA+EP enables near-linear throughput scaling with the number of GPUs for MoE workloads. - Gotcha: Pure DP duplicates both model weights and KV caches — for a 70B model this means each replica requires its own 140 GB VRAM for weights alone, which is prohibitive at high DP degrees. DPA solves this only for MLA-architecture models where KV cache is compressed; standard GQA models still duplicate KV under DPA (though the KV is smaller).
title: --dp-size

body: Parallelism · appears on: Data Parallelism: DP, DPA & Cache-Aware Router frame — 'DPA: chỉ replicate attention; MoE/FC layers chia sẻ qua EP' - What: A hybrid parallelism strategy where the attention layers of a MoE model are replicated across DP replicas (each with its own KV cache) while the MoE expert feed-forward layers are shared via Expert Parallelism — combining the cache-locality benefit of DP with the memory efficiency of EP. - How it works: In standard DP, every replica holds the full model (attention + FFN) and KV cache, causing KV cache duplication at the cost of N× VRAM. In DPA mode ('--dp-size N --enable-dp-attention'), each DP replica independently maintains its own attention weights and KV cache but shares MoE expert weights across the EP group. During the forward pass, each replica independently computes attention (no communication), then performs A2A dispatch to the shared expert pool for the FFN computation. For MLA-based models (DeepSeek-V3), this is especially efficient because MLA's compressed KV cache (10× less than MHA) makes per-replica KV storage affordable. - Why it matters: DPA captures the prefix-cache hit locality of DP (requests with matching system prompts go to the same replica, maximising KV reuse) while avoiding the MoE expert VRAM duplication of pure DP. The DeepSeek-V3 production config ('--tp 8 --dp-size 8 --ep 8 --enable-dp-attention') achieves 92% throughput uplift over baseline DP on 8×A100 by combining DPA with cache-aware routing. - Gotcha: DPA is only beneficial for MoE models where MLA compression makes per-replica KV affordable; for standard GQA-attention dense models, DPA's KV duplication is as costly as full DP. The '--enable-dp-attention' flag requires that 'ep_size = tp_size', adding a constraint to the configuration space.

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Tokens-per-Joule & The Power Wall - What: A hardware power management technique that adjusts GPU or CPU operating voltage and clock frequency dynamically based on workload demands to reduce energy consumption. - How it works: During phases of LLM inference that are memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound (e.g., the decode phase for small batches), the GPU does not need to run at maximum frequency. DVFS reduces the voltage and clock during these phases, saving energy with minimal latency impact. GreenLLM (arXiv:2508.16449) applies phase-specific DVFS — different frequency settings for prefill vs decode phases. - Why it matters: GreenLLM achieves 10–34% energy reduction with fewer than 3.5% additional SLO violations by intelligently scaling down power during memory-bound phases. This is a software-controllable energy lever requiring no model changes. - Gotcha: DVFS must be applied phase-specifically; applying it uniformly during compute-bound prefill would reduce throughput and increase latency. Improper DVFS tuning can cause SLO violations. Not all GPU configurations expose DVFS at the software level (requires NVML or equivalent access).
title: DVFS

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Pre-LLM Era: Serving Infrastructure 2017–2022 - What: Triton Inference Server's per-model batching strategy where incoming requests are accumulated within a configurable latency window and then sent to the model as a single batch, without a fixed batch-size requirement. - How it works: Each model in Triton's repository has a dynamic_batching configuration specifying a preferred_batch_size list and max_queue_delay_microseconds. Triton accumulates requests until either a preferred batch size is filled or the delay expires, then dispatches the batch. Multiple instances of the same model can run concurrently (instance_group config). - Why it matters: Dynamic batching improved GPU utilization for non-LLM models vs static batching by not requiring a full batch before dispatch. However, it still operates on the request level (not the token/decode-step level), making it fundamentally insufficient for autoregressive LLMs where latency comes from decode steps, not from batching overhead. - Gotcha: Triton's dynamic batching and vLLM's continuous batching are both called 'dynamic' informally, but they operate at completely different granularities. Triton batches at the request level (entire inference call). vLLM's continuous batching operates at the decode-step level (per token iteration), which is what enables TPOT guarantees independent of batch fill time.
title: Dynamic Batching

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Model Compilation: torch.compile + CUDA Graphs + TensorRT - What: A `torch.compile` option that enables dynamic shape support, generating a single compiled kernel that works across variable input shapes without recompilation per shape. - How it works: With `dynamic=True`, TorchInductor generates kernels parameterized by symbolic shape variables (using `torch.SymInt`). The generated Triton code includes runtime shape logic rather than hardcoded constants. This eliminates recompilation when tensor shapes change (e.g., batch size, sequence length), at a small runtime overhead vs static-shape kernels. - Why it matters: Essential for continuous batching where batch size and sequence length change every decode step. Without `dynamic=True`, torch.compile would recompile for every new (batch_size, seq_len) combination, causing latency spikes on shape changes. - Gotcha: Dynamic shape kernels are slightly slower than static-shape kernels because they cannot fully constant-fold shape-dependent expressions. Mixing static and dynamic shapes (e.g., static batch size, dynamic seq length) via `torch.compile(dynamic=True)` with explicit constraints can recover some of the static optimization.

body: Metric · appears on: Latency Taxonomy: TTFT · TPOT · Goodput - What: Total wall-clock time from request submission to reception of the final output token, capturing both the prefill and the entire decode phase. - How it works: Computed as E2E Latency = TTFT + TPOT × (N − 1), where N is the total number of generated tokens. For a 200-token response with TTFT = 450 ms and TPOT = 25 ms, E2E ≈ 450 + 25 × 199 ≈ 5.4 s. - Why it matters: E2E Latency is the SLO metric for non-streaming use cases (batch APIs, offline jobs). For streaming chat, TTFT + TPOT are more relevant because E2E can be large while the user experience is still acceptable as long as tokens stream quickly. - Gotcha: SLOs are usually expressed as P95 or P99 E2E Latency, not mean, because tail latency determines whether high-percentile users abandon requests. Reporting mean E2E hides pathological long-tail caused by KV-cache eviction or queue pile-up.
title: E2E Latency

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ (research companion) - What: The dominant FP8 sub-format for weights: 1 sign + 4 exponent + 3 mantissa bits, providing higher precision at the cost of narrower dynamic range versus E5M2. - How it works: Used with dynamic per-tensor or per-group scaling. The NVIDIA cuBLAS FP8 GEMM kernel default is E4M3 for weights and either E4M3 or E5M2 for activations depending on range requirements. - Why it matters: E4M3 preserves more mantissa precision, making it suitable for weight representation where values cluster near zero — critical for keeping accuracy loss under 1%. - Gotcha: E4M3 has a smaller max representable value than E5M2; activations with large dynamic range (e.g., attention logits) should use E5M2 or be scaled carefully to avoid saturation.
title: E4M3

body: Decoding · appears on: Speculative Decoding & Continuous Batching - What: The current state-of-the-art speculative decoding method (NeurIPS 2025), achieving 3.0–6.5× single-request speedup by using multi-layer feature fusion from the target model to train a stronger draft head. - How it works: EAGLE-3 fuses hidden states from multiple target-model layers (not just the top layer like EAGLE-2) to produce richer draft features. A 'training-time test' procedure ensures the draft head generalizes to diverse token distributions. The draft tree explores topk candidates per step, and the target model verifies a batch of candidate trees in one pass. - Why it matters: ~1.4× aggregate over EAGLE-2 (up to 6.47× on Vicuna-13B/HumanEval). EAGLE-3 is now integrated natively into SGLang and vLLM. Extended by EAGLE 3.1 (May 2026) which fixes an attention-drift bug and achieves 2.03× per-user speedup at concurrency=1 on Kimi K2.6. - Gotcha: EAGLE-3 requires either a draft model checkpoint trained against the target model, or a target model with an MTP head. It cannot be applied zero-shot to arbitrary models without a draft training step. The per-task speedup range is wide (3–6.5×); the '~1.4× over EAGLE-2' aggregate is the safer summary figure. There is no EAGLE-4 — as of Aug 2026 EAGLE-3 is still the newest in-family version, and the successor direction is parallel drafting (P-EAGLE, DFlash, DSpark), not a version bump. Students will search for EAGLE-4 and find nothing.

body: Concept · appears on: Multimodal (VLM) Serving: Encode–Prefill–Decode - What: A VLM architecture design where visual information is integrated into the token stream from the earliest layers without a separate, standalone vision encoder stage. - How it works: Rather than running a ViT encoder to produce patch embeddings that are then concatenated with text, early-fusion models (e.g., Llama 4) natively embed visual tokens alongside text tokens in the model's main transformer from the start. This removes the distinct Encode phase from the EPD pipeline. - Why it matters: Eliminates the ViT bottleneck and the encoder-disaggregation engineering burden; simplifies deployment from three phases (EPD) to two (Prefill-Decode). However the model must be trained natively in this fashion. - Gotcha: Early-fusion models lose the ability to apply CPU AMX or separate encoder hardware since there is no separable encoder stage. The tradeoff is deployment simplicity vs the ability to independently scale encoding.

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Structured Generation: XGrammar, Tool & Reasoning Parsers - What: A formal grammar notation used to specify arbitrary context-free output grammars (not just JSON) for constrained decoding, enabling enforcement of SQL, code, or domain-specific language syntax. - How it works: The client provides an EBNF grammar string to the serving engine's grammar-backend (XGrammar or llguidance). The backend compiles the EBNF into an automaton and uses it for logit masking at each decode step. XGrammar supports both JSON Schema and EBNF inputs natively. - Why it matters: Enables constrained generation for non-JSON domains: SQL queries, Python code, command-line invocations, custom protocols — wherever the output must match a formal grammar. - Gotcha: Complex recursive EBNF grammars can have large state spaces; XGrammar's PDA approach handles these more efficiently than FSM-based Outlines, but extremely ambiguous grammars can still cause slowdowns. Test performance with production schema complexity before deployment.

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Edge Deployment Flow - What: The end-to-end pipeline for taking a PyTorch-trained model and deploying it to edge or laptop targets via two distinct export/optimization paths: ONNX→TensorRT for GPU servers, and GGUF→Ollama for edge/laptop. - How it works: A PyTorch model forks at export time: the ONNX path converts weights and graph to the Open Neural Network Exchange format, which TensorRT then compiles into a fused FP8/INT8 engine for NVIDIA GPU servers (3–5x faster than vanilla PyTorch). The GGUF path quantizes weights into llama.cpp's native file format and wraps them with Ollama for single-command container deployment on laptops and edge devices. Both paths converge into either a GPU server or an Edge/Laptop runtime. - Why it matters: The bifurcation makes explicit that production GPU serving and resource-constrained edge serving require fundamentally different toolchains and optimization formats; choosing the wrong branch wastes engineering effort. - Gotcha: The ONNX→TensorRT path incurs a 5–30 minute per-model compile time at deployment; TensorRT engines are also device-specific (an engine compiled for H100 will not run on A100). The GGUF→Ollama path avoids this but is capped at llama.cpp's supported hardware backends.

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Data Parallelism: DP, DPA & Cache-Aware Router - What: SGLang CLI flag that activates DP-Attention mode, replicating only attention layers across DP ranks while sharing MoE expert weights via EP, eliminating KV cache duplication. - How it works: When set, SGLang modifies the parallelism plan so that attention computation (and its KV cache) is handled independently per DP replica, while expert FFN layers participate in Expert Parallelism A2A. Combined with `--dp-size N` and `--ep N` to form the full DPA+EP configuration. - Why it matters: The primary flag for deploying DeepSeek-V3/R1 efficiently in multi-replica setups. Without it, standard DP replicates all MoE expert weights per replica, wasting VRAM on unnecessary copies. - Gotcha: Requires ep_size = dp_size in most configurations. Only meaningful for MoE models with latent attention (MLA). Setting --enable-dp-attention on a dense model or GQA model provides no benefit and may introduce overhead.
title: --enable-dp-attention

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Pipeline Parallelism: Ultra-Long Context - What: An SGLang CLI flag that enables adaptive chunk sizing for chunked prefill in Pipeline Parallelism, automatically adjusting chunk size based on prefix length and a smooth factor. - How it works: Instead of a fixed chunk size (e.g., 4K tokens), dynamic chunking computes the optimal chunk size as a function of the current prefix length and a smooth_factor (default 0.75, tunable 0.6–0.85 via env var). Initial chunks are 2–3× the baseline to amortize overhead; subsequent chunks shrink as the context fills. Examples: DeepSeek-V3.1 12K dynamic (smooth=0.65), Qwen3-235B 18K dynamic (smooth=0.8). - Why it matters: Fixed chunk sizes are suboptimal: too small wastes pipeline fill time; too large causes memory spikes and load imbalance across PP stages. Dynamic chunking adapts to workload, balancing TTFT and throughput for 128K+ context serving. - Gotcha: Dynamic chunking interacts with Piecewise CUDA Graph (PCG): PCG is automatically disabled when PP is enabled, so the CUDA graph overhead is absent but PCG's capture/replay benefits are also lost. The smooth_factor default of 0.75 is a starting point—model-specific tuning (via the env var) yields the cited gains.
title: --enable-dynamic-chunking

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Expert Parallelism (Key Optimizations): 'EPLB: --enable-eplb' - What: An SGLang CLI flag that activates Expert Parallelism Load Balancing (EPLB), a static redundant-expert replication strategy that reduces GPU utilisation variance caused by uneven token routing in MoE models. - How it works: In MoE models with auxiliary-loss-free routing (e.g., DeepSeek-V3), the router distributes tokens unequally across experts at inference time — popular experts receive far more tokens than less-used ones, creating GPU utilisation imbalance. EPLB places redundant copies of hot experts on multiple GPUs so no single GPU is a bottleneck. vLLM's dynamic EPLB (merged Jun 26 2025, PR #18343) rebalances expert placement online based on observed routing statistics. - Why it matters: Without EPLB, load-skewed expert routing causes some GPUs to finish their expert GEMM in microseconds while others stall for milliseconds, serialising the All-to-All synchronisation barrier. SGLang's EPLB ablation showed 1.49x prefill / 2.54x decode throughput improvements over non-balanced EP at large scale. - Gotcha: The 1.49x/2.54x figures are from SGLang's large-EP ablation, not vLLM's EPLB implementation. Auxiliary-loss-free routing (arXiv:2408.15664) — used by DeepSeek-V3 for training quality — is the root cause of the inference load skew that EPLB must correct: this is a training–serving design coupling that practitioners must be aware of.
title: --enable-eplb

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Multi-LoRA Serving: 'vLLM --enable-lora: N adapters / 1 endpoint' - What: A vLLM CLI flag that activates multi-LoRA serving mode, allowing a single deployed base model endpoint to dynamically load and serve multiple LoRA adapters per request without requiring separate model instances. - How it works: When '--enable-lora' is set, vLLM allocates a pool of LoRA weight slots in VRAM (sized by '--max-loras' and '--max-lora-rank'). Each incoming request can specify an adapter ID; the scheduler loads the matching adapter weights into a slot (using S-LoRA's paged adapter storage if needed) and applies the Punica/SGMV fused batched-adapter GEMM kernel during the forward pass. Adapters not in active VRAM slots can be swapped from CPU memory. In vLLM v1, multi-LoRA is fully merged and optimised (V0 removed as of v0.10). - Why it matters: Enables N-to-1 multi-tenant serving: one 7B–70B base model serves SQL specialists, medical assistants, code generators, and finance adapters from a single GPU instance, with 12x throughput versus N independent single-adapter deployments. Each adapter adds only ~2ms/token overhead. - Gotcha: All LoRA adapters must share the same base model architecture and rank configuration. The '--max-loras' flag caps simultaneous in-VRAM adapters; beyond that, adapters are swapped from CPU, adding latency. MoE-LoRA (introduced v0.22.0) requires Triton kernels and has additional constraints.
title: --enable-lora

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Production Tuning: Memory, Scheduling & Observability - What: SGLang CLI flag that activates the Prometheus metrics endpoint at :30000/metrics, required for any production observability setup. - How it works: When passed at startup, SGLang spawns a prometheus_client HTTP server on port 30000. The endpoint is then scraped by Prometheus at a configured interval (typically 15s). Without this flag, no metrics are emitted and the endpoint returns 404. - Why it matters: Mandatory for production monitoring; enables all downstream observability tooling (Grafana dashboards, PagerDuty alerts, KEDA autoscaling). The vLLM equivalent is implicit (vLLM always exports metrics via prometheus_client when the package is installed). - Gotcha: Port 30000 is SGLang's default serving port — if running both the API server and metrics on the same port, ensure the Prometheus scrape config points to the /metrics path and not /v1/chat/completions. vLLM uses a separate --metrics-port flag to control where metrics are exposed.
title: --enable-metrics

body: CLI / flag · appears on: PagedAttention vLLM v0 box: 'Prefix caching opt-in (--enable-prefix-caching)' - What: A vLLM v0 CLI flag that activated Automatic Prefix Caching (APC), causing completed KV blocks from any prior request to be retained in the free-block pool and reused if a future request shares the same prefix. - How it works: When enabled, vLLM hashes each filled 16-token block's token-ID sequence. On a new request, the scheduler walks the prefix trie of cached block hashes; matching blocks are mapped directly into the new request's page table without recomputation, skipping the prefill cost for those tokens. In v0, this was opt-in because the hash computation and cache eviction logic added measurable overhead at 0% hit rate. - Why it matters: Prefix caching is the single highest-ROI serving optimisation for multi-turn chat, RAG, and agent workloads where a long system prompt or retrieved context is shared across many requests. The deck notes it saves up to 70% TTFT on repeated system prompts. - Gotcha: In vLLM v1 (default since v0.8.0, Mar 2025), APC is on by default with near-zero overhead (<1% at 0% hit rate) — the flag is no longer needed and its absence no longer disables caching. Using '--enable-prefix-caching' on v1 is a no-op.
title: --enable-prefix-caching

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Expert Parallelism (Key Optimizations) and TBO defbox: '--enable-two-batch-overlap' - What: An SGLang CLI flag (also '--enable-dbo' in vLLM) that enables Two-Batch Overlap, a pipeline scheduling technique that interleaves the All-to-All communication of one micro-batch with the GEMM computation of another to hide A2A latency in MoE expert-parallel serving. - How it works: During MoE EP forward passes, the timeline per step is: GEMM1 → All-to-All dispatch → expert GEMM → All-to-All combine → GEMM2. TBO splits each training-style batch into two micro-batches and schedules them in an overlapping pipeline: while micro-batch A is in the All-to-All phase (waiting for expert activations), micro-batch B's GEMM runs on the same GPUs. This 'compute hides communication' pattern eliminates A2A as a sequential bottleneck, yielding +27–35% prefill throughput and up to 50% peak memory reduction (because only one micro-batch occupies activations at a time). - Why it matters: All-to-All communication is the dominant latency bottleneck in expert-parallel serving at EP32–EP144 scales. Without TBO, GPU compute sits idle waiting for A2A to complete. At DeepSeek-V3's production scale (~$0.20/1M output tokens), this efficiency gain directly translates to reduced serving cost. - Gotcha: TBO requires that the A2A and GEMM workloads be roughly balanced in duration for effective overlap; highly asymmetric operations reduce the benefit. It also requires that the MoE A2A backend (DeepEP) supports the dual-buffer scheduling — not all backends do. The SGLang flag is '--enable-two-batch-overlap'; vLLM's equivalent is '--enable-dbo'.
title: --enable-two-batch-overlap

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Auto-scaling Architecture (via Gateway API Inference Extension research) - What: The per-request replica selection component of the Gateway API Inference Extension that routes each request to the replica with the highest estimated KV-cache hit probability and lowest queue depth. - How it works: Queries each replica's real-time state (exposed via a side-channel metrics endpoint): current queue depth, KV-cache utilization, and which prefix hashes are cached. Scores replicas on a weighted combination and selects the best. Falls back to least-busy if no cache-hit candidate exists. - Why it matters: Routing by KV-cache state converts the load balancer into a cache-aware orchestrator. This is the mechanism behind the 3–10x lower TTFT claim in vLLM production-stack benchmarks vs round-robin. - Gotcha: The Endpoint Picker's effectiveness degrades if replicas do not expose real-time KV-cache metadata. Backends must implement the side-channel metrics protocol expected by the picker. Not all inference engines (only vLLM and llm-d as of mid-2026) fully support this protocol.
title: Endpoint Picker

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Scaling Strategies (via research companion §12) - What: An LLM-aware API gateway (Tetrate + Bloomberg, Feb 2025) built on Envoy Proxy that provides token-rate limiting, multi-provider routing, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints. - How it works: Extends Envoy with LLM-specific filters: token counting (not just byte counting), per-user token budgets, fallback routing across 16+ providers under one endpoint, and request/response logging. Integrated into KServe v0.16 as the ingress gateway for LLM traffic. - Why it matters: Classic API gateways rate-limit on request count; for LLM serving, token count is the cost unit. Envoy AI Gateway enables token-based rate limiting and cost attribution that aligns with how LLM providers bill, and provides multi-model/multi-provider failover under a single endpoint. - Gotcha: Token-rate limiting requires counting tokens at the gateway before forwarding to the backend, which adds per-request overhead (tokenization or estimation). Accurate token counting requires access to the model's tokenizer, which gateways may approximate rather than exactly compute.
title: Envoy AI Gateway

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Expert Parallelism: MoE Scaling - What: A CLI/config flag specifying how many GPUs participate in Expert Parallelism sharding—i.e., how many ways the expert weight pool is partitioned. - How it works: Set via `--ep N` in SGLang or equivalent. At ep_size=32, each of 32 GPUs holds 1/32 of the total expert weights. The constraint `ep_size = tp_size` is required by most A2A backends (DeepEP, mooncake, nixl) to ensure communication topology consistency. - Why it matters: Controls the tradeoff between expert memory distribution and A2A communication overhead. DeepSeek uses EP32 for prefill (4 nodes) and EP144 for decode (18 nodes), optimized separately for each phase. - Gotcha: The constraint ep_size = tp_size is enforced by most backends and is not optional. Setting ep_size > tp_size or mismatched values will cause runtime errors. The optimal ep_size is workload-phase dependent—prefill and decode benefit from different ep_sizes.
title: ep_size

body: Concept · appears on: Expert Parallelism: MoE Scaling - What: An architectural requirement in most MoE A2A backends (DeepEP, mooncake, nixl) that the Expert Parallelism degree must equal the Tensor Parallelism degree in the same deployment. - How it works: This constraint arises because A2A dispatch and TP All-Reduce must use the same GPU communicator group. If ep_size ≠ tp_size, the communication patterns for expert routing and weight-shard synchronization do not align, causing correctness or performance issues. Most backends enforce this at initialization. - Why it matters: Ensures that the GPU topology used for expert dispatch (EP) is consistent with the intra-layer weight-shard synchronization (TP), avoiding communication pattern conflicts and enabling efficient fused kernels. - Gotcha: This constraint limits flexibility: you cannot independently tune EP and TP. For DeepSeek configs like `--tp 8 --ep 8`, the constraint is automatically satisfied, but trying `--tp 4 --ep 8` typically fails or requires special workarounds.
title: ep_size = tp_size constraint

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Multimodal (VLM) Serving: Encode–Prefill–Decode - What: A three-phase disaggregation architecture for VLM serving that routes the ViT encode, LLM prefill, and LLM decode stages to independently scaled pools of hardware. - How it works: The ViT encoder (Encode) runs on a dedicated pool (or CPU AMX), its outputs are transferred to a prefill pool where the LLM processes the combined visual+text sequence (Prefill), then KV cache is handed off to a decode pool for autoregressive generation (Decode). SGLang introduced this in January 2026; 2E1P (two encoders, one prefill node) achieves ~6–8x lower TTFT on Qwen3-VL-235B. - Why it matters: Encode, prefill, and decode have very different compute profiles and scaling axes; co-locating them wastes GPU resources and inflates latency. EPD allows each phase to scale independently based on traffic. - Gotcha: EPD differs from standard PD disaggregation by adding the encoder as a separate scalable unit. vLLM supports encoder disaggregation via `--mm-encoder-tp-mode data` starting v0.11.1; not all models expose the encoder as separable (early-fusion models like Llama 4 collapse encode into prefill).
title: EPD

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Multimodal (VLM) Serving (EPD Disaggregation): 'SGLang 2E1P: ~6-8x TTFT down on Qwen3-VL-235B' - What: A three-phase disaggregated serving topology for Vision-Language Models where image encoding (ViT), text prefill (LLM), and token decoding are separated into independently scalable worker pools — specifically using 2 encoder workers per 1 prefill worker to balance throughput. - How it works: In collocated VLM serving, the ViT encoder, LLM prefill, and LLM decode all share the same GPU, creating contention. EPD splits these into separate pools: Encode workers run ViT forward passes in parallel (one image batch at a time, embarrassingly parallel across workers); Prefill workers receive the encoded visual tokens plus text tokens and run chunked prefill; Decode workers handle autoregressive generation. The 2E1P ratio (two encode workers for every one prefill worker) is tuned for Qwen3-VL-235B's specific ViT-to-prefill compute ratio. SGLang's Jan 2026 EPD implementation achieved ~6–8x TTFT reduction for this model. - Why it matters: ViT encoding is compute-intensive but does not need the same GPU as the LLM (it has no KV-cache dependency on the LLM state). By scaling encode workers independently, EPD prevents ViT computation from blocking LLM decode — the dominant source of TTFT latency in multi-image VLM requests. - Gotcha: ViT does not benefit from tensor parallelism (per the research companion, performance degrades at TP=8), so encode workers should use DP, not TP. EPD adds KV transfer overhead between encode and prefill stages; the net gain is only positive when image count per request is high. Early-fusion models like Llama 4 eliminate the separate encode stage entirely.
title: EPD 2E1P

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Expert Parallelism: MoE Scaling - What: A static or dynamic load-balancing system that places redundant expert copies on lightly-loaded GPUs to reduce GPU utilization variance across expert-parallel nodes. - How it works: Analyzes the expert activation frequency distribution (which is skewed because auxiliary-loss-free routing creates 'hot' experts) and places redundant copies of popular experts on additional GPUs, distributing load more evenly. SGLang: `--enable-eplb`; vLLM: dynamic rebalancing merged Jun 26 2025 (PR #18343). DeepSeek uses 32 redundant experts in both prefill and decode stages. - Why it matters: Without EPLB, popular experts bottleneck their host GPUs while others sit idle, reducing effective throughput. The 1.49x prefill / 2.54x decode gains cited on the frame are from SGLang's large-EP ablation (not vLLM). - Gotcha: The throughput figures (1.49x/2.54x) are SGLang ablation numbers, not vLLM EPLB results—these are frequently misattributed. EPLB effectiveness depends heavily on how skewed expert routing is, which is a function of the training objective (auxiliary-loss-free routing = more skew = more EPLB benefit).
title: EPLB

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Scaling Strategies - What: An autoscaling paradigm in which replica count changes are triggered by discrete events or metric threshold crossings (queue messages, Prometheus alerts) rather than by polling CPU/memory at a fixed cadence. - How it works: KEDA and Knative implement event-driven autoscaling on Kubernetes. KEDA registers metric scalers (Prometheus, Kafka topic lag, Redis list length, etc.) and fires scale-out/scale-in actions when thresholds are crossed. Knative's KPA reacts to per-second request concurrency. Both can react faster than the default Kubernetes HPA polling interval (15s) by using push-based event sources. - Why it matters: LLM inference queues can fill in seconds; polling-based HPA (defaulting to a 15-second sync loop) is too slow. Event-driven autoscaling achieves sub-15-second scale-out reactions for metric-threshold events, reducing queue buildup under sudden traffic spikes. - Gotcha: Faster reaction time does not eliminate cold-start latency. Even if the scale decision is made in 1 second, the new GPU pod still needs 30–120 seconds to load model weights. EDA reduces the decision latency but not the provisioning latency — which is why warm pools remain necessary for low-latency SLOs.
title: Event-Driven Autoscaling

body: Parallelism · appears on: Disaggregated Prefill/Decode Serving - What: A parallelism strategy for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models that places different expert FFN weights on different GPUs, routing each token's computation to the GPU holding its activated expert. - How it works: Each GPU holds a subset of the total expert FFN weights. A learned router selects top-K experts per token; tokens are dispatched (all-to-all) to the GPU holding each selected expert, computed locally, and results are returned (another all-to-all). For DeepSeek-R1: prefill uses EP32 (32 GPUs, 4 nodes, 32 redundant experts), decode uses EP144 (144 GPUs, 18 nodes). DeepEP (v1.2.1) provides the fused all-to-all dispatch/combine kernel (NVLink: 726–740 GB/s). - Why it matters: Enables serving 671B+ MoE models efficiently; at EP=32, DeepSeek-R1 achieves 3.3x over TP16 prefill throughput (LMSYS, 96×H100). The dominant parallelism strategy for large MoE models in production 2026. - Gotcha: Expert Parallelism requires auxiliary-loss-free routing to work well at inference, which can cause load skew across experts; EPLB (Expert Parallel Load Balancing) with redundant expert copies is needed to address this. Skip EP for models with <1% activation density (e.g., Llama-4-Maverick at 0.78%).
title: Expert Parallelism

body: Parallelism · appears on: Expert Parallelism: MoE Scaling - What: A parallelism strategy for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models that shards expert weights across GPUs rather than replicating them, so each GPU owns a subset of experts. - How it works: During each forward pass, a router selects top-K experts per token; tokens are dispatched (All-to-All) to the GPUs holding their chosen experts, processed locally, then combined back (All-to-All) to the originating GPU. The pipeline is: dispatch → pre-permute → core runner (GEMM on expert weights) → combine. Each GPU runs GEMM only on its local expert subset. - Why it matters: The only practical way to serve MoE models like DeepSeek-V3 671B. Tensor Parallelism replicates all experts to every GPU (infeasible at scale); EP avoids replication. DeepSeek uses EP32 for prefill and EP144 for decode, achieving ~$0.20/1M output tokens. - Gotcha: EP requires All-to-All (A2A) collective communication for token dispatch and combine, which adds latency proportional to the number of nodes. Most backends require ep_size = tp_size. Auxiliary-loss-free routing during training can cause expert load skew at inference, making EPLB essential.
title: Expert Parallelism

body: Attention / KV · appears on: FlashAttention: IO-Aware Attention (FA1→FA4) - What: The original FlashAttention (Dao et al., NeurIPS 2022): first IO-aware exact attention implementation achieving 3–4× speedup over PyTorch's standard attention via SRAM tiling and online softmax. - How it works: Tiles Q, K, V into SRAM blocks of size determined by available SRAM capacity; iterates over K/V blocks while maintaining running softmax normalization statistics (max and sum) per Q tile. A single HBM write produces the final output. Memory: O(N) instead of O(N²). - Why it matters: Proved the IO-awareness principle and opened the path to all subsequent versions. The 3–4× speedup at FA1 already made long-context serving viable where it was previously OOM. - Gotcha: FA1 was limited to specific GPU SRAM sizes and did not expose a flexible API for custom masking patterns. These limitations motivated FA2's sequence parallelism and FlexAttention's BlockMask API.
title: FA1

body: Attention / KV · appears on: FlashAttention: IO-Aware Attention (FA1→FA4) - What: FlashAttention-2 (arXiv Jul 2023): refined tiling strategy and sequence-dimension parallelism doubling FA1's throughput, becoming the standard attention kernel for A100/H100 inference. - How it works: Reworked the work partitioning between CUDA warps to improve parallelism along the sequence dimension, reducing synchronization overhead and better utilizing tensor cores. Achieved ~2× FA1 throughput on A100. - Why it matters: The de facto standard kernel for production LLM serving through 2023–2024. Integrated natively into PyTorch's `F.scaled_dot_product_attention`, making it effectively automatic for well-maintained model code. - Gotcha: FA2 targets A100/Ampere architecture CUDA cores; it does not exploit Hopper-specific hardware features (TMA, WGMMA, async pipelining) that FA3 was designed for.
title: FA2

body: Attention / KV · appears on: FlashAttention: IO-Aware Attention (FA1→FA4) - What: FlashAttention-3 (NeurIPS 2024 Spotlight): Hopper-native attention kernel achieving ~840 TFLOPS/s BF16 and ~1.3 PFLOPS/s FP8 on H100 via TMA async pipelining and warp specialization. - How it works: Exploits Hopper-specific hardware: Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) for asynchronous data movement from HBM to SRAM, WGMMA (Warpgroup Matrix Multiply-Accumulate) instructions for sustained tensor-core throughput, and warp specialization that dedicates separate warp groups to data movement vs compute to pipeline both simultaneously. - Why it matters: ~1.3× faster than cuDNN-based baselines on H100. FP8 support in FA3 enables KV cache quantization at the kernel level. Became the standard for H100 Hopper deployments in 2024. - Gotcha: FA3 is Hopper-specific and not directly portable to Ampere (A100). The WGMMA and TMA instructions do not exist on prior architectures. For A100 deployments, FA2 remains the appropriate choice.
title: FA3

body: Attention / KV · appears on: Attention Backend Selection: FA3 / FA4 / FlashInfer / FlashMLA - What: The third generation of the FlashAttention kernel (arXiv:2407.08608, NeurIPS 2024 Spotlight), targeting NVIDIA Hopper (H100/H200) with TMA async pipelining, warp specialization, and FP8 KV support. - How it works: FA3 uses Hopper-specific CUDA extensions: Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) for async data movement from VRAM to shared memory, WGMMA (Warp-Group Matrix Multiply-Accumulate) for compute, and a warp-specialized pipeline that overlaps memory transfers with matmul. Achieves ~840 TFLOPs/s BF16 and ~1.3 PFLOPs/s FP8 on H100. vLLM auto-selects FA3 for H100/H200 with CUDA 12.3+. - Why it matters: The standard attention kernel for H100/H200 production deployments; ~2x over FA2 on Hopper due to warp specialization and TMA. Required for FP8 KV cache on Hopper. - Gotcha: FA3 requires CUDA 12.3+ and Hopper SM90a architecture — it will not compile/run on A100/A40 (Ampere). On those GPUs, FlashInfer is the auto-selected backend. FA3 is not Blackwell-optimized; use FA4 or trtllm_mha on B200.
title: FA3

body: Attention / KV · appears on: FlashAttention: IO-Aware Attention (FA1→FA4) - What: FlashAttention-4 (arXiv:2603.05451, Mar 2026): Blackwell-native attention kernel achieving ~1,613 TFLOPS/s BF16 on B200 (71% utilization), 1.3× over cuDNN 9.13, with native FP4 KV cache support. - How it works: Targets Blackwell's asymmetric MMA architecture (2-CTA MMA pattern), implements software-emulated softmax for Blackwell's non-native softmax paths, and includes CuTe-DSL Python frontend for kernel parameterization. FP4 KV cache support halves KV memory vs FP8 with <1% accuracy loss. SGLang auto-selects FA4 on B200. - Why it matters: On Blackwell GPUs, FA4 is the standard attention backend. FP4 KV support makes GB200/B200 memory use maximally efficient. 2.7× faster than a Triton-based baseline on the same hardware. - Gotcha: FA4 is Blackwell-only. The 1,613 TFLOPS/s is the arXiv figure; the Colfax blog quotes 1,605 — cite the arXiv primary source. The 1.3× over cuDNN 9.13 improvement is hardware-generation-specific and should not be compared directly to FA3's speedup over cuDNN on Hopper.
title: FA4

body: Attention / KV · appears on: Attention Backend Selection: FA3 / FA4 / FlashInfer / FlashMLA - What: The Blackwell-generation FlashAttention kernel (arXiv:2603.05451, Mar 2026) exploiting B200's SM100 architecture for ~1,613 TFLOPs/s BF16 and FP4 KV cache support. - How it works: FA4 uses Blackwell's asymmetric scaling (different compute and memory speeds for different precisions), software-emulated softmax for FP4 stability, and a 2-CTA (Cooperative Thread Array) MMA design to double pipeline stages. It includes a CuTe-DSL Python frontend for custom kernels. Achieves 71% hardware utilization on B200, 1.3x over cuDNN 9.13, 2.7x over Triton. vLLM auto-selects FA4 on B200. - Why it matters: Unlocks FP4 KV cache on Blackwell (halving FP8 memory footprint with <1% accuracy loss) and achieves the highest known BF16 attention FLOP/s; critical for GB200 NVL72 multi-tenant deployments. - Gotcha: FA4 is Blackwell SM100-only — it will not run on H100/A100. The cited ~1,613 TFLOPs/s BF16 is from the arXiv paper; co-author Colfax blog cites 1,605 — cite the arXiv figure. Do not confuse FA4 (attention kernel) with FP4 (quantization format).

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Inference Engine Evolution: 2020 → 2025 - What: NVIDIA's 2021 CUDA-kernel-level transformer inference library that provided optimized attention and FFN kernels for Hopper/Ampere before dedicated LLM serving engines existed. - How it works: FasterTransformer implemented multi-head attention, layer normalization, and beam search in highly optimized CUDA kernels with INT8/FP16 support, exposed as a C++ library with Python bindings. TensorRT-LLM is its direct successor and absorbed most of its kernels. - Why it matters: Historical milestone: established that CUDA kernel optimization (not just algorithmic changes) is necessary for production LLM throughput; its kernel work directly influenced TRT-LLM. - Gotcha: FasterTransformer was not a serving framework — it had no batching scheduler, API server, or memory management. It was a kernel library plugged into larger systems. Conflating it with full engines is a common student error.
title: FasterTransformer

body: Serving pattern · appears on: PagedAttention: vLLM v0 → v1 Deep Dive - What: vLLM v0's default request scheduling policy: requests are processed in arrival order, with preemption when VRAM is exhausted (swapping the lowest-priority request to CPU). - How it works: The FCFS scheduler maintains a waiting queue ordered by arrival time. When the scheduler runs, it picks the oldest waiting request, allocates KV pages, and starts prefill. If VRAM runs out mid-generation, it preempts (swaps) the youngest active request to CPU RAM to free space, resuming it later. vLLM V1 replaced this with a prefix-aware scheduler that prioritizes requests sharing KV pages with cached prefixes. - Why it matters: Simple and predictable but suboptimal when prefix sharing is possible — a prefix-aware scheduler improves cache hit rate and thereby reduces average TTFT without changing hardware. - Gotcha: FCFS preemption can cause non-deterministic TTFT: a high-priority real-time request arriving just after a batch starts will wait until the current batch step completes. V1's prefix-aware scheduler partially addresses this but doesn't implement strict priority queuing. Updated Aug 2026: vLLM now ships `--scheduling-policy priority` alongside the `fcfs` default (lower value runs earlier, arrival time breaks ties), so strict priority queuing is available — but preempting an already-running request by priority remains an open feature request (vllm#40004), not shipped.
title: FCFS scheduler

body: Concept · appears on: Pre-LLM Era: Serving Infrastructure 2017–2022 - What: A design assumption in pre-LLM serving frameworks where both input and output tensor shapes are fixed and known at model-load time, incompatible with autoregressive LLM generation where output length is determined dynamically. - How it works: Classical ML serving (classifiers, regressors, encoders) takes fixed-dimension inputs and produces fixed-dimension outputs. Frameworks like TF Serving and TorchServe optimize around this: they pre-allocate buffers, build static computation graphs, and batch requests using a single tensor shape. Autoregressive generation requires a growing KV cache (output grows by one token per step) and a variable number of forward passes. - Why it matters: Fixed-length I/O is a root cause for why pre-LLM frameworks cannot serve LLMs efficiently. Every LLM-serving innovation — dynamic KV allocation, continuous batching, chunked prefill, speculative decoding — exists because output length is not known in advance. - Gotcha: Some systems work around fixed-length I/O with padding to maximum length, which wastes compute and memory proportionally to how much shorter the actual output is. ONNX export of LLMs with dynamic axes partially addresses this but adds export fragility.
title: Fixed-Length I/O

title: Flash Attention

body: Attention / KV · appears on: FlashAttention: IO-Aware Attention (FA1→FA4) - What: A family of IO-aware exact attention algorithms (FA1 through FA4) that compute attention entirely within GPU SRAM via tiling and online softmax, eliminating the O(N²) HBM intermediate writes of standard attention. - How it works: Standard attention writes the N×N score matrix to HBM, reads it back for softmax, then reads it again for the V-weighted sum — three HBM round trips. FlashAttention tiles Q, K, V blocks into SRAM, computes a numerically stable online softmax update across tiles, and writes the output to HBM exactly once. Memory complexity drops from O(N²) to O(N). - Why it matters: For long contexts, standard attention OOMs because the N×N matrix grows quadratically. FlashAttention enables 128K+ context on a single GPU. The IO-reduction also yields 3–4× wall-clock speedup on H100 (FA1) that compounds with each version. - Gotcha: FlashAttention computes exact attention — it is not an approximation. Papers sometimes conflate FA with sparse/approximate attention variants. FA1 was NeurIPS 2022 Best Paper (Dao et al.); each subsequent version targets a specific hardware generation.
title: FlashAttention

body: IO-aware attention kernel. Keeps tiles in SRAM (on-chip cache, ~tens of MB, fast) instead of round-tripping through HBM (High Bandwidth Memory, the GPU's main 80 GB pool, slower). v3 adds Hopper / FP8 / async.
title: FlashAttention v1/v2/v3

body: Attention / KV · appears on: Attention Architecture: MHA → MLA & Long-Context - What: A shared attention kernel library (MLSys 2025 Best Paper) using BSR (Block Sparse Row) JIT-compiled kernels that serves as the unified attention backend across vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM. - How it works: Represents attention matrices in BSR format and uses JIT compilation to generate kernels for the exact sparsity pattern and dtype at runtime. NVIDIA contributes TRT-LLM kernels upstream; SGLang uses it as default; vLLM uses it as an optional (increasingly default) backend. - Why it matters: Having one battle-tested kernel library shared across major engines reduces maintenance burden and ensures consistent hardware utilization. In mid-2026, it is the convergence point for MLA, FP8, NVFP4, and variable-length attention patterns. - Gotcha: BSR format and JIT compilation add startup overhead (first-call compile); not suitable for very short one-shot inference where warmup cost dominates.
title: FlashInfer

body: Attention / KV · appears on: Attention Backend Selection: FA3 / FA4 / FlashInfer / FlashMLA - What: A unified attention kernel library (MLSys 2025 Best Paper) using Block Sparse Row (BSR) format JIT kernels that serves as the shared attention backend across vLLM, SGLang, and TRT-LLM. - How it works: FlashInfer represents the KV cache in BSR format, enabling variable page sizes (page_size > 1), FP8 KV quantization, speculative decoding with topk > 1, sliding window attention, and mixed-length request batching in a single fused kernel. JIT compilation generates kernels tuned to the specific page size, head dim, and dtype at engine startup. NVIDIA contributes TRT-LLM kernels upstream. Auto-selected for A100/A40 in vLLM. - Why it matters: Became the convergence point for open-source attention kernels; MLSys 2025 Best Paper validates its design. Supports both Ampere (where FA3 doesn't run) and Hopper as a universal fallback; key for multi-engine ecosystems. - Gotcha: FlashInfer's JIT compilation adds startup latency (seconds); pre-compilation is recommended for production containers. Page size must be > 1 (unlike standard vLLM which defaults to 16) — check engine configs when mixing FlashInfer with other backends.
title: FlashInfer

body: Attention / KV · appears on: Attention Architecture: MHA → MLA & Long-Context - What: DeepSeek's open-source BF16/FP8 CUDA kernel for MLA decode, optimized for paged KV blocks of size 64 on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs. - How it works: Implements the MLA absorb trick in a memory-efficient tiled kernel; BF16 decode achieves up to 3,000 GB/s memory throughput and 660 TFLOPS on H800 SXM5 (CUDA 12.8). Added FP8 sparse (NSA) kernels in Sep 2025. - Why it matters: Standard FlashAttention kernels do not support MLA's latent-to-KV reconstruction inline; FlashMLA provides the hardware-optimized primitive that makes DeepSeek's KV compression practical at production throughput. - Gotcha: The 3,000 GB/s figure's batch and sequence configuration is undisclosed by DeepSeek. FlashMLA is primarily H800/H100 Hopper-targeted; Blackwell users are directed to FlashInfer or CutlassMLA.
title: FlashMLA

body: Attention / KV · appears on: Attention Backend Selection: FA3 / FA4 / FlashInfer / FlashMLA - What: DeepSeek's open-source BF16 MLA decode kernel (Feb 24, 2025) for paged block-64 KV layout, achieving up to 3,000 GB/s memory-bandwidth utilization on H800 SXM5. - How it works: FlashMLA implements the compressed-latent attention (MLA) decode in a single fused CUDA kernel using paged KV blocks of size 64 (not the standard 16). It exploits H800 SXM5's 3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth to reach 3,000 GB/s effective BW (memory-bound path) and 660 TFLOPS (compute-bound path). Sep 2025 added FP8 sparse (NSA) kernels. vLLM auto-selects --attention-backend flashmla for DeepSeek V3/R1 models. - Why it matters: 3.1x throughput and 10x less KV memory vs MHA on DeepSeek V3/R1 models; mandatory for efficient serving of the dominant open-source frontier models. - Gotcha: FlashMLA requires paged block size=64 — engines must be configured with this non-default block size when using FlashMLA. The 3,000 GB/s figure is a benchmark peak; batch/sequence config is undisclosed. Sep 2025 added FP8 NSA support but NSA requires models trained with sparse attention.
title: FlashMLA

body: Attention / KV · appears on: FlashAttention: IO-Aware Attention (FA1→FA4) - What: A PyTorch 2024 API (`torch.nn.attention.flex_attention`) that allows arbitrary attention masking patterns to be expressed as Python functions, compiled via `torch.compile` into efficient Triton kernels without writing CUDA. - How it works: The user provides a `score_mod` function (applied element-wise to attention logits) and a `BlockMask` (specifying which Q-K block pairs to compute). PyTorch's compiler traces these Python callables and generates a Triton kernel that implements the custom masking pattern in a tiled IO-aware fashion. Common patterns (causal, sliding window, prefix+causal, document boundaries) can be expressed and fused. - Why it matters: Eliminates the need to write custom CUDA kernels for non-standard attention patterns. Research on new attention patterns (sliding window for streaming, prefix attention for caching) can be prototyped in Python and deployed with near-native efficiency. - Gotcha: FlexAttention only applies the custom mask at training/prefill time in the standard formulation; for decode-time use with KV caches, integration with PagedAttention requires additional work. The Triton kernels generated may not match hand-tuned FA3/FA4 kernels in peak performance on critical production paths.
title: FlexAttention

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization: Precision vs Performance; Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ - What: Half-precision floating-point: 1 sign + 5 exponent + 10 mantissa bits, 2 bytes per value. The conventional 'full quality' serving baseline for most GPU deployments. - How it works: An 8B model in FP16 occupies ~15.8 GB VRAM (parameters × 2 bytes). GPU tensor cores (Volta onwards) execute FP16 matrix multiplications natively, accumulating in FP32 for numerical stability. - Why it matters: FP16 is the baseline against which all quantization accuracy losses are measured. It fits an 8B model on a single 24 GB consumer GPU, but 70B models require ~140 GB — typically 2× H100 80 GB. - Gotcha: FP16 has a narrower dynamic range than BF16 (max exponent 5 bits vs 8 bits), making it more prone to overflow/underflow with certain weight distributions; BF16 is now preferred for training and often for serving on Ampere+.
title: FP16

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization: Precision vs Performance - What: The standard IEEE 754 single-precision floating-point format using 4 bytes per value (1 sign + 8 exponent + 23 mantissa bits). - How it works: Weights are stored and computed in full 32-bit precision. For an 8B-parameter model this yields ~31.6 GB VRAM (parameters × 4 bytes). Modern serving frameworks load weights in FP32 only when an explicit --dtype float32 override is set. - Why it matters: FP32 is the quality baseline and the training format for older models, but is almost never used for production inference because it doubles memory vs FP16 with no accuracy benefit in serving. - Gotcha: Double-quantization in NF4/QLoRA stores the quantization constants in FP32 then compresses them to FP8, so 'FP32 constants' still appear as an intermediate representation inside lower-bit schemes.
title: FP32

body: Quantization · appears on: Hardware Landscape 2026: Beyond H100 - What: A 4-bit floating-point numeric format (in the NVFP4 or MXFP4 variant) used for model weights and KV cache on Blackwell and Vera Rubin GPUs, delivering approximately 2x the throughput of FP8 and 3.5x memory savings vs FP16 with less than 1% quality loss. - How it works: FP4 weights are stored in 4-bit blocks with per-block or per-tensor scaling factors at higher precision. NVFP4 (NVIDIA) and MXFP4 (OCP standard) differ in block size. Blackwell Tensor Cores execute FP4 matrix multiply natively. B200 peaks at ~9,000 TFLOPS FP4 dense; B300 at 15 PFLOPS; Vera Rubin at 50 PFLOPS. FA4 (FlashAttention 4) uses FP4 KV cache natively on Blackwell. - Why it matters: FP4 is the defining format of the Blackwell generation: it doubles serving capacity per GPU vs FP8, enabling serving of 2x larger models at the same memory or 2x more concurrent users. NVFP4 is the default format for TensorRT-LLM on Blackwell in 2026. - Gotcha: FP4 is hardware-gated: requires Blackwell (SM90a) or Vera Rubin. MR-GPTQ (ICLR 2026) and QAD (arXiv:2601.20088) are the 2026 PTQ calibration methods that close the FP4 accuracy gap. NVFP4 and MXFP4 are not interchangeable formats.
title: FP4

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization: Precision vs Performance; Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ - What: An 8-bit floating-point format (most commonly E4M3: 4 exponent + 3 mantissa bits) that cuts memory to half of FP16 and doubles throughput on Hopper/Blackwell tensor cores. - How it works: Weights and activations are represented in E4M3 (preferred for weights) or E5M2 (activations, more range). Dynamic per-tensor scaling is applied. CUDA 12 and the cuBLAS/cuDNN libraries provide native FP8 GEMM on H100+. DeepSeek-V3 was trained entirely in FP8 with <0.25% loss. - Why it matters: FP8 is the production default on Hopper hardware. It delivers ~14.9% higher decode throughput for Llama-3.1-8B vs FP16 KV, and is described as 'essentially lossless' (W8A8-FP, ACL 2025) — under 1% accuracy drop on MMLU. - Gotcha: FP8 is natively supported only on Hopper (H100/H200) and Blackwell (B200/B300); older Ampere GPUs (A100) simulate it in software. Early vLLM FP8 KV-cache had a two-level accumulation bug that dropped a 128k needle task from 89% to 13% — fixed in flash-attention PR #104.
title: FP8

body: Quantization · appears on: Hardware Landscape 2026: Beyond H100 - What: An 8-bit floating-point numeric format natively supported on NVIDIA Hopper (H100/H200) and later GPUs, Google TPU v7, and AWS Trainium3, delivering approximately 2x throughput vs FP16 with less than 1% quality drop. - How it works: FP8 comes in two variants: E4M3 (4-bit exponent, 3-bit mantissa, used for weights) and E5M2 (5-bit exponent, 2-bit mantissa, used for activations/gradients). Hopper Tensor Cores execute FP8 matrix multiplications natively. In vLLM and SGLang, FP8 is enabled via `--dtype fp8` or `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`. FP8 KV cache provides approximately 14.9% higher throughput for Llama-3.1-8B by halving KV memory. - Why it matters: FP8 is the production standard for Hopper GPU clusters in 2026; it provides the best quality-per-compute tradeoff available on H100/H200 hardware and approximately 30% energy reduction at batch sizes ≥64. - Gotcha: FP8 is Hopper-native but can also run on A100 with software emulation (significantly slower). On Blackwell, FP4 (NVFP4) is preferred over FP8 where quality allows. The two FP8 variants (E4M3/E5M2) are not interchangeable and must be matched to the training precision configuration.
title: FP8

body: Quantization · appears on: Embedding & Reranker Serving: The Retrieval Half - What: The application of FP8 quantization to embedding model weights and activations, achieving approximately 50% throughput improvement while retaining >99% cosine similarity compared to FP16/BF16 embeddings. - How it works: Embedding models (which are purely prefill-bound, no decode) benefit from FP8 quantization of their transformer weights. The reduced precision doubles the number of weight values per memory access, improving compute throughput. For embedding models, >99% cosine similarity retention at FP8 has been validated (Arctic Inference team, 2026), making it essentially lossless for retrieval quality. - Why it matters: A 50% throughput improvement from FP8 halves the GPU count needed for a given embedding throughput target, directly reducing infrastructure cost for retrieval-heavy pipelines. - Gotcha: The >99% cosine similarity figure is for short-to-medium sequences. Long sequences (>4K tokens) may show slightly larger precision effects. Additionally, the similarity threshold for semantic caching must be re-calibrated when switching from BF16 to FP8 embeddings, as the embedding space shifts slightly.
title: FP8 Embedding Throughput

body: Low-precision numeric formats that cut memory and $/token. FP4 (Blackwell) is the 2026 frontier; AWQ 4-bit is the INT4 tier for smaller/open models.
title: FP8 / FP4 / AWQ

body: Quantization · appears on: FlashAttention: IO-Aware Attention (FA1→FA4) - What: Storing KV cache tensors in 8-bit floating point (E4M3) rather than BF16, approximately halving KV memory footprint per token with ~15% throughput improvement at the kernel level. - How it works: KV tensors are quantized to FP8 (E4M3 format) when written to the cache and dequantized to BF16 for the attention computation. FA3 supports inline FP8 KV on Hopper. vLLM fixed a critical two-level accumulation bug (PR #104) that had reduced long-context accuracy; after the fix, performance on 128k needle tasks recovered from 13% to 89% accuracy (close to the 91% BF16 baseline). - Why it matters: Production default on Hopper and Blackwell. Halving KV memory per token either doubles context length at fixed batch or doubles batch size at fixed context, directly improving serving throughput. - Gotcha: The accuracy fix matters: before vLLM's FP8 KV accumulation bug fix, FP8 KV cache had catastrophic accuracy loss at long contexts. The 97–98% AUC recovery figure is for Llama-3.3-70B; the 89% needle score (vs 91% BF16) is the post-fix H100 result. These figures are for different tasks and should not be conflated.
title: FP8 KV Cache

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Model Routing & Cascades: Cross-Model Cost - What: A cascade-based LLM cost optimization system (TMLR 2024) that sequences queries through progressively stronger and more expensive models, deferring to the next tier only when confidence is low. - How it works: FrugalGPT runs a cheap model first; if the model's confidence in its response exceeds a threshold, the response is returned. Otherwise, the query is deferred to a more expensive model. This cascade continues until a confident response is obtained. On benchmark evaluations, this matches GPT-4 quality at up to 98% lower cost. - Why it matters: Cascades automatically adapt to query difficulty at runtime: easy queries resolve at the cheap tier with minimal cost, hard queries escalate to the frontier tier. This is complementary to RouteLLM's pre-generation routing. - Gotcha: Cascades pay the generation cost of the cheap model even when they ultimately defer to the expensive model. A 2026 decision-theoretic result (arXiv:2605.06350) shows pre-generation routing structurally beats cascades on 4 of 5 benchmarks because cascades waste compute on early-exit failures before deferring.

SGLang achieves 26,156 prefill / 13,386 decode tok/s/GPU on DeepSeek-R1 on this hardware. - Why it matters: GB200 NVL72 is the gold standard (as of mid-2026) for hyperscale MoE serving and is the hardware on which NVIDIA's Dynamo 1.0 demonstrations (up to 30x throughput for DeepSeek-R1) were conducted. The 30x Dynamo speedup claim was made at GTC Mar 2025 and compares against a non-disaggregated baseline — not a strawman but also not representative of all configurations.

body: Hardware · appears on: Hardware Landscape 2026: Beyond H100 - What: A rack-scale NVIDIA system combining 72 B200 GPUs with 36 Grace ARM CPUs in a single coherent NVLink 5 domain, providing 13.4 TB of unified GPU memory and 130 TB/s NVLink bandwidth, drawing 120–132 kW per rack. - How it works: The 72 B200 GPUs are connected via NVLink Switch chips providing all-reduce and all-to-all at 130 TB/s. The Grace CPUs share coherent memory with the GPUs via NVLink-C2C. This eliminates InfiniBand as the scale-up interconnect within the rack, making cross-GPU communication fast enough to support tensor parallelism across all 72 GPUs for a single model. - Why it matters: GB200 NVL72 is the hardware target for disaggregated prefill-decode serving at the frontier (NVIDIA Dynamo, llm-d) and for models too large for a single-node 8-GPU configuration. It is the reference platform for multi-hundred-billion-parameter dense model serving. - Gotcha: The 120–132 kW/rack power draw requires liquid cooling infrastructure and specialized data center design. Comparing GB200 NVL72 throughput numbers to single-H100 numbers conflates system-level and chip-level figures.

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ - What: The binary model file format used by llama.cpp and related CPU/edge inference engines, supporting quantization from 1.58 bits (binary weights) to 8 bits per weight in various schemes. - How it works: GGUF encodes model architecture metadata, tokenizer, and quantized weight tensors in a single binary file. Quantization variants include legacy Q-quants (Q4_0, Q8_0) and modern K-quants and I-quants. The format supports memory-mapped loading (mmap), enabling models larger than RAM by paging weight blocks from disk. - Why it matters: GGUF is the standard for CPU inference, edge devices, and consumer hardware where GPU VRAM is limited. llama.cpp b9771 (Jun 2026) is the reference implementation; the format is supported on Windows/Mac/Linux with no Docker requirement. - Gotcha: GGUF is primarily a CPU/CPU-offload inference format. When a GPU is available, the preferred path is engine-native formats (AWQ/FP8 for vLLM; TRT engine for TensorRT-LLM). GGUF on GPU uses llama.cpp's metal/CUDA backend but is less optimized than purpose-built GPU serving stacks.
title: GGUF

body: Quantization · appears on: Edge Deployment Flow - What: llama.cpp's binary file format for storing quantized LLM weights plus metadata (tokenizer, architecture config, quantization scheme) in a single self-contained file. - How it works: llama.cpp's conversion scripts take a HuggingFace or PyTorch checkpoint and pack weights into GGUF using one of several quantization schemes (Q2_K through Q8_0). Each tensor block is quantized independently, with scaling factors stored alongside. The resulting file is memory-mapped at runtime, enabling mixed CPU/GPU offload without a separate loading step. K-quant variants (Q4_K_M, Q6_K) apply mixed quantization per tensor type (attention vs FFN) to preserve quality. - Why it matters: GGUF is the standard format for edge and local inference: it supports 1.58- to 8-bit quantization, runs on CPU with SIMD (AVX2/AVX-512/NEON), GPU (Metal/CUDA/Vulkan), and mixed offload, and is the native format consumed by Ollama. - Gotcha: GGUF quality degrades non-linearly below Q4; I-quant variants (IQ3_XS, IQ4_XS) with imatrix calibration beat same-bit K-quants at ≤3 bits. Math reasoning capability degrades first under aggressive quantization.
title: GGUF
