title: Goodhart's law

body: Metric · appears on: Latency Taxonomy: TTFT · TPOT · Goodput - What: Requests (or tokens) per second that satisfy both TTFT and TPOT SLO targets simultaneously — the fraction of throughput that is 'good' from the user's perspective. - How it works: Measured empirically by running load at various request rates, recording per-request TTFT and TPOT, and counting only those requests where both metrics fell within their respective SLO thresholds (e.g., TTFT < 1 s AND TPOT < 50 ms). The goodput curve peaks at the system's SLO-constrained capacity point. Coined in the DistServe paper (OSDI 2024). - Why it matters: Goodput is described in the deck as 'the most important production metric.' It directly captures how many users receive acceptable service, unlike raw throughput. Prefill–decode disaggregation, chunked prefill, and speculative decoding are all evaluated by goodput improvements, not just throughput. - Gotcha: Goodput is workload- and SLO-dependent: changing the TTFT threshold from 1 s to 500 ms on the same hardware can cut goodput in half. Always specify the SLO parameters when reporting goodput. The term originates from networking (useful throughput excluding retransmits); in LLM serving it was repurposed specifically to gate on dual TTFT+TPOT SLOs.
title: Goodput

body: Metric · appears on: Inference Engine Evolution: 2020 → 2025; Disaggregated Prefill/Decode Serving - What: The number of requests per second that meet both TTFT and TPOT SLOs simultaneously — the correct optimization target for production LLM serving. - How it works: Goodput = (requests_per_second) × P(TTFT < SLO_ttft AND TPOT < SLO_tpot). DistServe introduced goodput as the target metric because maximizing raw throughput often violates latency SLOs for individual requests. SLAI (arXiv:2508.01002) achieves 53% median TTFT reduction and 26% capacity improvement by scheduling for dual-SLO goodput. - Why it matters: Raw throughput metrics (tokens/sec) mislead in production — a system can maximize tok/s by batching aggressively while violating TTFT SLOs for every request. Goodput aligns the optimization objective with user experience. - Gotcha: Goodput is workload-specific: a system with excellent goodput on short-prompt workloads may have poor goodput on long-context RAG. Always specify the traffic mix when comparing goodput across systems or papers.
title: Goodput

body: Metric · appears on: SLA Dashboard: Key Metrics (implicit), Production SLA: Best Practices - What: The subset of throughput that actually satisfies latency SLOs (both TTFT and TPOT bounds). The deck example: 1,800 tok/s total throughput but only 1,200 tok/s goodput when TTFT < 1 s and TPOT < 50 ms are required. - How it works: Computed by filtering out requests that violate either TTFT or TPOT bounds and summing output tokens only from compliant requests, divided by wall time. Formalized by DistServe (OSDI'24) and now the standard production KPI. SLAI (arXiv:2508.01002) reports 26% goodput improvement over Sarathi via dual-SLO scheduling. - Why it matters: Goodput is the only metric that simultaneously captures latency and throughput, making it the correct north-star for LLM serving optimization. The deck explicitly warns that reporting throughput while ignoring SLO constraints is misleading. - Gotcha: Goodput can be maximized in ways that hurt individual user experience (e.g., aggressive batching raises average throughput but increases P99 TTFT for some users). Always inspect per-percentile latency alongside goodput.
title: Goodput

body: SLO-attained throughput: requests/s meeting both TTFT and TPOT SLOs (≠ raw throughput). The headline LLM-serving capacity SLI. NVIDIA AIPerf (successor to GenAI-Perf) measures it via `--goodput "time_to_first_token:X inter_token_latency:Y"` (single flag, not `--goodput-ttft`).
title: Goodput

body: Requests/s that meet both TTFT and TPOT SLOs — distinct from raw throughput (requests served but missing SLO are paid-for but unusable).
title: Goodput

body: Metric · appears on: SLA Dashboard: Key Metrics - What: The tokens-per-second rate counting only requests that satisfy both TTFT and TPOT latency objectives simultaneously. The canonical production KPI for LLM serving stacks. - How it works: For each request, check: did TTFT <= TTFT_SLO AND TPOT <= TPOT_SLO? If yes, count all output tokens toward goodput. Sum over all requests in a time window and divide by window duration. The deck example: H100 Llama-3-70B batch 32 with TTFT_SLO=1s and TPOT_SLO=50ms yields Goodput@SLO ≈ 1,200 tok/s out of total throughput 1,800 tok/s. - Why it matters: Goodput@SLO is the metric that correctly penalizes both throughput inflation (achieved by violating latency) and underutilization. It is the mathematically correct objective function for serving stack optimization under real production constraints. - Gotcha: Goodput@SLO can be gamed by loosening SLO bounds. Always report the SLO parameters alongside the goodput number. TaiChi (arXiv:2508.01989) reports 77% goodput improvement over a PD-disaggregated baseline — the improvement magnitude depends heavily on the chosen TTFT/TPOT targets.
title: Goodput@SLO

body: Hardware · appears on: Hardware Landscape 2026: Beyond H100 - What: Google's seventh-generation custom AI accelerator, delivering 4,614 TFLOPS FP8, 192 GB HBM3e at 7.4 TB/s, deployable in 9,216-chip pods, and used at scale to power Anthropic's Claude inference. - How it works: TPU v7 uses Google's custom ASIC architecture optimized for matrix multiply and memory bandwidth. It operates in large pod configurations (up to 9,216 chips with high-bandwidth ICI interconnect). Google provides TPU v7 via Google Cloud TPU and runs Anthropic's Claude workloads at approximately 1 million chips. Analyst estimates suggest ~44% lower TCO than GB200 from Google's perspective. - Why it matters: TPU v7 demonstrates that frontier-scale inference does not require NVIDIA GPUs; Anthropic's diversification onto Ironwood plus AWS Trainium provides supply and cost resilience. It also shows that purpose-built ASICs can match or exceed GPU efficiency for matrix-multiply-dominated workloads. - Gotcha: The ~$1.60/TPU-hour pricing for Anthropic and ~44% TCO advantage are SemiAnalysis analyst estimates, not official Google figures. The 4,614 TFLOPS figure is FP8; there is no published FP4 performance since TPU v7 does not natively support FP4 in the same way Blackwell does.

body: Concept · appears on: Tokens-per-Joule frame (energy levers): 'MoE sparsity: GPT-OSS-20B -26% energy/1K tok vs dense 32B' - What: OpenAI's open-weight model released Aug 5 2025 (Apache 2.0) with 21B total parameters / 3.6B active (a sparse MoE design using MXFP4 quantisation), fitting in 16 GB VRAM, used in the deck as the reference for MoE sparsity energy efficiency versus dense models. - How it works: GPT-OSS-20B's MoE architecture activates only 3.6B parameters per token (17% activation density), while a comparable dense model (e.g., Qwen3-32B) activates all 32B parameters per token. Energy per 1K tokens is proportional to active FLOPs; thus GPT-OSS-20B uses approximately 26% less energy per 1K tokens than Qwen3-32B despite ostensibly being a '20B' model. It also serves as a multi-LoRA benchmark in vLLM's Feb 2026 blog showing 8 adapters at ~454% throughput overhead. - Why it matters: GPT-OSS-20B's energy comparison demonstrates that MoE sparsity is not just a quality/memory optimisation but also a power-efficiency technique — critical context for the Tokens-per-Joule frame. At datacenter scale (485–950 TWh by 2030), choosing MoE-sparse over dense architectures has a measurable carbon footprint impact. - Gotcha: The '-26% energy/1K tok' figure is relative to Qwen3-32B (a dense 32B model), not to a hypothetical dense 20B model. The comparison is favorable because GPT-OSS-20B has far fewer active parameters than its dense comparator; a fair comparison would be GPT-OSS-20B vs a dense 3.6B model, which might show different energy characteristics. The MXFP4 quantisation also contributes to the energy reduction beyond just MoE sparsity.

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Semantic Caching: The Stack Is 3 Caches Deep - What: An open-source semantic caching library (Zilliz) that sits in front of any LLM API and caches responses based on semantic similarity of prompts, supporting multiple vector backends and embedding models. - How it works: GPTCache intercepts LLM API calls, embeds the prompt using a configurable embedding model, searches a vector store (FAISS, Milvus, Redis, etc.) for similar cached prompts, and returns the cached response if similarity exceeds a configured threshold. Falls through to the LLM API on cache miss and stores the new response. - Why it matters: Provides drop-in semantic caching for any OpenAI-compatible API without infrastructure commitment. Useful for development and moderate-scale production. Multiple vector backend options allow tuning for speed vs scale. - Gotcha: GPTCache is vulnerable to the NDSS 2026 cache-poisoning attack and the NDSS 2025 key-collision attack (86% hijack rate in some configurations). Production deployments handling sensitive data require additional security mitigations (per-tenant namespacing, response validation).
title: GPTCache

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ - What: A layer-by-layer post-training quantization algorithm that minimizes layer-wise output error using an inverse-Hessian update, supporting INT4 (and INT3/INT2) weight-only quantization. - How it works: Uses the OBQ (Optimal Brain Quantization) framework: the layer's weight matrix is quantized column-by-column, and after each column the remaining weights are updated with a Hessian-based correction. In practice, ~128 calibration samples (real text from the training domain) are passed through the model. The deck notes: 'Slow to quantize, fast at inference.' A typical GPTQ 4-bit pass on a 70B model takes hours. - Why it matters: GPTQ was the dominant 4-bit GPU quantization method before AWQ; it yields ~35 GB for a 70B model at 4-bit vs 140 GB at FP16, enabling 70B models on 2× A100 40 GB. It is widely supported (AutoGPTQ, TGI, vLLM). - Gotcha: GPTQ is strictly a weight-quantization method (W4A16 or W4A8); activations remain in FP16/BF16. Its successor MR-GPTQ (ICLR 2026) extends the Hessian method to FP4 via Hadamard rotation, achieving 2.2× throughput on B200.
title: GPTQ

title: GPU-backed debt

body: Security · appears on: Confidential Inference: TEE & the Attack Surface - What: NVIDIA's hardware feature set that encrypts GPU memory and computations so that data remains protected while being processed on the GPU, even from the cloud operator or host system. - How it works: NVIDIA GPU Confidential Computing extends CPU TEE (e.g., Intel TDX or AMD SEV-SNP) into the GPU domain: GPU memory is encrypted using hardware keys managed by the GPU itself; PCIe traffic between CPU and GPU is encrypted via PPCIE; the GPU provides a remote attestation certificate. On Hopper (H100/H200), this covers single-GPU setups. On Blackwell (B200/GB200), NVLink encryption extends this to multi-GPU pods. - Why it matters: Enables deployment of LLMs with sensitive model weights or user data in multi-tenant cloud environments without requiring trust in the cloud operator. Overhead is <9% throughput for large models and approximately 0% for Llama-70B-class models. - Gotcha: Hopper PPCIE (8-GPU HGX configuration, GA Apr 23, 2025) has a critical gap: NVLink communication between GPUs in the same node is plaintext. Full multi-GPU confidentiality requires Blackwell's TEE-I/O. Do not assume Hopper CC protects multi-GPU inference.
title: GPU Confidential Computing

body: CLI / flag · appears on: PagedAttention: vLLM v0 → v1 Deep Dive; Production Tuning: Memory, Scheduling & Observability - What: A vLLM CLI flag (0.0–1.0) that sets the fraction of total GPU VRAM allocated to the unified memory pool (model weights + KV cache + activations). - How it works: At startup, vLLM loads model weights, then allocates --gpu-memory-utilization × total_VRAM to its pool, reserving the remainder for CUDA context, driver overhead, and safety margin. Default 0.9. Too high (>0.95) risks OOM from activation spikes or driver overhead; too low wastes VRAM that could hold more KV pages. - Why it matters: The primary single-knob for memory tuning; setting it correctly for a given model×GPU combination is the first step in production deployment — leave 5–8 GB of headroom (typically 0.85–0.90 for H100 80GB). - Gotcha: SGLang uses --mem-fraction-static for the same purpose, but semantics differ slightly (SGLang's fraction covers static model weights only, with KV pool computed from remainder). Don't assume 1:1 mapping between the two flags.
title: --gpu-memory-utilization

body: % of time ≥1 kernel is running on the GPU — a "busy" clock, not an efficiency metric. Can read 100% while real compute use is ~20%.
title: GPU-Util%

body: Metric · appears on: Auto-scaling Architecture, Scaling Strategies - What: The fraction of time a GPU's compute units are actively doing work, expressed as a percentage (0–100%). - How it works: Reported by NVIDIA's NVML library (nvidia-smi / DCGM). In LLM serving, it reflects whether the GPU SM cores are executing attention/matmul kernels. SGLang's zero-overhead scheduler raised GPU utilization from 78–85% to 95–98% by overlapping CPU scheduling with GPU execution. The deck uses thresholds: scale out at >80%, scale in at <30%. - Why it matters: A primary ops metric for both capacity decisions and cost efficiency. Low GPU utilization means idle expensive hardware; near-100% utilization can mask queue saturation. It is used as one KEDA scaling trigger, though queue depth is now preferred as a more responsive signal. - Gotcha: GPU utilization is a lagging and ambiguous signal for LLM auto-scaling. A GPU at 80% utilization may be handling decode batches efficiently (good) or may be spending time on memory-bound attention (artificially high). For scale-out decisions, `vllm:num_requests_waiting` (queue depth) is the 2025–26 recommended primary KEDA trigger; GPU util is a secondary/confirmation metric.
title: GPU Utilization

body: Attention / KV · appears on: Attention Architecture: MHA → MLA & Long-Context - What: An attention variant where multiple query heads share a single K/V head, reducing KV cache size by a configurable factor (commonly 4–8×) while retaining most of MHA's quality. - How it works: Heads are divided into G groups; all Q heads in a group share one K head and one V head. LLaMA-2/3 uses 8 query heads per KV head (4× reduction shown on the deck). During inference, only G KV pairs are stored and read per token, reducing memory bandwidth and KV cache size proportionally. - Why it matters: GQA is the dominant attention type in production open-weight models as of 2025–26 (LLaMA, Mistral, Gemma, Qwen families). It provides a straightforward ~4–8× KV savings with negligible accuracy loss, directly increasing the number of concurrent requests that can fit in VRAM. - Gotcha: GQA's savings are at the attention KV level; the model's overall parameter count and weight load are unchanged. At very large group sizes it approaches MQA and may lose quality on fine-grained tasks.
title: GQA

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Production SLA: Best Practices - What: The practice of returning a reduced-quality but still useful response when the primary serving path is overloaded or unavailable. The deck lists two mechanisms: returning a cached or shorter response, or routing to a smaller model. - How it works: Implemented as a tiered fallback chain in the API gateway or application layer. Tier 1: serve from semantic cache (if available). Tier 2: shorten max_tokens to reduce generation time. Tier 3: route to a smaller/cheaper model (e.g., fall back from a 70B model to a 7B model). Tier 4: return a canned error message. Each tier has a latency budget; the system descends tiers when the P95 latency budget is at risk. - Why it matters: For user-facing applications, a degraded response is almost always better than a timeout error. Graceful degradation is the runtime complement to circuit breakers: instead of fast-failing, the system delivers partial value. It also flattens latency spikes during traffic bursts. - Gotcha: Routing to a smaller model during degradation must be invisible to the caller (same API contract) but may produce lower-quality outputs. Silently degrading quality without signaling to the caller can violate user trust and SLA terms. Consider adding a response header or metadata field indicating degraded mode.
title: Graceful Degradation

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Structured Generation: 'SGLang --grammar-backend xgrammar' - What: SGLang's CLI flag (equivalent to vLLM's '--guided-decoding-backend') that selects the grammar enforcement engine for structured output generation. - How it works: In SGLang, the grammar backend integrates with its jump-forward decoding optimisation: when a grammar constraint implies a deterministic next sequence of tokens (e.g., a JSON key that must be exactly '"name"'), SGLang's 'find_jump_forward_string' mechanism skips sampling entirely and directly appends those tokens, driven by the XGrammar engine. This eliminates per-token overhead for forced token spans. - Why it matters: SGLang's tight integration between the grammar backend and jump-forward decoding makes it particularly efficient for structured generation workloads — the 'up to 10x JSON throughput' headline figure cited in the deck reflects this combined optimisation over a naive per-token-mask approach. - Gotcha: Jump-forward only works when the grammar implies a single forced continuation; branching grammars still require per-token sampling. The legacy Outlines-backed jump-forward path still exists in SGLang v0.5.x but is now driven by XGrammar internally.

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Tokens-per-Joule & The Power Wall - What: An energy-aware LLM serving system (arXiv:2508.16449) that applies phase-specific Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling to reduce GPU energy consumption by 10–34% with minimal SLO impact. - How it works: GreenLLM profiles the compute vs memory-bandwidth demands of each inference phase (chunked prefill chunks, decode steps) and selects the minimum GPU frequency that satisfies the SLO for that phase. Phases with slack in their SLO budget run at reduced frequency; TTFT-critical prefill phases run at full frequency. This is applied dynamically per request. - Why it matters: Given the power wall constraints of 2026, reducing energy per token by 10–34% translates directly to higher effective cluster density and lower electricity cost. It also reduces carbon footprint when energy sources are carbon-variable. - Gotcha: GreenLLM's gains require that the serving system has sufficient SLO headroom to absorb frequency-reduced phases. At high load with tight SLOs, frequency reduction is not possible. The gains are also model- and hardware-specific.
title: GreenLLM

body: Hardware · appears on: Hardware Landscape 2026: Beyond H100 - What: Groq's purpose-built inference accelerator achieving 500+ tokens/second for 8B models and approximately 10x lower latency than H100 at batch size 1, sacrificing flexibility for extreme deterministic single-request throughput. - How it works: The Groq LPU uses a streaming dataflow architecture: weights are preloaded into on-chip SRAM (no DRAM, so no memory bandwidth bottleneck), and inference is executed via a compile-time-scheduled deterministic pipeline with zero dynamic dispatch overhead. This makes it extremely fast for latency-critical batch=1 workloads but poorly suited for high-batch serving or dynamic shapes. In December 2025 NVIDIA signed a non-exclusive LPU technology license and acqui-hire deal with Groq (reported as ~$20B, officially undisclosed). - Why it matters: Groq's use case is latency-critical serving where a user expects an immediate streaming response at batch=1 — customer-facing chatbots, real-time coding assistants. For throughput-optimized serving (high batch, many users), GPU engines outperform Groq. - Gotcha: The '$20B NVIDIA-Groq deal' dollar figure was reported by CNBC/EE Times via Groq's lead investor but has never been officially confirmed by NVIDIA or Groq. Do not state it as a confirmed figure. Groq's throughput advantage disappears at large batch sizes.
title: Groq LPU

body: Concept · appears on: Pre-LLM Era: Serving Infrastructure 2017–2022 - What: A high-performance, binary-serialized RPC framework (Google, open-sourced 2015) using HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers, used by TF Serving and Triton as their primary inference API protocol. - How it works: Clients send typed protobuf-encoded requests over an HTTP/2 connection; the server decodes, runs inference, and returns a protobuf response. gRPC supports bidirectional streaming (used for token streaming in some inference servers) and is significantly more efficient than REST/JSON for high-throughput, low-latency inference calls due to binary encoding and connection multiplexing. - Why it matters: gRPC was the standard protocol for pre-LLM model serving APIs. Modern LLM serving has largely converged on the OpenAI REST /v1/chat/completions API as the universal wire protocol, with streaming via HTTP SSE, though Triton and some internal systems still use gRPC for efficiency. - Gotcha: gRPC requires stub generation from .proto files on both client and server, adding coupling. The OpenAI REST API's simplicity (JSON over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2, SSE for streaming) was a key reason it became the universal standard — any curl or requests call works without generated stubs.
title: gRPC

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Structured Generation: 'vLLM --guided-decoding-backend xgrammar' - What: A vLLM CLI flag that selects the grammar engine used to enforce structured output constraints (JSON Schema, EBNF, Regex, Pydantic) during token sampling. - How it works: At each decoding step, the grammar engine computes a token mask — a boolean vector over the vocabulary — indicating which next tokens are valid given the current partial output and the grammar constraint. The sampler applies this mask before softmax, zeroing out invalid token logits. The '--guided-decoding-backend xgrammar' option selects XGrammar (the default and fastest backend, ~40µs/token cached via vocabulary partitioning and a Pushdown Automaton), over alternatives like Outlines (FSM, 40s–10min compile on large schemas) or llguidance (Rust Earley parser). - Why it matters: The choice of backend determines structured-output latency overhead. XGrammar's ~40µs/token is negligible versus decode time; Outlines' compilation latency makes it unusable for dynamic schemas in production. The flag enables operators to pin to a specific backend for compliance or debugging. - Gotcha: XGrammar v0.2.2 (Jun 2026) is the default across vLLM, SGLang, and TRT-LLM, but coverage of complex JSON schemas differs by backend: on GitHub-Hard schemas, XGrammar achieves ~28% empirical coverage versus Guidance's 41%, with Outlines at 3%. For agentic dynamic schemas, XGrammar-2's Cross-Grammar Cache provides ~7x lower function-calling latency.
title: --guided-decoding-backend

The H200 (same GPU die, 141 GB HBM3e at 4.8 TB/s) improves memory capacity and bandwidth, yielding ~43% higher decode throughput. Supports FlashAttention-3 (Hopper TMA/WGMMA warp specialization, ~840 TFLOPs/s BF16). - Why it matters: The H100/H200 is the reference hardware for most 2023–2025 serving benchmarks. The deck's worked example (H100, Llama-3-70B, batch 32: TTFT ≈ 450 ms, TPOT ≈ 25 ms, 1800 tok/s throughput, 1200 tok/s goodput) establishes concrete baseline intuition for metric interpretation. - Gotcha: H100 and H200 have the same compute (same GPU die, same TFLOPS); H200's advantage is purely memory capacity and bandwidth. The Blackwell generation (B200, GB200) roughly doubles FP8 throughput and supports NVFP4 (FP4 native), making H100-era benchmarks significantly outdated by mid-2026.

body: Hardware · appears on: FlashAttention: IO-Aware Attention (FA1→FA4) - What: The off-chip, high-capacity DRAM stack used as the main GPU memory (visible as 'GPU VRAM'), with bandwidth of 3–8 TB/s on modern accelerators but much slower than on-chip SRAM. - How it works: HBM is physically stacked beside the GPU die and connected via a wide interposer. H100 has 80GB HBM3 at 3.35 TB/s; B200 has 192GB HBM3e at 8 TB/s. KV caches, model weights, and activations all live in HBM; attention computations must fetch from HBM to on-chip SRAM for arithmetic. - Why it matters: HBM bandwidth — not TFLOP compute — is the bottleneck for LLM decode. All IO-awareness optimizations (FlashAttention, kernel fusion) aim to minimize the number of HBM reads and writes. The ratio of compute TFLOPS to HBM TB/s (arithmetic intensity threshold) determines whether an op is compute-bound or memory-bound. - Gotcha: HBM bandwidth and capacity are often conflated. Bandwidth matters for compute-bound decode throughput; capacity determines maximum context length + batch size. HBM4 (shipping 2026) roughly doubles bandwidth; HBM supply is sold out for 2026 per the research notes.
title: HBM

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Hardware Landscape 2026: Beyond H100 - What: The situation in 2026 where global HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) production capacity is sold out, making HBM the single binding constraint on AI accelerator supply and a primary factor in cloud GPU pricing and availability. - How it works: SK Hynix and Samsung are the two primary HBM manufacturers. HBM production requires advanced packaging (TSV, interposer) which constrains yield. In 2026, demand from hyperscalers (Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta) for H200/B200/B300 far exceeds HBM production capacity. HBM4 mass production began February 2026 but volume is still ramping. - Why it matters: Understanding the HBM supply constraint explains why GPU availability is limited regardless of fab capacity, why memory bandwidth (not TFLOPS) drives accelerator value, and why memory efficiency (FP4/FP8 quantization) has outsized production relevance — fewer chips needed for the same workload. - Gotcha: The constraint is on HBM packaging and stacking capacity, not on the DRAM cells themselves. Adding more DRAM fabrication capacity does not directly relieve HBM supply; advanced packaging fabs are the actual bottleneck.
title: HBM Supply Constraint

body: Hardware · appears on: Hardware Landscape 2026: Beyond H100 - What: The memory technology used in H200, B200, B300/GB300, AMD MI355X, Google TPU v7, and AWS Trainium3, providing higher bandwidth and capacity than HBM2e or HBM3. - How it works: HBM3e is a stacked DRAM technology connected via a silicon interposer to the GPU die. It uses 12 high layers with TSV (through-silicon via) connections, achieving 4–8 TB/s bandwidth per GPU. The 'e' designation indicates extended bandwidth and capacity versus HBM3. For H200, 141 GB is arranged in 8 stacks. - Why it matters: For LLM decode, memory bandwidth is the primary bottleneck (each token generation requires reading all model weights once). Higher HBM bandwidth directly increases tokens/second in decode-bound regimes. In 2026, HBM supply is sold out globally, making HBM the single binding constraint on AI accelerator production. - Gotcha: TFLOPS figures are misleading for comparing LLM inference hardware; HBM bandwidth is the correct metric to compare for decode throughput. A chip with 2x TFLOPS but same bandwidth will not improve decode throughput at all.
title: HBM3e

body: Hardware · appears on: Hardware Landscape 2026: Beyond H100 - What: The next-generation stacked DRAM standard after HBM3e, entering mass production in February 2026, used in NVIDIA Vera Rubin (22 TB/s) and planned for AMD MI455X (19.6 TB/s). - How it works: HBM4 achieves higher bandwidth through wider interfaces and more efficient signaling. Vera Rubin uses HBM4 at 22 TB/s per GPU. HBM4E (Extended) samples appeared May–June 2026 with approximately 4 TB/s per stack. SK Hynix and Samsung began mass production of HBM4 in February 2026. - Why it matters: HBM4 is what enables Vera Rubin's 50 PFLOPS NVFP4 performance to be memory-delivery-matched; without commensurate bandwidth, the added compute would be bottlenecked waiting for data. - Gotcha: HBM4 supply is even tighter than HBM3e in mid-2026; Vera Rubin ships H2 2026 but volume availability will be constrained. Do not conflate HBM4 with HBM4E — HBM4E is still in samples/pre-production as of mid-2026.
title: HBM4

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Production SLA: Best Practices - What: A periodic probe (HTTP GET /health or /v1/models) sent by a load balancer or orchestrator to each replica to determine whether it is ready to receive traffic. - How it works: Kubernetes liveness and readiness probes hit the inference server's health endpoint every few seconds. A configurable number of consecutive failures marks the pod unhealthy, removing it from the load balancer pool. Serving engines (vLLM, SGLang, llama-server) expose /health by default on their OpenAI-compatible API port. - Why it matters: Health checks are the first line of defense for uptime. Without them, a crashed or OOM'd GPU worker continues to receive requests that silently fail, directly degrading P99 latency and increasing error rate. - Gotcha: A shallow /health check (returns 200 even when the model is still loading or KV cache is full) can pass while the server is functionally degraded. For LLM servers, add a deep health check that verifies the model is loaded and can complete a minimal generation.
title: Health Check

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Scaling Strategies (via research companion §12 vLLM production-stack) - What: A Kubernetes package manager template that bundles all Kubernetes manifests (Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, KEDA ScaledObjects, etc.) for an application into a versioned, configurable release. - How it works: vLLM production-stack ships as a Helm chart (vllm-stack-0.1.11). Operators run `helm install` to deploy the full stack: vLLM pods, the prefix-aware router, Prometheus ServiceMonitor, KEDA ScaledObject, and Grafana dashboards. Configuration parameters (replica count, GPU type, model path, KEDA thresholds) are passed via `values.yaml`. - Why it matters: Helm charts reduce the ops burden of deploying complex multi-component stacks from dozens of manual manifest edits to a single parameterized install command. The vLLM production-stack Helm chart makes production-grade LLM serving deployable in minutes. - Gotcha: Helm chart defaults (replica count, threshold values, resource limits) are reference values for a specific benchmark environment and should be tuned for actual workloads. Blindly using chart defaults in production is a common source of under- or over-provisioned serving infrastructure.

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Inference Engine Evolution: 2020 → 2025 - What: The original Python-first model-loading and inference library (2020–2022 era) that introduced a unified API for all HF-hosted models but relied on manual/static batching and had no memory management. - How it works: HF Transformers wraps model weights as PyTorch nn.Modules, providing generate() with simple autoregressive decoding. Serving required user-written batching loops; each request allocated a fixed pre-allocated sequence buffer, wasting VRAM on short completions. No continuous batching, no paged memory. - Why it matters: Historical anchor in the timeline: the 24x throughput jump when PagedAttention replaced HF Transformers' naive approach in Jun 2023 defines the scale of the improvement vLLM represented. - Gotcha: HF TGI (the serving layer built on Transformers) entered maintenance mode Dec 2025 and the repo was archived Mar 21, 2026. HF now recommends vLLM/SGLang for serving — do not conflate HF Transformers (still active for fine-tuning) with TGI (EOL).

body: Caching · appears on: Prefix Caching: RadixAttention, APC, HiCache & Pricing - What: SGLang's 3-tier hierarchical KV cache system (Sep 2025) that spills KV pages from GPU VRAM → host RAM → external storage (HF3FS, Mooncake, disk) without engine restart. - How it works: Tier 1 is GPU VRAM (active, hot KV pages); Tier 2 is host DRAM (spillover, GPU-assisted I/O up to 3x faster than standard cudaMemcpy); Tier 3 is external persistent storage (HF3FS or Mooncake cluster). The cache hierarchy is managed by SGLang's RadixAttention tree — cold nodes get spilled to lower tiers. Attach/detach of backends requires no server restart. Ant Group's DeepSeek-R1-671B deployment saw 84% TTFT reduction with HiCache. - Why it matters: Extends effective KV cache capacity beyond GPU VRAM limits for long-context and multi-turn workloads; enables 6x throughput and 80% TTFT reduction at scale without adding GPUs. - Gotcha: Tier-3 read latency (from disk or remote storage) can exceed the prefill compute time for short prompts — HiCache helps most when cache-miss penalty (full prefill of a long shared context) far exceeds tier-3 read time. Profile before deploying tier-3.
title: HiCache

body: Hardware · appears on: Quantization: Precision vs Performance - What: NVIDIA's H100/H200 GPU architecture (2022–2024), the Blackwell predecessor, introducing native FP8 tensor cores, Transformer Engine, and NVLink 4. - How it works: Hopper adds Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) for async memory movement, WGMMA warp group matrix-multiply units, and native FP8 (E4M3/E5M2) compute at ~2× the FP16 TFLOP rate. H100 SXM5 delivers ~2,000 TFLOPS FP8; H200 adds 141 GB HBM3e at 4.8 TB/s (~43% more decode throughput than H100). - Why it matters: Hopper is the production baseline for cloud GPU inference in 2026. The quantization decision tree in the deck recommends 'FP8 / AWQ 4-bit' for Hopper as the primary operating point. It is the target architecture for FlashAttention-3 and the current vLLM/SGLang default GPU. - Gotcha: Hopper's FP8 requires CUDA 12.x and cuBLAS/cuDNN with FP8 support — earlier driver stacks silently fall back to FP16. NVFP4 is NOT supported on Hopper; do not attempt to use NVFP4 model weights on H100/H200.
title: Hopper

body: Security · appears on: Confidential Inference: TEE & the Attack Surface - What: NVIDIA's confidential computing implementation on Hopper (H100/H200) GPUs, providing PCIe encryption for CPU-GPU data transfer in an 8-GPU HGX configuration. Reached GA on April 23, 2025. - How it works: Each H100/H200 GPU pairs with a CPU TEE (Intel TDX or AMD SEV-SNP) and encrypts PCIe traffic between them. Up to 8 GPUs can be used in a confidential configuration (8-GPU HGX). However, NVLink between GPUs in the same node remains plaintext, limiting true confidential isolation to one GPU per CVM. - Why it matters: Hopper PPCIE made confidential single-GPU inference practical for regulated industries. The <9% throughput overhead (~0% for 70B models) makes it viable for production workloads that were previously incompatible with cloud deployment due to trust requirements. - Gotcha: The 1-GPU-per-CVM limitation on Hopper means models requiring tensor parallelism (most frontier models) cannot be served confidentially on Hopper. This requires Blackwell with TEE-I/O. A common misconception is that an 8-GPU Hopper cluster provides multi-GPU confidentiality — it does not.
title: Hopper PPCIE

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Scaling Strategies (via research companion §12 KEDA pattern note) - What: The built-in Kubernetes controller that automatically adjusts the number of pod replicas based on observed CPU/memory metrics or custom metrics. - How it works: HPA polls the Kubernetes metrics server (or custom metrics API) on a configurable interval (default 15s) and computes the desired replica count as: desired = ceil(current × current_metric / target_metric). KEDA acts as an HPA extension, feeding external metrics into the same HPA mechanism. - Why it matters: HPA is the Kubernetes-native autoscaling primitive that KEDA builds on. Understanding HPA clarifies why KEDA was necessary: standard HPA only supports CPU/memory metrics, which are inadequate for LLM serving workloads where queue depth and TTFT are the relevant signals. - Gotcha: GPU-utilization HPA was the pre-2025 approach and is now considered suboptimal for LLM serving. The 2025–26 production standard (KEDA on `vllm:num_requests_waiting` + TTFT PromQL) supersedes GPU-util HPA because queue depth is a more responsive and semantically correct trigger for inference overload.

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization: Precision vs Performance; Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ - What: GGUF quantization variants (IQ2_XS, IQ3_XS, IQ4_XS, etc.) that use an importance matrix (imatrix) computed from calibration data to guide which weights to round more carefully. - How it works: An imatrix is built by running representative text through the full-precision model and collecting per-channel weight activation norms. The quantizer then applies tighter rounding to high-importance channels. I-quants beat same-bit K-quants at 3 bits and below (research companion, arXiv:2601.14277). - Why it matters: At extreme compression (≤3 bits), standard K-quants produce noticeable accuracy loss; I-quants with a good imatrix can recover significant quality. The deck recommends I-quants when below Q4 for edge/laptop use. - Gotcha: Building a good imatrix requires calibration data representative of your task; math/reasoning capabilities degrade first under low-bit GGUF quantization regardless of method. IQ4_XS can be competitive in size with Q4_K_S while often beating its quality.

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Milestone 1: AI Infrastructure Platform: 'Cloud setup: IaC + K8s cluster' - What: The practice of defining and managing cloud infrastructure (VMs, networks, Kubernetes clusters, storage) through machine-readable configuration files (Terraform, Pulumi, Ansible, CDK) rather than manual console operations — required for reproducible, version-controlled AI infrastructure deployment. - How it works: In the Milestone 1 context, IaC means the K8s cluster, GPU node pools, networking (VPC, subnets, load balancers), storage (object store buckets, persistent volumes), and IAM policies are all defined in Terraform or Pulumi modules checked into a git repository. Applying 'terraform apply' idempotently creates or updates the entire infrastructure stack. For AI specifically, IaC manages GPU quota allocation, node taints for GPU scheduling, and Helm chart deployments of vLLM/SGLang serving endpoints. - Why it matters: IaC is a prerequisite for the 'platform' framing of Milestone 1: a reproducible, auto-provisioned infrastructure that can be torn down and recreated eliminates 'it works on my machine' issues and enables CI/CD pipelines to provision environments for integration testing. It also enables cost control (auto-destroy dev environments outside working hours). - Gotcha: GPU quota in cloud providers is gated by approval processes; an IaC script that requests 8× A100s will fail if the cloud project has not been pre-approved for GPU quota. Milestone 1 labs should test with smaller instances (T4, L4) that have broader quota availability unless GPU quota has been arranged in advance.

body: Concept · appears on: Tokens-per-Joule frame (The Power Wall): 'IEA dự báo ~485 → 950 TWh (2025→2030)' - What: The International Energy Agency, an intergovernmental energy policy body, whose 2025 electricity consumption forecast for global data centres (~485 TWh in 2025, projected ~950 TWh by 2030) is cited in the deck as the quantitative basis for the 'Power Wall' constraint on AI scaling. - How it works: IEA's Electricity 2025 report models data centre electricity demand growth driven by AI training and inference workloads, cloud hyperscaler expansion, and crypto mining. The doubling from ~485 to ~950 TWh in five years represents an annual compound growth rate of ~14%, driven primarily by AI compute demand. This figure contextualises why rack power density (120–190 kW/rack for frontier GPU systems) and tokens-per-joule efficiency are first-class infrastructure metrics in 2026. - Why it matters: The IEA forecast establishes that AI inference energy consumption is a geopolitical and infrastructure constraint, not just an operating cost concern. Countries and operators planning data centre buildouts must plan electrical infrastructure years in advance; the 2x demand growth projection is the demand signal driving power-delivery upgrades at hyperscaler facilities. - Gotcha: The IEA forecast includes all data centre electricity (cloud, enterprise, crypto), not just AI inference. The AI-specific fraction is estimated at 30–50% of total data centre demand and growing. National electricity grids in regions with high data centre density (Virginia, Singapore, Ireland) are already experiencing capacity constraints that precede the 2030 forecast horizon.
title: IEA

body: Concept · appears on: Multimodal (VLM) Serving: Encode–Prefill–Decode - What: The phenomenon where a single image at typical resolutions consumes 1,100–4,100 LLM tokens, and video at 30 FPS produces approximately 350K visual tokens per minute before any compression. - How it works: ViT encoders tile images into fixed patches (e.g., 14×14 or 16×16 pixels), each becoming one token. At 1024² resolution, Qwen3-VL produces ~1,139 tokens and Pixtral produces 4,096 tokens per image. Video multiplies this by frame count. TTFT is therefore dominated by image count rather than output length. - Why it matters: A single multi-image request can demand more prefill compute than thousands of text tokens, making standard continuous-batching strategies insufficient and motivating EPD disaggregation. - Gotcha: TTFT for VLMs is a function of number of images, not output length — a reversal of the text-only assumption. This breaks naive SLO budgeting that treats all prefill as equal cost.
title: Image-Token Explosion

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization: Precision vs Performance (research companion) - What: A calibration artifact used by llama.cpp's I-quant family: a per-channel matrix of average squared activation norms collected by running calibration text through the full-precision model. - How it works: Generated by the llama-imatrix tool using a calibration corpus (e.g., wikitext). The resulting .imatrix file is passed to llama-quantize alongside the model weights. Channels with high imatrix values get finer quantization grids. The technique is essential for sub-4-bit I-quants to beat K-quants. - Why it matters: Without an imatrix, 2–3 bit GGUF quantization is nearly unusable. With a task-relevant imatrix, IQ3_XS can approach Q4_K_M quality in practice, enabling 70B models on 16 GB RAM. - Gotcha: The calibration corpus must match the model's domain. Using a generic wikitext imatrix for a code model or a math model will underperform a task-specific imatrix. Generating the imatrix itself requires loading the full-precision model, which demands the full FP16 memory.
title: imatrix

TRT-LLM's implementation is tightly integrated with its layer-fusion and CUDA graph pipeline, so the in-flight mechanism operates at the engine's internal scheduler level rather than a Python orchestration layer. - Why it matters: Terminological alignment: instructors and practitioners must know that 'in-flight batching' (NVIDIA) and 'continuous batching' (vLLM/open-source community) are the same serving pattern. - Gotcha: The deck explicitly notes these two terms are equivalent ('thuật ngữ tương đương'). Conflating them with 'piecewise CUDA graph' (SGLang) or 'chunked prefill' is a common source of confusion.

body: Concept · appears on: Auto-scaling Architecture (via Gateway API Inference Extension research) - What: A Kubernetes CRD from the Gateway API Inference Extension that defines a logical model identity (name, version, criticality) and maps it to an InferencePool. - How it works: Clients address requests to an InferenceModel name rather than a specific pod or service. The gateway resolves InferenceModel → InferencePool → best replica. This indirection allows routing policies (priority, canary, criticality-based preemption) to be expressed declaratively without changing client code. - Why it matters: Decouples the model identity that clients use from the physical serving infrastructure, enabling model version upgrades, A/B testing, and criticality-based preemption without client-side changes. - Gotcha: InferenceModel supports a 'criticality' field (Critical/Standard/Sheddable) for priority-based request preemption under overload — a feature not available in standard Kubernetes Services. Teams migrating from plain Services must explicitly set criticality to benefit from this.
title: InferenceModel

body: Concept · appears on: Auto-scaling Architecture (via Gateway API Inference Extension research) - What: A Kubernetes CRD (Custom Resource Definition) introduced by the Gateway API Inference Extension that represents a group of model-serving backend replicas sharing the same base model. - How it works: Operators define an InferencePool resource specifying which pods belong to the pool (via label selectors) and the target model. The Gateway API Inference Extension's Endpoint Picker uses InferencePool metadata to select the best replica per request based on KV-cache state and queue depth. - Why it matters: InferencePool abstracts the fleet of replicas behind a logical identity, enabling inference-aware routing without modifying the backend engines. It is the standard API surface for LLM load balancing in the 2025–26 Kubernetes-native serving stack. - Gotcha: InferencePool is distinct from a standard Kubernetes Service (which does dumb round-robin or iptables-based load balancing). Routing through InferencePool requires the Gateway API Inference Extension gateway and its Endpoint Picker — standard ingress controllers bypass it.
title: InferencePool

body: Hardware · appears on: Distributed Inference: Parallelism Strategy Guide - What: A high-bandwidth, low-latency networking technology used for GPU-to-GPU communication across nodes in datacenter AI clusters, providing ~200 GB/s per port with 1–2 µs latency. - How it works: Connects compute nodes in an AI cluster fabric. In distributed inference, InfiniBand carries Pipeline Parallelism P2P activation tensors between nodes (tolerable because P2P is smaller and less frequent than All-Reduce) and EP A2A dispatch/combine operations. RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access) enables zero-copy GPU-to-GPU transfers. Configured via `NCCL_IB_HCA=mlx5`. - Why it matters: The standard interconnect for multi-node inference clusters (H100/B200 DGX). Enables PP across nodes and large-scale EP. Critical for disaggregated serving where multi-GB KV caches must be transferred between prefill and decode nodes. - Gotcha: 200 GB/s IB is ~4.5x slower than NVLink (900 GB/s), which is why TP should NOT cross nodes over IB—All-Reduce would bottleneck every layer. IB is suitable for P2P (PP stages) and bulk KV transfer, not for all-reduce-heavy TP.
title: InfiniBand

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ (research companion) - What: 4-bit integer weight representation, the most compressed standard format still considered usable for production on 8B+ models. - How it works: Weights are rounded to one of 16 integer values. A scale (and optionally zero-point) is stored per group of 32–128 weights. At inference, weights are de-quantized on the fly to FP16 before the GEMM (W4A16), or left as INT4 with INT8 activation (W4A8) in newer kernels. - Why it matters: INT4 is the basis for AWQ, GPTQ, and NF4 — the three dominant 4-bit formats. The ~4× memory reduction vs FP16 enables 8B models on 6 GB GPUs and 70B models on a single 40 GB GPU. - Gotcha: Quantization noise at 4-bit is meaningful: ~1 MMLU-point drop for 8B+ models, much more for sub-7B models. Research (ACL 2025) found that W4A16 speculative decoding can cancel spec-decode gains — W8A8 + EAGLE is the safer pairing.
title: INT4

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization: Precision vs Performance; Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ - What: 8-bit signed integer quantization, storing each weight (or activation) as a value in [-128, 127] with a per-tensor or per-channel float scale and optional zero-point. - How it works: Supported as W8A8 (weights and activations both INT8) in TensorRT and as W8A16 (weights only) in bitsandbytes. Integer arithmetic on tensor cores is faster than floating point and supported from Turing (RTX 20xx) onwards. - Why it matters: INT8 achieves the same ~2× memory reduction as FP8 and is supported on a much wider GPU range. It is the calibration target for TensorRT LLM's FP8/INT8 calibration pass (→ .trt engine) yielding 3–5× throughput vs vanilla PyTorch. - Gotcha: W8A8-INT8 can show more accuracy loss than W8A8-FP8 on certain tasks because integer scaling lacks the floating-point mantissa. On Hopper+ the preferred path is FP8, not INT8.
title: INT8

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ - What: The mathematical tool used by GPTQ to compute the optimal weight correction after quantizing each column: it encodes the curvature of the loss surface with respect to the remaining weights. - How it works: GPTQ computes the Fisher information matrix (approximated via the Hessian of the quantization error) for each weight matrix using the calibration activations. After quantizing each weight column, the inverse Hessian is used to update the remaining unquantized columns to compensate for the introduced error. This is derived from the Optimal Brain Surgeon framework. - Why it matters: The Hessian update is what makes GPTQ much more accurate than naive round-to-nearest at 4-bit: unquantized weights absorb the error of already-quantized weights, reducing the total output error at each layer. - Gotcha: Computing and inverting the Hessian is the expensive step in GPTQ — quantizing a 70B model takes many hours on a single GPU. MR-GPTQ (ICLR 2026) applies a Hadamard rotation to the weight matrix before this process, enabling extension to FP4.
title: Inverse Hessian

body: Concept · appears on: FlashAttention: IO-Aware Attention (FA1→FA4) - What: The principle that algorithm design should minimize the number of round trips between slow external memory (HBM) and fast on-chip memory (SRAM/L2 cache), even if that requires more arithmetic operations. - How it works: Modern GPUs have a large gap between peak FLOP throughput and peak HBM bandwidth. For memory-bound operations (including attention for long sequences), compute is 'free' relative to memory latency. IO-aware algorithms restructure computation to keep working sets in SRAM, accepting more FLOPs in exchange for fewer HBM reads/writes. - Why it matters: The foundational insight that motivates FlashAttention, fused kernels, and model compilation strategies in this section. Understanding IO-awareness explains why kernel fusion (combining multiple ops into one kernel) yields practical speedups even when it doesn't change the asymptotic FLOP count. - Gotcha: IO-awareness does not always mean 'minimize FLOPs.' An IO-aware algorithm may perform more FLOPs than a naive implementation but run faster because it stays in fast memory. This is counterintuitive to practitioners who focus purely on FLOP counts.
title: IO-Awareness

body: Replaces DPO's sigmoid loss with a quadratic. Fixes DPO's tendency to overfit when preferences are deterministic (always y_w wins). Note: deck line 458 says IPO fixes "length bias" — that's wrong; SimPO fixes length bias, IPO fixes deterministic-preference overfit. (Frame 4.1b table at line 568 is correct.)
title: IPO

body: Quantization · appears on: Edge Deployment Flow - What: A GGUF I-quant (importance-aware quantization) format that uses an imatrix calibration dataset to assign higher precision to the most important weights, often outperforming K-quants at the same or smaller bit depth. - How it works: imatrix (importance matrix) is computed by running the full-precision model on a calibration dataset and recording the activation magnitudes per weight group. Weights that influence high-magnitude activations are quantized with higher effective precision within the I-quant scheme. IQ4_XS at 4.38 bits per parameter achieves competitive quality to Q4_K_M (4.55 bits) at smaller file size. - Why it matters: I-quants with imatrix beat same-bit K-quants at ≤3 bits and provide the best quality/size tradeoff for aggressive quantization. This is important for fitting models into very tight memory constraints (e.g., 8 GB RAM for an 8B model). - Gotcha: I-quants require running an imatrix calibration step (llama.cpp's `llama-imatrix` tool) with a representative dataset before quantization; they cannot be produced from the GGUF file alone. The calibration corpus quality affects result quality significantly.
title: IQ4_XS

In a continuous-batching engine, ITL is the time for one decode iteration across the entire running batch, divided by the number of sequences (each gets one token per iteration). - Why it matters: Used interchangeably with TPOT in papers and monitoring dashboards. Knowing the synonym prevents confusion when reading vLLM/SGLang metrics output or research papers that use ITL in tables. - Gotcha: Some papers (e.g., DistServe) distinguish 'TPOT SLO' from 'ITL' based on whether they measure server-side or client-side intervals; in practice the distinction is negligible for most serving stacks. Do not confuse with 'inter-request latency.'

The SSM layers handle long-range context with constant KV memory (SSM state size is fixed regardless of sequence length), while attention layers handle local precision. The interleaving ratio is tuned for quality/efficiency. - Why it matters: SSM layers bypass the quadratic attention complexity and avoid KV cache growth for the tokens they process, enabling longer contexts at lower memory cost. body: Serving pattern · appears on: Structured Generation: XGrammar, Tool & Reasoning Parsers - What: A JSON document schema specification used as the grammar input to constrained decoding engines, ensuring model outputs are always valid JSON matching a declared structure. - How it works: The client sends a JSON Schema object in the `response_format` field of the OpenAI-compatible API request. The serving engine parses the schema, converts it to a grammar automaton (PDA in XGrammar, FSM in Outlines, Earley parser in llguidance), and at each decode step masks logits for any token that would violate the schema. The result is guaranteed to be parseable by any standard JSON parser. - Why it matters: Eliminates output parsing errors in agentic and structured-data applications; reduces retry rates; enables type-safe downstream processing. The most commonly requested structured output format in production. - Gotcha: Grammar constraints apply only to the final output tokens, not to the model's reasoning process. For reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3), the <think>...</think> block is unconstrained; grammar is applied only after the reasoning concludes. This is by design — constraining reasoning degrades output quality.
title: JSON Schema

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization: Precision vs Performance; Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ - What: The modern family of GGUF quantization schemes (Q2_K through Q8_K) that apply mixed-precision block quantization, assigning more bits to sensitive weight tensors. - How it works: In a K-quant, the model's weight tensors are categorized by sensitivity (attention vs FFN vs embedding). More sensitive tensors receive higher-bit quantization within the same overall BPW budget. The 'K' stands for 'better quantization' in the llama.cpp naming convention. Q4_K_S = 70.83% compression with only 0.43% quality loss (research companion). - Why it matters: K-quants beat legacy Q-quants (Q4_0, Q8_0) at every bit-width because they allocate bits where they matter most. For production edge inference, K-quants are the correct GGUF choice at 4-bit and above. - Gotcha: K-quants require the llama.cpp quantization tool (llama-quantize); they cannot be derived from the safetensors HF checkpoint directly without going through llama.cpp's conversion pipeline.

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Auto-scaling Architecture, Scaling Strategies - What: A Kubernetes add-on that scales deployments (including GPU pods) based on arbitrary external metrics rather than only CPU/memory. - How it works: KEDA registers custom metrics sources (called scalers) and periodically polls them. When a threshold is crossed — e.g. `vllm:num_requests_waiting > 10` or GPU utilization > 80% — KEDA adjusts the replica count by writing to the standard Kubernetes HorizontalPodAutoscaler. It can also scale a deployment all the way to zero replicas when a queue is empty, and bring it back up when a new event arrives. - Why it matters: GPU-utilization-based HPA (the classic Kubernetes approach) reacts too slowly for LLM workloads because a GPU can show low utilization while its request queue is already saturating. KEDA on `vllm:num_requests_waiting` + a TTFT PromQL metric is the 2025–26 production standard; KServe v0.16 and vLLM production-stack both ship KEDA integration out of the box. - Gotcha: GPU utilization alone is a lagging signal for LLM scale-out decisions. The correct 2026 KEDA pattern is to trigger on `vllm:num_requests_waiting` (a leading indicator) rather than GPU util %, which can stay high even after queues are draining. Also: KEDA-managed scale-to-zero requires a separate activator component (as in llm-d) to catch the first request when the pool is at zero replicas.
title: KEDA

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Production SLA: Best Practices - What: A Kubernetes autoscaler that scales deployments based on external event sources and custom metrics (Prometheus, queue depths, cloud event streams), beyond the built-in CPU/memory HPA. - How it works: KEDA adds ScaledObject custom resources that reference metric sources. For LLM serving, the standard 2025-2026 pattern is KEDA on `vllm:num_requests_waiting` or a TTFT PromQL expression — when the waiting-request count exceeds a threshold, KEDA increases replica count; when it drops to zero, KEDA scales down (optionally to zero). The vLLM production-stack Helm chart and KServe v0.16 both implement this pattern. - Why it matters: CPU/memory HPA is blind to LLM-specific load signals (queue depth, KV cache pressure, TTFT degradation). KEDA on inference-specific Prometheus metrics enables SLO-aware autoscaling rather than utilization-aware scaling, which better tracks actual latency impact. - Gotcha: KEDA with scale-to-zero creates a cold-start gap. The standard mitigation is to keep minReplicas=1 for latency-sensitive deployments. The metric vllm:num_requests_waiting is preferred over GPU utilization because GPU utilization stays high during prefill-only periods, causing over-scaling.
title: KEDA

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Model Compilation: torch.compile + CUDA Graphs + TensorRT - What: The optimization of combining multiple GPU operations that would each launch a separate kernel into a single kernel, eliminating intermediate HBM reads and writes between them. - How it works: Two element-wise operations (e.g., ReLU followed by layer norm) normally each launch separately: the first writes its output to HBM, the second reads it back. A fused kernel computes both in registers without the HBM trip. TorchInductor and TensorRT's layer-fusion passes identify chains of fuseable operations in the FX/ONNX graph and emit combined kernels. - Why it matters: For LLM serving, common fusion targets include: RoPE embedding application + QKV projection, layer norm + residual, activation functions. Each fused op eliminates one HBM round trip. Collectively, fusions from torch.compile add 1.1–1.5× speedup on the decode phase. - Gotcha: Not all operations are fuseable: ops that require a global reduction (softmax) or have data dependencies that span the full tensor require materialization. FlashAttention is the canonical example of a complex multi-op fusion (Q×K, scale, softmax, ×V all in one kernel).
title: Kernel Fusion

The parser is a streaming finite-state machine that detects model-specific output patterns and re-serialises them into the OpenAI-compat 'tool_calls' array format expected by clients. EAGLE 3.1 (May 2026) reported 2.03x per-user throughput at C=1 on Kimi-K2.6-NVFP4. - Why it matters: Without a model-specific parser, tool-call streaming from Kimi-K2 would be returned as raw text and require client-side parsing — breaking OpenAI-compat tool-use integrations. The parser abstraction lets the serving layer handle format diversity while presenting a uniform API surface. - Gotcha: The 'kimi_k2' parser token is model-family-specific and not interchangeable with the 'deepseek-r1' reasoning parser even for similarly structured output. Mixing parsers (e.g., '--reasoning-parser kimi_k2' with '--tool-call-parser deepseek') is valid but the combination must match what the specific model checkpoint actually emits.

When replicas reach zero, Knative's activator buffers incoming requests and triggers a cold start. - Why it matters: Knative provides the serverless runtime primitive that makes scale-to-zero practical on Kubernetes without custom operator code. Combined with KEDA for metric-triggered scaling, it is a common pairing for cost-sensitive LLM serving environments (dev, batch, low-traffic tenants). - Gotcha: Knative and KEDA overlap in capability and are sometimes used together (KEDA for external metrics triggering, Knative for the routing/activator layer) but can also conflict if both attempt to manage the same replica count. The deck lists them as a combined pattern ('KEDA + Knative: Event-Driven Autoscaling') without distinguishing their boundary.

body: Caching · appears on: KV Cache & PagedAttention - What: A memory buffer that stores the key and value tensors computed during the attention prefill phase, so that autoregressive decode steps can reuse them instead of recomputing from scratch. - How it works: During the prefill pass, each transformer layer projects every input token into K and V tensors; these are stored in GPU HBM. Each subsequent decode step appends one new K/V row and attends over all cached rows, so the cost per step is O(n) memory reads rather than O(n²) recomputation. - Why it matters: Without a KV cache, every decode step would re-run the full prefill computation over the entire sequence, making inference O(n²) per generated token. The cache reduces decode to O(n) bandwidth, which is why memory bandwidth — not FLOP throughput — is the binding bottleneck for LLM serving. - Gotcha: KV memory scales linearly with batch size × sequence length × layers × head-dim × 2 (K+V) × dtype bytes; a Qwen3-4B model at 32k context consumes ~4.5 GB KV. For reasoning models generating 10k–100k CoT tokens, the KV cache can overflow VRAM before inference completes.
title: KV Cache

body: Stored attention keys/values that let a model avoid recomputing prior context; its reuse (hit%) is a primary cost driver.

body: Decoding · appears on: DFlash: Block Diffusion Drafting + KV Injection - What: DFlash's second mechanism: writing the target model's hidden states directly into the draft model's KV cache so the drafter never re-models the context. - How it works: Instead of having the small drafter run its own forward pass over the prompt, the verifier's already-computed context features are injected into the drafter's attention cache. The drafter then only has to predict the block. - Why it matters: It removes duplicated context work from the draft path, which is a large share of drafting cost at long context. - Gotcha: An LMSYS ablation shows DFlash still beats EAGLE-3 with KV injection removed — the block-diffusion parallelism is the primary win and KV injection is an accelerant, so do not attribute the whole speedup to it.
title: KV injection

body: Security · appears on: Confidential Inference: TEE & the Attack Surface - What: An inference-time privacy attack that exploits measurable differences in TTFT caused by KV cache hits vs misses to infer information about other users' cached prompts on a shared serving instance. - How it works: When a prefix cache (APC) is shared across tenants, a cache hit for user B's prompt will occur if user A previously submitted the same prefix. This hit is observable as a reduced TTFT. By systematically varying prefixes and measuring TTFT, an attacker can determine what prefixes are cached, effectively reconstructing other users' prompts. This is the mechanism behind PROMPTPEEK (NDSS 2025). - Why it matters: Shared KV caches — a standard efficiency feature in vLLM, SGLang, and most production serving stacks — create a covert timing channel that leaks prompt content. This is a fundamental tension between efficiency (shared caches) and privacy (isolated caches). - Gotcha: This attack does not require any access to GPU memory or model internals — it only requires the ability to send HTTP requests to the API and measure response times. It is a black-box network-level attack, making it accessible to any API user.
title: KV Timing Side-Channel

body: Attention / KV · appears on: Disaggregated Prefill/Decode Serving - What: The data movement step in disaggregated serving that ships computed KV tensors from prefill GPUs to decode GPUs using high-speed NVLink (intra-node) or InfiniBand/RoCE (inter-node) interconnects. - How it works: After prefill, the KV cache (num_layers × 2 × seq_len × num_heads × head_dim × bytes_per_element bytes) is transmitted to the decode node. Over NVLink (GB200 NVL72: 130 TB/s intra-node), this is microseconds. Over InfiniBand NDR400 (~400 Gb/s per link, ~50 GB/s): a 1M-token DeepSeek-R1 KV cache (~70 GB) takes ~1.4 seconds. NIXL handles transport scheduling (IB/RoCE/TCP/NVMe-oF/S3). FlowKV (arXiv:2504.03775) reduced average KV-transfer latency from 0.944s to 0.053s via pipelining, though end-to-end speedup is 15–49% context-dependent. - Why it matters: The bottleneck step in disaggregated serving for inter-node deployments; its latency directly adds to TTFT and determines the feasibility of disaggregation for a given workload and context length. - Gotcha: The cited ~10 GB/s figure in the deck refers to typical IB Ethernet bandwidth in early deployments — modern NDR400 IB achieves 50 GB/s per link, and Mooncake's RDMA zero-copy approach removes CPU involvement entirely. Always benchmark actual transfer bandwidth in your cluster config.

body: Hardware · appears on: Tokens-per-Joule frame: 'GB200 NVL72 120-132 kW/rack; GB300 135-150 kW; Vera Rubin NVL144 ~190 kW' - What: A data centre infrastructure metric measuring peak electrical power draw per server rack, which has become the primary constraint on AI accelerator deployment density as GPU power consumption has scaled faster than traditional data centre cooling and electrical distribution infrastructure. - How it works: Traditional enterprise data centre racks are designed for 5–15 kW/rack (air cooled). AI GPU racks broke this boundary progressively: H100 DGX A100 = ~10.2 kW, H100 SXM5 HGX = ~10.2 kW per tray, GB200 NVL72 = 120–132 kW (liquid-cooled, 72 GPUs per rack-scale unit). This 10x increase over 4 years requires dedicated direct liquid cooling (DLC) infrastructure, 480V power distribution, and building-level electrical upgrades. The Vera Rubin NVL144 (~190 kW) and future systems (MI455X Helios) will require further infrastructure redesign. - Why it matters: Rack power density is the binding constraint that determines how many GPUs can be co-located in a physical facility. A data centre rated for 1 MW per floor (100 racks × 10 kW) can only support ~8 GB200 NVL72 racks — a 12x reduction in rack count. Operators must either build purpose-designed AI data centres or accept that hyperscale GPU deployments require greenfield facilities with custom power and cooling infrastructure. - Gotcha: The 120–132 kW/rack figure for GB200 NVL72 is the nameplate/TDP figure; actual average power draw under mixed workloads is typically 60–80% of TDP. However, infrastructure must be sized for peak TDP, not average, to avoid circuit breaker tripping. The '190 kW' Vera Rubin NVL144 figure is an estimate from pre-production specifications; actual shipped power may differ.

title: Late-Arriving Data

body: Embedding the whole document first and only then cutting, making fixed-size chunks perform like semantic chunking.
title: Late chunking

body: Concept · appears on: Embedding & Reranker Serving: The Retrieval Half - What: A retrieval technique where long documents are first embedded as a whole (preserving long-range context) and then chunked for indexing, rather than chunking before embedding. - How it works: The full document is passed through the encoder in one forward pass; the resulting per-token hidden states are then pooled into chunk-level embeddings at chunk boundaries. This allows each chunk's embedding to incorporate context from the full document, unlike standard chunking which embeds each chunk in isolation. - Why it matters: Standard chunk-then-embed loses cross-chunk context (e.g., coreference across paragraphs). Late chunking produces more contextually rich chunk embeddings, improving retrieval precision for long-document RAG pipelines. - Gotcha: Late chunking requires running the encoder over the entire document at once, which may exceed the model's context window for very long documents. It also requires per-token output from the encoder, which not all frameworks expose efficiently.
title: Late Chunking

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Auto-scaling Architecture, Scaling Strategies - What: A load-balancing policy that routes each new request to the GPU worker with the currently lowest queue depth (fewest pending requests). - How it works: The load balancer tracks a real-time queue-depth counter per replica. On each new request, it picks the replica with the minimum outstanding requests (or lowest utilization proxy). This is a form of the Least Connections algorithm from classical load balancing, adapted for GPU inference queues. - Why it matters: LLM inference request durations are highly variable (short prompts vs long CoT completions). Round-robin ignores this variance and creates hot replicas. Least-busy routing achieves +30% throughput over round-robin according to the deck, because it naturally shifts load away from workers that are slow on long-context requests. - Gotcha: Least-busy routing on queue depth alone is still suboptimal in 2026 production stacks: it ignores KV-cache state. The Gateway API Inference Extension's Endpoint Picker adds KV-cache hit rate as a routing signal, which provides further TTFT reduction (3–10x vs round-robin in vLLM production-stack benchmarks) by preferring workers that already hold matching prefix KV blocks.
title: Least-busy Routing

body: Concept · appears on: Latency Taxonomy: TTFT · TPOT · Goodput - What: Meta's 70-billion-parameter open-weight large language model from the Llama 3 family, used in the deck as the reference model for the TTFT/TPOT/Goodput worked example. - How it works: A dense transformer decoder with 70B parameters, GQA (Grouped-Query Attention) for KV efficiency, and BF16 native precision. At batch 32 on an H100 with vLLM: TTFT ≈ 450 ms (primarily 70B prefill compute), TPOT ≈ 25 ms (decode is memory-bandwidth-bound), throughput ≈ 1,800 tok/s, goodput ≈ 1,200 tok/s at TTFT < 1 s + TPOT < 50 ms SLO. - Why it matters: The 70B scale is a canonical production reference point: large enough that multi-GPU serving (TP=2 or TP=4) is common, but small enough to run on accessible hardware. Using Llama-3-70B as the worked example gives students a concrete, reproducible intuition for metric values before abstract definitions. - Gotcha: By mid-2026, Llama 3's successor (Llama 4, with Scout/Maverick MoE variants) is the current Meta open-weight frontier. Llama-3-70B benchmarks remain useful for comparison but are one generation behind. The Llama 4 Maverick (17B active, MoE) serves faster than Llama-3-70B at equivalent quality on many tasks.
title: Llama-3-70B

body: Concept · appears on: Quantization: Precision vs Performance frame (VRAM bars), and GGUF/NF4/GPTQ/AWQ table — used as the 8B reference model for all VRAM/quant figures - What: Meta's open-weight 8-billion-parameter dense transformer (Llama 3 family), used in the deck as the canonical small-model reference for quantization VRAM measurements. - How it works: The 8B parameter count at FP16 precision occupies ~15.8 GB VRAM (2 bytes/param); halving precision to FP8 gives ~7.9 GB; 4-bit AWQ reduces to ~4.5 GB. These linear ratios make it the standard didactic benchmark: small enough to run on a single GPU, large enough that quant tradeoffs are measurable. - Why it matters: It is the most widely benchmarked open model at the 7–8B tier, making its VRAM and perplexity figures reproducible across hardware. Quant decisions validated on Llama-3-8B generalize to the broader 7–13B class; it is also the baseline used by SGLang's throughput benchmarks (~16,215 tok/s FP8 on H100) and Lab 20. - Gotcha: Quality degradation from quantization is nonlinearly worse for sub-7B models; the '~1pt MMLU drop at AWQ 4-bit' figure applies to 8B+ models and should not be extrapolated to smaller models. The VRAM figures exclude KV-cache memory, which can dwarf model weight memory at long contexts.
title: Llama-3-8B

body: A contrast in frontier recipes: Llama 3 runs SFT → rejection-sampling → iterative DPO (6 rounds); Llama 4 inverts the order to light-SFT → online-RL → a final light DPO, because tight SFT/DPO was found to 'squeeze' the exploration space of online RL. _(deck: §9.1b 'Công thức post-training 2025', lines 1537-1538 and warningbox line 1550)_
title: Llama 3 / Llama 4 order inversion

body: Concept · appears on: Multimodal prefix caching defbox: 'Early-fusion (Llama 4) bỏ luôn encoder stage riêng' - What: Meta's Llama 4 family uses an 'early fusion' multimodal architecture where image tokens are embedded directly into the language model's token sequence at the input layer rather than being processed by a separate ViT encoder — eliminating the distinct encode stage. - How it works: In late-fusion VLMs (LLaVA, Qwen-VL, InternVL), a ViT encoder produces visual feature vectors that are projected into the LLM's token space and concatenated with text tokens; the encoder and LLM are separate sub-models. In early-fusion (Llama 4, also Chameleon-class models), raw image patches are embedded directly by the LLM's input embedding layer using a shared token vocabulary that includes both text and image patch tokens — there is no separate ViT forward pass. This means EPD disaggregation (Encode–Prefill–Decode) reduces to PD disaggregation (Prefill–Decode) for Llama 4. - Why it matters: Early fusion eliminates the encoder-prefill KV transfer bottleneck and removes the TP-incompatibility of ViT encoders. For serving, this means Llama 4 can be served with standard LLM parallelism strategies without special encoder handling. However, it makes prefix caching of image tokens harder because the image embedding is now interleaved with text rather than being a separable encoded vector. - Gotcha: Early fusion does not necessarily reduce the number of visual tokens per image — Llama 4's Maverick/Scout variants still produce hundreds to thousands of tokens per image depending on resolution. Multimodal prefix caching for early-fusion models hashes the raw pixel/patch values (via SHA-256) rather than ViT encoder outputs, as noted in the deck's defbox.
title: Llama 4

body: Meta's experimental "Maverick" variant (longer, emoji/format-heavy) topped the board, but enabling Style Control dropped it 2nd → 5th. Case study: "response length/formatting can buy Elo."
