body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Serving Stack 2026: 8 Engines That Matter - What: A portable C/C++ LLM inference engine supporting GGUF quantization, CPU+GPU mixed offloading, and Apple Metal, designed for local and edge deployments without Docker. - How it works: llama.cpp reads GGUF files and runs inference via optimized CPU BLAS + optional GPU (CUDA, Metal, Vulkan, OpenCL) offloading. Mixed-precision offloading lets layers split between CPU RAM and GPU VRAM. Build b9771 (Jun 23, 2026) adds libmtmd multimodal, native Android/ChromeOS GPU, and MTP speculative decoding (merged May 2026, ~2x on supported models). Exposes REST and OpenAI-compatible endpoints. - Why it matters: The reference engine for CPU, Mac, Windows, and edge deployments; zero Docker dependency; runs quantized models on consumer hardware; underpins Ollama. - Gotcha: The Prometheus /metrics endpoint no longer exposes kv_cache_usage_ratio — monitoring scripts referencing that metric need to be updated. MTP spec-decode requires a supporting model (e.g., DeepSeek V3) and isn't universally available.
title: llama.cpp

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Edge Deployment Flow - What: An open-source C++ inference engine for GGUF-format LLMs, supporting CPU, GPU (CUDA/Metal/Vulkan), and mixed CPU+GPU offload across Windows, macOS, Linux, and Android. - How it works: llama.cpp memory-maps GGUF files and executes the transformer forward pass using hand-optimized SIMD kernels (AVX2, AVX-512, NEON for ARM). GPU offload sends a configurable number of layers to CUDA/Metal/Vulkan while the remainder runs on CPU. As of build b9771 (Jun 23 2026), it includes MTP speculative decoding (~2x throughput), libmtmd multimodal support, and native Android/ChromeOS GPU backends. - Why it matters: llama.cpp is the only inference engine that runs efficiently on commodity hardware (laptops with 8 GB RAM) without a container or GPU. It is the backend for Ollama and the primary tool for the Day 20 lab. - Gotcha: Build flags must match the host CPU (AVX2 vs AVX-512 vs NEON); a generic build loses significant performance. The /metrics endpoint dropped kv_cache_usage_ratio in a recent build — use num_slots_used/num_slots instead.
title: llama.cpp

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Lab 20 frame (Core Tracks): '01-quickstart: llama-cpp-python baseline P50/P95/P99' - What: A Python binding library for llama.cpp that exposes the GGUF-based inference engine as a Python API, enabling direct Python-code inference (not via HTTP server) for benchmarking and scripted evaluation — used in Lab 20 Track 01 for baseline P50/P95/P99 latency measurement. - How it works: llama-cpp-python (pip install llama-cpp-python) wraps the llama.cpp C++ library via ctypes/cffi bindings, exposing the 'Llama' class with a '__call__' method that accepts a prompt string and generation parameters and returns generated tokens. This enables in-process inference from Python scripts without the overhead of HTTP serialisation/deserialisation. Track 01 uses this for controlled benchmarking: a single Python script generates a fixed set of prompts, measures wall-clock time per response, and computes P50/P95/P99 latency percentiles. - Why it matters: In-process llama-cpp-python benchmarking eliminates HTTP server overhead from the latency measurement, giving a clean baseline of raw inference latency. This is then compared against Track 02's 'llama-server' results to quantify the serving-stack overhead. It also runs on CPU without a GPU, making it the universal fallback for all student hardware configurations. - Gotcha: llama-cpp-python builds with default flags may not enable platform-specific CPU optimisations (AVX2, AVX-512, NEON, Metal). The bonus llama.cpp tuning track specifically addresses this: recompiling with 'CMAKE_ARGS="-DLLAMA_AVX2=ON"' can yield 1.5–3x throughput improvements on modern CPUs. The Python GIL also limits multi-threaded benchmarking from the same process.
title: llama-cpp-python

body: (Meta) classifier phân loại hazard / phát hiện injection-jailbreak.

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Lab 20 (02-server): 'OpenAI-compat llama-server + Prometheus + locust load test'; Deliverable frame - What: The HTTP server component of llama.cpp (formerly 'server' binary, renamed 'llama-server' in recent builds) that exposes an OpenAI-compatible REST API ('/v1/chat/completions', '/v1/completions', '/health', '/metrics') for GGUF model inference — used in Lab 20 Track 02 for load testing with locust. - How it works: llama-server starts a multi-threaded HTTP server (default port 8080) that accepts OpenAI-format JSON requests, runs inference via the llama.cpp engine, and returns streaming or batch responses. It exposes Prometheus metrics at '/metrics' (request count, processing time, tokens/second) for Grafana dashboards. In Track 02, students deploy llama-server, point locust at it to simulate 10 and 50 concurrent users, and collect P50/P95/P99 latency and throughput under load — the primary deliverable for the benchmark report. - Why it matters: llama-server provides an OpenAI-compatible serving endpoint runnable on any hardware (CPU/GPU/Apple Metal) without Docker or cloud dependencies, making it the universal lab environment for serving concepts. The locust load test replicates the 'saturation testing' workflow used in production to find the goodput@SLO envelope. - Gotcha: llama-server's performance at 50 concurrent users on CPU is limited by sequential inference (no batch parallelism on CPU) — students will observe P99 latency growing near-linearly with concurrency. This is pedagogically intentional: it motivates the continuous-batching and GPU-serving concepts taught in §3–4. The '/metrics' Prometheus endpoint was present in earlier builds but the specific metric names (e.g., 'llamacpp:prompt_eval_duration_seconds') changed across recent builds.
title: llama-server

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Structured Generation: XGrammar, Tool & Reasoning Parsers - What: Microsoft's (and OpenAI's adopted) Rust-based Earley parser for grammar-constrained decoding, with ~50µs/token latency and zero startup time; OpenAI shipped it for JSON Schema on May 20, 2025. - How it works: llguidance uses an Earley parsing algorithm implemented in Rust, which handles any context-free grammar including ambiguous ones without pre-compilation — startup is near-zero because it parses grammars lazily token-by-token. It achieves ~50µs/token overhead. v1.0.0 released Jun 23, 2025 (OpenAI shipped it May 20, 2025 on v0.7.x). It achieves 41% coverage on JSONSchemaBench GitHub-Hard (highest among open-source backends tested). - Why it matters: Zero startup time makes it ideal for dynamic grammars that change per request (tool-call schemas, agentic workflows); OpenAI's adoption makes it a critical reference implementation. - Gotcha: llguidance is primarily available via the Guidance library (Microsoft) and as OpenAI's internal backend — it is not the default backend in open-source vLLM/SGLang (those default to XGrammar). The v1.0.0 release date (Jun 23, 2025) is after OpenAI's May 2025 deployment of v0.7.x.
title: llguidance

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Serving Stack 2026: 8 Engines That Matter; Disaggregated Prefill/Decode Serving - What: A Kubernetes-native P/D-disaggregated LLM serving platform (CNCF Sandbox) that sits above vLLM using Gateway API Inference Extension and NIXL for KV transport. - How it works: llm-d routes requests via a KV-cache-aware Endpoint Picker (part of Gateway API Inference Extension) that preferentially sends requests to the decode worker that already holds the relevant KV prefix, minimizing KV transfer. NIXL handles zero-copy KV movement over NVLink/IB. v0.5 added scale-to-zero via an activator. Reports 3x lower mean TTFT at 4 QPS and ~50% higher QPS vs a non-KV-aware baseline. - Why it matters: The Kubernetes-native path to disaggregated LLM serving; co-developed by Red Hat/IBM/NVIDIA; integrates with KServe v0.16 LLMInferenceService CRD; target for teams running vLLM on K8s at scale. - Gotcha: Scale-to-zero is described qualitatively in v0.5 — no published cold-start latency numbers exist. v0.6/v0.7 now supersede v0.5.
title: llm-d

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Scaling Strategies (via deck line 970 and research) - What: A CNCF Sandbox Kubernetes-native LLM serving orchestrator that adds prefill/decode disaggregation, scale-to-zero, and LoRA-aware routing on top of vLLM. - How it works: Uses vLLM as the inference backend, Gateway API Inference Extension for routing, and NIXL for high-speed KV-cache transfer between prefill and decode nodes. An activator component handles the scale-to-zero cold-start problem by buffering the first request and triggering pod startup. v0.5 added scale-to-zero and saturation autoscaling. v0.6/v0.7 supersede v0.5 as of mid-2026. - Why it matters: Demonstrates the 2026 Kubernetes-native inference stack: disaggregated P/D + inference-aware routing + event-driven autoscaling as a single installable project. Reports 3x lower mean TTFT at 4 QPS and ~50% higher QPS vs aggregated serving. - Gotcha: No published end-to-end GPU-provision-to-first-token cold-start latency figures exist for llm-d's scale-to-zero activator as of mid-2026 — only TTFT (136–157ms) and KV-transfer (~360ms) figures are available, which measure steady-state disaggregated serving, not cold start.
title: llm-d

body: Caching · appears on: Prefix Caching: RadixAttention, APC, HiCache & Pricing - What: An open-source cross-instance KV cache sharing system (arXiv:2510.09665) that lets multiple vLLM/SGLang workers share cached KV tensors via CPU RAM, SSD, Redis, S3, or Mooncake, with multi-node P2P support GA since Jan 2026. - How it works: LMCache sits as a cache layer between the serving engine and VRAM; on a cache miss, it checks CPU/SSD/remote backends before triggering a full prefill. CacheBlend (EuroSys'25 Best Paper, integrated into LMCache) extends this to non-prefix KV reuse, recomputing only ~10–15% of hidden-KV-delta tokens for 2.2–3.3x TTFT and 2.8–5x throughput improvement. KServe integration enables cross-pod caching in K8s. - Why it matters: Extends prefix caching beyond a single GPU to a cluster-wide or cross-datacenter KV store, with 2.3–14x single-node CPU offload throughput improvement; enables persisting system-prompt KV caches across worker restarts. - Gotcha: LMCache adds serialization/deserialization overhead on the critical path; the benefit requires high hit rates (>20–30%) to offset the transport latency. Backend selection (CPU vs S3 vs Redis) depends on network bandwidth and latency — S3 is only viable for very large cached contexts where transport cost is amortized.
title: LMCache

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Serving Stack 2026: 8 Engines That Matter - What: InternLM's high-throughput LLM serving engine built around the TurboMind execution backend, optimized for NVIDIA GPUs with support for MXFP4 and disaggregated P/D via Mooncake. - How it works: LMDeploy's TurboMind engine delivers ~1.5x throughput over vLLM on H800 for GPT-class models by using highly optimized CUDA kernels and MXFP4 quantization (v0.13.0, CUDA 12.8). P/D disaggregation is supported via DLSlime and Mooncake integration. Exposes an OpenAI-compatible API. - Why it matters: Preferred engine in the InternLM/Shanghai AI Lab ecosystem; chosen by practitioners needing high throughput on NVIDIA H-series GPUs with minimal configuration. - Gotcha: MXFP4 support requires CUDA 12.8 and is limited to V100+ (Volta and later) — check hardware compatibility before assuming production readiness.
title: LMDeploy

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Auto-scaling Architecture - What: A network component that distributes incoming inference requests across a pool of GPU worker replicas. - How it works: Sits between clients and the GPU pool. Receives all incoming requests (e.g. 100 RPS in the deck diagram) and forwards each to one of the available GPU workers using a routing policy — in this context, least-busy routing. Signals to KEDA when the pool must expand or contract. - Why it matters: Without a load balancer, requests pile up on a single worker while others are idle, destroying throughput and inflating tail latency. It is the traffic-distribution primitive that makes horizontal scaling possible. - Gotcha: A naive round-robin policy ignores worker queue depth and KV-cache state, causing imbalanced load. The 2026 production standard replaces or augments classic load balancers with an inference-aware Endpoint Picker (Gateway API Inference Extension) that routes on KV-cache hit rate and queue depth, yielding 3–10x lower TTFT vs round-robin.
title: Load Balancer

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: SLA Dashboard: Key Metrics, Production SLA: Best Practices - What: An open-source Python-based HTTP load testing tool that simulates concurrent users sending requests to a service and measures latency distributions and throughput. - How it works: Users define User classes with on_start and task methods. locust spawns coroutines (greenlets) simulating concurrent users, all sending HTTP requests to the target endpoint. It records response times per request and computes P50/P95/P99 histograms in real time. For LLM load testing, tasks typically POST to /v1/chat/completions with varying prompt lengths and concurrency levels (the lab specifies 10 and 50 concurrent users on llama-server). - Why it matters: LLM serving performance is non-linear with concurrency; a 10-user test looks fine but 50 users may saturate KV cache causing evictions and P99 blowout. Load testing with locust before production is mandatory (the deck warningbox: 'Benchmark with locust/k6 BEFORE going to production. Do not guess latency — measure it.'). - Gotcha: locust reports client-side latency (includes network round-trip). For LLM inference, also collect server-side TTFT and TPOT from engine metrics (/metrics endpoint) to separate network from compute. Default locust CSV export truncates at P99 — configure the percentiles list explicitly for P99.9 if needed.

body: Attention / KV · appears on: PagedAttention: vLLM v0 → v1 Deep Dive - What: The virtual (logical) unit of KV cache in PagedAttention — a contiguous sequence of token positions as seen by the model (e.g., L0–L3), whose actual storage can be spread across non-contiguous physical GPU memory pages. - How it works: Each request has its own logical block space, indexed sequentially (L0, L1, L2 …). The page table maps each logical block index to a physical page (P0, P3, P1, P5 …) in arbitrary GPU VRAM locations. Attention computation addresses logical blocks; the hardware accesses physical pages via the mapping. - Why it matters: Separating logical from physical layout allows the serving engine to allocate, share, and evict KV pages without forcing contiguous GPU memory, which enables the zero-waste memory utilization that makes high throughput possible. - Gotcha: Logical block size (tokens per page) is 16 by default in vLLM v0; increasing it reduces page-table overhead but coarsens sharing granularity. V1 made this tunable.

The target model verifies proposed n-gram sequences in parallel. When no separate draft model is available, the target model's own generation history provides the drafts. - Why it matters: Enables speculative decoding speedup even when no draft model checkpoint exists or can be trained. Particularly useful for fine-tuned models where a draft head was not trained. - Gotcha: Self-drafting is less accurate than a purpose-trained draft model; acceptance rates and speedup are lower than EAGLE-3. The deck notes it is appropriate 'when no draft model is available' rather than as a first choice.

body: Concept · appears on: Pre-LLM Era: Serving Infrastructure 2017–2022 - What: TorchServe's deployment artifact format: a zip-like archive bundling model weights, a handler script, and dependency metadata into a single .mar file that TorchServe loads and serves. - How it works: Created with torch-model-archiver, a MAR file packages the serialized model (TorchScript or eager-mode state_dict), a handler.py defining pre/post processing, and a manifest. TorchServe reads the model store directory at startup or via management API and loads each .mar into a worker pool. - Why it matters: MAR archives established a deployable model unit concept that influenced later packaging systems (BentoML Bentos, Ollama Modelfiles, GGUF single-file bundles). For LLM teaching, MAR is the pre-LLM contrast point showing how bundling worked before weight sharding and multi-file checkpoints became the norm. - Gotcha: MAR archives bundle everything including the handler code, making them large and cumbersome for LLMs (tens of GB of weights). They also require the inference logic to live in the handler — no separation between inference engine and serving layer, unlike modern vLLM/SGLang where the engine is entirely separate from the API layer.

body: Decoding · appears on: DSpark: Semi-Autoregressive + Confidence Scheduling - What: DSpark's sequential module: a low-rank logit bias conditioned on the previous in-block token, added on top of the parallel drafter's output. - How it works: The bias is factorised as B = W₁W₂, where W₁ embeds the previous token into a rank-r space (default r=256) and W₂ projects to the draft vocabulary. Variants exist — vanilla (previous token only), gated (modulated by the backbone state) and recurrent (carrying state across block positions). - Why it matters: It restores the intra-block dependency that pure parallel drafting throws away, directly countering suffix decay, and it costs only +0.2–1.3% additional latency. - Gotcha: Setting `--markov-rank 0` disables it and reduces DSpark to DFlash behaviour — a useful ablation switch, and a reminder that DSpark is DFlash plus two small heads rather than a separate lineage.

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Model Compilation: torch.compile + CUDA Graphs + TensorRT - What: `torch.compile(mode='max-autotune')` — a compilation mode that runs an exhaustive search over kernel configurations (tile sizes, thread block shapes, vector widths) to find the fastest implementation for each operation on the target GPU. - How it works: TorchInductor generates multiple candidate Triton kernel implementations for each operation and benchmarks each against the target GPU. The best-performing config is cached in a `.triton` directory. Compilation takes significantly longer (minutes vs seconds) but runtime is maximally optimized for that exact hardware. - Why it matters: For latency-sensitive production serving where compilation happens once at startup (or offline), `max-autotune` pays the compilation cost upfront for faster inference throughput. Contrast with `reduce-overhead` which prioritizes faster compilation. - Gotcha: Autotune results are hardware-specific: autotuned kernels for H100 will not match performance on A100, requiring separate autotuning per hardware generation. The autotune cache must be managed across deployments.
title: max-autotune mode

body: CLI / flag · appears on: PagedAttention: vLLM v0 → v1 Deep Dive - What: A vLLM CLI flag that caps the maximum sequence length (prompt + output tokens) the engine will accept, overriding the model's config.json max_position_embeddings. - How it works: At startup, vLLM pre-allocates KV page slots for up to --max-model-len tokens per sequence. Setting this below the model's native context window reduces per-sequence VRAM footprint (more sequences fit simultaneously) at the cost of rejecting longer requests. e.g., --max-model-len 8192 on a 128k-context model allows ~8–16x more concurrent sequences. - Why it matters: Critical for deployments where actual workload context lengths are far shorter than the model's theoretical maximum — leaves more VRAM for KV pages and higher concurrency. - Gotcha: Requests exceeding --max-model-len are rejected with a 400 error, not truncated silently. If your client sends 10k tokens to an engine with --max-model-len 8192, the request fails. Set this based on p99 of your actual traffic, not the model's nominal context limit.
title: --max-model-len

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Production Tuning (Memory & Scheduling Knobs): '--max-running-requests / --max-num-seqs' - What: A vLLM CLI flag (equivalent to SGLang's '--max-running-requests') that caps the maximum number of sequences (requests) the scheduler is allowed to run concurrently in the decode phase. - How it works: The scheduler maintains a 'running' queue of requests currently generating tokens. At each scheduling step, it enforces that len(running) ≤ max_num_seqs. New requests are held in the waiting queue until a slot opens. This bounds peak KV-cache memory consumption at any instant (each running sequence occupies KV blocks proportional to its current length) and prevents the OOM cascade where too many concurrent decode streams collectively exhaust VRAM. - Why it matters: The primary tool for preventing decode OOM in burst traffic. Without this cap, a sudden spike of long-context requests can fill all KV pages simultaneously, forcing the scheduler into a preemption cascade that degrades latency for all requests. The deck recommends this alongside '--schedule-conservativeness' for production tuning. - Gotcha: Setting this too low wastes GPU utilisation (decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and benefits from high concurrency). Setting it too high risks OOM. The right value depends on model size, KV dtype, and max context length; it should be determined empirically via load testing.
title: --max-num-seqs

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Production Tuning: Memory, Scheduling & Observability - What: An SGLang CLI flag (--max-num-seqs in vLLM) that caps the number of requests simultaneously in the active decode batch, preventing decode-phase OOM from too many concurrent KV caches. - How it works: When the active batch reaches this limit, new requests queue in the waiting pool rather than being admitted. The scheduler only admits new requests when active requests complete and free their KV pages. Setting this too high allows the KV pool to be exhausted by too many simultaneous long sequences; too low causes artificial queuing and underutilizes GPU. - Why it matters: The primary safety valve against decode OOM at high concurrency; combined with --gpu-memory-utilization, these two flags are the most important production tuning knobs after model loading. - Gotcha: There is no perfect value — optimal setting depends on average output length and context length distribution of your traffic. A useful heuristic: set to (available KV pages) / (average tokens per active request) and tune empirically with load testing.
title: --max-running-requests

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Production Tuning: Memory, Scheduling & Observability - What: SGLang's equivalent of vLLM's --gpu-memory-utilization: sets the fraction of total GPU VRAM allocated to static model weights, with the remainder used for KV cache pages. - How it works: SGLang pre-loads model weights into the static fraction (e.g., 0.85 means 85% for weights), then allocates the remaining 15% as the KV page pool. The recommended practice is to leave 5–8 GB of raw VRAM headroom by setting this below the theoretical maximum — e.g., on an 80GB H100 with a 40GB model, set 0.85 to leave ~12GB for KV cache. - Why it matters: Primary single-knob for memory tuning in SGLang; setting it too high causes OOM during decode, too low wastes KV cache capacity and reduces throughput. - Gotcha: Semantics differ from vLLM's --gpu-memory-utilization: SGLang's flag covers only static weights, while vLLM's covers the entire unified pool (weights + activations + KV). Don't copy values directly between the two engines without accounting for this difference.
title: --mem-fraction-static

body: Concept · appears on: Hardware Landscape 2026: Beyond H100 - What: The empirical observation that LLM token generation (decode phase) is limited by how fast model weights can be streamed from GPU memory, not by the GPU's raw compute throughput, making HBM bandwidth the primary performance determinant. - How it works: During autoregressive decode, each generated token requires one full forward pass through the model, which means reading all model weights from HBM once per token. For a 70B FP16 model (140 GB), generating one token requires 140 GB of memory reads. If HBM bandwidth is 4.8 TB/s (H200), maximum decode rate is 4.8e12 / 140e9 ≈ 34 tokens/second before any other overhead. Compute throughput (TFLOPS) is not the bottleneck because the multiply-accumulate operations per byte of weights are relatively few in decode. - Why it matters: This principle explains why H200 (+43% decode vs H100) achieves its gain purely from more memory bandwidth, and why FP4/FP8 quantization (halving/quartering model size) directly increases decode throughput proportionally. TFLOPS comparisons across chips are misleading for serving without accompanying bandwidth figures. - Gotcha: The bottleneck shifts at very large batch sizes: when processing many requests simultaneously, compute can become the bottleneck (arithmetic intensity increases). The memory-bound regime is the dominant case for interactive single-user or low-concurrency serving.
title: Memory Bandwidth Bottleneck

body: Corrupting agent memory, embeddings or the RAG store so a hijacked goal persists across sessions.
title: Memory & context poisoning

title: Memory drift

body: Concept · appears on: Pre-LLM Era: Serving Infrastructure 2017–2022 - What: In pre-vLLM LLM serving, the phenomenon where KV-cache tensors for each request were allocated as contiguous GPU memory blocks sized for the maximum possible output length, leading to 60–80% VRAM waste from internal and external fragmentation. - How it works: Classical memory allocators require contiguous physical blocks. For LLM KV caches, the true output length is unknown at allocation time, so systems pre-allocated worst-case blocks. Many blocks were partially used (internal fragmentation), and completed requests left holes that could not be reused for differently-sized new requests (external fragmentation). The result was most VRAM being held by allocations that were largely empty. - Why it matters: Memory fragmentation was the single largest driver of wasted GPU capacity in pre-vLLM LLM serving. It limited batch sizes and thus throughput. PagedAttention (vLLM, 2023) solved this by managing KV cache like virtual memory — non-contiguous physical pages mapped to a logical address space — reducing fragmentation to below 4%. - Gotcha: Under PagedAttention, KV eviction strategies (H2O, SnapKV) reclaim almost no GPU memory in practice, because a physical block frees only when all sequences sharing it are complete. This is a subtle secondary fragmentation effect under paged allocation. Production systems therefore prefer KV quantization over eviction for memory pressure relief.
title: Memory Fragmentation

Inception's Mercury 2 announcement notably omits a tokens/sec number; any specific figure you see attributed to it traces to aggregators, not the company.

body: Attention / KV · appears on: Attention Architecture: MHA → MLA & Long-Context - What: The original attention mechanism from 'Attention Is All You Need' (Vaswani 2017): every attention head maintains its own full Q, K, and V projections, with no KV sharing between heads. - How it works: For H attention heads each of dimension d_h, MHA stores H independent K and V matrices per layer. At decode time, the KV cache stores H×d_h values per token per layer, making memory consumption proportional to the number of heads. - Why it matters: Baseline against which all KV-reduction variants are measured. MHA gives the strongest per-head expressiveness but has the largest KV memory footprint (labeled '1×' in the deck's progression diagram); it is used as the reference point for GQA/MQA/MLA comparisons. - Gotcha: Many papers report KV savings relative to MHA; these ratios only transfer directly if the model uses the same head size and layer count. The deck shows MHA as used in 'standard' pre-LLaMA-2 models.
title: MHA

body: Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections — projects Hyper-Connections' residual space onto a manifold to restore the identity-mapping property that plain HC breaks, curing its instability. Shipped in DeepSeek-V4.
title: mHC

title: Micro-Batch

body: Concept · appears on: Pipeline Parallelism: Ultra-Long Context - What: A sub-batch of requests that flows through one pipeline stage at a time in Pipeline Parallelism, allowing multiple micro-batches to be in-flight simultaneously across different stages. - How it works: The total batch is divided into M micro-batches. Stage 0 processes micro-batch 1 and passes its activations to stage 1, then immediately starts micro-batch 2—so stages 1 and 0 are simultaneously active on batches 1 and 2 respectively. With M micro-batches and P stages, effective GPU utilization = M/(M+P-1). - Why it matters: Without micro-batching, pipeline parallelism would have near-100% bubble time (only one stage active at a time). With M >> P, bubble fraction approaches zero. Dynamic chunking automatically sizes micro-batches to maximize utilization. - Gotcha: More micro-batches reduce bubble latency but increase memory pressure (multiple micro-batch KV caches in flight). The optimal M is a tradeoff between throughput (more M) and memory (less M). Model-specific smooth_factor tuning controls this.
title: Micro-batch

body: The bridging stage between pre-training and post-training: intermediate data and compute used to raise specific capabilities (math, code, reasoning, long context) while preserving general competence. Term is used inconsistently in the literature — define it before using it.
title: Mid-training

body: Concept · appears on: Distributed Inference: Parallelism Strategy Guide table — EP 'Best for: Mixtral / DeepSeek-V3 671B' - What: Mistral AI's sparse Mixture-of-Experts open-weight model family (Mixtral 8x7B, Mixtral 8x22B) that was among the first widely deployed open MoE models and established the production case for Expert Parallelism in serving. - How it works: Mixtral uses 8 expert FFN blocks per layer with top-2 routing (each token is processed by 2 of 8 experts). At 8x7B scale (~46.7B total parameters, ~12.9B active), it fits across 2–4 GPUs with TP but becomes efficient at batch with EP where each GPU holds 2–4 expert weight matrices. Its 3.13% expert activation density is in the range where EP outperforms TP according to the vLLM MoE Playbook (EP better above ~3% density). - Why it matters: Mixtral is the canonical open-source MoE reference: widely benchmarked, supported by all major serving engines, and the first model to make EP a practical necessity (rather than a theoretical option) for the open-source community. It appears alongside DeepSeek-V3 671B in the EP row of the parallelism table to contrast small-scale vs frontier-scale MoE. - Gotcha: Mixtral's 8-expert design is simpler than DeepSeek-V3's 256-expert (with 64 active) design; EPLB and Two-Batch Overlap are more critical for DeepSeek-class models. For Mixtral 8x7B, simple TP=4 or EP=8 on a single 8-GPU node is usually sufficient without the full disaggregated EP stack.
title: Mixtral

body: Attention / KV · appears on: Attention Architecture: MHA → MLA & Long-Context - What: DeepSeek's attention architecture (introduced in DeepSeek-V2) that compresses Q, K, and V projections through a low-dimensional latent vector before computing attention, yielding ~10× less KV memory than standard MHA. - How it works: Instead of storing full K/V matrices, the model stores only a small shared latent vector (~512-dim for DeepSeek-V3) per token per layer. At inference time K and V are reconstructed from this latent via up-projection matrices ('absorb trick'). The KV footprint drops from ~192–328 KB/token (GQA) to ~70 KB/token. - Why it matters: 10× KV reduction allows the model to serve much longer contexts or larger batches on the same VRAM. DeepSeek-V3/R1's deployment at scale relies critically on MLA. It is also retrofittable to existing GQA models (arXiv:2502.14837 shows ~92% KV reduction on adapted models). - Gotcha: MLA's absorb trick changes the memory-access pattern versus standard attention; it requires dedicated kernels (FlashMLA, CutlassMLA, FlashInfer) and is not drop-in compatible with standard FlashAttention paths. The stored latent cannot be reused across different projections without care.
title: MLA

body: Attention / KV · appears on: Attention Backend Selection: FA3 / FA4 / FlashInfer / FlashMLA - What: DeepSeek-V2/V3/R1's KV cache compression architecture that projects key-value tensors to a low-dimensional latent vector (~512 dim) before storing them, reducing KV memory by 2.7–4.7x vs GQA. - How it works: Instead of caching full K and V tensors per head, MLA stores a single compressed latent vector (~512 dim) per token. During attention, the latent is projected back to K and V via a learned up-projection (absorb trick for inference — the projection is folded into the QK matmul to avoid runtime expansion). This reduces KV cache from 192–328 KB/token (GQA) to ~70 KB/token — a 2.7–4.7x reduction. - Why it matters: Makes serving DeepSeek-V3-671B and R1-671B practical: KV cache for 10k tokens drops from ~3.2 GB (GQA) to ~0.7 GB. Required for any deployment of DeepSeek frontier models. FlashMLA, CutlassMLA, and TRTLLM-MLA are all specialized kernels for this architecture. - Gotcha: MLA was designed for DeepSeek-V2+ and requires the model to have been trained with this architecture. It cannot be retrofitted to standard MHA/GQA models without retraining (arXiv:2502.14837 showed retrofit is possible with ~92% KV reduction but requires fine-tuning).
title: MLA

body: Attention / KV · appears on: Data Parallelism: DP, DPA & Cache-Aware Router - What: DeepSeek's KV compression mechanism (V2+) that projects keys and values into a shared low-dimensional latent space (~512 dim) before caching, reducing KV cache size by 2.7–4.7x vs GQA. - How it works: Input is projected down to a latent vector (~512 dim); at inference, an 'absorb' trick folds the up-projection into the weight matrices to avoid materializing full KV. Per token: ~70 KB MLA vs 192–328 KB GQA. Combined with DPA, the small per-token footprint allows large batch sizes and efficient multi-GPU serving. - Why it matters: MLA enables DPA to be practically meaningful: with tiny per-token KV, you can fit large batches in each DP replica's attention cache without duplicating expensive expert weights. This combination is the key architectural insight behind DeepSeek's serving efficiency. - Gotcha: The 'absorb trick' is inference-only: it folds the projection matrices into Q/K/V weight matrices at load time to avoid materializing the latent during the forward pass. This is why FlashMLA is needed—standard attention kernels can't exploit MLA's structure.
title: MLA

body: Metric · appears on: Hardware Landscape 2026: Beyond H100 - What: The industry-standard benchmark suite for AI hardware, maintained by MLCommons, used to compare accelerators on standardized LLM inference workloads including offline throughput and online latency (TTFT, TPOT). - How it works: MLPerf Inference submitters run standardized models (Llama-3.1-70B, Llama-3.1-405B, Mixtral-8x7B, SDXL, etc.) under fixed SLO constraints (e.g., 99th-percentile TTFT ≤ 2s) and report tokens/second. MLPerf v6.0 showed AMD MI355X at B200 parity. MLPerf Power v5.1 added energy efficiency (tokens/joule) as an official metric. - Why it matters: MLPerf results are the most authoritative public comparisons of AI hardware performance; the v6.0 AMD MI355X = B200 finding is the basis for treating AMD as a credible NVIDIA alternative in 2026. - Gotcha: MLPerf measures specific models under specific SLOs; real-world workload performance may differ (e.g., longer context, MoE vs dense, batch size distributions). Vendors often optimize specifically for MLPerf scenarios, and submissions are self-reported with varying levels of optimization effort.
title: MLPerf

body: Metric · appears on: Tokens-per-Joule frame: 'Tokens-per-joule giờ là first-class metric (MLPerf Power v5.1)' - What: The September 2025 edition of the MLCommons MLPerf inference benchmark that added tokens-per-joule as a first-class reported metric alongside throughput and latency, making energy efficiency a standardised hardware ranking criterion for AI accelerators. - How it works: MLPerf Power measures system-level power draw (using calibrated power meters at the PDU or server input) during the MLPerf inference benchmark workloads (LLM text generation, computer vision, etc.). Tokens-per-joule = total output tokens generated / total joules consumed during the test window. This metric is reported alongside samples/second and TTFT/TPOT percentiles, enabling direct cross-platform energy efficiency comparison. TokenPowerBench (arXiv:2512.03024) extends this to more LLM-specific scenarios. - Why it matters: By making tokens-per-joule a formally tracked MLPerf metric (v5.1, Sep 2025), the community established that hardware vendors must optimise for energy efficiency, not just throughput. This drives architectural decisions toward FP4/FP8 quantisation, MoE sparsity, and power-scaled clock management (GreenLLM DVFS) — all of which appear in the deck's energy levers section. - Gotcha: MLPerf Power measures system-level efficiency, not just GPU efficiency — cooling, networking, and memory contribute to total power. A GPU with higher peak TFLOPS but worse memory bandwidth may score worse on tokens-per-joule than a lower-TFLOPS chip with more efficient memory subsystem. This is why HBM bandwidth (not TFLOPS) is cited as the LLM-serving bottleneck.

title: MLPerf Power v5.1

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Edge Deployment Flow - What: Apple's open-source machine learning framework optimized for Apple Silicon (M-series chips), providing NumPy-like operations with unified CPU/GPU memory and Apple Neural Engine (ANE) access, achieving up to 525 tokens/second on M4 Max for LLM inference. - How it works: MLX uses Apple's Metal GPU backend and unified memory architecture (no copy between CPU and GPU memory). vllm-mlx (arXiv:2601.19139) adds continuous batching and paged KV cache to MLX, enabling production-grade serving on Apple Silicon. As of Ollama v0.30.10 (Jun 2026), MLX preview is available for Apple Silicon Macs with >32 GB unified memory. - Why it matters: MLX enables near-native LLM inference performance on Apple Silicon without requiring discrete GPU infrastructure, making it viable for local development and on-device serving where llama.cpp Metal provides a fallback. - Gotcha: MLX preview in Ollama (v0.30.10) supports only limited models (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B) and requires >32 GB unified memory; llama.cpp Metal remains the fallback. The vllm-mlx project is experimental and not the same as production vLLM.
title: MLX

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Multimodal (VLM) Serving (EPD Disaggregation): 'vLLM v0.11+: --mm-encoder-tp-mode data' - What: A vLLM CLI flag (introduced v0.11.1, Dec 2025) that controls how the multimodal encoder (ViT) is parallelised across GPUs in a tensor-parallel setup — 'data' mode runs independent encoder replicas rather than sharding the encoder's weights. - How it works: With '--mm-encoder-tp-mode data', each GPU in the TP group runs a full, independent copy of the ViT encoder on its portion of the image batch (data parallelism for the encoder). This contrasts with the default mode where the encoder's attention weights would be sharded across GPUs like the LLM (tensor parallelism for the encoder). Since ViT attention does not scale well with TP (synchronisation overhead dominates for small sequence lengths), data-parallel encoder mode yields +44.9% throughput on AMD MI300X compared to TP-encoded baseline. - Why it matters: This flag is the vLLM mechanism for achieving EPD-like encoder independence without requiring a full separate encoder worker pool. For smaller deployments that cannot afford dedicated encode workers, '--mm-encoder-tp-mode data' provides most of the throughput benefit within a single multi-GPU node. - Gotcha: 'data' mode requires sufficient VRAM on each GPU to hold a full copy of the ViT encoder weights — for large vision encoders (InternViT-6B, InternVL2-Llama3-76B), this adds significant VRAM overhead per GPU. The throughput figure (+44.9%) was measured on MI300X; results on H100/H200 will differ.
title: --mm-encoder-tp-mode

body: Kernel two-sample test (`E[k(x,x')]+E[k(y,y')]−2E[k(x,y)]`); for high-dim embeddings where per-component tests fail (threshold ~0.015).

body: Metric · appears on: Quantization: Precision vs Performance; Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ - What: A widely used multiple-choice benchmark covering 57 academic subjects (math, history, law, medicine, etc.) used as a proxy for general model quality and quantization accuracy assessment. - How it works: The model is asked to select the correct answer from 4 choices for ~14,000 questions. Score is reported as accuracy (0–100%). The deck uses MMLU drop as the quality metric in the quantization comparison table: '~1pt MMLU' means approximately 1 percentage-point drop. - Why it matters: MMLU is a universally understood shorthand for 'how much quality did I lose' in quantization comparisons. The ~1 MMLU-point threshold is the informal industry benchmark for 'acceptable' quantization loss at 4-bit for 8B+ models. - Gotcha: MMLU is a static benchmark and is increasingly saturated (frontier models score 85–92%). More importantly, MMLU accuracy may not reflect actual user-facing quality loss, particularly for generation tasks (coding, reasoning, creative writing).
title: MMLU

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Embedding & Reranker Serving: The Retrieval Half - What: A modernized BERT-family encoder model (Dec 2024) with an 8192-token context window and 2–4x throughput improvement over BERT-large, supported by HuggingFace TEI. - How it works: ModernBERT replaces BERT's learned positional embeddings with RoPE (Rotary Position Embeddings), enabling 8192-token context (vs BERT's 512); uses FlashAttention-2 for memory-efficient self-attention; and applies architectural improvements from the LLM era (pre-norm, SwiGLU FFN) to the encoder paradigm. TEI v1.9.3+ serves ModernBERT natively. - Why it matters: ModernBERT's 8192-token context makes it suitable for long-document embedding without chunking, and its throughput improvement over BERT-large reduces serving costs. It represents the current state of encoder-only model efficiency for retrieval tasks. - Gotcha: ModernBERT's improvements over BERT are measured relative to BERT-large (340M params), not against state-of-the-art decoder-derived embedding models like Qwen3-Embedding-8B which uses a much larger model with significantly different quality/cost tradeoffs.
title: ModernBERT

body: Concept · appears on: Expert Parallelism: MoE Scaling - What: A model architecture where each token is processed by only a sparse subset (top-K of N) of feed-forward 'expert' sub-networks per layer, dramatically increasing parameter count while keeping per-token FLOPs constant. - How it works: A learned router assigns each input token to K experts (typically K=2–8 out of 64–256 total). Each expert is a standard FFN; only chosen experts activate per token. This yields 'conditional compute': a 671B parameter model like DeepSeek-V3 activates only ~37B parameters per token. - Why it matters: Enables frontier-scale models (671B–1T parameters) with manageable per-token compute. DeepSeek-V3/R1 671B, Kimi K2 1T, Llama-4, and Qwen3-235B are all MoE. Serving requires Expert Parallelism for efficiency. - Gotcha: Skip EP for <1% expert activation density (e.g., Llama-4-Maverick 0.78%); enable for >3% (DeepSeek-R1 3.13%). MoE models have higher memory bandwidth demand and communication overhead than equally-FLOPs dense models.
title: MoE

body: Only a subset of experts active per token (e.g. 2-of-8). FT subset = update only some experts (DeepSeek-MoE, Mixtral).
title: MoE

body: Activating only a subset of parameters per token (DeepSeek 37B of 671B), cutting compute cost per token.
title: MoE

body: kiến trúc chỉ kích hoạt một phần tham số (“active params”) mỗi lần suy luận; quyết định VRAM thật sự cần để tự host.
title: MoE

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Expert Parallelism (Architecture): 'A2A backends: --moe-a2a-backend deepep' - What: An SGLang CLI flag that selects the All-to-All communication library used to dispatch tokens to and combine results from MoE expert shards across GPUs during expert-parallel forward passes. - How it works: In expert parallelism, each GPU holds a subset of expert weight matrices. The router's top-K selection sends each token to 1–2 expert GPUs; after local GEMM computation, outputs must be gathered back. This dispatch+combine pattern is an All-to-All operation. The '--moe-a2a-backend' flag selects the transport: 'deepep' uses DeepEP's JIT-compiled NVLink/IB kernels (726/740 GB/s, FP8 dispatch halves traffic); 'mooncake' uses the Mooncake Transfer Engine; 'nixl' uses NVIDIA's NIXL transport (v1.3.0, Jun 2026). Most backends require ep_size = tp_size. - Why it matters: All-to-All is the performance bottleneck in expert parallel serving at high EP counts. The choice of backend determines whether the A2A fits within a single-step compute budget or stalls the pipeline. DeepEP is the recommended choice for NVLink-connected clusters; NIXL for heterogeneous transports. - Gotcha: The constraint that 'ep_size = tp_size' is enforced by most backends and means tensor parallelism and expert parallelism degrees must match, which limits configuration flexibility. Two-Batch Overlap (TBO/DBO, '--enable-two-batch-overlap') is the complementary optimisation that hides A2A latency behind GEMM computation.
title: --moe-a2a-backend

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Expert Parallelism (Architecture): 'MoE runner: --moe-runner-backend deep_gemm hoặc cutlass' - What: An SGLang CLI flag that selects the GEMM kernel used to compute expert feed-forward computations in MoE layers, choosing between DeepSeek's open-sourced DeepGEMM kernels or NVIDIA's CUTLASS templates. - How it works: After the All-to-All dispatch routes tokens to their assigned expert GPUs, each GPU runs a batched GEMM (General Matrix Multiply) across its expert weight matrices and the dispatched token activations. 'deep_gemm' uses DeepGEMM (DeepSeek open-source, Feb 2025), which implements FP8 grouped GEMM optimised for the expert activation patterns of DeepSeek-V3/R1. 'cutlass' uses NVIDIA's CUTLASS library templates, which are more general but may be slower for specific MoE configurations. - Why it matters: MoE GEMM is not a simple dense matrix multiply — the batch sizes per expert are highly variable (load imbalance) and the token-expert mapping is dynamic. DeepGEMM's specialised kernels handle these irregular patterns more efficiently than generic CUTLASS templates for DeepSeek-class models. - Gotcha: DeepGEMM requires Hopper or later (H100/H800/B200) due to use of WGMMA instructions. On older architectures, only the CUTLASS backend is available. EPLB ('--enable-eplb') is the complementary load-balancing mechanism that reduces expert activation imbalance, improving both backends' efficiency.
title: --moe-runner-backend

body: Route-aware LoRA: profile routing counts on a small calibration set, adapt only the top ~25% routed experts per layer. Within ±1pp of full LoRA at 70–73% fewer trainable parameters; random expert selection at matched budget is ~2.5pp worse.
title: MoE-Sieve

body: Concept · appears on: Tokens-per-Joule & The Power Wall - What: The property of Mixture-of-Experts models that activates only a subset (e.g., 2 of 64) of expert feed-forward networks per token, reducing active compute and energy proportionally to the activation sparsity ratio. - How it works: A learned router (gating function) selects K experts out of N total for each token; only the selected experts are computed. This means a 671B-parameter model like DeepSeek-R1 activates only ~37B parameters per token (approximately 5.5% activation ratio). Energy consumption scales with active parameters, not total parameters. - Why it matters: MoE models provide frontier-level quality at the energy cost of a much smaller dense model. GPT-OSS-20B (MoE, 3.6B active) consumes 25.8% less energy per 1K tokens than a comparable dense 32B model while matching its quality on most benchmarks. - Gotcha: MoE sparsity saves compute but not necessarily memory bandwidth — all expert weights must be loaded to GPU DRAM even if only 2 are active. For small-batch decode, the memory-bandwidth cost of loading all expert weights dominates over the compute savings.
title: MoE Sparsity

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Disaggregated Prefill/Decode Serving - What: The traditional architecture where each GPU (or TP-group) handles both prefill and decode for the same requests simultaneously, as in vLLM v0 and all pre-2024 engines. - How it works: In a monolithic setup (labeled 'GPU A P+D' and 'GPU B P+D' in the deck's TikZ diagram), each GPU runs prefill on new requests and decode on active requests in the same scheduling batch. When a long prefill arrives, it occupies the GPU for its full compute duration, preventing decode steps for other active requests. Continuous batching mitigates but does not eliminate this contention. - Why it matters: Historical baseline: all throughput and latency comparisons for disaggregated serving use monolithic vLLM v0 as the reference point. Understanding monolithic contention is prerequisite to understanding why disaggregation works. - Gotcha: Monolithic serving still makes sense for workloads with short, uniform prompts and low concurrency — the KV transfer overhead of disaggregation can exceed the prefill-contention cost for short prompts. Don't assume disaggregation is always better.
title: Monolithic serving

body: Category-defining data-observability SaaS (Barr Moses, 2019); coined the 5 pillars; launched Agent Observability (9/2025).
title: Monte Carlo

body: Caching · appears on: Disaggregated Prefill/Decode (Systems 2026): 'Mooncake (Kimi, FAST'25): 100B+ tok/day, global KV pool, RDMA zero-copy' - What: A KV-cache-centric disaggregated serving system developed by Moonshot AI (Kimi) that won the FAST 2025 Best Paper award, handling 100+ billion tokens per day across thousands of nodes with a global distributed KV pool and RDMA zero-copy transfer. - How it works: Mooncake decouples KV cache management from the GPU compute engines entirely: a centralised KV Block Manager tracks which physical blocks across the cluster contain which token-hash blocks. Prefill GPUs fill blocks and register them with the manager; decode GPUs request blocks by hash and receive them via RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access) zero-copy — bypassing the CPU and OS network stack. This enables cross-instance prefix sharing at scale (any decode node can reuse any prefill node's cached KV). The system also serves as an A2A backend for EP dispatch ('-moe-a2a-backend mooncake'). - Why it matters: At Kimi's scale (100B+ tokens/day), the marginal cost of KV transfer across the global pool is dominated by network bandwidth, not compute. Mooncake's RDMA path achieves near-GPU-memory-bandwidth KV transfer rates, making global prefix reuse economical. The FAST Best Paper recognition signals this is now the architectural blueprint for hyperscale KV disaggregation. - Gotcha: Mooncake's 100B+ tok/day figure and the Kimi K2 224k/288k tok/s throughput numbers are SGLang+OME (optimised multi-engine) benchmarks, not standalone Mooncake benchmarks. The system requires RDMA-capable network fabric (InfiniBand or RoCE); TCP fallback works but loses the zero-copy advantage.
title: Mooncake

body: Caching · appears on: Prefix Caching: RadixAttention, APC, HiCache & Pricing; Disaggregated Prefill/Decode Serving - What: Kimi's production KV cache disaggregation system (FAST'25 Best Paper), operating at 100B+ tokens/day across thousands of nodes using RDMA zero-copy for cross-instance KV transfer. - How it works: Mooncake maintains a global KV pool distributed across a cluster; prefill workers write KV tensors to this pool via RDMA (zero-copy, no CPU involvement), and decode workers read from it. This enables P/D disaggregation where prefill and decode GPUs are physically separate nodes. Mooncake Transfer Engine handles bandwidth scheduling. LMDeploy integrates Mooncake via DLSlime. - Why it matters: Enables serving 100B+ tokens/day at Kimi-scale without a monolithic KV cache per GPU; demonstrates that RDMA-based KV transfer is production-viable. FAST'25 Best Paper signals research-community validation. - Gotcha: Mooncake's RDMA zero-copy requires InfiniBand or RoCE network fabric — it does not help over standard Ethernet without RDMA support. KV transfer overhead is still ~10 GB/s per transfer; benefit is only clear for prefill-heavy traffic (long contexts, RAG).
title: Mooncake KVCache

This is what makes sub-2-minute rollback real — and it only works if prompts are deployable artifacts separate from the image.

body: Attention / KV · appears on: Attention Architecture: MHA → MLA & Long-Context - What: Extreme KV compression where all query heads share a single K head and a single V head, achieving the maximum KV reduction (8× vs MHA in the deck's diagram) at the cost of some model quality. - How it works: All H query heads project independently, but K and V are each a single shared vector per token per layer. KV cache at decode time is 1/H the size of MHA. Used in early models like those from the GPT-3 era. - Why it matters: Demonstrates the endpoint of the GQA spectrum. Important pedagogically as the precursor to MLA (which achieves 10× savings via a different latent compression approach rather than simply collapsing heads). - Gotcha: MQA quality degradation is significant at larger model sizes and is why GQA (intermediate sharing) became preferred. MLA surpasses both in KV reduction without MQA's quality penalty.
title: MQA

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ (research companion) - What: A 2026 extension of GPTQ (ICLR 2026) that applies a Hadamard rotation to model weight matrices before quantization, enabling accurate PTQ to FP4 (NVFP4/MXFP4) with up to 2.2× throughput on B200. - How it works: A random Hadamard matrix is applied to the weight matrix (and correspondingly to the input activations), spreading quantization error more uniformly across channels. The rotated matrix is then quantized to FP4 using the standard GPTQ Hessian update. MR-GPTQ achieves 2.2× throughput on B200 and 4× on RTX 5090 vs FP16 baseline. - Why it matters: MR-GPTQ is the leading PTQ method for achieving production-quality FP4 quantization without QAT, bridging the gap between NVFP4 hardware capability and model accuracy requirements. - Gotcha: MR-GPTQ is part of the 'rotation family' lineage: QuaRot (ICLR 2024) → SpinQuant (learned rotations, ICLR 2025) → MR-GPTQ (Hadamard → FP4, ICLR 2026). Earlier rotation papers do not achieve FP4; do not conflate QuaRot with MR-GPTQ's FP4 capability.
title: MR-GPTQ

body: Concept · appears on: Embedding & Reranker Serving: The Retrieval Half - What: An embedding training technique that produces representations where any prefix of the full embedding vector is itself a useful embedding at a lower dimensionality. - How it works: During training, the model is supervised at multiple embedding dimension checkpoints simultaneously (e.g., 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024 dims). This induces a nested structure where the first 64 dimensions already encode the most important information, subsequent dimensions refine it. - Why it matters: MRL allows a single deployed model to serve different quality/cost tradeoffs: use 64-dim embeddings for fast coarse retrieval and 1024-dim for precise reranking, without deploying separate models. Reduces memory and index size. - Gotcha: The efficiency gain comes from flexible truncation at serving time, not from a smaller model. The model itself must be trained with MRL objective; post-hoc truncation of a standard embedding model does not yield equivalent quality at lower dimensions.
title: MRL

body: Metric · appears on: Embedding & Reranker Serving (Stack 2026): 'Qwen3-Embedding-8B (MTEB rank 1)' - What: A standardised multilingual benchmark for evaluating text embedding models across tasks including classification, clustering, pair classification, reranking, retrieval, semantic textual similarity, and summarisation — used as the primary ranking signal for selecting embedding models in production RAG pipelines. - How it works: MTEB measures embedding model quality across 56 datasets in 112 languages by averaging normalised task scores. Models are ranked on the MTEB Leaderboard (HuggingFace). Qwen3-Embedding-8B achieved rank 1 on the MTEB Multilingual leaderboard (70.58 average score, 32K context). Performance on MTEB retrieval subtasks (nDCG@10, Hit Rate@k, MRR@k) is most relevant for RAG serving decisions. - Why it matters: MTEB rank is the standard quality signal for selecting embedding models for production deployment. Higher MTEB scores correlate with better retrieval Hit Rate and MRR in real RAG pipelines, directly impacting agent answer quality. The serving implication is that higher-quality embeddings (8B-class) require more compute — the break-even analysis (50–100M tokens/month vs API) depends on model size. - Gotcha: MTEB is dominated by English and high-resource language benchmarks; multilingual MTEB scores for Vietnamese and other Southeast Asian languages reflect smaller evaluation sets and may not reflect production performance. BGE-M3's multi-vector (dense+sparse+ColBERT) score on MTEB is not directly comparable to single-vector models because it uses a different retrieval paradigm.
title: MTEB

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Production SLA: Best Practices - What: Running inference replicas in two or more independent data-center failure domains (Availability Zones) within a cloud region so that a single AZ outage does not take the service offline. - How it works: A load balancer distributes requests across replicas in AZ-A and AZ-B. Each AZ has its own power, networking, and cooling. If AZ-A fails, the load balancer routes all traffic to AZ-B (or a surviving subset). Health checks on each replica detect failures within seconds. GPU instances in each AZ are independently provisioned from separate hardware pools. - Why it matters: Required to achieve >= 99.9% uptime SLO. Single-AZ deployments have availability bounded by that AZ's reliability (typically 99.5–99.9%); multi-AZ pushes the ceiling above 99.99% with active-active or above 99.9% with active-passive. - Gotcha: Cross-AZ data transfer incurs latency and cost. KV cache state (prefix cache) is not shared across AZs — a request routed to AZ-B after AZ-A failure suffers a full cache miss. Prefix-aware routing (sgl-router, vLLM production-stack router) must be AZ-aware to maximize cache hit rates.
title: Multi-AZ Deployment

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Multi-LoRA Serving - What: A serving pattern where a single base model instance on one GPU simultaneously hosts many fine-tuned LoRA adapters, each applied to requests on-the-fly without maintaining separate model copies. - How it works: The base model weights stay resident in GPU memory; adapter delta weights (low-rank A and B matrices) are stored in a paged pool and dynamically loaded per-request using fused batched-adapter GEMM kernels (Punica/SGMV). Requests in the same batch can each use a different adapter with negligible extra compute thanks to SGMV fusion. - Why it matters: Eliminates the N×VRAM cost of running N independent single-adapter model servers; the deck cites ~12x throughput vs N separate deployments. Critical for SaaS deployments offering domain-specialized endpoints (SQL, medical, code, finance) under one GPU budget. - Gotcha: Adapter application adds ~+2 ms/token overhead per adapter switch. vLLM V1 LoRA is fully merged and optimized (not 'in progress'); TensorRT-LLM ~3% overhead is vs the base model with no adapters, not vs a single-adapter baseline—do not compare those numbers directly.
title: Multi-LoRA Serving

body: Caching · appears on: Multimodal (VLM) Serving: Encode–Prefill–Decode - What: An extension of KV prefix caching that hashes on image pixel data or image embeddings (using SHA-256) to reuse computed KV entries when the same image appears in multiple requests. - How it works: vLLM V1 hashes raw image content to cache KV blocks for repeated images; LMCache demonstrated reduction from 18s to 1s TTFT on a cache hit for repeated images. SGLang uses a SHA-256-pixel global embedding cache (Feb 2026). The MPIC approach (arXiv:2502.01960) extends this to position-independent caching. - Why it matters: Many VLM workloads reuse the same images (product catalog images, document headers, UI screenshots); caching their KV drastically reduces TTFT without rerunning the expensive ViT encoder and prefill. - Gotcha: Image hash cache keys must be based on raw pixels or pixel embeddings, not file paths or URLs, to correctly identify semantically identical images. Cache key collision risk is higher for near-duplicate images.
title: Multimodal Prefix Caching

body: An optimizer that treats a weight matrix's momentum as a matrix and applies approximate zeroth-power orthogonalization (equalizing singular values) before the update, so rare-but-important directions are not drowned out.

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ (research companion) - What: An Open Compute Project (OCP) standardized 4-bit floating-point format using block-level microscaling, supported natively by AMD MI355X and Intel Gaudi future generations in addition to NVIDIA Blackwell. - How it works: Groups of 32 elements share a single 8-bit exponent scale (E8M0); each element is E2M1. This is the OCP MX (Microscaling) specification. AMD MI355X achieves ~10 PFLOPS with MXFP4/MXFP6 support. LMDeploy's TurboMind engine supports MXFP4 on H800+. - Why it matters: MXFP4 matters because it is vendor-neutral unlike NVFP4, providing a path to 4-bit inference without NVIDIA hardware lock-in. MR-GPTQ (ICLR 2026) uses Hadamard rotation to achieve 2.2× throughput on B200 and 4× on RTX 5090 with MXFP4. - Gotcha: MXFP4 and NVFP4 use similar block-scaling ideas but differ in block size and scale format. They are not interchangeable weight formats — a model quantized for one requires re-quantization for the other.
title: MXFP4

body: 4-bit float format with 32-element blocks and single-level scaling.

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Distributed Inference: Parallelism Strategy Guide - What: NVIDIA's library implementing collective communication primitives (All-Reduce, All-to-All, Broadcast, etc.) for multi-GPU and multi-node distributed deep learning workloads. - How it works: Automatically selects the optimal communication path (NVLink > NVSwitch > PCIe > InfiniBand) and algorithm (ring, tree, recursive halving). In vLLM Ray cluster deployments, `NCCL_IB_HCA=mlx5` configures NCCL to use InfiniBand HCA for cross-node communication. NCCL executes TP All-Reduce and EP A2A operations. - Why it matters: The default communication backend for both vLLM and SGLang collective operations. Its hardware-aware routing and algorithm selection are critical for performance—misconfigured NCCL (wrong IB HCA, wrong topology) can cut throughput by 2–5x. - Gotcha: NCCL's A2A is a general collective and is less optimized for MoE expert dispatch patterns than DeepEP's specialized JIT kernels. For large-scale MoE (EP32+), DeepEP outperforms NCCL A2A. The `NCCL_IB_HCA` env var must be set correctly for InfiniBand—omitting it causes NCCL to fall back to slower Ethernet or PCIe.
title: NCCL

body: Hardware · appears on: Distributed Inference (Multi-node vLLM): 'NCCL_IB_HCA=mlx5 cho InfiniBand NIC' - What: An NCCL environment variable that specifies which InfiniBand Host Channel Adapter (network card) NCCL should use for collective communications (all-reduce, all-gather, broadcast) in multi-node GPU clusters. - How it works: In multi-node GPU clusters, multiple InfiniBand NICs may be present (e.g., mlx5_0, mlx5_1 on ConnectX-6/7 cards). NCCL auto-detects them but may choose a suboptimal device or fail to use GPU-Direct RDMA if it selects a non-GPUDirect-capable port. Setting 'NCCL_IB_HCA=mlx5' pins NCCL to the Mellanox (now NVIDIA) mlx5-family HCA, which supports GPUDirect RDMA and enables zero-copy GPU-to-GPU transfers across InfiniBand fabric. In vLLM Ray cluster deployments, this environment variable is set on all worker nodes. - Why it matters: Without the correct HCA selection, NCCL may fall back to CPU-mediated transfers that saturate host memory bandwidth rather than InfiniBand bandwidth, reducing inter-node all-reduce throughput by 2–5x. For tensor parallelism across nodes (which requires synchronous all-reduce every layer), this directly degrades per-token latency. - Gotcha: The 'mlx5' prefix covers multiple ConnectX generations (ConnectX-4 through ConnectX-8); if multiple ports are available, more specific selection (e.g., 'mlx5_0:1' for port 1 of device 0) may be needed. On RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet) setups, the variable syntax differs. This setting does not apply to NVLink-only clusters (NVL72) where intra-domain communication does not use InfiniBand.
title: NCCL_IB_HCA

body: Order-aware; handles both binary and graded relevance. Uses a log2 positional discount (rank 1 undiscounted = 1.0, rank 2 ÷ ~1.585, rank 3 ÷ 2). Range [0,1].

body: Security · appears on: Semantic Caching: The Stack Is 3 Caches Deep - What: A published attack (NDSS 2026) demonstrating ~90.6% success rate in poisoning semantic caches of major cloud LLM deployments (AWS, Azure, Alibaba, GPTCache) by crafting prompts that cause malicious responses to be cached and returned to legitimate users. - How it works: The attacker submits crafted queries to the target service that: (a) are semantically similar to common legitimate queries (so they create cache entries that future legitimate users will hit), and (b) elicit harmful, incorrect, or misleading responses from the LLM. Once cached, legitimate users asking the genuine question receive the poisoned response without triggering a new LLM call. - Why it matters: Demonstrates that production semantic caching systems from major cloud providers were vulnerable to systematic cache poisoning, with the attack succeeding ~90% of the time. This forced post-hoc security patches and highlighted the need for cache isolation and response validation. - Gotcha: This attack works because semantic caches use loose similarity matching (not exact match) and do not validate response quality before caching. Mitigations include per-tenant cache namespacing (salting), response validation before cache write, and limiting cache write privileges to authenticated internal services rather than all API users.

body: Hardware · appears on: Edge Deployment Flow - What: ARM's SIMD instruction set (128-bit vector operations) present on all ARM64/AArch64 processors including Apple Silicon M-series, Qualcomm Snapdragon, and Android ARM chips, used by llama.cpp for efficient matrix multiply on non-x86 hardware. - How it works: llama.cpp compiles NEON-optimized kernels when targeting ARM64 (enabled automatically on Apple Silicon, Raspberry Pi 4/5, Android). NEON supports 128-bit vectors (4x FP32, 8x INT16, 16x INT8), and llama.cpp's ARM kernels use dot-product instructions (SDOT/UDOT) for INT8 GEMM on Apple M1+ and Snapdragon 8cx. - Why it matters: NEON is the ARM equivalent of x86 AVX2; without it, LLM inference on ARM-based edge devices (MacBooks, Android phones, Raspberry Pi) would be prohibitively slow. It enables llama.cpp to achieve competitive tokens/second on Apple Silicon laptops. - Gotcha: NEON is mandatory on all ARMv8-A (64-bit) chips; there is no opt-in build flag for llama.cpp on ARM — it is always enabled. Apple Silicon's ANE (Neural Engine) is a separate, more specialized unit from the NEON SIMD; mlx and ANEMLL target ANE while llama.cpp Metal targets the GPU and llama.cpp CPU targets NEON.
title: NEON

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ - What: A 4-bit quantization format from the bitsandbytes library, designed to be information-theoretically optimal for normally-distributed neural network weights by mapping quantile boundaries of the normal distribution to equally-spaced integer codes. - How it works: Unlike uniform INT4, NF4 places quantization levels at the quantile boundaries of a standard normal distribution (matching the empirical distribution of pretrained weights). The bitsandbytes library implements this on CUDA. BPW is 4.0, yielding ~4.0 GB for an 8B model. - Why it matters: NF4 is the quantization format used by QLoRA for fine-tuning: the base model is loaded in NF4 while the LoRA adapter trains in BF16, enabling fine-tuning of 70B+ models on a single consumer GPU. - Gotcha: NF4 is primarily a fine-tuning quantization (via bitsandbytes) and is NOT hardware-accelerated as efficiently as AWQ/GPTQ for pure inference. For serving, AWQ or GPTQ are preferred at 4-bit; NF4 is specifically for the 'fine-tune on 1 GPU' use case.
title: NF4

body: A 4-bit datatype information-theoretically optimal for normally-distributed weights — not ordinary int4.

body: Decoding · appears on: Chọn Thuật Toán Spec Decoding (Aug 2026) - What: Model-free speculative decoding that drafts by matching recent n-grams from the prompt and generation history — `--speculative-algorithm NGRAM` in SGLang. - How it works: Candidate continuations are looked up from text already in the context rather than predicted by a network, then verified normally by the target model. - Why it matters: It requires no training, no checkpoint and no extra VRAM, which makes it the only zero-setup option. It works well where output repeats input: code editing, JSON/structured emission, retrieval-heavy answers. - Gotcha: Acceptance collapses on open-ended prose where nothing is repeated. Treat it as a workload-specific accelerator, not a general default.
title: NGRAM / n-gram drafting

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Serving Stack 2026: 8 Engines That Matter - What: NVIDIA's pre-packaged, containerized model-serving runtime that bundles TensorRT-LLM (or vLLM) with an OpenAI-compatible API, health checks, and model registry integration. - How it works: NIM containers ship with a pre-compiled TRT-LLM engine for specific model×GPU combinations, eliminating the 28-minute compile step. They expose /v1/chat/completions, /v1/completions, and /health endpoints. NIM is part of the NVIDIA AI Enterprise stack and integrates with NVIDIA Dynamo for P/D-disaggregated deployments. - Why it matters: Production shortcut for NVIDIA GPU fleets: no custom TRT-LLM compilation, certified model×GPU pairings, and enterprise support; widely used in cloud (AWS Marketplace, Azure) deployments. - Gotcha: NIMs are locked to specific model×GPU SKU combinations — a NIM for Llama-4-70B on H100 is a different artifact from one on A100; model updates require new NIM builds, adding operational lag vs vLLM's rolling updates.
title: NIM

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Disaggregated Prefill/Decode Serving - What: NVIDIA's KV cache transport library for disaggregated serving (v1.0.0 Mar 13, 2026; v1.3.0 Jun 15, 2026), supporting IB/RoCE/TCP/NVMe-oF/S3 transport with a unified zero-copy API. - How it works: NIXL provides a unified asynchronous API for KV tensor movement between GPUs across transport backends. Applications call nixl_send(kv_tensor, target_node) and NIXL handles registration, RDMA pinning, and bandwidth scheduling automatically. Used by NVIDIA Dynamo, llm-d, and vLLM's KV Connector API. AWS EFA support was added Mar 2026. - Why it matters: Enables engine-agnostic KV transfer in multi-engine disaggregated clusters (vLLM prefill → TRT-LLM decode, or mixed); v1.0.0 GA makes production deployment practical without custom transport code. - Gotcha: NIXL v1.0.0 shipped Mar 13, 2026 (not 'pending' as older materials stated). The S3 backend is suitable only for large cached prefixes (high write latency) — do not use S3 for hot-path KV transfer in latency-sensitive serving. Current version is v1.3.0 (Jun 15, 2026).
title: NIXL

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Auto-scaling Architecture (via llm-d and Dynamo research references) - What: A high-performance KV-cache transfer library from NVIDIA that moves KV tensors between prefill and decode nodes over IB/RoCE/TCP/NVMe-oF/S3. - How it works: NIXL provides a unified transport API over multiple network backends (InfiniBand, RoCE, TCP, NVMe-oF, S3). It handles buffer registration, zero-copy transfers where possible, and flow control. v1.0.0 shipped Mar 13, 2026; current v1.3.0 (Jun 15, 2026) adds AWS EFA support. - Why it matters: P/D disaggregation requires moving multi-GB KV caches between prefill and decode nodes per request. NIXL provides the high-bandwidth, low-latency transport layer that makes this feasible without the transfer cost dominating TTFT. - Gotcha: NIXL is a component of the NVIDIA Dynamo ecosystem (also used by llm-d). It is not a standalone product for general data transfer — it is specifically designed for KV tensor transfer in disaggregated LLM serving. Comparing its bandwidth to general storage benchmarks is misleading.
title: NIXL

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Pipeline Parallelism: Ultra-Long Context - What: CLI flag specifying the total number of compute nodes in a distributed vLLM or SGLang cluster deployment. - How it works: Combined with `--pp-size` and `--tensor-parallel-size`, determines the full distributed topology. `--nnodes M` tells the framework to expect M Ray workers/nodes; each node runs `--tensor-parallel-size K` GPU workers. Total GPUs = nnodes × tensor_parallel_size. - Why it matters: Required for multi-node cluster initialization. Must match the actual Ray cluster topology. Used alongside `ray start --head` / `ray start --address=...` to form the distributed serving cluster. - Gotcha: If `--nnodes` doesn't match the actual Ray cluster size, initialization hangs or fails with a timeout. `--nnodes` is about physical nodes, while `--pp-size` is about logical pipeline stages—they should be equal for standard PP deployments.
title: --nnodes
