body: Hardware · appears on: Edge Deployment Flow - What: A dedicated hardware accelerator for neural network inference integrated into mobile SoCs and laptop chips (e.g., Apple ANE, Qualcomm Hexagon, Intel NPU), providing high tokens-per-watt efficiency for edge LLM inference. - How it works: NPUs implement fixed-function matrix multiply engines optimized for INT4/INT8 operations at low power. Apple's ANE (Neural Engine) achieves approximately 170+ tokens/second for LLMs via the ANEMLL framework (arXiv:2603.06728). Qualcomm Hexagon 8 Elite achieves ~45 TOPS and ~70 tokens/second quantized. ONNX Runtime targets NPUs via QNNExecutionProvider (Qualcomm) and CoreMLExecutionProvider (Apple ANE). - Why it matters: NPUs are essential for on-device LLM deployment where battery life and thermal envelope are the binding constraints; they deliver tokens at 2–6 W vs GPU inference at 150–400 W. - Gotcha: Thermal throttling, not TOPS, is the real mobile bottleneck: iPhone 16 Pro loses approximately half its NPU throughput after two inference iterations due to thermal buildup. Published NPU tok/s figures are typically peak, not sustained.
title: NPU

body: Attention / KV · appears on: Attention Architecture: MHA → MLA & Long-Context - What: DeepSeek's natively trainable sparse attention mechanism (ACL Best Paper 2025, arXiv:2502.11089) that trains models end-to-end with structured sparsity, achieving 9× forward and 11.6× decode speedup at 64K context on 8×A100. - How it works: NSA selects a sparse subset of K/V blocks to attend to per query using a lightweight routing mechanism trained jointly with the model. The sparsity pattern is structured (block-level) allowing efficient hardware execution. FlashMLA added FP8 NSA kernels in Sep 2025. The 9× forward and 6× backward speedups are wall-clock vs Triton FA-2; 11.6× decode is a memory-access-derived expected speedup, not a kernel race. - Why it matters: Sparse attention can reduce the O(N²) attention cost for very long contexts (64K+) where full attention is prohibitive. Natively training with the sparse pattern — rather than post-hoc approximation — preserves model quality better than attention approximation methods. - Gotcha: NSA's speedup figures are benchmark-specific: 9× forward is wall-clock vs Triton FA-2 at 64K on 8×A100; 11.6× decode is a derived memory-bandwidth estimate, not an end-to-end kernel measurement. Performance at different context lengths or hardware generations will differ.
title: NSA

body: Dimension-wise RoPE rescaling: high-frequency dimensions are stretched less than low-frequency ones, preserving local token distinctions.
title: NTK-aware scaling

body: Metric · appears on: Production Tuning: Memory, Scheduling & Observability - What: A Prometheus metric exported by SGLang (equivalent: vllm:num_requests_waiting in vLLM) indicating the number of requests in the waiting queue not yet admitted to the decode batch. - How it works: The serving engine increments this on every incoming request that cannot be immediately admitted (due to --max-running-requests cap or insufficient KV pages) and decrements it when a request is admitted. Used in KEDA HPA rules to trigger horizontal scale-out when sustained queue depth exceeds a threshold. - Why it matters: The primary autoscaling signal for LLM serving; GPU utilization is a misleading metric (always ~100% on decode-bound workloads), but queue depth directly measures whether the system is keeping up with demand. - Gotcha: vLLM uses the metric name vllm:num_requests_waiting (not num_queue_reqs) — cross-engine monitoring dashboards must account for different metric names. Both engines expose this as a Prometheus gauge, not counter.
title: num_queue_reqs

body: Metric · appears on: Production Tuning: Memory, Scheduling & Observability - What: A Prometheus metric exported by SGLang (equivalent: vllm:num_requests_running in vLLM) indicating the current number of requests actively in the decode batch. - How it works: The engine increments this counter when a request is admitted from the waiting queue into the active decode batch and decrements it on completion or preemption. Along with num_queue_reqs and KV cache hit rate, it is the core real-time health signal for the serving engine. - Why it matters: Enables real-time capacity monitoring: if num_running_reqs approaches --max-running-requests, new requests will queue, and TTFT will spike. Used in Grafana alert rules and KEDA autoscaling alongside queue depth. - Gotcha: A high num_running_reqs combined with low num_queue_reqs is healthy (system is saturated but not overloaded). High num_running_reqs AND high num_queue_reqs together indicate the system is overloaded — scale out or reduce batch size.
title: num_running_reqs

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization: Precision vs Performance - What: NVIDIA's proprietary 4-bit floating-point format natively supported by Blackwell (B200/B300/GB200) tensor cores, delivering approximately 2× the throughput of FP8. - How it works: Implemented via block-scaled E2M1 (2 exponent + 1 mantissa) values with a shared per-block FP8 scale. B200 achieves 9,000 TFLOPS dense / 18,000 TFLOPS sparse with NVFP4. Accuracy recovery uses NVIDIA QAD (KL-divergence distillation to a BF16 teacher). TensorRT-LLM v1.3.x and SGLang support NVFP4 MoE dispatch (cuts all-to-all traffic 4×). The deck notes 3.5× memory savings vs FP16 and 1.8× vs FP8 with <1% accuracy loss. - Why it matters: NVFP4 is the new production default on Blackwell hardware and the 2026 serving frontier. Frontier models (Qwen3.x, NVIDIA Nemotron, DeepSeek-R1) ship official NVFP4 weights at release. - Gotcha: NVFP4 is Blackwell-exclusive — there is no fallback path on Hopper or older hardware. Do not conflate with OCP MXFP4 (which AMD MI355X also supports) — they share the 4-bit FP concept but differ in the block-scaling specification.
title: NVFP4

body: Quantization · appears on: Hardware Landscape 2026: Beyond H100 - What: NVIDIA's proprietary 4-bit floating-point format native to Blackwell and Vera Rubin GPUs, delivering approximately 3.5x memory savings vs FP16 and 1.8x vs FP8 with less than 1% quality loss, making it the default production format for Blackwell. - How it works: NVFP4 uses a 4-bit mantissa representation with per-block scaling, similar in structure to MXFP4 but with NVIDIA-specific block sizing. Blackwell Tensor Cores execute NVFP4 matrix multiplications natively. In practice, B200 achieves ~9,000 TFLOPS FP4 dense (~85% of peak). TensorRT-LLM uses NVFP4 by default on Blackwell for weights and optionally for KV cache. - Why it matters: NVFP4 is the key differentiator of Blackwell for serving: halving memory vs FP8 means 2x more tokens in KV cache or running a model twice as large on the same GPU. This directly translates to higher throughput at production batch sizes. - Gotcha: NVFP4 is hardware-specific: it requires Blackwell SM90a or later. Do not confuse with OCP MXFP4 (a standards body format) — they differ in block size and are not directly interchangeable. The 3.5x vs FP16 memory gain applies to weights; KV cache in FP4 halves KV vs FP8 with less than 1% loss.
title: NVFP4

body: 4-bit float with 16-element blocks and two-level scaling (per-block E4M3 + per-tensor FP32) → lower quantization error. ~2–3× FP8 arithmetic throughput.
title: NVFP4

body: Quantization · appears on: FlashAttention: IO-Aware Attention (FA1→FA4) - What: Blackwell-native 4-bit floating point KV cache storage, reducing KV memory by ~50% vs FP8 KV with <1% accuracy loss and up to 3× lower latency on long-context workloads. - How it works: NVFP4 (NVIDIA's proprietary 4-bit format) stores K and V tensors at 4 bits per element. Blackwell's native NVFP4 compute units dequantize on-the-fly during attention. A documented 'plateau effect' means accuracy degradation does not continuously worsen as context lengthens beyond the training context. - Why it matters: On GB200/B200 servers, NVFP4 KV enables 2× the context or batch size vs FP8 KV with minimal accuracy cost. For long-context tasks (100K+ tokens), +20% cache hit rate has been reported for Qwen3-Coder-480B. - Gotcha: NVFP4 KV is Blackwell-only (B200/GB200/B300); it does not exist on Hopper or Ampere. Production teams must maintain separate serving configurations for H100 (FP8 KV) vs B200 (NVFP4 KV) deployments.
title: NVFP4 KV Cache

body: Hardware · appears on: Hardware Landscape 2026: Beyond H100 - What: NVIDIA's first Blackwell-generation GPU, with 192 GB HBM3e at 8 TB/s bandwidth and 9 PFLOPS FP4 peak compute, marking the introduction of native FP4 inference (NVFP4) on NVIDIA hardware. - How it works: The B200 uses the GB202 Blackwell die with fifth-generation Tensor Cores that natively execute FP4 matrix multiplications (NVFP4 format), doubling FP8 TFLOPS. The GB200 NVL72 configuration pairs 72 B200 GPUs with 36 Grace CPUs in a single NVLink domain, providing 13.4 TB unified GPU memory and 130 TB/s NVLink bandwidth for all-to-all communication without InfiniBand. - Why it matters: B200 is the first GPU to make FP4 inference practical at scale; NVFP4 gives 3.5x memory savings vs FP16 and 1.8x vs FP8 with less than 1% quality loss, fundamentally changing the serving economics for frontier models. - Gotcha: GB200 NVL72 is a specific system form-factor (NVLink rack), not just 72 B200s. Tensor parallelism across the full NVL72 domain is feasible because the NVLink fabric provides 130 TB/s, but TP across nodes without this NVLink fabric remains inadvisable.
title: NVIDIA B200

body: Hardware · appears on: Hardware Landscape 2026: Beyond H100 - What: Blackwell Ultra, the highest-performance NVIDIA GPU in production as of mid-2026, with 288 GB HBM3e, 15 PFLOPS FP4 peak, 1,400 W TDP, and ConnectX-8 networking, designated the current gold standard for production LLM inference. - How it works: B300 uses the same Blackwell architecture as B200 but with a larger HBM3e stack (288 GB vs 192 GB) and 15 PFLOPS FP4 vs 9 PFLOPS. GB300 refers to the Grace+B300 combined package. The ConnectX-8 NIC enables higher inter-node bandwidth for multi-node tensor parallelism compared to the B200's ConnectX-7. - Why it matters: B300/GB300 is the capacity-performance leader for frontier model serving in 2026; its 288 GB memory can hold a 70B model in FP4 on a single GPU or a 405B model across 4 GPUs without aggressive tensor parallelism overhead. - Gotcha: The 135–150 kW/rack power draw for GB300 systems (in NVL configurations) is higher than B200 NVL72. Cost of ownership is driven by cooling infrastructure, not just chip price. 'GB300' refers to Grace+B300 packages; bare B300 SXM modules also exist.
title: NVIDIA B300 / GB300

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Serving Stack 2026: 8 Engines That Matter; Disaggregated Prefill/Decode Serving - What: NVIDIA's cross-engine P/D-disaggregation orchestrator (GA 1.0 Mar 2026) that sits above vLLM/SGLang/TRT-LLM and routes prefill and decode to separate GPU pools. - How it works: Dynamo v1.0 provides a KV-aware Smart Router that routes new requests to the prefill pool with the best KV prefix hit, then transfers KV state via NIXL (NVLink/IB/RoCE) to a decode pool. Its SLO Planner manages token budgets across heterogeneous GPU groups. The system reports up to 30x throughput on DeepSeek-R1/GB200 NVL72 vs a non-disaggregated optimized TP/PP baseline (a vendor benchmark, not a naive strawman). - Why it matters: The production-default disaggregation conductor for NVIDIA fleets in 2026; current version v1.2.1 (Jun 2026). Enables 30x throughput claims on frontier MoE models at hyperscale. - Gotcha: The '30x throughput' figure is a NVIDIA GTC-launch vendor benchmark comparing disaggregated GB200 NVL72 vs an optimized (not naive) TEP16PP4DP4 baseline — treat as upper-bound, not typical deployment speedup.
title: NVIDIA Dynamo

body: Hardware · appears on: Hardware Landscape 2026: Beyond H100 - What: NVIDIA's Hopper-generation GPU upgrade over the H100, featuring 141 GB of HBM3e memory at 4.8 TB/s bandwidth, delivering approximately 43% higher decode throughput than H100 through memory capacity and bandwidth improvements alone. - How it works: The H200 uses the same Hopper SM90 compute die as the H100 but replaces HBM2e with HBM3e, increasing capacity from 80 GB to 141 GB and bandwidth from 3.35 TB/s to 4.8 TB/s. FP8 compute is identical to H100. The extra memory enables larger KV caches and fitting larger models without tensor parallelism, which drives the decode throughput gain. - Why it matters: The H200 is the cost-effective production baseline in 2026: it is available on existing Hopper infrastructure, has no recompilation requirement compared to Blackwell, and the +43% decode gain is purely from the memory upgrade — no software changes needed. - Gotcha: H200 does not support FP4 (no native Blackwell NVFP4 tensor cores). Systems already optimized for H100 get a free performance boost on H200, but cannot use NVFP4 quantization available on B200/B300.
title: NVIDIA H200

body: Packaged inference microservices priced per GPU (NVIDIA AI Enterprise ~$4,500/GPU/yr ≈ $1/GPU-hr) on top of GPU rental.
title: NVIDIA NIM

body: Hardware · appears on: Hardware Landscape 2026: Beyond H100 - What: NVIDIA's next-generation GPU (after Blackwell), announced as entering full production at CES January 5, 2026, with 50 PFLOPS NVFP4, 288 GB HBM4 at 22 TB/s, and NVLink 6, shipping H2 2026 in volume. - How it works: Vera Rubin uses a new GPU die (Rubin) paired with Grace CPUs (Grace-Rubin). The HBM4 memory provides 22 TB/s per GPU. The NVL144 rack configuration uses 144 Rubin GPUs with approximately 190 kW/rack power draw. NVFP4 native tensor cores deliver 50 PFLOPS dense. - Why it matters: Vera Rubin sets the next benchmark for FP4 compute density; at 50 PFLOPS vs Blackwell's 9–15 PFLOPS, it represents a 3–5x generational leap in raw compute, though memory bandwidth (22 TB/s) is the practical serving bottleneck. - Gotcha: There is no official 'R100' product name; the correct name is 'Vera Rubin' or 'Rubin GPU'. The CES Jan 5 2026 announcement was production entry, not product launch; H2 2026 volume shipments are the supply-constrained reality. The NVL144 variant uses 144 GPUs, not 72 like NVL72.
title: NVIDIA Vera Rubin

body: Hardware · appears on: Distributed Inference: Parallelism Strategy Guide - What: NVIDIA's proprietary high-bandwidth, low-latency GPU-to-GPU interconnect, providing up to 900 GB/s (NVLink 4) within a node and up to 130 TB/s across NVL72 domains. - How it works: Point-to-point or switched NVLink (NVSwitch) connects GPUs within a node or NVL module. All-Reduce operations in TP use NVLink for collective communication, achieving sub-millisecond synchronization. NVL72 (GB200 NVL72) connects 72 GPUs in a single NVLink domain at 130 TB/s aggregate bandwidth, enabling TP across what would otherwise be 9+ nodes. - Why it matters: NVLink bandwidth (900 GB/s/GPU) vs InfiniBand (~200 GB/s) is the reason TP is node-local: All-Reduce on NVLink takes ~0.1 ms vs ~5 ms on IB. NVL72's 130 TB/s makes intra-domain EP32 or EP64 feasible entirely over NVLink, bypassing IB entirely for DeepSeek-scale workloads. - Gotcha: NVLink is only between GPUs in the same physical NVLink domain (same node or NVL module). Cross-node NVLink requires NVLink Fusion fabric (NVL72). Do NOT assume TP across standard multi-node IB clusters is NVLink-backed—it isn't.
title: NVLink

body: Hardware · appears on: Hardware Landscape 2026: Beyond H100 - What: NVIDIA's proprietary high-speed GPU-to-GPU interconnect providing up to 900 GB/s (NVLink 4, Hopper) and 130 TB/s aggregate bandwidth in GB200 NVL72 configurations (NVLink 5), used for all-reduce in tensor parallelism and KV transfer in disaggregated prefill-decode serving. - How it works: NVLink connects GPUs on the same node (or within an NVLink Switch fabric) via a point-to-point SerDes interface. In Hopper systems, 8 GPUs are connected at 900 GB/s each. In GB200 NVL72, 72 GPUs are connected via NVLink Switch chips providing full-bisection bandwidth at 130 TB/s aggregate. Tensor parallelism all-reduce operations complete at near-NVLink bandwidth rather than PCIe or InfiniBand rates. - Why it matters: NVLink bandwidth (900 GB/s intra-node) vs InfiniBand (400 GB/s inter-node) explains the rule: do tensor parallelism within a node (NVLink), pipeline parallelism across nodes (IB). GB200 NVL72's 130 TB/s fabric extends this to a 72-GPU domain. - Gotcha: The deck explicitly warns: do not use tensor parallelism across nodes unless the hardware is an NVLink fabric like NVL72/GB200. Standard IB (400 GB/s) cannot support TP all-reduce at scale. Blackwell adds NVLink encryption, which was absent on Hopper.
title: NVLink

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Serving Stack 2026: 8 Engines That Matter - What: A one-command local LLM runner (`ollama run <model>`) that wraps llama.cpp under the hood, exposing a REST and OpenAI-compatible API for local development. - How it works: Ollama bundles llama.cpp and provides a model registry with automatic download/conversion to GGUF. It manages Metal (macOS) and CUDA GPU offloading transparently. v0.30.10 (Jun 2026) added an MLX preview for >32GB Apple Silicon Macs (decode 58→112 tok/s on M5), though llama.cpp Metal remains the fallback for most models. - Why it matters: Lowest-friction path for local development and testing; handles model management, GPU offloading, and API compatibility in a single binary — the recommended 'container' deployment mode for local/edge use. - Gotcha: MLX preview in v0.19.0+ (Mar 2026) only supports models >32GB Mac configs and limited models (e.g., Qwen3.5-35B-A3B); most users still get llama.cpp Metal. Ollama is not intended for high-concurrency production serving.
title: Ollama

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Edge Deployment Flow - What: A container-based local LLM serving tool that wraps llama.cpp (with an MLX preview on Apple Silicon) behind a single CLI command and a Docker-compatible REST API. - How it works: Ollama downloads GGUF models from the Ollama registry, manages model storage and versioning, and serves them via a local OpenAI-compatible REST endpoint. A single `ollama run llama3` command pulls, quantizes if needed, and starts inference. As of v0.30.10 (Jun 17 2026), it includes an MLX preview for >32GB Apple Silicon Macs (decode ~2x faster than llama.cpp Metal for Qwen3.5-35B-A3B). - Why it matters: Ollama is the fastest path from zero to a running local LLM, making it the standard for local development and testing before deploying to production engines like vLLM or SGLang. - Gotcha: Ollama uses llama.cpp as its backend (with Metal fallback even in MLX preview mode for most models). Its default Q4_K_M quantization for downloaded models is appropriate for most cases, but custom quantization or fine-tuned models require manual GGUF conversion.
title: Ollama

body: Attention / KV · appears on: FlashAttention: IO-Aware Attention (FA1→FA4) - What: A numerically stable algorithm that computes the softmax denominator incrementally as K/V tiles are processed, without ever materializing the full N-length score vector in memory. - How it works: Maintains two running statistics per Q row: m_i (running maximum of attention scores seen so far) and ℓ_i (running sum of exp(score - m_i)). When processing each new K/V tile, updates m_i and rescales the accumulated output by exp(m_old - m_new) to preserve correctness. After all tiles, divides by ℓ_i to normalize. - Why it matters: Without online softmax, computing the softmax denominator requires first reading all N scores, which forces two passes over HBM. Online softmax allows a single pass, enabling the IO-aware single-HBM-write property of FlashAttention. - Gotcha: Blackwell's hardware does not natively support the softmax operations needed for FA4's tiling; FA4 must emulate softmax in software using the 2-CTA MMA pattern. This is why FA4's design differs architecturally from FA3.
title: Online Softmax

body: A low-latency (Redis/Dynamo, ms) feature store used for inference.
title: Online store

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Model Compilation: torch.compile + CUDA Graphs + TensorRT - What: An open intermediate representation format for neural network models, used as the standard exchange format between training frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow) and inference runtimes (TensorRT, ONNX Runtime). - How it works: PyTorch models are exported to ONNX via `torch.onnx.export()`, which traces the computation graph and serializes it as a protobuf file with operator nodes, tensor shapes, and weights. TensorRT's ONNX parser ingests this file as the starting point for its compilation pipeline. - Why it matters: Serves as the handoff between the research/training ecosystem and production inference compilers. Understanding ONNX explains why TensorRT compilation requires an export step and why changes to model architecture require recompilation. - Gotcha: ONNX export has known limitations with dynamic shapes, custom operators, and control flow. Dynamic shape models (variable batch/sequence length) require explicit shape specifications. Not all PyTorch operators have ONNX equivalents, and custom CUDA kernels (like FlashAttention) require ONNX custom ops.
title: ONNX

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Edge Deployment Flow - What: An open cross-framework model serialization format and runtime that represents neural network graphs in a hardware-neutral intermediate representation. - How it works: A PyTorch model is exported to ONNX via torch.onnx.export(), producing a .onnx file containing the computation graph and weights. ONNX Runtime (introduced 2019) can execute this on CPU, GPU, or NPU with hardware-specific optimized kernels. For NVIDIA targets the .onnx file is fed to TensorRT for further compilation into a hardware-fused engine. - Why it matters: ONNX decouples the training framework from the inference runtime, enabling the same model to be deployed across CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs without framework-specific code. - Gotcha: ONNX export can fail or produce suboptimal graphs for models with dynamic control flow or custom ops; dynamic shapes (variable batch/sequence length) require explicit export arguments and can limit TensorRT optimization.
title: ONNX

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Pre-LLM Era: Serving Infrastructure 2017–2022 - What: A cross-framework inference execution engine (Microsoft, 2019) that runs models exported to the ONNX format across CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs via pluggable execution providers. - How it works: Models from PyTorch, TensorFlow, scikit-learn, or JAX are exported to the ONNX intermediate representation (computation graph). ORT selects an execution provider (CPU, CUDA, ROCm, DirectML, TensorRT, CoreML, etc.) at runtime and applies graph-level optimizations (fusion, quantization, layout transformations). - Why it matters: ORT enabled hardware-agnostic deployment of traditional ML models and early Transformer models, and remains the preferred runtime for inference on CPUs (Azure/ONNX-based endpoints) and NPUs. For LLMs, ORT with Optimum offers ONNX-exported versions of Llama/Mistral for deployment on non-CUDA devices. - Gotcha: ONNX export of LLMs with dynamic KV-cache shapes can be fragile — each new token changes the KV-cache tensor shape, which some export paths handle poorly. For production LLM serving on GPUs, purpose-built engines (vLLM, SGLang, TRT-LLM) outperform ORT significantly because they manage KV cache natively.
title: ONNX Runtime

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Edge Deployment Flow - What: Microsoft's cross-platform inference runtime (introduced 2019) that executes ONNX model graphs with hardware-specific optimized kernels for CPU, GPU, and NPU targets. - How it works: ONNX Runtime loads a .onnx file and applies execution providers: CPUExecutionProvider (SIMD-optimized), CUDAExecutionProvider (cuDNN/TensorRT), DirectMLExecutionProvider (Windows GPU), QNNExecutionProvider (Qualcomm NPU), CoreMLExecutionProvider (Apple ANE). It selects the best available provider at runtime and falls back to CPU if specialized hardware is absent. - Why it matters: ONNX Runtime is the standard inference runtime for non-LLM-specific models (vision, audio, embedding) deployed at the edge or in cross-platform environments where a framework-specific runtime (PyTorch, TensorFlow) would be too heavy. - Gotcha: ONNX Runtime is less suited for large LLM autoregressive generation than llama.cpp or TensorRT-LLM; it lacks continuous batching and paged KV cache for LLMs. Microsoft's Olive tool (ONNX optimization for edge) and ONNX Runtime GenAI are needed for LLM-specific optimizations.
title: ONNX Runtime

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Serving Stack 2026: 8 Engines That Matter; Structured Generation: XGrammar, Tool & Reasoning Parsers - What: The de-facto wire protocol for LLM serving: HTTP POST /v1/chat/completions (and /v1/completions) with the same JSON schema as the OpenAI API, supported by vLLM, SGLang, LMDeploy, NVIDIA Dynamo, llama.cpp, and others. - How it works: Each engine spawns an HTTP server that accepts JSON bodies with fields like `model`, `messages`, `temperature`, `response_format`, `tools`, and `stream`, returning SSE chunks or a complete JSON response matching the OpenAI specification. This allows drop-in substitution of the backend without client-side code changes. - Why it matters: Universal adoption means any OpenAI SDK, LangChain, LlamaIndex, or agent framework works unchanged against a local or self-hosted engine — critical for cost control and data-residency compliance. - Gotcha: Coverage is not 100% identical across engines: TensorRT-LLM exposes a Triton backend protocol rather than native OpenAI-compat, requiring a wrapper (Dynamo or NIM); some engines lag on `strict` mode, parallel tool calls, or `logprobs` semantics.

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Structured Generation: XGrammar, Tool & Reasoning Parsers - What: The original FSM (Finite State Machine)-based grammar-constrained decoding library for LLMs, now relegated to fallback-only status behind XGrammar due to 40s–10min schema compile times. - How it works: Outlines builds a finite state machine for the JSON Schema or regex at request time, then masks logits token-by-token according to FSM state. FSM construction is slow on complex schemas (large vocab × state space) — 40 seconds to 10 minutes for complex recursive grammars. Was the default in SGLang before v0.4 switched to XGrammar. - Why it matters: Historical reference: Outlines pioneered grammar-constrained LLM decoding; understanding it explains why the field moved to PDA/vocab-partition approaches (XGrammar) for production. - Gotcha: Despite being 'fallback-only' in production engines, Outlines has the highest JSONSchemaBench GitHub-Hard coverage (in some comparisons, but results vary by model and benchmark version). Don't assume XGrammar covers all schemas Outlines handles.
title: Outlines

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Request Scheduling: Ai Được Chạy Trước? - What: The structural reason LLM scheduling is hard: the output sequence length is unknown when the request is admitted. - How it works: Classic scheduling wins — shortest-job-first, deadline ordering, accurate admission control — all assume job size is known. For LLM generation it is not, so schedulers either default to arrival order or must predict length (ELIS and similar). - Why it matters: It explains why FCFS remains the default in production engines despite being provably suboptimal, and why reasoning models (with long, uncontrolled output tails) make admission control and token budgets mandatory rather than optional. - Gotcha: Length predictors shift the failure mode rather than removing it: a mispredicted long request scheduled as short causes exactly the head-of-line blocking SJF was meant to avoid.
title: Output-length uncertainty

body: Decoding · appears on: Drafting Ladder: EAGLE-3 → Parallel Drafting (2026) - What: EAGLE-3's architecture converted to parallel drafting (arXiv 2602.01469), emitting all K draft tokens in one forward pass. - How it works: It keeps EAGLE-3's Llama-style decoder and multi-layer hidden-state conditioning, but substitutes learnable mask-token embeddings and shared hidden states as placeholders for the future positions. Training uses Conditional-On-Distribution (COD) sampling plus sequence partitioning to keep memory tractable. - Why it matters: It is the lowest-friction upgrade for a team already running EAGLE-3: same architecture and training pipeline, up to 1.69× over EAGLE-3 on gpt-oss-20B/B200 at concurrency 1 (1.05–1.25× at concurrency 64), with optimal K moving 3 → 7. - Gotcha: The headline 1.69× is a concurrency-1 figure on SPEED-Bench; at concurrency 64 the gain narrows to 5–25%. Quote the concurrency alongside the number.
title: P-EAGLE

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Distributed Inference: Parallelism Strategy Guide; Pipeline Parallelism: Ultra-Long Context - What: A communication pattern where one GPU sends activation tensors directly to the next pipeline stage's GPU, used in Pipeline Parallelism to pass layer outputs between stages. - How it works: After stage K finishes processing its layers for a micro-batch, it sends the output activations via `torch.distributed.send/recv` (or NCCL P2P) to stage K+1's GPU. This is a directed, pairwise transfer (not a broadcast or all-reduce), which tolerates InfiniBand latency better than All-Reduce because it is less frequent and involves only two participants. - Why it matters: P2P's asymmetric communication pattern (only adjacent stages communicate) is the key reason PP can span multiple nodes over IB while TP cannot—All-Reduce needs every TP rank simultaneously, amplifying IB latency N-fold. - Gotcha: P2P activation size scales with `batch_size × hidden_dim × sizeof(dtype)`. For 128K context windows with chunked prefill, activation tensors between PP stages can be large; dynamic chunking controls this. P2P over NVLink (within an NVL domain) is ~5x faster than over IB.
title: P2P

body: Metric · appears on: SLA Dashboard: Key Metrics - What: The 50th-percentile (median) end-to-end latency: half of all requests complete faster than this value. The dashboard example shows 120 ms with a target of < 200 ms. - How it works: Computed by sorting all request completion times over a rolling window (e.g., 1 min) and returning the midpoint. Load-testing tools like locust and k6 emit this automatically. In continuous-batching engines the P50 is dominated by TPOT x output_length for typical mid-length generations. - Why it matters: P50 represents the typical user experience. It is the easiest percentile to optimize (cache hits, batch efficiency lift it) but least representative of tail behavior under burst load. - Gotcha: P50 can look excellent while P99 is catastrophic (factor of 7x in the dashboard example: 120 ms vs 850 ms). Never report only P50 in a production SLA context; always include P95 and P99.
title: P50 Latency

body: Metric · appears on: SLA Dashboard: Key Metrics - What: The 95th-percentile latency: 95% of requests complete within this time. The dashboard example shows 380 ms with a target of < 500 ms. - How it works: Requires 5% of requests to be slower. In LLM serving these are typically long-output requests, cache-miss requests entering a full prefill queue, or requests hitting a batch that just expanded. P95 is the most common SLO threshold in production LLM APIs (e.g., E2E latency = TTFT + TPOT x (N-1) at P95/P99 per deck §1). - Why it matters: Represents the experience of users who regularly interact with the service. A P95 SLO is sensitive enough to catch systematic issues (queue depth spikes, GC pauses) without being dominated by one-off outliers. - Gotcha: P95 TTFT and P95 TPOT are different SLOs; a request can satisfy the former but violate the latter. Track them independently in production dashboards.
title: P95 Latency

body: Metric · appears on: SLA Dashboard: Key Metrics - What: The 99th-percentile latency: 99% of requests complete within this time. The dashboard example shows 850 ms with a target of < 1000 ms. - How it works: Only 1% of requests are slower. P99 is sensitive to worst-case scheduling delays, KV-cache evictions under memory pressure, cold-start prefill, and network retransmits. It requires larger statistical sample sizes to be stable (need >> 100 requests per measurement window). - Why it matters: P99 represents the worst experience that a significant fraction of active users will encounter during a high-traffic period. Regulated or user-facing products often set P99 as the binding SLA constraint. AIBrix routing improvements showed 79% P99 reduction (though this is a routing result, not multi-LoRA). - Gotcha: P99 is highly sensitive to outlier events and requires a long enough measurement window (typically >= 1 minute, >= 1000 requests) to be statistically meaningful. Reported P99 from a 10-request benchmark is meaningless.
title: P99 Latency

body: Attention / KV · appears on: PagedAttention: vLLM v0 → v1 Deep Dive - What: The per-request data structure that maps logical KV block indices to their physical GPU page addresses, exactly analogous to a CPU MMU page table. - How it works: During attention computation, vLLM's attention kernel looks up the page table to find where each logical block's K/V data physically resides. For shared prefixes, multiple requests' page tables point to the same physical pages (copy-on-write). The page table is small (one entry per 16-token block) and kept on the CPU, with GPU-side pointers passed at kernel launch. - Why it matters: Enables non-contiguous VRAM usage and prefix sharing without changing the attention algorithm — the attention kernel is adapted to follow indirection through the page table rather than assuming contiguous layout. - Gotcha: Page-table lookup adds one level of indirection per attention call; modern engines amortize this with CUDA graph capture for decode steps, but prefill kernels (non-fixed shape) cannot use CUDA graphs and must resolve the table at runtime.
title: Page table

body: Offloads optimizer state to CPU RAM on memory spikes instead of throwing OOM.
title: Paged optimizer

body: managing the KV cache in fixed-size non-contiguous blocks (like OS virtual-memory paging) to eliminate fragmentation and enable KV sharing — the basis of vLLM, ~2–4× throughput.
title: PagedAttention

body: Attention / KV · appears on: Pre-LLM Era: Serving Infrastructure 2017–2022 - What: vLLM's core KV-cache management innovation (SOSP 2023) that allocates KV cache in fixed-size non-contiguous physical pages (like OS virtual memory), eliminating the need for contiguous memory blocks and reducing fragmentation below 4%. - How it works: Inspired by virtual memory paging in operating systems. The KV cache is divided into fixed-size physical blocks (pages). A logical block table maps each sequence's KV indices to physical pages. Pages can be scattered across GPU memory — they need not be contiguous. When a sequence finishes, its pages are individually freed and immediately reusable by other sequences. Copy-on-Write enables KV sharing for beam search and prefix caching. - Why it matters: PagedAttention is the architectural breakthrough that enabled the LLM serving era. The deck notes 24x throughput improvement over naive HuggingFace Transformers. By enabling non-contiguous KV allocation, it makes continuous batching practical (no more pre-reserving worst-case contiguous blocks) and forms the foundation for all modern LLM engines. - Gotcha: The V1 vLLM engine (Jan 2025+) refactored PagedAttention internals significantly: constant-time eviction, prefix caching on by default, multimodal block hashing, and up to 1.7x throughput improvement over V0. The original SOSP 2023 paper describes V0's block manager; do not assume V0 and V1 block management are identical.
title: PagedAttention

body: Attention / KV · appears on: KV Cache & PagedAttention - What: A KV cache memory manager, introduced in vLLM (SOSP 2023), that allocates KV tensors in fixed-size non-contiguous physical 'pages' (blocks) rather than one contiguous buffer per sequence. - How it works: Inspired by OS virtual memory: each request has a virtual sequence of KV blocks; a page table maps virtual block IDs to physical GPU memory blocks. When a request finishes, its blocks are freed individually. Physical blocks are allocated on demand, keeping fragmentation below 4% in V1. - Why it matters: Traditional serving pre-allocates a contiguous buffer sized for max_sequence_length per request; unused slots are wasted (shown in red on the deck's TikZ diagram). PagedAttention eliminates this waste, enabling 24× higher throughput vs naive HuggingFace Transformers and allowing memory sharing across requests (prefix caching). - Gotcha: KV eviction techniques like H2O/SnapKV that 'compress' the KV cache under PagedAttention reclaim almost no GPU memory in practice: a physical block only frees when every slot inside it is evicted, so sparse eviction scatters survivors across blocks. Production favors quantization or MLA compression over token-level eviction.
title: PagedAttention

body: Attention / KV · appears on: Inference Engine Evolution: 2020 → 2025; PagedAttention: vLLM v0 → v1 Deep Dive - What: vLLM's core memory management technique (Jun 2023, SOSP 2023) that treats GPU KV cache like virtual memory — dividing it into fixed-size pages and mapping them non-contiguously, eliminating memory fragmentation. - How it works: KV cache for each request is divided into logical blocks (16 tokens/page by default); a page table maps each logical block to a non-contiguous physical page in GPU VRAM. When a request needs more cache, a new physical page is allocated from the global page pool. Pages can be shared across requests with identical prefixes (copy-on-write). Fragmentation drops below 4%. vLLM V1 adds constant-time eviction and multimodal hashing. - Why it matters: Enabled 24x throughput improvement over HF Transformers' naive contiguous allocation; continuous batching becomes practical when VRAM isn't wasted on pre-allocated fixed buffers. All modern engines now use paged or equivalent KV management. - Gotcha: KV eviction heuristics (H2O, SnapKV) reclaim almost no GPU memory under PagedAttention because a physical block frees only when ALL tokens in the block are evicted — survivors scatter across blocks, leaving pages partially full. Production preference is quantization (FP8/NVFP4) or MLA over eviction.

body: Decoding · appears on: Drafting Ladder: EAGLE-3 → Parallel Drafting (2026) - What: The defining shift of 2026 speculative decoding: emitting all K draft tokens in a single drafter forward pass instead of K sequential ones. - How it works: An autoregressive drafter such as EAGLE-3 must run K times to propose K tokens, so drafting latency grows linearly in K. Parallel drafters feed the drafter learnable mask-token embeddings (P-EAGLE) or a block-diffusion objective (DFlash) so one pass produces the whole block. - Why it matters: It moves the optimal speculation depth from K≈3 to K≈7 and turns drafting from a sequential tax into block-parallel GPU work — which is what lets speculative decoding help at concurrency, not just at batch 1. - Gotcha: The cost is losing dependencies between tokens inside a block, which shows up as suffix decay. body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Pipeline Parallelism: Ultra-Long Context - What: An optimization technique that captures and replays GPU execution sequences as a CUDA Graph for prefill, while using a separate full CUDA Graph for decode, reducing kernel launch overhead. - How it works: Standard CUDA Graph captures the entire sequence of GPU operations and replays them with minimal CPU overhead. PCG ('piecewise') applies graph capture only to the non-attention portion of prefill (where shapes vary but the non-attention ops are shape-fixed), and uses a full graph for decode. This was described as FULL_AND_PIECEWISE in vLLM V1. - Why it matters: CUDA Graph replay eliminates kernel launch latency (CPU→GPU dispatch delay per kernel) that otherwise accounts for 10–30% of inference time at small batch sizes. PCG makes this applicable to prefill where token counts vary, not just decode. - Gotcha: PCG is automatically disabled when Pipeline Parallelism is active. This means PP workloads do not get the kernel launch overhead reduction benefit of PCG. If PP is required for model size or context length, accept that PCG benefits are unavailable.
title: PCG

body: Metric · appears on: Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ - What: A standard language model quality metric measuring how well the model predicts a held-out text corpus; lower perplexity = better language model. Used as the primary quantization quality benchmark. - How it works: Calculated as exp(cross-entropy loss) on a held-out corpus (e.g., wikitext-2-raw). llama.cpp provides a built-in perplexity evaluation command (llama-perplexity). The deck warningbox states: 'Benchmark perplexity sau khi quantize' (after quantizing). Gemma 3 QAT reduced perplexity drop by 54% vs naive Q4_0. - Why it matters: Perplexity is the standard sanity check after applying any quantization — it quickly flags catastrophic quality loss before full task evaluation. However, perplexity does not perfectly predict downstream task performance; MMLU or domain-specific evals are also needed. - Gotcha: Math and reasoning task accuracy degrades before perplexity worsens — a model can have acceptable perplexity but significantly degraded chain-of-thought quality at 2–3 bit quantization. Always supplement perplexity with task-specific evals for math/code use cases.
title: Perplexity

body: Metric · appears on: Hardware Landscape 2026: Beyond H100 - What: A unit of compute throughput equal to 10^15 floating-point operations per second, used to compare peak theoretical compute performance across accelerators. - How it works: PFLOPS figures are derived from peak matrix multiply rates at a given precision: B200 = 9 PFLOPS FP4, B300 = 15 PFLOPS FP4, Vera Rubin = 50 PFLOPS NVFP4, AMD MI355X = 20 PFLOPS FP4, AWS Trainium3 = 2.52 PFLOPS FP8. These are theoretical peaks; real utilization is typically 60–85% of peak for LLM workloads. - Why it matters: PFLOPS provides a quick cross-vendor comparison metric for compute, but for LLM decode specifically it is a misleading primary metric because decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, not compute-bound at typical batch sizes. - Gotcha: Peak PFLOPS at one precision (e.g., FP4) is not comparable to another precision (FP8, FP16) without accounting for the precision difference. The memory bandwidth metric (TB/s) is almost always more predictive of real LLM serving throughput than TFLOPS/PFLOPS.
title: PFLOPS

body: Security · appears on: Confidential Inference: TEE & the Attack Surface - What: A confidential computing deployment by Phala Network that runs GPU-accelerated LLM inference inside a TEE and exposes it via OpenRouter's API marketplace, enabling users to access confidential inference at market rates. - How it works: Phala deploys LLMs on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs with Confidential Computing enabled (PPCIE) inside Intel TDX-protected VMs. Remote attestation certificates are provided to users who want to cryptographically verify the TEE configuration. The inference is accessible through OpenRouter's standard routing infrastructure. - Why it matters: Provides a practical demonstration that GPU TEE inference is commercially deployable. Regulated-industry users can access confidential LLM inference without deploying their own TEE infrastructure, paying a per-token premium for the confidentiality guarantee. - Gotcha: Phala's setup uses Hopper PPCIE, which is limited to single-GPU confidential computation per CVM. Multi-GPU models requiring TP may need to trade confidentiality for performance, or wait for Blackwell TEE-I/O deployments.

body: Attention / KV · appears on: PagedAttention: vLLM v0 → v1 Deep Dive - What: The physical unit of VRAM allocated to hold the K and V tensors for 16 tokens (by default) — analogous to a page frame in OS virtual memory. - How it works: Physical pages live in a pre-allocated global page pool covering the GPU VRAM not used by model weights and activations. The pool is managed by vLLM's block allocator; pages are assigned on demand to requests and returned to the pool on request completion or eviction. Shared-prefix pages are reference-counted and only freed when no active request points to them. - Why it matters: Fixed-size physical pages eliminate external fragmentation and allow the block manager to maintain a simple free-list, making allocation O(1) and enabling the non-contiguous mapping that is PagedAttention's key insight. - Gotcha: Physical page size (16 tokens × num_heads × head_dim × bytes_per_element) can be significant on large models — FlashInfer requires page size > 1 for its BSR-format kernels, which is why vLLM's FlashInfer mode uses page_size=16 (or larger).
title: Physical page

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Speculative Decoding & Continuous Batching - What: SGLang's approach to CUDA graph capture for variable-length batches: the non-attention parts of the forward pass are captured as a static CUDA graph (and replayed cheaply), while the attention step — which is variable-length — runs eagerly. - How it works: A full forward pass is split into: (a) static parts (embedding lookup, FFN, layer norms — shape is fixed given batch-size buckets) which are graph-captured; and (b) the attention call (variable over sequence lengths) which is always eager. At replay, only the eager attention portion incurs Python dispatch overhead. vLLM V1 implements a similar split: FULL_AND_PIECEWISE mode uses full graph for decode and piecewise (ex-attention) for prefill. - Why it matters: Extends the CUDA graph throughput benefit (~10–20% extra) to continuous/mixed batches where full-graph capture would require one graph per (batch-size, seq-length) pair — combinatorially impractical. - Gotcha: Piecewise graphs add warmup complexity: multiple batch-size buckets must be recorded at startup, increasing initialization time. The Python overhead savings are smaller than full-graph replay but still meaningful.
title: Piecewise CUDA Graph

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Distributed Inference (Multi-node vLLM Ray Cluster): '--tensor-parallel-size 4 --pipeline-parallel-size 2' - What: A vLLM CLI flag that sets the pipeline parallelism degree — how many sequential pipeline stages the model's layers are split across, with each stage running on a separate node or set of GPUs. - How it works: With '--pipeline-parallel-size 2', vLLM divides the model's transformer layers into 2 equal segments. GPU set 1 (stage 0) processes layers 0..L/2-1; GPU set 2 (stage 1) processes layers L/2..L-1. Activations are transferred between stages via P2P communication (NVLink for intra-node, InfiniBand/RoCE for inter-node). Combined with '--tensor-parallel-size 4', the example '--tp 4 --pp 2' deploys across 2 nodes × 4 GPUs = 8 GPUs total. Chunked prefill micro-batches fill pipeline bubbles to improve GPU utilisation. - Why it matters: PP is the only practical way to serve models whose weights exceed the VRAM of a single node's GPU set. For DeepSeek-V3.1 at full precision (~1.3 TB), PP across multiple 8×H100 nodes is unavoidable. PP also enables ultra-long-context serving (128K+) where the KV cache per pipeline stage is bounded. - Gotcha: PP introduces 'bubble latency' — GPUs in later stages idle while the first stage processes the initial micro-batch. Chunked prefill reduces but does not eliminate bubbles. Piecewise CUDA Graphs disable automatically when PP is active, adding overhead per decode step. TP within each PP stage is constrained to NVLink-connected GPUs on the same node.
title: --pipeline-parallel-size

body: Parallelism · appears on: Distributed Inference: Parallelism Strategy Guide; Pipeline Parallelism: Ultra-Long Context - What: A parallelism strategy that distributes consecutive transformer layers across multiple GPUs/nodes, with activations flowing as a pipeline from stage 0 (early layers) to stage N-1 (final layers). - How it works: Model layers are split into P stages, each assigned to a node. The forward pass streams activation tensors between stages via Point-to-Point (P2P) communication over InfiniBand or NVLink. Micro-batching is used to keep all stages busy: while stage 1 processes micro-batch 2, stage 0 already handles micro-batch 3. Flag: `--pp-size N --nnodes M`. - Why it matters: The right strategy when the model is too large for single-node TP (e.g., DeepSeek-V3.1 full precision) or when 128K+ context windows are needed. P2P activation transfer tolerates higher IB latency than TP All-Reduce. Rule: PP = number of nodes. - Gotcha: PP introduces 'bubble latency'—GPUs idle at the start and end of each micro-batch pipeline fill/drain phase. Dynamic chunking (`--enable-dynamic-chunking`) and PCG optimization reduce bubble overhead. Piecewise CUDA Graph (PCG) is automatically disabled when PP is enabled.
title: Pipeline Parallelism

This design prioritises visual fidelity over token efficiency, making it well-suited for document understanding and fine-grained visual tasks but creating severe TTFT spikes in serving when multiple high-res images are included in a single request. - Why it matters: Pixtral's 4,096 tokens/image figure is the worst-case data point in the deck's image-token-explosion discussion, establishing the upper bound of VLM serving overhead. At 30 FPS video, 4,096 tokens/frame × 1,800 frames/minute = ~7.4M visual tokens/minute — making naive VLM serving of video content infeasible without aggressive token compression or EPD disaggregation. - Gotcha: The 4,096 figure assumes no token compression (dynamic high-res tiling). Recent Pixtral variants and competitor models (Qwen3-VL's ~1,139, LLaVA-NeXT's ~2,880) use learned compression to reduce this overhead. Always check the model card's 'tokens_per_image' function rather than assuming the raw ViT patch count.

body: Concept · appears on: Tokens-per-Joule & The Power Wall - What: The physical and infrastructure constraint that limits AI serving scale due to datacenter power capacity; in 2026, GPU clusters rather than compute FLOPS are limited by how much electricity the facility can deliver. - How it works: Modern AI server racks draw 120–132 kW (GB200 NVL72), 135–150 kW (GB300), and projected ~190 kW (Vera Rubin NVL144). A 50 MW datacenter can only accommodate a limited number of such racks. IEA projects global AI datacenter electricity consumption to roughly double from ~485 TWh (2025) to ~950 TWh (2030). - Why it matters: The power wall makes energy efficiency a first-class design constraint. Techniques that save compute (quantization, MoE sparsity, routing) now also save physical capacity and operational cost. Hardware procurement and cluster design must now account for peak power draw, not just FLOP count. - Gotcha: Power constraints are facility-specific; a rack that draws 132 kW cannot be installed in a datacenter row designed for 30 kW/rack without significant electrical infrastructure upgrades. The effective compute density is limited by power delivery, not the GPU specs alone.
title: Power Wall

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Pipeline Parallelism: Ultra-Long Context - What: CLI flag specifying the number of pipeline stages (and thus the number of nodes in a PP deployment), determining how model layers are partitioned across nodes. - How it works: Setting `--pp-size N` divides the model's transformer layers into N equal groups, one per pipeline stage. Each stage is typically one node. Combined with `--nnodes M` (total node count) and `--tensor-parallel-size K` (TP per node), the total GPU count = pp_size × tp_size. Example: `--tp 4 --pp 2 --ep 8` = 2 nodes × 4 GPUs for DeepSeek-V3.1. - Why it matters: PP is the primary mechanism for extending serving to multi-node clusters when model size exceeds single-node TP capacity. The flag directly controls the cluster topology for serving ultra-large models or 128K+ context workloads. - Gotcha: Setting pp_size > actual node count causes allocation failures. PP and TP are orthogonal but interact with EP: the recommended configuration is TP within nodes, PP across nodes, EP partitioning experts. Increasing pp_size increases bubble latency—balance against micro-batch count.

body: Security · appears on: Confidential Inference: TEE & the Attack Surface - What: NVIDIA's encryption of the PCIe bus between the CPU host and GPU in a confidential computing configuration, protecting data in transit between host memory and GPU memory. - How it works: In a Hopper PPCIE setup (GA Apr 23, 2025), the PCIe data path between the host CVM (CPU Trusted Execution Environment) and the GPU is encrypted at the hardware level using keys negotiated during attestation. This ensures that even the PCIe bus snooping cannot expose model weights or activations during transfer. - Why it matters: Without PCIe encryption, an attacker with access to the host PCIe bus (e.g., DMA attacks, compromised hypervisor) could intercept model weights or user activations during CPU-GPU transfers. PPCIE closes this attack vector. - Gotcha: PPCIE only covers the PCIe link; on Hopper, NVLink (GPU-to-GPU communication within a node) remains plaintext. The result is that Hopper CC is limited to single-GPU confidential computation, not multi-GPU. Blackwell adds NVLink encryption to close this gap.
title: PPCIE

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Model Routing & Cascades: Cross-Model Cost - What: A model selection strategy that classifies the incoming query and selects the target model before any generation begins, as opposed to cascades that run a cheap model first and defer if confidence is low. - How it works: A lightweight classifier (e.g., RouteLLM's matrix-factorization router, or an embedding-based similarity classifier) analyzes query features — length, complexity signals, topic — and routes the request directly to the appropriate model tier. The routing decision is made in a few milliseconds before any LLM tokens are generated. - Why it matters: Pre-generation routing is faster and cheaper than cascades because it avoids the sunk cost of generating tokens with a cheap model that later gets overridden. A 2026 theoretical result confirms pre-generation routing is structurally superior on most benchmarks. - Gotcha: Pre-generation routing requires a classifier that is accurate enough to justify the routing decision without seeing the model's output. In contrast, cascades have a built-in quality feedback loop (the cheap model's confidence). Routing errors commit to the wrong model — there is no automatic fallback.

body: Serving pattern · appears on: PagedAttention vLLM v0 box: 'FCFS scheduler + preemption' - What: A vLLM v0 scheduling mechanism where an in-progress generation request can be evicted from GPU KV-cache memory (its KV state swapped to CPU or recomputed later) to make room for higher-priority requests, preventing system-wide stall. - How it works: Under the FCFS (First Come First Served) scheduler, when new requests arrive and GPU KV-cache pages are exhausted, vLLM preempts the longest-running (lowest-priority) requests by either swapping their KV blocks to CPU DRAM or dropping them entirely for recomputation. The page table mechanism (non-contiguous physical pages mapped via a logical page table) makes this feasible without memory copies of the full sequence. The preempted request is re-queued and its KV state recomputed when memory becomes available. - Why it matters: Preemption prevents head-of-line blocking where one very long request monopolises all KV-cache memory and starves shorter requests. It is what makes continuous batching workable in practice — without preemption, the system would OOM on the first long-context request. - Gotcha: Preemption with recomputation adds a latency spike for the preempted request (it must re-run prefill). In vLLM v1, the scheduler became prefix-aware, reducing unnecessary preemptions for shared-prefix requests. The default FCFS policy may be suboptimal for mixed-priority workloads. Note the mode: v1's default preemption mode is `RECOMPUTE`, not `SWAP` — recomputing prefill is cheaper than moving KV blocks over PCIe.
title: Preemption

body: Concept · appears on: Embedding & Reranker Serving: The Retrieval Half - What: A serving regime where latency and throughput are dominated by the prefill (forward pass) computation rather than autoregressive decode, because there is no token generation loop. - How it works: Embedding and reranker models perform a single forward pass over the input sequence and output a fixed-size representation or score. There is no KV cache to maintain, no decode loop, and no memory bandwidth bottleneck from incremental generation — compute is fully determined by input length and batch size. - Why it matters: Prefill-bound workloads have different optimal batching strategies than LLM decode; they benefit from large static batches sorted by token length to maximize GPU compute utilization, rather than continuous batching which is designed for the generate loop. - Gotcha: Continuous batching (designed for decode) is suboptimal for embedding/reranker serving. Static batches with `--max-batch-tokens` sorting by token length maximize throughput. Don't apply LLM serving architecture blindly to embedding models.
title: Prefill-Bound

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Disaggregated Prefill/Decode Serving - What: In a disaggregated architecture, the set of GPUs dedicated exclusively to computing KV caches from input prompts (the prefill phase), optimized for high FLOP/s throughput. - How it works: Requests from the router are sent to a prefill pool GPU, which runs the forward pass for all input tokens in parallel (prefill is a batched matmul — compute-bound). The prefill pool benefits from high-FLOP/s hardware and large batch sizes. After prefill, KV tensors are transferred to the decode pool. Prefill GPUs can be lower-memory GPUs if context lengths are short enough to fit KV in their VRAM. - Why it matters: Separating prefill workload allows it to be scaled independently from decode — during prefill-heavy traffic (RAG, long context), the prefill pool can be scaled up without adding decode capacity. - Gotcha: Prefill pool GPUs must have enough VRAM to hold the KV cache for the prompt before transfer — for 128k-token prompts and large models, this requires the same class of GPU as decode. Pool sizing must account for worst-case context lengths, not average.
title: Prefill pool

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Model Routing & Cascades: Cross-Model Cost - What: A three-level model routing architecture for cost optimization: a nano model (~$0.10/M tokens) for classification, a mid-tier model ($1–3/M) for standard generation, and a frontier model ($10–15/M) for complex hard-tail queries. - How it works: The router (e.g., RouteLLM classifier or Azure AI Foundry Model Router) directs each incoming request to the appropriate tier based on predicted difficulty. The nano tier handles simple classification and filtering; the mid tier handles the majority of generation tasks; the frontier tier handles complex reasoning, edge cases, and high-stakes queries. The routing decision adds <5% latency overhead. - Why it matters: This tiered architecture achieves 60–80% overall cost reduction versus routing all queries to the frontier tier, while maintaining quality parity on the vast majority of requests. Production deployments at scale make this the primary serving-layer cost lever. - Gotcha: The tier boundaries must be calibrated to the production query distribution; a tier calibrated on benchmark data may mis-route in production. Routing quality degrades for novel query types not well-represented in the classifier training data.

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Production Tuning (Observability): 'vLLM expose tương tự qua prometheus_client' - What: The official Python client library for Prometheus, which vLLM uses internally to expose inference metrics (queue depth, TTFT/TPOT histograms, cache-hit rate, etc.) at a '/metrics' HTTP endpoint scraped by Prometheus. - How it works: vLLM instruments its scheduler and engine with 'prometheus_client' Gauge, Histogram, and Counter objects. When '--enable-metrics' is set, the engine starts a metrics HTTP server (default port varies; SGLang uses :30000/metrics). Prometheus scrapes this endpoint on a configurable interval; Grafana dashboards visualise the time series. Key metrics include 'vllm:num_requests_running', 'vllm:num_requests_waiting', TTFT/TPOT histogram buckets, and KV cache utilisation. - Why it matters: Prometheus+Grafana is the production-standard observability stack for Kubernetes deployments. Exposing metrics via the standard prometheus_client library makes vLLM natively compatible with existing monitoring infrastructure — no custom exporters needed. KEDA autoscaling rules can also trigger on these Prometheus metrics (e.g., scale out when 'vllm:num_requests_waiting > 10'). - Gotcha: The metric names differ between vLLM and SGLang (SGLang uses a separate '--enable-metrics' flag and exposes at a different path). The previously documented 'kv_cache_usage_ratio' metric was removed from llama.cpp /metrics in a recent build — always verify metric names against the current engine version before building dashboards.

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Scaling Strategies (via research companion and deck line 921 Grafana reference) - What: The de facto open-source metrics collection (Prometheus) and visualization (Grafana) stack used for monitoring LLM serving systems. - How it works: vLLM, SGLang, and llm-d all expose Prometheus-format `/metrics` endpoints. Prometheus scrapes these at a configurable interval (typically 15s). Grafana renders time-series dashboards. KEDA queries Prometheus via PromQL to evaluate scale triggers. The deck references 'Grafana anomaly' detection in the debug flow. - Why it matters: Provides the observability infrastructure that KEDA-based autoscaling depends on. Without Prometheus scraping `vllm:num_requests_waiting`, the KEDA trigger cannot fire. Also the primary tool for diagnosing GPU utilization anomalies, queue buildup, and latency regressions. - Gotcha: Prometheus scrape intervals (default 15s) introduce a lag between a metric change and KEDA acting on it. For very fast traffic spikes (sub-15s), this lag means autoscaling reacts after the queue has already grown. Shorter scrape intervals increase Prometheus cardinality load.

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Production Tuning: Memory, Scheduling & Observability - What: The Prometheus-format HTTP metrics endpoint exposed by SGLang (port 30000/metrics) and vLLM (via prometheus_client) for scraping real-time serving health and performance data. - How it works: Enabled via --enable-metrics flag. The endpoint emits metrics including: num_running_reqs (active decode batch size), num_queue_reqs (waiting queue depth), TTFT histograms, TPOT histograms, KV cache hit rate, num_gpu_blocks (available/used), and request success/error counts. Standard Prometheus scrape → Grafana dashboard visualization. Supports alert rules on queue depth and latency percentiles. - Why it matters: The primary observability interface for production LLM serving; enables auto-scaling (KEDA on num_requests_waiting), latency SLO alerting, and capacity planning based on real workload data. - Gotcha: In llama.cpp, the kv_cache_usage_ratio metric was removed from /metrics in a recent build — scripts that monitor this metric will silently produce no data. Also, vLLM and SGLang use different metric names for the same concepts — check the specific engine's docs rather than assuming metric names are portable.

body: Security · appears on: Confidential Inference: TEE & the Attack Surface - What: A KV-cache timing side-channel attack (NDSS 2025) that reconstructs a victim's prompt with 99% accuracy by measuring TTFT variations caused by shared automatic prefix cache (APC) hits and misses. - How it works: An attacker probes the LLM API by submitting carefully crafted queries that share increasing prefix lengths with suspected victim prompts. When a prefix matches a victim's cached KV entry (APC hit), TTFT drops measurably (cache hit is faster). By binary-searching over token space and measuring TTFT differences, the attacker can recover the victim's prompt token-by-token. A Stanford ICML 2025 audit found 7 of 8 major caching APIs shared cache entries across users, 5 of which have since patched. - Why it matters: This attack makes shared prefix caches a direct privacy violation in multi-tenant serving. Any system using APC (which is on-by-default in vLLM v0.8+) without per-tenant isolation is potentially vulnerable to prompt reconstruction by other tenants. - Gotcha: PROMPTPEEK only works when the KV cache is shared across users. Per-tenant cache salting (vLLM Issue #16016) fully mitigates the attack by making cross-tenant APC hits impossible. But salting also eliminates cross-tenant cache efficiency gains — a direct security-vs-cost tradeoff.
title: PROMPTPEEK

For LLM autoscaling, a typical expression computes something like `histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(vllm:e2e_request_latency_seconds_bucket[2m]))` to get P99 TTFT. KEDA evaluates this expression on each polling tick and compares the result to a threshold. - Why it matters: PromQL allows KEDA to scale on derived, statistically meaningful signals (P99 TTFT, rate of waiting requests) rather than raw gauge values, enabling much tighter SLO-aligned autoscaling. - Gotcha: Writing correct PromQL for LLM scaling requires understanding histogram semantics and label cardinality. A common mistake is computing rate() over a window shorter than the scrape interval, yielding unreliable results. PromQL expressions used in KEDA should be validated in Grafana before deployment.

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ (research companion) - What: Quantization applied after a model has been fully trained in full precision, using only a small calibration dataset rather than retraining. GPTQ, AWQ, and GGUF K-quants are all PTQ methods. - How it works: PTQ methods minimize the quantization error at each layer (or globally) by solving a weight-adjustment optimization. The model's weights are adjusted once and the quantized model is frozen for inference. Calibration typically requires 128–512 samples from the training domain run in a forward pass. - Why it matters: PTQ is the dominant production approach because it requires no GPU-hours of retraining — a 70B model can be quantized in hours rather than weeks. All the serving frameworks (vLLM, SGLang, TRT-LLM) consume PTQ-quantized model artifacts. - Gotcha: PTQ accuracy is fundamentally limited by the information loss at quantization time. At very low bits (2–3 bit), PTQ methods struggle — QAT (quantization-aware training) becomes necessary but requires retraining. MR-GPTQ pushes PTQ to FP4 via Hadamard rotation.
title: PTQ

Requests in a continuous batch each point to their adapter's segment; SGMV fuses all adapter computations into one kernel call, amortizing kernel launch overhead and maximizing GPU utilization. - Why it matters: The foundational work that proved multi-LoRA batching is practical. Its SGMV kernel was directly adopted by vLLM (--enable-lora) and SGLang, becoming the de facto industry standard. - Gotcha: Punica's original 12x claim is over single-adapter serving, not over N separate servers. Throughput advantage depends on batch diversity—if all requests share one adapter, SGMV's advantage shrinks.

Serving clients (or the engine's Python SDK) call this to obtain the schema and pass it as 'response_format={"json_schema": model_json_schema()}'. XGrammar then compiles the JSON Schema into a grammar constraint. Instructor (a popular wrapper library) automates this flow. - Why it matters: Pydantic is the de-facto Python type annotation and validation standard; allowing Pydantic models as grammar input removes the need to write JSON Schema by hand, making structured generation accessible to Python-first users. It is the most ergonomic entry point to grammar-constrained decoding in practice. - Gotcha: Not all Pydantic features map to JSON Schema cleanly: validator functions, computed fields, and discriminated unions may produce schemas that are too complex for XGrammar's PDA, falling back to slower Outlines compilation. Always test schema compilation latency with production schemas before deploying.

title: PyTorch

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ - What: The most aggressive standard GGUF K-quant, averaging ~2.6 bits per weight. For an 8B model this yields ~2.7 GB VRAM; for a 70B model ~24 GB. - How it works: Uses the K-quant block scheme with very coarse quantization grids (effectively 2-bit for most tensors, with 4-bit scale blocks). The deck classifies quality as 'Noticeable' degradation. - Why it matters: Q2_K is a last-resort option when VRAM is extremely constrained — e.g., running a 70B model on a single 24 GB consumer GPU. It enables use cases that would otherwise be impossible but at significant quality cost. - Gotcha: The deck explicitly labels Q2_K 'last resort' (cực kỳ constrained). For most production scenarios quality loss is too large for customer-facing applications; use Q4_K_M or I-quants at ≥3 bits instead.
title: Q2_K

body: Quantization · appears on: Edge Deployment Flow - What: The most aggressive GGUF k-quant level, storing weights at approximately 2.6 bits per parameter, producing the smallest possible GGUF file at a noticeable quality cost. - How it works: Each weight block is quantized to 2 bits with per-block scaling factors stored at higher precision. The 'K' suffix denotes k-quant: mixed-precision within the block (some super-block scales stored at Q4 or Q6). For an 8B model, Q2_K yields roughly 2.7 GB and 24 GB for a 70B model. - Why it matters: Q2_K is the last resort for extremely memory-constrained deployment (e.g., 4 GB RAM devices) where loading any other format is impossible. - Gotcha: Quality drop is 'noticeable' per the deck (the research doc specifies math reasoning degrades first). It is not suitable for production use; I-quants with imatrix (IQ2_XS) can achieve better quality at similar sizes below Q3.
title: Q2_K

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization: Precision vs Performance; Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ - What: The recommended GGUF quantization variant for 8–12 GB GPU/CPU setups: a mixed 4-bit and 6-bit K-quant where attention weights use Q6 and FFN weights use Q4. - How it works: K-quants (the 'K' prefix) use a block-quantization scheme with higher-precision quantization for more sensitive tensors (attention vs FFN). Q4_K_M specifically assigns Q4_K to most blocks and Q6_K to attention tensors and feed-forward norm weights. BPW is ~4.5, yielding ~4.8 GB for 8B and ~43 GB for 70B models. Quality is ~1 MMLU-point below FP16. - Why it matters: Q4_K_M is the default recommended by llama.cpp for balanced quality/size trade-off. It achieves ~92–95% of FP16 quality and fits the 8B Llama-3 in under 5 GB, enabling single-tab browser inference via WebAssembly or local inference on M1/M2 Macs. - Gotcha: The 'M' (medium) vs 'S' (small) suffix affects which tensors get promoted to Q6; 'M' is generally preferred over 'S'. Do not confuse K-quants with legacy Q4_0 — K-quants are strictly better at the same bit-count.
title: Q4_K_M

body: Quantization · appears on: Edge Deployment Flow - What: The recommended GGUF k-quant level, storing weights at approximately 4.5 bits per parameter with mixed Q4/Q6 quantization across tensor types, achieving approximately 92–95% of FP16 quality at roughly 4.6 GB for an 8B model. - How it works: The 'K' indicates k-quant (per-block mixed precision); 'M' means medium size variant (vs 'S' for small). Attention weight tensors receive slightly higher precision (Q6 bits within the block) while FFN tensors use Q4. Super-block scaling factors are stored at Q4/Q6. For 70B models, Q4_K_M uses approximately 43 GB. - Why it matters: Q4_K_M is the default for local and edge inference in 2026 because it fits 8B models in 6–8 GB of RAM while retaining near-production quality. Ollama, llama.cpp, and the deck all recommend it as the primary edge format. - Gotcha: The MMLU quality drop is approximately 1 point. For models smaller than 7B, quality degradation is more severe; use Q6_K or Q8_0 for sub-7B models when accuracy matters.
title: Q4_K_M

body: Quantization · appears on: Edge Deployment Flow - What: A GGUF k-quant level storing weights at approximately 6.6 bits per parameter, described as 'near-lossless' quality at roughly 6.1 GB for an 8B model. - How it works: Uses 6-bit quantization within each block with Q8 super-block scaling factors. Quality is very close to FP16 (approximately 0.1–0.2 perplexity above). For 70B models, Q6_K uses approximately 56 GB. - Why it matters: Q6_K is the choice when quality is paramount but FP16 memory is unavailable (e.g., a 12 GB GPU running a 7B–8B model, or a Mac with 16 GB unified memory). It avoids the noticeable quality gap of Q4 while still fitting in constrained contexts. - Gotcha: Near-lossless does not mean lossless; benchmarks such as MMLU still show minor degradation. On the same hardware, Q6_K is faster to load from disk than Q8_0 while nearly matching its quality.
title: Q6_K

body: Quantization · appears on: Edge Deployment Flow - What: The highest-quality GGUF quantization level, storing weights at 8 bits per parameter with a simpler block-linear scheme, offering maximum quality at the cost of largest file size (approximately 8.1 GB for an 8B model). - How it works: Each block is quantized to 8 bits with a single FP32 scaling factor ('_0' = no super-block). No mixed-precision within blocks. At 8 bits the quantization noise is nearly imperceptible; perplexity is within 0.01–0.05 of FP16. For 70B models, Q8_0 uses approximately 72 GB. - Why it matters: Q8_0 is used when the highest possible local inference quality is needed and memory is sufficient, such as on systems with 16+ GB RAM. It is also the standard format for academic GGUF quality benchmarking. - Gotcha: Q8_0 is not always faster than Q4_K_M at runtime; it requires more memory bandwidth to load weights, which can reduce tokens/second on memory-bandwidth-limited CPUs. On GPU, the larger file can exceed VRAM and force CPU offload.
title: Q8_0

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization: Precision vs Performance (research companion) - What: NVIDIA's technique for recovering accuracy after NVFP4 quantization by distilling from a BF16 teacher model using KL-divergence loss during a short fine-tuning pass. - How it works: A BF16 reference model and the NVFP4 student model run in parallel on calibration data. The KL divergence between their output distributions is minimized, adjusting the student's weights to match the teacher's behavior. Used to produce official NVFP4 checkpoints for Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B and other NVIDIA models. - Why it matters: QAD bridges the accuracy gap between PTQ FP4 and BF16 baselines, enabling NVFP4 deployment at 'near-BF16' quality. It is the required post-processing step for the highest-quality NVFP4 models. - Gotcha: The widely circulated '99.4% of BF16' figure for QAD is a marketing/forum claim absent from the paper, the blog, and any model card. The verifiable claim is 'near-BF16' — no specific number is published. Do not cite 99.4% in technical writing.
title: QAD

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ (research companion) - What: A training methodology where quantization noise is simulated during the forward pass of training (using straight-through estimators for gradients), allowing the model to learn weight distributions that tolerate quantization better. - How it works: Fake quantization nodes are inserted after weight tensors during training. The forward pass rounds weights to quantized values; the backward pass uses straight-through gradients through the rounding. Gemma 3 QAT (Apr 2025) reduced perplexity drop by 54% vs naive Q4_0. EfficientQAT trained a 2-bit Llama-2-70B on one A100 in 41 hours. - Why it matters: QAT achieves significantly better quality than PTQ at the same bit-width, particularly at 2–4 bits. It is the approach used by Google (Gemma 3) and NVIDIA (QAD for NVFP4) to ship official quantized models. - Gotcha: QAT requires access to training infrastructure and the training data, making it impractical for end-user model adaptation. It is primarily used by model providers to release official quantized checkpoints — users rely on these artifacts rather than running QAT themselves.
title: QAT

body: Simulating quantization during training so the model adapts to the error. Distinct from QLoRA.
title: QAT

body: Quantization · appears on: FP4 2026: MXFP4 vs NVFP4 & KV Cache Quantization - What: A 1-bit sketching transform used as TurboQuant's second stage to remove the inner-product bias introduced by MSE-optimal quantization. - How it works: The Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma says random projection into a lower dimension approximately preserves distances. QJL quantizes that projection to a single bit per coordinate and applies it to the residual left by the first-stage quantizer, producing an unbiased estimate of the query·key inner product. - Why it matters: Attention needs accurate inner products, not merely low reconstruction error. A quantizer tuned for MSE can be systematically biased in exactly the quantity attention consumes, so the correction is what makes aggressive KV quantization safe. - Gotcha: QJL is a bias-correction stage, not a standalone compressor — quoting it as “1-bit KV cache” misstates the method. The bit budget people should quote is the combined 3.5 bits/channel.
title: QJL

body: Directly rescales query/key projections when attention logits explode — attacks the root cause of divergence rather than the symptom.
title: QK-Clip

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ - What: A parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that loads the base model in NF4 4-bit quantization while training small low-rank adapter weights (LoRA) in BF16, enabling fine-tuning of large models on constrained GPU hardware. - How it works: The frozen base model weights are quantized to NF4 with double quantization. LoRA adapters (low-rank matrices inserted at each attention layer) are trained in BF16. Gradients flow through the NF4 weights using bitsandbytes' custom 4-bit backward pass. The deck recommends QLoRA specifically for 'fine-tune on 1 GPU'. - Why it matters: QLoRA made it practical to fine-tune 65B–70B models on a single 48 GB GPU (e.g., A6000 or A100 40 GB). It is the dominant technique for domain adaptation without multi-GPU infrastructure. - Gotcha: QLoRA inference after training requires either merging the adapter back into FP16 weights (and re-quantizing for serving) or using bitsandbytes at inference — the latter is slower than production AWQ/GPTQ. Merged QLoRA models often underperform equivalent full fine-tunes due to accumulated NF4 rounding error.
title: QLoRA

body: 4-bit NF4 quantized frozen base + bf16 LoRA adapters; only adapters train. Dettmers et al., 2023.
title: QLoRA

body: Gradients still flow through the quantized base to reach adapters, so QLoRA is slower than bf16 LoRA even though it is lighter.
title: QLoRA speed caveat

title: Quality Gate
