title: Quality gate

body: Concept · appears on: Quantization: Precision vs Performance; Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ - What: The process of representing model weights (and optionally activations) in lower-precision numeric formats to reduce VRAM usage and increase compute throughput at the cost of some accuracy. - How it works: Each weight value that normally occupies 16 or 32 bits is mapped to a smaller integer or floating-point representation. A scale factor (and sometimes a zero-point) is stored per-tensor, per-channel, or per-group to allow approximate reconstruction of the original value at inference time. - Why it matters: A single 8B-parameter model in FP32 consumes ~31.6 GB VRAM; at AWQ 4-bit that drops to ~4.5 GB, enabling deployment on consumer GPUs and cutting memory-bandwidth cost, which is the dominant latency driver during autoregressive decode. - Gotcha: Quality degradation is non-linear: models below 7B lose accuracy faster per bit reduced than 13B+ models. Always benchmark perplexity (and task-specific metrics) after quantizing; leaderboard rankings do not always predict real-task outcomes.
title: Quantization

body: GGUF (1.5–8 bit, CPU/edge) vs safetensors + AWQ/GPTQ (INT4, GPU engines) vs native FP8 (H100/Blackwell-class).
title: Quantization formats are not interchangeable

meta.section: GLOSSARY — Day 10: Data Pipeline & Data Observability

title: Query-Based CDC

body: Metric · appears on: Latency Taxonomy: TTFT · TPOT · Goodput - What: The number of incoming requests waiting in the prefill queue at any given moment, i.e., requests that have been accepted but not yet started prefill processing. - How it works: Tracked as a time-series counter by the serving engine scheduler. When queue depth grows, newly arriving requests wait longer before prefill begins, directly increasing their TTFT. Queue depth is the primary saturation indicator — a non-zero, growing queue means the system has hit prefill capacity. - Why it matters: Queue depth is used as a Kubernetes autoscaling signal (e.g., vLLM production-stack scales on `vllm:num_requests_waiting` via KEDA). Monitoring queue depth in real time distinguishes whether high TTFT stems from compute limits or from a scheduling/routing imbalance. - Gotcha: Queue depth is a leading indicator of TTFT degradation, not a lagging one. By the time P95 TTFT violations appear in dashboards, queue depth has usually been elevated for seconds to minutes. Under prefill–decode disaggregation, queue depth at the prefill pod and at the decode pod are separate metrics with different autoscaling triggers.
title: Queue Depth

body: Metric · appears on: Production Tuning: Memory, Scheduling & Observability - What: The number of requests waiting in the serving engine's pending queue (not yet admitted to the active decode batch), used as the primary saturation signal in production LLM serving. - How it works: Engines report this as num_queue_reqs (SGLang) or vllm:num_requests_waiting (vLLM) on the Prometheus endpoint. The practical operating range is 100–2,000 waiting requests; above ~2,000 the system is saturated and new requests will experience unacceptable TTFT. KEDA autoscalers use this metric to trigger horizontal scaling. - Why it matters: GPU utilization is misleading for LLM serving (LLMs are memory-bandwidth-bound and run at high GPU utilization even when underloaded); queue depth is the correct saturation proxy. The standard KEDA HPA pattern uses vllm:num_requests_waiting > threshold to trigger pod scale-out. - Gotcha: Queue depth can spike transiently during prefill-heavy batches (long prompts block admission) even when the system is not truly saturated. Use a sustained (>60s) queue depth threshold for autoscaling to avoid flapping. Target queue range 100–2,000; alert at >2,000.
title: Queue depth

body: Metric · appears on: Auto-scaling Architecture, Scaling Strategies - What: The number of inference requests currently waiting in the engine's scheduler queue, not yet dispatched to a GPU batch. - How it works: Exposed as a Prometheus metric (e.g. `vllm:num_requests_waiting` in vLLM). KEDA polls this metric via a PromQL query and compares it to a threshold (e.g. > 10 requests). When threshold is crossed, KEDA adds replicas. The Gateway API Inference Extension's Endpoint Picker also uses queue depth per-replica for routing decisions. - Why it matters: Queue depth is a leading indicator of overload — requests start queuing before GPU utilization saturates, making it a faster scale-out trigger. It is the 2025 production standard KEDA scaling metric for LLM serving, replacing CPU/GPU utilization HPA. - Gotcha: Queue depth of >10 is a heuristic, not a universal constant — the right threshold depends on model size, batch size, and SLO targets. A queue of 10 short requests at a small model may clear in milliseconds; at a 70B model they may accumulate hundreds of milliseconds of TTFT penalty before the new replica is ready.
title: Queue Depth

body: scale LLM replicas on `vllm:num_requests_waiting` (KEDA Prometheus trigger), not GPU% (ambiguous). KV pressure (`kv_cache_usage_perc`) is the leading indicator.
title: Queue-depth autoscaling

body: Alibaba's Qwen3 post-training uses offline + online RL with GSPO, whose sequence-level importance ratio stabilizes RL for its Mixture-of-Experts architecture. _(deck: §9.1b line 1540 (recipe table, row 'Qwen3 (Alibaba)'))_
title: Qwen3

body: Concept · appears on: Pipeline Parallelism (Optimal Chunk Size): 'Qwen3-235B: 6K fixed hoặc 18K dynamic' - What: Alibaba's 235-billion-parameter MoE model (Qwen 3 family) used in the deck as the second reference model for pipeline parallelism chunk-size tuning, alongside DeepSeek-V3.1. - How it works: Qwen3-235B uses a different MoE architecture than DeepSeek-V3 (different expert count, activation ratio, and per-layer size), resulting in different optimal PP chunk sizes: 6K tokens fixed or 18K dynamic (smooth factor 0.8) — larger than DeepSeek-V3.1's 4K/12K because Qwen3-235B's per-layer activation tensors are smaller relative to the pipeline communication overhead. Kimi K2 benchmarks report 224k prefill / 288k decode tok/s on 128×H200 using SGLang+OME for this model family scale. - Why it matters: Including Qwen3-235B alongside DeepSeek-V3.1 in the PP chunk-size frame teaches that optimal chunking is model-architecture-specific (not a universal constant) and must be tuned per-model. Qwen3-235B is also notable as an open MoE model that can run on a single GB200 NVL72 system in FP8. - Gotcha: The 6K/18K chunk-size figures apply to the specific Qwen3-235B A22B (22B active) architecture under pipeline parallelism; they will not apply to denser Qwen3 variants (Qwen3-32B is dense, not MoE). Always run a small chunk-size sweep when first deploying a new model under PP.
title: Qwen3-235B

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Embedding & Reranker Serving: The Retrieval Half - What: An embedding model from Alibaba's Qwen3 series; the 8B variant held MTEB Multilingual rank 1 as of mid-2026 with 70.58 score across 100+ languages and 32K context window. - How it works: Built on the Qwen3 decoder backbone, converted to an encoder-style embedding model via mean-pooling or [EOS] pooling. Supports MRL for flexible dimension truncation. Achieves state-of-the-art multilingual performance by leveraging Qwen3's large multilingual pretraining corpus. - Why it matters: Sets the current quality ceiling for production embedding deployments as of 2026. With 32K context and multilingual capability, it covers both long-document and cross-language retrieval use cases. - Gotcha: As a Qwen3-series model it benefits from FP8 quantization for throughput; at FP8 it achieves ~50% throughput improvement with >99% cosine similarity retention. The 8B size requires dedicated hosting — not suitable for colocation with large LLMs.
title: Qwen3-Embedding

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Embedding & Reranker Serving: The Retrieval Half - What: Alibaba's cross-encoder reranker model from the Qwen3 series, designed for high-precision document relevance scoring in the second stage of a retrieve-then-rerank pipeline. - How it works: Qwen3-Reranker-8B takes (query, document) pairs as input and produces a relevance score via a classification head on the pooled representation. Built on the Qwen3 backbone, it benefits from the same multilingual and long-context capabilities as Qwen3-Embedding but is optimized for pointwise relevance scoring rather than embedding production. - Why it matters: Paired with Qwen3-Embedding-8B, it provides a coherent high-quality retrieval pipeline using models from the same family. Cross-encoders like Qwen3-Reranker-8B significantly improve retrieval precision over bi-encoder-only approaches for high-stakes RAG applications. - Gotcha: Cross-encoder rerankers are significantly more computationally expensive per document than bi-encoders — typically 10–100x more FLOPs per scored pair. In production, they should only be applied to the top-K candidates (20–100 docs) from the bi-encoder retrieval stage.
title: Qwen3-Reranker

body: Concept · appears on: Multimodal (VLM) Serving: 'Qwen3-VL ~1,139' tokens; 'SGLang 2E1P ... Qwen3-VL-235B' - What: Alibaba's Qwen 3 Vision-Language Model family, including the Qwen3-VL-235B variant, used in the deck as the primary benchmark model for EPD disaggregation and image-token-explosion quantification. - How it works: Qwen3-VL encodes 1080p images into approximately 1,139 visual tokens (lower than Pixtral's 4,096 due to a more aggressive ViT compression scheme). For Qwen3-VL-235B, SGLang's 2E1P EPD disaggregation (two Encode workers, one Prefill worker, independent Decode pool) achieves approximately 6–8x TTFT reduction compared to collocated serving, because the ViT encoder stage can process images in parallel across multiple CPUs/GPUs without waiting for the LLM prefill/decode pipeline. - Why it matters: Qwen3-VL-235B is the largest open-weight VLM as of mid-2026 and demonstrates the scaling of EPD disaggregation to frontier models. Its ~1,139 tokens/image figure establishes that even 'efficient' VLMs add thousands of prefill tokens per image, making VLM serving fundamentally different from text-only LLM serving in its TTFT characteristics. - Gotcha: The 1,139 token figure is for 1080p input; lower-resolution images produce proportionally fewer tokens. Qwen3-VL's ViT encoder does not benefit from tensor parallelism (ViT is not TP-friendly; performance degrades at TP=8) — EPD disaggregation is required to scale encoder throughput independently.
title: Qwen3-VL

body: The prefactor that keeps the expected update per rank-1 component constant across ranks — which is why the optimal learning rate is nearly rank-independent.
title: `α/r` scaling

body: R1-Zero: base model + RLVR only, no SFT cold-start; learns to reason but produces ugly mixed-language traces. R1: small SFT cold-start + RLVR; cleaner format with the same reasoning.
title: R1-Zero vs R1

body: Caching · appears on: KV Cache & PagedAttention - What: SGLang's prefix-sharing mechanism that stores all cached KV blocks in a radix tree indexed at the token level, enabling exact prefix reuse across requests that share a common prefix. - How it works: Each node in the radix tree corresponds to a KV block. Incoming requests walk the tree to find the longest matching prefix; only the unmatched suffix needs to be computed. Unlike vLLM's 16-token block hashing, RadixAttention matches at token granularity, yielding 75–95% hit rates on multi-turn or RAG workloads with shared system prompts. - Why it matters: RAG pipelines, multi-turn conversations, and agent systems reuse system prompts and retrieved context repeatedly. Prefix sharing directly converts those repeat prefill FLOPs into a cache lookup, dramatically reducing TTFT and saving GPU compute budget for new tokens. - Gotcha: Also called 'Prefix Sharing' in the deck's §3. RadixAttention requires that system prompts and static context always appear first in the sequence (before dynamic content) to preserve prefix stability — any dynamic token inserted early breaks the shared prefix and collapses hit rates.
title: RadixAttention

body: Attention / KV · appears on: Inference Engine Evolution: 2020 → 2025; Prefix Caching: RadixAttention, APC, HiCache & Pricing - What: SGLang's token-level radix-tree (prefix trie) data structure for KV cache management, enabling O(L) prefix lookup and cache sharing at finer granularity than vLLM's block-hashing approach. - How it works: SGLang organizes all cached KV entries into a radix tree where each node corresponds to a sequence of tokens and holds a pointer to the KV cache for those tokens. On a new request, SGLang walks the tree to find the longest matching prefix and reuses its KV cache, computing only the suffix. On a cache miss, the tree is updated. This achieves 75–95% cache-hit rates on multi-turn workloads with shared system prompts, vs vLLM APC's 16-token block granularity. - Why it matters: Enables up to 5–6.4x higher throughput vs naive serving on RAG and multi-turn workloads; finer granularity than vLLM's block-level hashing means higher hit rates when prefixes don't align to 16-token boundaries. - Gotcha: RadixAttention benefits degrade on workloads with unique, non-repeating prefixes (e.g., single-turn creative generation) — for those, it adds tree-management overhead with no cache benefit. Also, the radix tree lives in GPU VRAM; with HiCache, overflowing to DRAM/disk extends this.
title: RadixAttention

body: Cosine similarity has no time dimension, so stale chunks score as high as fresh ones — a silent failure; mitigated with TTLs, NN-overlap, orphan-chunk GC.

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Distributed Inference: Parallelism Strategy Guide - What: The distributed computing framework used by vLLM to manage multi-node GPU deployments, handling device mesh creation, worker scheduling, and collective communication coordination. - How it works: Initialized with `ray start --head` on the head node and `ray start --address=...` on worker nodes. vLLM uses Ray actors to spawn per-GPU workers, which coordinate via NCCL for TP All-Reduce and PP P2P. Ray automatically manages the device mesh topology. Example: `--tensor-parallel-size 4 --pipeline-parallel-size 2` on 2 nodes of 4 GPUs each = 8 GPUs total. - Why it matters: Provides the process management, fault tolerance, and distributed scheduling layer that vLLM needs for multi-node serving without custom MPI or Kubernetes-level job orchestration. - Gotcha: Ray's device mesh is automatically managed but its network auto-detection can fail in complex cluster topologies. Always set `NCCL_IB_HCA` explicitly. Ray cluster requires all nodes to have matching Python/CUDA/vLLM versions—version drift causes silent failures.
title: Ray Cluster

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Scaling Strategies (via research companion §12) - What: Ray Serve's native LLM deployment abstraction (announced Nov 2025) that provides prefill/decode disaggregation, Wide Expert Parallelism, and production autoscaling for large models. - How it works: Uses `build_pd_openai_app` to construct a disaggregated P/D serving pipeline on Ray. Prefill and decode nodes are separate Ray actors that communicate via Ray's object store. Wide-EP (Expert Parallelism across many GPUs) is supported for MoE models. Benchmarked at 2,400 tok/s per H200. - Why it matters: Ray Serve LLM provides a Python-native, research-to-production path for teams already using Ray for training. The P/D disaggregation support matches the 2025–26 production architecture without requiring Kubernetes-specific tooling. - Gotcha: Ray Serve LLM's disaggregation (`build_pd_openai_app`) is a higher-level abstraction than llm-d or NVIDIA Dynamo and has less K8s-native observability integration out of the box. Teams adopting it should factor in Ray cluster management overhead.
title: Ray Serve LLM

body: Hardware · appears on: Disaggregated Prefill/Decode (Systems 2026): 'Mooncake ... RDMA zero-copy' - What: A network technology that allows one machine to read from or write to the memory of another machine without involving either machine's CPU or OS kernel, achieving near-memory-bandwidth inter-node data transfer with microsecond latency. - How it works: RDMA operates via NIC hardware (InfiniBand HCAs or RoCE-capable Ethernet NICs) that implement memory registration, completion queues, and direct DMA between the initiating machine's registered memory region and the target's registered memory region. In LLM serving (Mooncake, NIXL), GPU KV-cache blocks are registered with the RDMA NIC (via GPUDirect RDMA), allowing a decode GPU on node B to pull KV blocks directly from a prefill GPU's HBM on node A at rates approaching NVLink bandwidth across InfiniBand links. - Why it matters: KV transfer between prefill and decode pools in disaggregated serving involves moving 10s to 100s of GB of KV tensors per second. CPU-mediated network copies would introduce latencies and throughput bottlenecks that negate the serving gains from disaggregation. RDMA zero-copy is what makes P/D disaggregation viable at production scale. - Gotcha: GPUDirect RDMA requires specific NIC and GPU firmware combinations and is supported differently across NVIDIA (via NCCL/NIXL), AMD (ROCm GPUDirect), and other platforms. The 'NCCL_IB_HCA=mlx5' environment variable in the deck configures NCCL to use the Mellanox/NVIDIA ConnectX-5/6/7 InfiniBand HCA for collective communications.

body: Decoding · appears on: Structured Generation (Grammar-Constrained Output): 'Formats: JSON Schema, EBNF, Regex, Pydantic model' - What: A format constraint where the model's output is forced to match a regular expression pattern — the simplest form of grammar-constrained decoding, compiled to a Finite State Machine (FSM) token mask. - How it works: The regex is compiled to a deterministic FSM over the vocabulary (Outlines' original contribution, now also supported by XGrammar). At each decode step, the FSM's current state determines which tokens are valid next transitions; the engine masks logits accordingly. For patterns like phone numbers ('\d{3}-\d{3}-\d{4}') or fixed-format identifiers, the FSM is small and fast. XGrammar handles regex via its generalised PDA framework. - Why it matters: Regex is the lowest-overhead constraint for simple structured outputs: dates, IDs, codes, enumerations. Unlike JSON Schema, a regex constraint adds near-zero TPOT overhead because the FSM is tiny. It is the building block that all grammar-constrained decoding systems originally implemented before advancing to context-free grammars. - Gotcha: Regular expressions cannot express context-sensitive patterns (balanced brackets, matching keys to values) — those require EBNF/PDA. Large or ambiguous regexes can produce exponentially large FSMs that blow XGrammar's compilation budget, triggering fallback. Unicode character classes and lookaheads are often unsupported or slow.

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Production Tuning: Memory, Scheduling & Observability - What: A debugging utility in SGLang that replays a recorded request dump file to reproduce crashes or unexpected behavior in a controlled environment. - How it works: SGLang maintains a rolling 5-minute request buffer in memory (crash dump). On a server crash or on demand, this buffer is serialized to disk. replay_request_dump.py reads the dump and re-submits each request to a fresh engine instance in the same order, reproducing the exact sequence that triggered the issue. - Why it matters: LLM serving bugs are often sequence-dependent (a specific combination of concurrent long and short requests triggers OOM or a kernel bug) — replaying the exact request sequence on the same engine+config is the only reliable way to reproduce them. - Gotcha: Replay requires identical engine configuration (same model, same flags, same GPU) — using a different GPU model or driver version may not reproduce hardware-specific bugs. The 5-minute rolling window means crashes triggered by slow-accumulating state (e.g., prefix cache fragmentation over hours) may not be capturable.
title: replay_request_dump.py

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Scaling Strategies - What: A single instance of a model-serving pod (container) running on one or more GPUs, capable of independently handling inference requests. - How it works: In Kubernetes, a replica corresponds to one Pod in a Deployment or StatefulSet. Each replica loads a full copy of the model (or a tensor-parallel shard for multi-GPU models). The autoscaler adjusts the number of replicas by setting the `spec.replicas` field. Scale-to-zero means setting replicas = 0. - Why it matters: Replicas are the fundamental unit of horizontal scaling. Replica count directly controls serving capacity, cost, and fault tolerance. Most KEDA-based scaling policies express their target in terms of replicas per unit of queue depth or load. - Gotcha: For models served with tensor parallelism (TP > 1), a single 'replica' occupies multiple GPUs. Auto-scalers track replica count, not GPU count, so the node pool must have multi-GPU nodes available when TP replicas scale out. This complicates node auto-provisioning calculations.
title: Replica

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Scaling Strategies - What: A time interval (e.g. 50 ms) during which the serving engine accumulates incoming requests before dispatching them together as a single GPU batch. - How it works: The scheduler holds new arriving requests for up to the window duration, collecting them into a batch. Once the window expires (or a maximum batch size is reached, whichever comes first), the full batch is sent to the GPU together. This amortizes the fixed overhead of a GPU kernel launch and memory access across more tokens in parallel. - Why it matters: Batching is the primary mechanism for increasing GPU utilization and throughput. The deck claims a 50 ms batching window yields +40% throughput. It trades a small amount of added first-token latency (up to 50 ms) for substantially higher hardware efficiency. - Gotcha: A fixed batching window is a static approximation; modern engines use continuous batching (also called iteration-level scheduling) where requests join and leave mid-batch at each decode step, making a fixed window unnecessary for the decode phase. The 50 ms window primarily applies to the prefill accumulation stage. Choosing too large a window degrades TTFT SLOs; too small wastes GPU compute.

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Structured Generation: 'API: OpenAI-compat response_format={json_schema}' - What: An OpenAI-compatible API request field that instructs the serving engine to enforce a specific JSON Schema on the model's output, guaranteeing the response parses as valid JSON matching the schema. - How it works: Clients pass 'response_format={"type": "json_schema", "json_schema": {"name": "...", "schema": {...}}}' in the chat-completions request body. The server extracts the schema, compiles it into the grammar backend (XGrammar by default), and applies token masking at each decode step. The 'strict: true' sub-field requests zero-deviation enforcement (vs best-effort). The response body contains a JSON string in the 'content' field guaranteed to conform to the schema. - Why it matters: This is the standard wire protocol for structured generation in production — it decouples schema enforcement from client-side prompt engineering and allows engine-level optimization (compiled grammar, jump-forward). Any vLLM, SGLang, or TRT-LLM deployment with OpenAI-compat endpoints supports this field. - Gotcha: OpenAI's strict mode previously disabled parallel function calling; as of ~May 2025 these now coexist (except for fine-tuned models calling multiple functions). The 'json_schema' type requires the schema to be serialisable to EBNF/PDA; recursive schemas and $ref resolution edge cases can trigger fallback to slower compilation paths.

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Production SLA: Best Practices - What: Matching the GPU tier and memory capacity to the actual model size and traffic requirements, avoiding over-provisioning. The deck example: do not use an A100 for a 7B model. - How it works: A 7B model at FP16 requires ~14 GB of GPU memory for weights; an A100 80 GB is overkill and cost-inefficient vs an RTX 4090 (24 GB, ~4x lower cost per hour) or a single L40S (48 GB). Right-sizing analysis computes model weight memory + KV cache memory at peak batch, then selects the smallest GPU tier that satisfies SLO throughput requirements. LMDeploy, vLLM, and SGLang expose memory profiling flags to measure KV cache headroom at different batch sizes. - Why it matters: Over-provisioning on large GPUs is the single most common cost waste in production LLM deployments. A100 instances on AWS cost ~$3.27/hr vs an L4 at ~$0.81/hr; for a 7B model the L4 satisfies most SLOs at 4x lower cost. - Gotcha: Right-sizing must account for KV cache memory at peak batch, not just model weights. A 7B model at batch 256 with 4096-token context can consume 30+ GB of KV cache on top of 14 GB weights, overflowing a 24 GB card. Profile under realistic load before committing to an instance type.

body: Hardware · appears on: Attention Backend Selection: 'ROCm / Ascend / CPU → triton'; Triton 'cross-platform fallback (ROCm...)' - What: AMD's open-source GPU computing platform (ROCm — Radeon Open Compute) that provides CUDA-equivalent programming APIs, libraries (rocBLAS, rocFFT, hipBLAS), and compilers for AMD Instinct GPUs (MI300X, MI355X) — the primary non-NVIDIA GPU compute stack supported by vLLM and SGLang. - How it works: ROCm implements the HIP (Heterogeneous-compute Interface for Portability) API, which is largely source-compatible with CUDA. vLLM and SGLang use Triton as the cross-platform kernel layer on ROCm: the '--attention-backend triton' flag selects Triton-compiled attention kernels that run on both CUDA and ROCm/HIP. AMD MI300X and MI355X achieve H100-comparable throughput on ROCm for FP8/BF16 workloads; MI355X reached B200 parity at MLPerf v6.0. MORI-IO (AMD, Apr 2026) demonstrated 2.5x goodput on MI300X for P/D disaggregated serving. - Why it matters: ROCm support in vLLM/SGLang broadens deployment options beyond NVIDIA hardware: AMD MI300X/MI355X offer competitive performance at potentially lower cost (Intel Gaudi 3 ~2x price/perf vs H100). As HBM supply is sold out globally in 2026, ROCm-compatible AMD GPUs provide an alternative procurement path for operators who cannot access NVIDIA allocations. - Gotcha: Triton-compiled kernels on ROCm do not achieve the same throughput as CUDA-specific kernels (FA3/FA4) on equivalent AMD hardware because Triton's ROCm backend is less mature than its CUDA backend. FlashAttention-4 is CUDA/SM100-specific and does not run on ROCm; the highest-performance attention backend on MI300X remains FlashInfer's HIP port or Triton.

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Serving Cho RL: Rollout Là Một Workload Riêng - What: The inference server used to generate trajectories during reinforcement-learning post-training — in 2026 practice, the same vLLM or SGLang you serve production traffic with. - How it works: RL pipelines separate the trainer (FSDP, Megatron, DeepSpeed) from generation, and hand generation to an inference server built for it: continuous batching, paged KV cache, prefix reuse. The loop is generate → train → sync weights, repeated every step. - Why it matters: It makes RL post-training an inference-infrastructure problem as much as a training one — the serving techniques from this day apply directly to the rollout half of RLHF/GRPO. - Gotcha: Day 20 owns the serving side (rollout engine, sleep/wake, weight transfer, elasticity). The RL algorithms themselves — PPO, GRPO, DPO — belong to Days 21–22; do not re-teach them here.

body: Attention / KV · appears on: Attention Architecture: MHA → MLA & Long-Context - What: A position encoding scheme used in LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, and most modern open-weight LLMs, where position information is injected by rotating query and key vectors at each layer. - How it works: For a position p, query/key vectors are multiplied by a rotation matrix R(p) based on their dimension index and position. Relative position between tokens is captured by the dot product Q_p · K_q = Q · R(p-q)^T · K, encoding distance without explicit absolute position tokens. YaRN and similar methods extend this by interpolating the rotation frequencies. - Why it matters: RoPE's relative-position property makes it compatible with context extension techniques like YaRN (which rescale the rotation frequencies). Understanding RoPE is necessary to understand why YaRN works and what limits naive extension beyond training context. - Gotcha: RoPE frequencies have a maximum useful resolution that degrades when positions exceed the training context by a large factor without interpolation. YaRN applies different interpolation factors to different frequency bands to preserve resolution.
title: RoPE

body: Rotary Position Embedding — encodes token position as a rotation at a spectrum of frequencies. All the extension methods below reshape that spectrum.
title: RoPE

body: Rotary positional encoding extensions for long-context. NTK = "neural-tangent-kernel" rescaling; YaRN = combination interpolation; LongRoPE = per-dimension search.
title: RoPE / NTK / YaRN / LongRoPE

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Scaling Strategies - What: The baseline load-balancing policy that cycles requests sequentially across replicas in a fixed rotation, ignoring current worker state. - How it works: Each new request is sent to the next replica in a circular queue, regardless of how many requests each replica currently has or whether any KV-cache reuse is possible. Simple to implement and stateless. - Why it matters: Round-robin is the default in many reverse proxies (nginx, HAProxy) and is the baseline against which smarter policies are measured. It is explicitly the baseline in the deck's least-busy routing claim (+30%) and the vLLM production-stack benchmark (3–10x lower TTFT). - Gotcha: Round-robin can cause severe load imbalance when request durations vary widely — common in LLM serving where a reasoning-model response may take 10–100x longer than a short classification request. Using it in production LLM serving is a well-known anti-pattern.
title: Round-Robin

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Model Routing & Cascades: Cross-Model Cost - What: An open-source pre-generation router (ICLR 2025) that classifies incoming queries and routes them to a cheap or expensive LLM based on predicted difficulty, achieving ~85% cost reduction while maintaining 95% of frontier model quality. - How it works: RouteLLM trains a matrix-factorization classifier on human preference data (e.g., Chatbot Arena) to predict whether a query requires a strong (frontier) model or a weak (cheap) model. The classifier runs before any LLM generation; it adds minimal latency (<5% routing overhead) and selects between models in a configured pair. - Why it matters: Most production query distributions are bimodal: simple factual questions need only a cheap model, while complex reasoning requires a frontier model. RouteLLM exploits this to cut API costs dramatically without visible quality degradation on the majority of queries. - Gotcha: RouteLLM's 85% cost reduction is measured on the MT-Bench benchmark distribution, which may not match production traffic. Real-world gains depend heavily on the query distribution; a creative-writing-heavy workload may see smaller savings than a mixed FAQ workload.
title: RouteLLM

body: The learned gate that assigns tokens to experts in an MoE. Vendors disable router fine-tuning by default for stability.
title: Router

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Data Parallelism: DP, DPA & Cache-Aware Router - What: SGLang sgl-router CLI flag that activates cache-aware load balancing, routing requests to the worker with the best KV prefix cache match rather than round-robin. - How it works: Instructs sgl-router to compute prefix match scores against each worker's cached prefix tree for every incoming request, then select the worker with the highest score above `--cache-threshold`. Falls back to least-loaded routing if no worker exceeds the threshold. - Why it matters: Enables the +92% throughput / +275% cache hit rate gains on shared-prefix workloads by keeping traffic with the same system prompt or document prefix routed to the same worker instance consistently. - Gotcha: Must be combined with `--cache-threshold` tuning. Too high a threshold (e.g., 0.9) causes frequent fallback to round-robin; too low (e.g., 0.1) routes nearly everything to the same worker, causing load imbalance. The benchmark 92%/275% figures assume a workload with substantial prefix sharing.
title: --router-policy cache_aware

body: The observation that a small subset of experts handles most tokens in each layer — the reason uniform LoRA-on-all-experts wastes most of the adapter.

body: Metric · appears on: Auto-scaling Architecture - What: The number of inference requests arriving at the serving system per second; the primary throughput unit at the traffic/gateway layer. - How it works: Measured at the load balancer or API gateway by counting HTTP/gRPC requests in a 1-second sliding window. In the deck's TikZ diagram, '100 RPS' labels the client node, indicating the aggregate request arrival rate that the load balancer must distribute across GPU replicas. - Why it matters: RPS is the natural unit for capacity planning: given a target RPS, mean request latency, and per-replica concurrency limit, the minimum replica count can be derived via Little's Law (N = λ × W). RPS also drives KEDA scaling decisions when used as a metric scaler. - Gotcha: RPS is a coarser planning unit for LLM serving than token throughput (tokens/s), because requests vary widely in input/output length. A system handling 100 RPS of 10-token requests is very different from 100 RPS of 10,000-token requests. Production SLO tracking should complement RPS with TTFT and TPOT distributions.
title: RPS

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Multi-LoRA Serving - What: A serving system (arXiv:2311.03285) that pages LoRA adapter weights in unified GPU memory, enabling thousands of distinct adapters to be served from a single server with per-request adapter swapping. - How it works: Extends PagedAttention-style virtual memory to adapter weights: adapter matrices are split into pages, stored in a unified pool, and fetched on demand using SGMV batched kernel. Adapters not currently needed are evicted to CPU memory. 4x throughput over PEFT-naive serving in benchmarks. - Why it matters: Scales multi-LoRA to thousands of adapters where even the adapter weights don't fit simultaneously in GPU VRAM. Key for fine-tuning platforms (Predibase, SageMaker LMI-Dist) offering per-customer personalized models. - Gotcha: S-LoRA's paging is for adapter weights, not KV cache. The KV cache is still paged by PagedAttention separately. Swapping adapters in/out of CPU has latency cost—useful for long-tail adapters accessed infrequently.
title: S-LoRA

body: A serving system using heterogeneous batching and custom CUDA kernels; reports up to 4× throughput over naive LoRA serving.
title: S-LoRA

body: Security · appears on: Confidential Inference: TEE & the Attack Surface - What: A mitigation system for KV-cache timing side-channel attacks that adds noise or isolation to KV cache access patterns to prevent timing-based prompt reconstruction. - How it works: SafeKV (mentioned alongside vLLM cache salting and CacheSolidarity) applies techniques to break the deterministic relationship between cache hits and TTFT — either by adding uniform random delays, by using per-tenant isolated cache namespaces, or by making cache hit/miss behavior indistinguishable at the API level. - Why it matters: PROMPTPEEK demonstrated 99% prompt reconstruction from TTFT timing; mitigations that make cache timing uninformative are essential for multi-tenant deployments serving sensitive data. - Gotcha: Adding timing noise to obscure cache hits introduces latency overhead for legitimate users. The tradeoff between privacy (more noise) and performance (less noise) must be explicitly calibrated. Cache salting (per-tenant isolation) is generally preferred over noise addition because it provides stronger isolation without performance overhead for the isolated tenant.
title: SafeKV

body: A serialization format that cannot execute code on load; the fix for pickle-based model supply-chain attacks.
title: safetensors

body: A written safety policy document the model reads and reasons over at inference time in deliberative alignment, serving as the explicit anchor for refusals and safe behavior. _(deck: §6.3 line 1250 (defbox 'Deliberative Alignment', 'safety spec viết sẵn ngay lúc inference'))_
title: Safety spec / safety specification

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Multi-LoRA Serving - What: AWS's managed multi-LoRA hosting service built on SageMaker, providing production-grade multi-adapter LLM serving with automatic scaling and infrastructure management. - How it works: Wraps vLLM or TRT-LLM under a SageMaker inference endpoint, exposing multi-LoRA via the Multi-Adapter Inference (MAI) feature (Nov 2024). Handles adapter routing, scaling, and monitoring as managed services. - Why it matters: Reduces operational burden for teams that need multi-LoRA at scale but don't want to self-manage engine configuration, scaling policies, and observability infrastructure. - Gotcha: SageMaker LMI-Dist abstracts the underlying engine (vLLM/TRT-LLM), so engine-specific flags and optimizations (e.g., SGLang's csgmv) are not directly accessible. Cost profile reflects managed overhead on top of raw compute.

aliases: Amazon SageMaker Large Model Inference Distributed

title: SageMaker LMI-Dist

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ - What: A weight channel that, when rounded to low precision, causes disproportionately large output error — typically identified by its associated input activation having unusually high magnitude. - How it works: AWQ detects salient weights by measuring per-channel activation norms on a calibration set. Channels where activations frequently have large magnitudes are designated 'salient': these weights are scaled up before INT4 rounding (so the rounding error is relatively smaller) and the corresponding scale factor is stored. The deck text: 'tìm salient weights (high activation magnitude), scale trước INT4 rounding'. - Why it matters: Protecting salient weights is the key insight that makes AWQ outperform naive 4-bit quantization. Roughly 1% of weight channels are highly salient; protecting them recovers most of the accuracy lost in naively rounding all weights. - Gotcha: The definition of 'salient' in AWQ is specifically activation-magnitude-based, not weight-magnitude-based. Large weight values are not necessarily problematic; large corresponding activation values are.
title: Salient Weight

body: Chọn giữ trace nào để giảm chi phí. Head = quyết định đầu request; tail = sau khi xong (luôn giữ trace lỗi/chậm).

body: Concept · appears on: Pre-LLM Era: Serving Infrastructure 2017–2022 - What: TensorFlow's serialization format for exporting a trained model (computation graph + weights) as a directory that can be loaded by TF Serving or tf.saved_model.load() for inference without the original training code. - How it works: A SavedModel directory contains a protobuf-serialized computation graph (saved_model.pb) and a variables/ subdirectory with weight checkpoint shards. TF Serving monitors a model repository directory and hot-swaps SavedModel versions when new ones appear, enabling zero-downtime model updates. - Why it matters: SavedModel introduced the concept of a self-contained deployable model artifact — a pattern adopted by ONNX, TorchScript, and more recently GGUF. Understanding SavedModel explains the lineage from training-serving separation to today's multi-format model ecosystem (GGUF, FP8 safetensors, NVFP4 packages). - Gotcha: SavedModel freezes the computation graph at export time, which is efficient for inference but loses Python-level flexibility (no dynamic control flow). TensorFlow 2.x added tf.function tracing to capture dynamic-looking code, but the underlying serialization is still a static graph — incompatible with autoregressive LLM decode loops without custom handling.
title: SavedModel

body: Machine-readable inventory of every component in an image (SPDX or CycloneDX). Generated by `syft`. Now regulation-driven (US EO 14028, EU Cyber Resilience Act).
title: SBOM

body: The problem of supervising models that are more capable than their human (or weaker-model) evaluators. Approaches include weak-to-strong generalization, debate, and prover-verifier games. Hard because chain-of-thought is not reliably faithful. _(deck: §6.4 'Scalable oversight & CoT (un)faithfulness', line 1267 (vinbox 'Giám sát khi model mạnh hơn người chấm'))_
title: Scalable oversight

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Auto-scaling Architecture - What: Reducing the number of active GPU replica pods when load drops, to free GPU resources and reduce cost. - How it works: Triggered by KEDA when a scale-in threshold is met (e.g. GPU util < 30%) and a stabilization/cooldown window has elapsed. Kubernetes gracefully terminates surplus pods (draining in-flight requests via connection draining) before releasing the GPU. Scale-in to zero replicas requires a separate activator (as in Knative/llm-d) to handle the next arriving request. - Why it matters: Scale-in is the cost-saving counterpart to scale-out. Without it, fleets provision for peak load and pay full GPU cost 24/7. Effective scale-in can reduce costs by 50–90% for workloads with diurnal or bursty patterns. - Gotcha: Premature scale-in during a brief traffic lull followed by a spike can cause latency spikes or errors while new replicas come up. The stabilization window (typically 5 minutes in Kubernetes HPA) must be tuned to traffic patterns. Too-aggressive scale-in is often the root cause of production SLO violations.
title: Scale In

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Auto-scaling Architecture, Scaling Strategies - What: Adding more GPU replica pods to the serving pool in response to increased load. - How it works: Triggered by KEDA when a scale-out threshold is crossed (GPU util > 80% or queue depth > 10). Kubernetes schedules new pods on available GPU nodes; the load balancer begins routing requests to them once they pass health checks. The new replicas load model weights from shared storage or a model cache. - Why it matters: Horizontal scaling (scale out) is the primary mechanism for handling traffic growth in LLM serving, since vertical scaling (bigger GPU) has diminishing returns and requires model restarts. Scale-out is also how P/D disaggregated systems add decode capacity independently of prefill capacity. - Gotcha: Scale-out is bounded by available GPU node capacity in the cluster. In cloud environments this may trigger node provisioning (VM cold start), adding minutes to the scale-out latency. A warm pool of pre-provisioned nodes or GPU reservations is the mitigation.
title: Scale Out

body: hosted capacity purchasing: a committed-term tier with an SLA, and a flat-multiple priority tier.
title: Scale Tier / Fast mode

body: Shutting instances down to zero when idle (no cost), spinning up on the next request (with cold-start cost).
title: Scale-to-zero

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Scaling Strategies - What: A serving configuration where a model replica pool is allowed to shrink to exactly zero active GPU pods when there is no incoming traffic, eliminating idle GPU cost. - How it works: The autoscaler (KEDA or Knative) monitors request queue depth. When the queue is empty for a configurable idle window, it sets replicas = 0, freeing the GPU. An activator component buffers the first request that arrives, triggers a new pod, waits for it to be ready, then forwards the buffered request. In llm-d v0.5+, this activator mechanism is built in. - Why it matters: GPU hours are the dominant cost of LLM serving. For bursty, low-traffic, or multi-tenant workloads, scale-to-zero can eliminate 80–95% of idle GPU cost. llm-d v0.5 added scale-to-zero support; vLLM's production-stack and KServe both expose it via KEDA. - Gotcha: No published GPU-provision-to-first-token measurement exists for llm-d's scale-to-zero as of mid-2026 — the activator mechanism is described qualitatively only. Cold-start for a large model (loading weights to GPU) can take tens of seconds to minutes, making scale-to-zero unsuitable for latency-sensitive tiers; it is best reserved for batch or developer endpoints.
title: Scale-to-zero

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Production SLA: Best Practices - What: The ability to reduce the number of running inference replicas to zero when there is no incoming traffic, then provision new replicas on the first incoming request. Referenced in the deck via KEDA. - How it works: Implemented by KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling) monitoring the request queue depth metric. When requests_waiting = 0 for a configured idle period, KEDA scales the deployment to 0 replicas. On the first new request, the activator (e.g., llm-d v0.5 activator) intercepts it, triggers scale-up, and holds the request until a replica is ready. llm-d v0.5 introduced this capability; v0.6/v0.7 have since refined it. - Why it matters: GPU instances are expensive when idle. Scale-to-zero eliminates idle costs entirely, critical for dev/staging environments and low-traffic deployments. For batch workloads or non-interactive inference, scale-to-zero can reduce GPU costs to near-zero during off-hours. - Gotcha: GPU cold-start time (model load + CUDA initialization) is 30s–5min depending on model size and storage speed. No published GPU-provision-to-first-token latency numbers exist for llm-d v0.5 scale-to-zero. Scale-to-zero is incompatible with P99 < 1s SLOs unless a pre-warmed spare replica is kept alive (scale-to-one minimum for latency-sensitive paths).
title: Scale-to-Zero

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Scaling Strategies - What: A metric threshold or event condition that causes the autoscaler to add (scale out) or remove (scale in) GPU replicas. - How it works: KEDA subscribes to one or more metric sources and evaluates threshold conditions on a polling interval. The deck defines two scale-out triggers (GPU util > 80%, queue depth > 10) and one scale-in trigger (GPU util < 30%). When a trigger fires, KEDA adjusts the Kubernetes Deployment replica count up or down accordingly. - Why it matters: Automated scale triggers replace manual capacity decisions, allowing the serving fleet to respond to load changes in seconds rather than hours. Correctly chosen triggers keep GPU cost proportional to actual traffic. - Gotcha: Scale-in triggers must include a cooldown period to prevent thrashing (repeatedly adding and removing replicas). Aggressive scale-in (low threshold, short cooldown) risks under-provisioning during traffic ramps; conservative scale-in wastes GPU budget during long idle periods.
title: Scale Trigger

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Production Tuning: Memory, Scheduling & Observability - What: An SGLang-specific scheduler knob (0.0–1.3+) that controls how aggressively the scheduler admits new requests into the active batch relative to available KV memory. - How it works: At 1.0 (default), the scheduler admits requests when projected KV usage stays within the pool. At 0.3 (aggressive), it admits more requests per step, risking preemption under burst traffic but maximizing throughput. At 1.3 (conservative), it leaves a larger KV reserve before admitting, reducing preemption risk at the cost of lower GPU utilization. Useful during traffic spikes or when serving long-context requests with high variance. - Why it matters: Production systems often need to be conservative during peak hours to avoid preemption cascades (where evicting a request to CPU itself causes latency spikes). Monitoring queue depth and adjusting conservativeness is a standard ops procedure. - Gotcha: This flag has no direct equivalent in vLLM — vLLM's preemption behavior is controlled indirectly via --max-num-seqs and --swap-space. When documenting runbooks, specify the engine alongside the flag value.
title: --schedule-conservativeness

body: Flag · appears on: Request Scheduling: Ai Được Chạy Trước? - What: SGLang's scheduling knob. Contrary to widely mirrored older docs, its default is also `fcfs`; `lpm` (longest-prefix-match) is opt-in. - How it works: Choices are `lpm`, `random`, `fcfs`, `dfs-weight`, `lof`, `priority` and `routing-key` (see `python/sglang/srt/server_args.py`). `lpm` reorders the queue so requests sharing the longest cached prefix run together, trading scheduling overhead for cache hits. - Why it matters: Cache-aware ordering can materially raise prefix-cache hit rate on shared-prefix workloads (chat, RAG, agents) without touching hardware — but you have to enable it. - Gotcha: Doc-drift trap: several mirrored copies of SGLang's v0.4.x-era documentation (HuggingFace clones and GitHub forks) state that `lpm` is the default, and repeat a “falls back to FCFS above 128 queued requests” rule. Neither is in the current source. Read `server_args.py` for the version you actually run.
title: `--schedule-policy` (SGLang) & LPM

body: Flag · appears on: Request Scheduling: Ai Được Chạy Trước? - What: vLLM's request-ordering knob, with exactly two choices: `fcfs` (default) and `priority`. - How it works: Under `fcfs` requests are served in arrival order. Under `priority` each request carries a priority value where lower runs earlier, and arrival time breaks ties. It is set on the server command line or through `EngineArgs`. - Why it matters: It is the cheapest lever in the entire serving stack — no GPU, no model change, no redeploy of weights — and almost nobody turns it. Co-locating latency-sensitive interactive traffic with bulk batch traffic is exactly what it is for. - Gotcha: Priority ordering applies to the waiting queue. Preempting an already-running request because a higher-priority one arrived is still only an open feature request (vllm#40004) — do not promise it.
title: `--scheduling-policy`

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Embedding & Reranker Serving: The Retrieval Half - What: The token volume threshold (~50–100M tokens/month) at which the total cost of self-hosting an embedding or reranker model (GPU/CPU, software, ops) becomes lower than the equivalent API spend (e.g., OpenAI Embeddings API or Voyage). - How it works: Below the break-even, the API cost per token is lower than the amortized cost of GPU/CPU hosting + engineering. Above it, a self-hosted TEI or Arctic Inference deployment on even modest hardware becomes cost-competitive. The threshold varies with GPU cost, model size, and API pricing. - Why it matters: For RAG-heavy applications, embedding costs can rival or exceed LLM generation costs. Understanding the break-even point drives the build-vs-buy decision for retrieval infrastructure. - Gotcha: The 50–100M token/month break-even assumes efficient batch utilization on self-hosted hardware. Idle GPU time and low batch efficiency can push the break-even significantly higher. Engineering and operations overhead (model updates, monitoring, scaling) must be included in the cost model.

title: Semantic cache

body: Caching · appears on: Semantic Caching: The Stack Is 3 Caches Deep - What: A response-level cache layer that stores completed LLM responses and matches future requests based on semantic similarity of prompts (not exact text match), returning a cached response when similarity exceeds a threshold. - How it works: Incoming prompts are embedded into vectors using a fast embedding model; the embedding is used to query a vector store for the nearest cached prompt. If cosine similarity exceeds a configured threshold (e.g., 0.8), the cached response is returned without invoking the LLM. A cache miss falls through to KV prefix cache or full inference. - Why it matters: Semantic caching is the highest-leverage cache layer because it saves 100% of compute on a hit — no LLM forward pass at all. It catches paraphrased or slightly reworded versions of the same question that would miss an exact-match cache. - Gotcha: Realistic production hit rates are 30–68% for FAQ/support workloads and only 10–25% for open-ended queries — not the '95%' figures cited in marketing. Stale cached answers are a reliability risk; the threshold must be tuned carefully, and per-tenant cache salting is required to prevent cross-tenant poisoning.
title: Semantic Caching

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Data Parallelism: DP, DPA & Cache-Aware Router - What: SGLang's Rust-based production load balancer that routes incoming requests to the DP worker instance with the highest KV prefix cache overlap, maximizing cache hit rate across a multi-instance deployment. - How it works: Maintains a prefix-tree index of each worker's cached prefixes. For each new request, hashes the prompt prefix and selects the worker with the best prefix match score above `--cache-threshold` (default 0.5). Flags: `--router-policy cache_aware --cache-threshold 0.5`. Falls back to least-loaded routing when no cache match exceeds threshold. - Why it matters: On 8×A100 80GB, cache-aware routing yields +92% throughput and +275% cache hit rate (20%→75%) vs round-robin. These gains come from prefix reuse—the same system prompt or shared RAG context being served from a warm cache instead of recomputed. - Gotcha: sgl-router is Rust-based and intended to replace the native Python DP router; it is a separate process/binary. Cache-threshold 0.5 means 'at least 50% prefix overlap'; tuning this value is workload-dependent. The 92%/275% figures are for a specific 8×A100 benchmark and may not generalize.
title: sgl-router

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Serving Stack 2026: 8 Engines That Matter; Prefix Caching: RadixAttention, APC, HiCache & Pricing; Attention Backend Selection: FA3 / FA4 / FlashInfer / FlashMLA; Structured Generation: XGrammar, Tool & Reasoning Parsers - What: A high-throughput LLM serving engine optimized for prefix-heavy, multi-turn, and structured-generation workloads, featuring RadixAttention and built-in grammar-constrained decoding. - How it works: SGLang uses RadixAttention (token-level radix-tree prefix matching) to share KV cache across requests with common prefixes, achieving 75–95% cache-hit rates on multi-turn workloads. Its zero-overhead scheduler (v0.4) overlaps CPU/GPU one-batch-ahead, pushing utilization to 95–98%. It integrates XGrammar by default for structured outputs and supports EAGLE spec-decode tree-drafting as of v0.5.13. - Why it matters: Performance leader for prefix-heavy and MoE workloads; ~16,215 tok/s on Llama-3.3-70B FP8 on H100 (~29% over vLLM); chosen alongside vLLM as the 'production 2026' recommendation in the deck. - Gotcha: SGLang achieves 75–95% prefix-hit rates specifically with shared system prompts; gains collapse on prompts with no shared prefix. EAGLE-2 spec-decode in SGLang drops to 0.93x at batch=24, motivating --speculative-disable-by-batch-size.
title: SGLang

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Multi-LoRA Serving - What: A fused CUDA kernel primitive (from the Punica project) that batches LoRA adapter GEMM operations across multiple adapters in a single GPU pass, one for each request in the batch. - How it works: Groups requests by adapter in a single kernel launch using segment pointers; performs a matrix-vector multiply for each adapter's A and B matrices simultaneously, avoiding per-adapter kernel overhead. SGLang's chunked-SGMV (csgmv) variant further improves latency by chunking the segmented multiplications at high concurrency. - Why it matters: The key kernel that makes multi-LoRA economically viable. Without it, adapter application would serialize across requests. Adopted by vLLM and SGLang; chunked-SGMV yields 20–80% latency reduction at high concurrency. - Gotcha: SGMV is from Punica (MLSys 2024), not to be confused with GEMV (general matrix-vector). SGLang's chunked-SGMV (csgmv) was introduced in v0.5.3 (Oct 2025). 'Chunked SGMV' is an SGLang optimization; the basic Punica SGMV is the shared primitive across engines.
title: SGMV

body: Caching · appears on: Multimodal prefix caching defbox: 'Hash trên pixel/image-embedding (SHA-256)' - What: A cryptographic hash function used in multimodal serving to generate a fixed-length cache key for image inputs so that identical images across different requests can share their ViT-encoded or embedded token KV cache without re-encoding. - How it works: When a VLM request includes an image, the serving engine (vLLM V1 / SGLang) computes SHA-256 over the raw image bytes (for late-fusion models) or over the pixel patch tensor (for early-fusion models) to produce a 256-bit cache key. This key is used as the block hash in the prefix-caching trie: if the same image has been encoded before, its KV blocks are returned from cache, reducing TTFT from 18 seconds to ~1 second (LMCache measurement). SGLang extends this to a global embedding cache where any instance can serve cached visual tokens. - Why it matters: Images are large (JPEGs can be hundreds of KB to MB) and encoding them via ViT takes hundreds of milliseconds. SHA-256 hashing is fast (~1 GB/s) and collision-resistant, making it a practical cache key mechanism. Identical image content (same bytes) produces the same hash even if the requests come from different users or arrive at different workers. - Gotcha: SHA-256 hashing is byte-exact: the same image encoded as JPEG vs PNG, or resized to different dimensions, produces different hashes even if the visual content is semantically identical. This means the caching benefit only applies to bit-for-bit identical image uploads, not perceptually similar images. For semantic deduplication, a separate embedding-level similarity hash would be needed.
title: SHA-256

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: SLA Dashboard: Key Metrics, Production SLA: Best Practices - What: A formal contract between a service provider and a consumer that specifies measurable performance guarantees (latency, uptime, throughput) and consequences for violation. - How it works: In LLM serving, SLAs are expressed as percentile latency bounds (P95/P99 TTFT, TPOT) and uptime targets. A monitoring dashboard continuously compares live measurements against these bounds; alerts fire when thresholds are breached. The deck ties SLA directly to the Goodput@SLO concept: requests that violate latency bounds do not count as successfully served. - Why it matters: Defines the operational contract the inference stack must satisfy in production. Without explicit SLA targets, teams optimize the wrong metric (peak throughput instead of bounded tail latency), leading to silent SLO violations under real load. - Gotcha: SLA (business contract) and SLO (Service Level Objective, the internal target) are often conflated; SLA is the external promise. More critically, Throughput@saturation != Goodput@SLO — a server hitting 1,800 tok/s at 100% load may only deliver 1,200 tok/s that actually satisfies latency bounds (the remainder times out or breaches P99).
title: SLA

body: Flag · appears on: Serving Cho RL: Rollout Là Một Workload Riêng - What: A vLLM feature (`--enable-sleep-mode`) that releases most GPU memory without stopping the server, so a serving cluster can lend VRAM to a trainer between rollouts. - How it works: Level 1 offloads model weights to CPU RAM and discards the KV cache, keeping weights ready for a fast restore. Level 2 discards the weights as well (retaining small buffers such as rope-scaling tensors), which is the mode to use when the weights are about to be updated anyway. Control it over HTTP: `POST /sleep?level=N`, `POST /wake_up`, `GET /is_sleeping`, with partial wake via `tags=["weights"]`. - Why it matters: It frees >90% of GPU memory and removes the need to stand up a second cluster for training, which is the practical connective tissue between serving and RL post-training. - Gotcha: Level 1 needs enough CPU RAM to hold the weights; level 2 is the fallback when it does not. On ROCm, tune `VLLM_ROCM_SLEEP_MEM_CHUNK_SIZE` (default 256 MB, powers of two) if you hit OOM.
title: Sleep mode

body: Model-merging recipes (mergekit). SLERP = spherical interpolation of two checkpoints; Task Arithmetic = add/subtract task vectors; TIES/DARE = sparsify and merge.

title: SLO

body: A first-class service-level objective of two kinds — completion-rate and freshness — tiered by importance.
title: SLO

body: Metric · appears on: Latency Taxonomy: TTFT · TPOT · Goodput - What: An internal engineering target for a measurable quality-of-service attribute, such as P95 TTFT < 1 s or P99 TPOT < 50 ms, that the serving system must sustain under production load. - How it works: SLOs are specified as (metric, percentile, threshold, window) tuples. They drive autoscaling rules, alerting, and capacity planning. In LLM serving, the standard approach is dual SLOs: one for TTFT (covering prefill latency) and one for TPOT (covering decode smoothness). Goodput is the rate at which the system satisfies both SLOs simultaneously. - Why it matters: SLOs translate user experience requirements into operational targets. Without an SLO, a serving system can appear healthy by throughput while delivering poor user experience. SLOs also gate whether speculative decoding, quantization, or batching changes are net-positive for production. - Gotcha: SLOs (internal targets) differ from SLAs (Service-Level Agreements, contractual commitments with penalties). SLOs are typically set tighter than SLAs to provide a buffer. P95/P99 is standard; P50 (median) TTFT can be misleading because it hides the 1-in-20 or 1-in-100 bad experiences.
title: SLO

body: Metric · appears on: Scaling Strategies (via research companion §12) - What: A quantitative target for a service quality metric (e.g. P99 TTFT < 500 ms, or TPOT < 50 ms/token) that the serving system must meet under specified conditions. - How it works: SLOs are defined in terms of a metric, a percentile, a threshold, and a compliance window (e.g. 99% of requests must have TTFT < 1s over a 5-minute window). KEDA-based autoscaling can use SLO compliance as a scaling signal: if P99 TTFT rises above the SLO target (computed via PromQL), trigger scale-out. - Why it matters: SLO-driven autoscaling aligns infrastructure decisions directly with user experience goals, rather than proxy metrics like GPU utilization. KServe v0.16 and the 2026 KEDA pattern both support TTFT/queue-depth SLO-based scaling. - Gotcha: SLOs measured at the serving engine exclude network round-trip time, client-side buffering, and API gateway overhead. A 500ms P99 TTFT SLO at the vLLM engine may translate to 600–800ms at the client depending on infrastructure topology.
title: SLO

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: SLA Dashboard: Key Metrics (implicit via targets), Production SLA: Best Practices - What: The internal engineering target for a single measurable dimension of service quality, such as P95 TTFT < 500 ms or uptime >= 99.9%. - How it works: SLOs are set conservatively relative to the external SLA to leave an error budget. Each metric tile in the dashboard (P50/P95/P99/throughput/uptime) shows a target that is the SLO. Monitoring systems (Prometheus, Grafana) alert when the rolling error-budget burn rate is too high. - Why it matters: SLOs convert the abstract SLA into operational thresholds that engineering teams can observe, alert on, and optimize toward. The goodput definition used throughout the deck is specifically Goodput@SLO, meaning tokens/s that satisfy both TTFT and TPOT SLOs simultaneously. - Gotcha: A single-dimensional SLO (e.g., only TTFT) is insufficient for LLM serving; TTFT and TPOT must both be bounded to characterize user-perceived quality. DistServe (OSDI'24) first formalized the dual-SLO goodput definition.
title: SLO

body: Hardware · appears on: Attention Backend Selection (Backend Feature Highlights): 'FA4: FP4 KV cache — Blackwell SM100 (2025)' - What: NVIDIA's Streaming Multiprocessor architecture generation used in Blackwell GPUs (B200, B300), introducing FP4 native matrix multiply hardware (fourth-generation Tensor Cores), asymmetric scaling for software-emulated softmax, and 2-CTA (Cooperative Thread Array) MMA — the hardware substrate required for FlashAttention-4. - How it works: SM100 adds NVFP4 and MXFP4 4-bit tensor core operations to the existing FP8/BF16/FP16 Tensor Core stack. FlashAttention-4 (arXiv:2603.05451) exploits SM100's asymmetric MMA: the FP4 Tensor Core can perform matrix multiplications with a non-square output precision (BF16 accumulation), enabling FP4 QK^T computation with BF16 attention score accumulation. The 2-CTA MMA instruction (two CTAs cooperatively computing one WGMMA) increases arithmetic intensity and hides register file bandwidth. SM100 achieves ~1,613 TFLOPS/s BF16 (71% utilisation) in FlashAttention-4 benchmarks, versus ~840 TFLOPS/s on SM90 (H100). - Why it matters: SM100 is a hardware prerequisite for NVFP4 KV cache, NVFP4 activation quantisation, and FlashAttention-4 — three of the highest-priority serving optimisations on Blackwell. Engineers targeting Blackwell platforms must use SM100-aware kernels; the older CUDA code paths compiled for SM90 (Hopper) will run but miss the FP4 throughput uplift. - Gotcha: SM100 is Blackwell-only; Hopper GPUs use SM90 and cannot run NVFP4 or FA4 kernels. The FlashAttention-4 '1,613 TFLOPS/s BF16' figure is for B200, not B300 (Blackwell Ultra), and at a batch/sequence configuration not disclosed in the primary arXiv paper — cite as 'on B200' with the caveat.
title: SM100

body: Concept · appears on: Pipeline Parallelism: Ultra-Long Context - What: A hyperparameter (env var, default 0.75, range 0.6–0.85) that controls how aggressively dynamic chunking adjusts chunk sizes relative to prefix length in Pipeline Parallelism serving. - How it works: The dynamic chunking formula scales chunk size as a function of current prefix length weighted by smooth_factor. Higher smooth_factor = slower size ramp (more conservative, more bubble). Lower smooth_factor = faster size ramp (more aggressive, less bubble, more memory pressure). Model-specific tuning: DeepSeek-V3.1 uses 0.65 for 12K dynamic chunks; Qwen3-235B uses 0.8 for 18K dynamic chunks. - Why it matters: Different model sizes and context lengths have different optimal chunk growth profiles. The smooth factor allows operators to tune the TTFT vs throughput tradeoff without recompiling. - Gotcha: Smooth factor is tuned per model; the defaults in the deck (DeepSeek 0.65, Qwen3 0.8) are empirically validated but may not transfer to other models or hardware configurations.

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Chọn Thuật Toán Spec Decoding (Aug 2026) - What: SGLang's rewritten speculative-decoding engine, whose central goal is removing host–device synchronisation points; default from v0.5.16. - How it works: The overlap scheduler lets host-side work for one batch run concurrently with GPU work on another: request cleanup (stop-token detection, metadata updates) after batch N−1 overlaps GPU execution of batch N, and host KV allocation for batch N overlaps GPU work on N−1. Fall back with `--disable-overlap-schedule`. - Why it matters: Per-step host overhead is a large share of speculative decoding's cost, because each step involves draft, verify and bookkeeping. Removing the syncs gave +33% on Qwen3-8B (single B200, concurrency 32): ~11.4 → ~15.3 ktok/s. It benefits the EAGLE, MTP and DFLASH paths alike. - Gotcha: This is the same class of problem as the Python-GIL client bottleneck in benchmarking — host-side serialisation masquerading as model slowness. It is also why both vLLM and SGLang moved their frontends to Rust.
title: Spec V2 (SGLang) & the overlap scheduler

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Speculative Decoding & Continuous Batching - What: SGLang CLI flag that selects the EAGLE-3 speculative decoding algorithm for the serving engine. - How it works: When passed to the SGLang server launch command, enables the EAGLE-3 draft tree with the companion flags `--speculative-num-steps 5` (draft chain length) and `--speculative-eagle-topk 4` (top-k candidates per draft step). Requires either a pre-trained EAGLE-3 draft checkpoint or a model with MTP heads. - Why it matters: The deck's defbox shows the exact production CLI pattern. Instructors and practitioners use this as a template for enabling speculative decoding on SGLang-deployed models. - Gotcha: Requires a draft model checkpoint or an MTP head; not usable out-of-the-box on arbitrary model checkpoints. The `--speculative-num-steps` and `--speculative-eagle-topk` values must be tuned per model — defaults may not give peak speedup.
title: --speculative-algorithm EAGLE3

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Model Routing & Cascades: Cross-Model Cost - What: A serving pattern (Google, ICLR 2025) that combines speculative decoding with model cascades: the cheap model generates draft tokens AND acts as the first cascade tier, with the strong model both verifying spec-decode drafts and serving as the cascade fallback. - How it works: The small (cheap) model generates speculative draft tokens; the large (expensive) model verifies them as in standard speculative decoding. If the large model rejects too many tokens (low acceptance rate), the request is treated as a cascade deferral and the large model takes over generation fully. This fuses the efficiency benefits of speculative decoding with the cost savings of cascading. - Why it matters: Speculative cascades exploit synergies: the spec-decode verification (already running the large model forward) provides the confidence signal needed for cascade deferral at minimal extra cost. Net effect is lower latency AND lower cost compared to either technique alone. - Gotcha: Speculative cascades only work when the small model is the same architecture as the draft model in spec-decode. The additional complexity of combined cascade+spec-decode logic increases engineering overhead significantly. Gains are most pronounced for query distributions with bimodal difficulty.
title: Speculative Cascade

body: a small "draft" model proposes several tokens that the large "target" model verifies in parallel, cutting latency ~2–3× without changing the output distribution (EAGLE-3).
title: Speculative decoding

body: Decoding · appears on: Speculative Decoding & Continuous Batching - What: A latency-reduction technique where a small 'draft' model proposes 4–8 tokens in parallel, and the large 'target' model verifies them all in a single forward pass, accepting correct tokens and rejecting the first wrong one. - How it works: The draft model (or self-drafting mechanism) generates a candidate sequence autoregressively. The target model then runs one forward pass that evaluates the probability of each draft token in parallel. Any token whose draft probability deviates beyond a threshold is rejected; all preceding accepted tokens are taken without additional cost. This allows multiple tokens to be produced per target-model forward pass. - Why it matters: LLM decode is memory-bandwidth-bound: each forward pass loads all weights regardless of whether it produces 1 or 8 tokens. Producing multiple tokens per weight-load step multiplies effective throughput without changing the target model. Net effect: 3–6.5× latency reduction at batch sizes 1–4. - Gotcha: “Latency tool, not a throughput tool” was true for autoregressive drafters: at batch ≥24 the draft+verify overhead makes inference slower than baseline (~0.93× at batch 24 on H100, EAGLE-3 paper Table 3). The 2026 generation invalidates that as a blanket rule — parallel drafting removes the sequential draft cost, SGLang's Spec V2 overlap scheduler removes the host–device sync cost, and DSpark's confidence-scheduled verification removes the wasted-verify cost. DeepSeek replaced MTP-1 with DSpark in its production serving system, which is a throughput decision made under live traffic. Note: `--speculative-disable-by-batch-size` is no longer listed in current SGLang docs — rely on the behaviour, not the flag name.
title: Speculative Decoding

body: A small "draft" model predicts the next k tokens; the big model verifies in parallel. 2–3× throughput when the draft is correct.
title: Speculative decoding

body: Draft-then-verify decoding; saves cost only when latency-bound (−48% $/token) and can add cost when throughput-saturated (+19%). ROI scales with acceptance rate (target ≥60%).
title: Speculative decoding / acceptance rate

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Speculative Decoding & Continuous Batching - What: SGLang CLI flag that automatically disables speculative decoding when the live batch size exceeds a specified threshold, reverting to standard autoregressive decoding at high concurrency. - How it works: SGLang's scheduler monitors the current batch size at each step; when it exceeds the threshold set by this flag, the draft+verify pipeline is bypassed and tokens are generated one at a time via standard forward passes. Typically set to 24 based on the empirical crossover point where EAGLE-2/3 becomes net-negative. - Why it matters: Prevents the scenario where speculative decoding's overhead (draft generation + verify pass) makes throughput worse than baseline. At batch ≥24 on H100 with Llama-3.1-8B, EAGLE-2 achieved only 0.93× throughput vs no spec-decode (per EAGLE-3 paper Table 3). - Gotcha: The threshold is hardware- and model-specific; 24 is the SGLang/H100/Llama-3.1-8B empirical value. A different model or GPU may have a different crossover. The flag enables dynamic adjustment without restarting the server.
title: --speculative-disable-by-batch-size

body: Tooling · appears on: Chọn Thuật Toán Spec Decoding (Aug 2026) - What: vLLM's unified library for training, evaluating and packaging speculative-decoding draft heads. - How it works: It standardises checkpoint format and training data generation (both offline and online, via vLLM's hidden-state extraction) so a draft head trained once can be loaded by the serving engine without code changes. - Why it matters: It is the reason swapping drafting algorithms is a config edit rather than an engine patch. Its release ladder also dates the field: EAGLE/EAGLE-3/HASS in v0.1.0 → DFlash v0.5.0 → P-EAGLE v0.6.0 → DSpark v0.7.0. - Gotcha: Cite the version rather than the date — release dates reported across the vLLM blog, Red Hat articles and the GitHub releases page disagree; the releases page is authoritative.
title: Speculators

body: Benchmark · appears on: Benchmarking: Đo Sao Cho Không Nói Dối - What: NVIDIA's unified benchmark for speculative decoding (arXiv 2604.09557, Feb 2026), designed to standardise SD evaluation across domains and realistic serving regimes. - How it works: It spans diverse semantic domains and measures both draft accuracy and throughput at varying input lengths and concurrency levels, rather than reporting a single speedup on one dataset. - Why it matters: Speculative-decoding performance is intrinsically data-dependent, so a benchmark that does not vary workload cannot characterise it. Two findings matter directly for lab work: synthetic/random tokens overestimate throughput by ~23% when SD is enabled, and low-entropy domains (coding, math) yield substantially longer acceptance runs than high-entropy ones such as roleplay. - Gotcha: The corollary is a rule, not a caveat: never benchmark speculative decoding with random tokens. If you do, you will report a number ~23% better than anything a user will experience.
title: SPEED-Bench

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Disaggregated Prefill/Decode Serving - What: An ISCA'24 paper proposing heterogeneous disaggregated serving using prefill-optimized and decode-optimized GPU types in separate pools, achieving 1.4x per-dollar throughput improvement. - How it works: Unlike DistServe (which uses homogeneous GPU pools for each phase), Splitwise assigns compute-efficient GPUs (e.g., A100 for FLOPs) to prefill and memory-bandwidth-efficient GPUs (e.g., H100 for HBM bandwidth) to decode. This heterogeneous assignment better matches hardware characteristics to workload requirements, improving cost efficiency. - Why it matters: Motivated the industry practice of mixing GPU types in disaggregated clusters; practically relevant now that B200/GB200 (extreme memory bandwidth) are used for decode while older H100/A100 handle prefill in cost-optimized deployments. - Gotcha: Splitwise's 1.4x per-$ figure assumes the specific GPU price ratios at ISCA'24 publication time (2024). With GPU pricing changes (H200 vs A100 price spread, GB200 availability), the optimal heterogeneous mix may differ significantly in 2026.
title: Splitwise

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Production SLA: Best Practices - What: Spare cloud compute capacity offered at steep discounts (60–90% vs on-demand GPU prices) that can be preempted by the cloud provider with 2-minute warning. The deck recommends spot instances specifically for batch inference workloads. - How it works: The orchestration layer (Kubernetes with KEDA or a custom controller) labels certain worker nodes as spot-eligible. Batch jobs (offline embedding, document processing, non-interactive generation) are scheduled onto spot nodes. When a preemption notice arrives, the controller checkpoints the job and reschedules it on on-demand capacity or another available spot node. Interactive/real-time inference is kept on on-demand instances. - Why it matters: GPU compute is the dominant cost in LLM serving. Spot instances for batch inference can reduce compute cost by 60–90% with negligible impact on SLA because batch jobs tolerate interruption. The deck frames this under 'cost per 1M tokens: continuously optimize'. - Gotcha: Spot instance preemption is incompatible with stateful serving for real-time requests — a preemption mid-stream drops the response. The critical split is: batch inference = spot-eligible; real-time streaming = on-demand only. Also, spot availability for A100/H100 GPUs is limited; build multi-instance-type bid strategies.
title: Spot Instances

body: Hardware · appears on: FlashAttention: IO-Aware Attention (FA1→FA4) - What: The small, extremely fast on-chip memory (L1 cache / shared memory) on each GPU Streaming Multiprocessor (SM), with ~1–2 TB/s bandwidth but only 100–200 KB capacity per SM. - How it works: In CUDA terminology, SRAM refers to shared memory within an SM — the target for CUDA's `__shared__` allocations and CUTLASS's shared memory tiles. FlashAttention explicitly manages SRAM allocation to ensure Q/K/V tiles fit without spilling to HBM. - Why it matters: SRAM vs HBM access speed difference is ~10× in latency and ~10–20× in bandwidth. Keeping working sets in SRAM is the key to IO-aware performance; FlashAttention's core design constraint is fitting attention tiles into SM SRAM. - Gotcha: SRAM capacity on a single SM is limited (~164 KB on A100 SM). Large tile sizes improve compute efficiency but risk SRAM overflow (causing spilling to L2/HBM). FA kernel variants choose tile sizes to balance SRAM utilization against thread occupancy.
title: SRAM
