body: Concept · appears on: Attention Architecture: MHA → MLA & Long-Context - What: A class of sequence models (Mamba, S4, etc.) that use a fixed-size recurrent state to process sequences, with training complexity O(n log n) via parallel scan and inference complexity O(1) per step regardless of context length. - How it works: SSMs model sequences via a learned transition matrix A and input/output matrices B, C: hidden state h_t = A·h_{t-1} + B·x_t; y_t = C·h_t. The state size is fixed, so long-context processing does not increase the per-step memory footprint as a KV cache would. - Why it matters: The constant-memory property of SSMs makes them attractive for very long context serving where KV cache size becomes prohibitive. Used as the backbone or hybrid component in Jamba, Mamba, and similar models. - Gotcha: SSMs are generally weaker than attention at in-context learning and precise retrieval tasks ('needle-in-haystack'). Pure SSM models trade quality on retrieval-heavy tasks for memory efficiency.
title: SSM

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Embedding & Reranker Serving: The Retrieval Half - What: A batching strategy where all sequences in a batch are collected, sorted by token length, and processed together in one fixed forward pass, as opposed to continuous batching which dynamically adds/removes sequences during generation. - How it works: For embedding/reranker models, all inputs are accumulated until a batch size or token budget is reached (controlled by `--max-batch-tokens`), then sorted by sequence length to minimize padding waste, and processed in a single forward pass. No generation loop means there is no benefit to dynamic insertion or preemption. - Why it matters: Static batching maximizes GPU compute utilization for prefill-only models. Continuous batching's overhead (request queue management, KV cache allocation) is unnecessary overhead that reduces throughput for embedding workloads. - Gotcha: Static batching introduces queuing latency — requests must wait for a batch to fill. The batch size and token budget must be tuned per model and SLO; too large increases latency, too small leaves GPU underutilized.
title: Static Batch

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Pre-LLM Era: Serving Infrastructure 2017–2022 - What: A batching strategy where incoming requests are collected until a fixed batch size is reached (or a latency timeout expires), then the whole batch is processed together as a single GPU call, and all responses are returned at once. - How it works: The serving system holds a queue of requests and forms a batch when either N requests are waiting or a timer (e.g., 100 ms) fires. The entire batch runs through the model in one forward pass. Responses cannot be released until the slowest request in the batch finishes — the batch is as slow as its longest member. - Why it matters: Static batching adds 200–500 ms latency overhead (waiting to fill the batch) and causes head-of-line blocking (one long request delays all shorter ones). Understanding static batching's failure mode clarifies why continuous batching is essential for LLM serving under variable request lengths. - Gotcha: Static batching was acceptable for fixed-output-length models (classifiers, encoders) but catastrophically inefficient for autoregressive generation where output lengths vary by 10–100x. A single long request (e.g., 2000 output tokens) holds the batch slot occupied while shorter requests (10 tokens) could have completed and freed the slot.
title: Static Batching

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Speculative Decoding & Continuous Batching - What: The legacy serving approach where the server waits until a full batch of requests is assembled before running any forward pass, holding all requests until the slowest in the batch completes. - How it works: All requests in a batch must finish before any results are returned. The GPU runs one forward pass per full batch, with short sequences padded to match the longest sequence in the batch. Padding tokens contribute memory and compute cost but produce no output. - Why it matters: Pedagogical baseline that shows why continuous batching was developed: static batching adds 200–500 ms of padding latency and wastes compute on pad tokens, making tail latency proportional to the slowest sequence in the batch. - Gotcha: Some vendor documentation (e.g., older Triton Inference Server docs) still uses 'static batching' to mean fixed-size batch compilation (a different concept). In the LLM serving context, the term always means 'wait for full batch before executing.'
title: Static Batching

body: Attention / KV · appears on: Attention Architecture: MHA → MLA & Long-Context - What: A technique for theoretically infinite-context LLM inference by maintaining only the first few 'attention sink' tokens plus a sliding window of the most recent tokens in the KV cache, discarding the rest. - How it works: Empirically, LLMs consistently assign high attention mass to the very first tokens in a sequence (the 'attention sinks'), even when those tokens are semantically unimportant. Keeping the first 4 sink tokens plus a sliding window of the last W tokens preserves model coherence without context-length-proportional memory. Formalized in ICLR 2024. - Why it matters: Enables truly unbounded streaming inference with O(W) KV memory instead of O(n). Used in edge/mobile scenarios where KV memory is severely constrained, or in streaming chat applications where complete history retention is unnecessary. - Gotcha: StreamingLLM loses information about the middle of long conversations; it is not equivalent to true long-context attention. The model can appear incoherent when asked about content in the evicted middle section. vLLM V1 adds `--kv-cache-dtype-skip-layers` support for hybrid model configurations.

body: Decoding · appears on: DSpark: Semi-Autoregressive + Confidence Scheduling - What: The failure mode of pure parallel drafting: acceptance probability falls off sharply toward the end of a drafted block. - How it works: When every position in a block is predicted independently from the same conditioning, position j has no knowledge of what was proposed at position j−1. Errors therefore compound along the block and the tail is rejected far more often than the head. - Why it matters: It caps the useful block size of a parallel drafter — pushing γ higher stops paying off. Naming the failure is what motivated DSpark's semi-autoregressive design. - Gotcha: Suffix decay is invisible in an average-speedup number; you only see it by plotting per-position acceptance across the block.

body: Hardware · appears on: Hardware Landscape 2026 table: 'NVIDIA H200 SXM' - What: NVIDIA's high-bandwidth server GPU form factor that uses a proprietary mezzanine socket (replacing PCIe) to provide direct NVLink connections between GPUs within a server, enabling significantly higher GPU-to-GPU bandwidth than PCIe-connected modules. - How it works: SXM GPUs plug into a proprietary NVSwitch-based board (HGX, MGX) rather than standard PCIe slots. This physical attachment allows NVLink signals to route at full bandwidth between GPUs: on H100/H200 SXM, NVLink 4.0 provides 900 GB/s bidirectional GPU-to-GPU bandwidth versus ~16 GB/s for PCIe 4.0 x16. The SXM5 mechanical spec (used on H100/H200) supports 4-way and 8-way NVLink configurations. SXM GPUs also have higher TDP headroom than PCIe variants (700W vs 400W for H100 SXM vs H100 PCIe). - Why it matters: For tensor-parallel LLM serving, the all-reduce communication bandwidth between GPUs is the primary latency bottleneck. SXM's 900 GB/s NVLink versus 16 GB/s PCIe means all-reduce is ~50× faster on SXM, enabling TP-8 without significant overhead. This is why all production-scale LLM serving uses SXM-form GPUs (H100 SXM, H200 SXM, B200 SXM) rather than PCIe variants. - Gotcha: SXM GPUs cannot be used in standard PCIe servers; they require HGX/MGX server platforms with the NVSwitch interconnect board, which adds substantial system cost. The 'H200 SXM' designation in the hardware table is important because H200 also exists in a lower-bandwidth PCIe variant (H200 NVL, 141GB but different interconnect).

body: Security · appears on: Confidential Inference: TEE & the Attack Surface - What: A hardware-isolated secure enclave where code and data are protected from inspection or modification even by the host OS, hypervisor, or cloud operator, enabling confidential computation. - How it works: TEEs use CPU/GPU hardware features (Intel SGX/TDX, AMD SEV-SNP, NVIDIA CC) to encrypt memory at rest and in transit, enforce access controls at the hardware level, and provide remote attestation (a cryptographic proof that code is running in an authentic TEE with specific measurements). For GPU inference, GPU confidential computing extends this to protect model weights and activations during computation. - Why it matters: Regulated industries (healthcare, finance, government) require that model weights and user data remain protected even from the infrastructure operator. GPU TEE makes confidential LLM inference viable with <9% throughput overhead on large models, opening these markets to cloud-hosted AI. - Gotcha: On Hopper GPUs, each confidential VM (CVM) is limited to one GPU (NVLink between Hopper GPUs is plaintext, not encrypted). This limitation is fixed in Blackwell, which adds NVLink encryption + TEE-I/O for multi-GPU confidential inference.
title: TEE

body: Security · appears on: Confidential Inference: TEE & the Attack Surface - What: NVIDIA Blackwell's feature that extends confidential computing to the inter-GPU NVLink fabric, enabling encrypted multi-GPU inference within a single node's TEE boundary. - How it works: In Blackwell systems, TEE-I/O encrypts NVLink traffic between GPUs in addition to PCIe (PPCIE). This means a multi-GPU pod (e.g., an 8-GPU GB200 server) can operate as a unified confidential computing domain where all inter-GPU communication (activations, KV cache transfers) is encrypted and attestable. - Why it matters: Hopper's PPCIE left NVLink unencrypted, limiting confidential inference to single-GPU models. Blackwell TEE-I/O enables confidential serving of large models that require tensor parallelism across multiple GPUs — the practical prerequisite for confidential frontier-model inference. - Gotcha: TEE-I/O is Blackwell-specific (2025+). Organizations planning confidential multi-GPU inference must procure Blackwell-class hardware; Hopper + NVLink will always have the plaintext NVLink gap regardless of software configuration.
title: TEE-I/O

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Embedding & Reranker Serving: The Retrieval Half - What: HuggingFace's high-performance Rust-based server for embedding and cross-encoder reranker models, replacing TGI for retrieval model serving. - How it works: TEI v1.9.3 (Mar 2026) serves both embedding and reranker models with optimized CUDA kernels, dynamic batching up to `--max-batch-tokens`, Flash Attention for long sequences, and supports Qwen3, ModernBERT, and Gemma3 architectures. Written in Rust for low overhead. - Why it matters: With TGI archived (Mar 2026), TEI is the canonical HuggingFace-supported server for retrieval models. Its token-sorted static batching and FP8 support make it purpose-built for embedding workloads. - Gotcha: TEI is for encoder-only and sequence-classification models, not generative LLMs. Do not confuse with TGI (which served generative models and is now archived). TEI does not support KV cache or decode — it's a single-pass forward-only server.

body: CLI / flag · appears on: PagedAttention: vLLM v0 → v1 Deep Dive - What: A vLLM CLI flag that sets the number of GPUs over which model weights are sharded via tensor parallelism (splitting attention heads and FFN rows/columns across N GPUs). - How it works: When N>1, vLLM uses NCCL all-reduce after each matmul, so all N GPUs participate in every forward pass. Each GPU holds 1/N of the attention heads and FFN weights. For a 70B model on 8×H100, each GPU holds ~8.75B params. Strongly affects both throughput (more VRAM, larger batch) and latency (all-reduce overhead grows with N). - Why it matters: Required to serve models that exceed single-GPU VRAM (e.g., 70B+ models need ≥4×H100 at BF16); also improves decode throughput on memory-bandwidth-bound models by spreading the bandwidth load across N GPUs' HBM. - Gotcha: TP increases communication overhead — above TP=8 on non-NVLink fabrics (e.g., PCIe), all-reduce latency dominates and throughput degrades. For MoE models, Expert Parallelism often outperforms TP at high concurrency (EP wins above ~256–512 concurrent requests).
title: --tensor-parallel-size

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Distributed Inference: Parallelism Strategy Guide - What: CLI flag for vLLM/SGLang specifying how many GPUs to use for Tensor Parallelism within each node, sharding weight matrices across that many devices. - How it works: Sets the TP degree: `--tensor-parallel-size 4` means 4 GPUs share each weight matrix via column/row splitting. All-Reduce operations over NVLink synchronize partial results per layer. Combined with `--pipeline-parallel-size` and `--ep` for full multi-node MoE configurations. - Why it matters: The primary knob for fitting large models on multi-GPU single-node servers. For a 70B model needing ~140GB at BF16, TP=2 on 2×80GB GPUs is the minimum viable configuration. - Gotcha: TP must be ≤ GPUs per node (for NVLink efficiency). TP across nodes over IB is almost never recommended. Increasing TP beyond what is needed adds All-Reduce overhead with diminishing memory benefits.
title: --tensor-parallel-size

body: Parallelism · appears on: Inference Engine Evolution: 2020 → 2025; PagedAttention: vLLM v0 → v1 Deep Dive - What: A parallelism strategy that partitions individual transformer layer weights (attention heads, FFN rows/columns) across N GPUs, with an all-reduce synchronization after each matmul. - How it works: For attention: Q/K/V projection weights are column-partitioned across N GPUs; each GPU computes attention for num_heads/N heads; results are all-reduced. For FFN: gate/up projections are column-partitioned, down projection is row-partitioned, with one all-reduce at the end. Each GPU holds 1/N of every weight matrix. Requires N-way NVLink all-reduce at each layer boundary — optimal on NVLink rings (GB200 NVL72: 130 TB/s). - Why it matters: The standard parallelism for models that fit in N GPUs' combined VRAM but not one; reduces per-GPU memory requirement and increases effective HBM bandwidth proportionally. Set via --tensor-parallel-size in vLLM. - Gotcha: TP latency grows with N due to all-reduce overhead — at TP=8 over PCIe (not NVLink), all-reduce dominates and throughput degrades vs TP=4. For MoE models with >3% activation density, Expert Parallelism outperforms TP at concurrency >256–512 (vLLM MoE Playbook, Nov 2025).
title: Tensor parallelism

body: Parallelism · appears on: Distributed Inference: Parallelism Strategy Guide - What: A parallelism strategy that shards individual weight matrices (within a single transformer layer) across multiple GPUs, with each GPU computing a portion of every layer's forward pass. - How it works: Typically uses Megatron-LM column/row splitting: attention heads and FFN columns are split across N GPUs. After each shard's partial computation, an All-Reduce collective (via NCCL) synchronizes partial results across all TP ranks. All-reduce is required every layer. Best when GPUs are on the same node connected via NVLink (900 GB/s). - Why it matters: Enables serving models too large for a single GPU without introducing pipeline bubbles (unlike PP). The rule of thumb: TP ≤ GPUs per node. On NVLink-connected nodes, All-Reduce latency is sub-millisecond, making TP efficient. - Gotcha: TP across nodes (over InfiniBand) is almost always a bad idea—All-Reduce latency at IB speed (~200 GB/s) is ~5–10x higher than NVLink, bottlenecking every layer. Exception: NVLink fabric spanning nodes (NVL72/GB200). Do NOT mix TP across nodes unless NVLink fabric is present.
title: Tensor Parallelism

body: splitting a model's weight matrices across GPUs within a node (tensor) or by depth across nodes (pipeline) to serve models too large for one GPU.
title: Tensor / pipeline parallelism

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Model Compilation: torch.compile + CUDA Graphs + TensorRT - What: NVIDIA's inference optimization SDK that compiles an ONNX model graph through layer fusion, precision calibration (FP8/INT8), and hardware-specific kernel selection into a binary `.trt` engine delivering 3–5× speedup vs vanilla PyTorch. - How it works: Pipeline: ONNX export → TensorRT parser → graph optimization (layer fusion, constant folding) → kernel autotuning (CUDA kernel selection from cuDNN/CUTLASS) → calibration (for FP8/INT8 quantization with calibration data) → serialized `.trt` engine binary. Compilation takes 5–30 minutes per model. The engine is then deployed via NVIDIA Triton Inference Server or TensorRT-LLM. - Why it matters: Peak throughput on NVIDIA hardware, particularly beneficial for large-batch encoder tasks or deterministic latency requirements. Used as the compilation backend in TensorRT-LLM for the highest-throughput LLM serving. 3–5× vs vanilla PyTorch makes it worthwhile despite the long compile step. - Gotcha: Compile time is 5–30 minutes per model vs seconds for vLLM/SGLang (which load weights directly). Engines are hardware-specific: a TRT engine compiled for H100 will not run on A100. Every model update requires recompilation. The TRT engine is opaque binary — no Python-level debugging.
title: TensorRT

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Edge Deployment Flow - What: NVIDIA's inference optimization compiler and runtime that takes an ONNX graph and produces a device-specific fused engine (a .trt file) with FP8/INT8 calibration, achieving 3–5x speedup over vanilla PyTorch. - How it works: TensorRT ingests an ONNX model, applies layer fusion (combining adjacent ops into single kernels), selects the best kernel implementation for each fused layer, performs FP8/INT8 calibration using a calibration dataset, and emits a serialized .trt engine. The engine is then executed by NVIDIA's Triton Inference Server or TensorRT-LLM. Compile time is 5–30 minutes per model. - Why it matters: TensorRT is the highest-throughput NVIDIA inference path; TensorRT-LLM (the LLM-specific variant) achieves best-in-class NVIDIA GPU throughput by combining TensorRT compilation with LLM-specific optimizations (continuous batching, paged KV cache, FP4 support on Blackwell). - Gotcha: Engines are device-specific and must be recompiled per GPU SKU (A100 vs H100 vs B200). The long compile time makes TensorRT unsuitable for frequent model updates or LoRA hot-swapping without engine caching.
title: TensorRT

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Serving Stack 2026: 8 Engines That Matter; Attention Backend Selection: FA3 / FA4 / FlashInfer / FlashMLA - What: NVIDIA's native LLM inference engine built on TensorRT, providing peak FP8/FP4/NVFP4 throughput on NVIDIA GPUs at the cost of a multi-minute engine compile step. - How it works: TRT-LLM compiles a model into an optimized TensorRT engine (taking ~28 minutes) with operator fusion, INT8/FP8/NVFP4 quantization, paged KV cache, and a Triton Inference Server backend. v1.0 promoted the PyTorch backend to stable default; v1.3.x adds NVFP4 MoE, KV Cache Connector API for disaggregation, and Gemma 4 multimodal support. FlashInfer is used for attention kernels, contributed upstream by NVIDIA. - Why it matters: Highest peak throughput on NVIDIA GPU fleets, especially Blackwell with NVFP4; mandatory for NVIDIA NIM containers and the canonical back-end for Dynamo. ~3% overhead vs foundation model with multi-LoRA at rank 64 on RTX 4090. - Gotcha: Engine compile takes ~28 minutes vs seconds for vLLM/SGLang — makes rapid model iteration painful. Use vLLM/SGLang for dev/test; TRT-LLM for long-running production workloads.
title: TensorRT-LLM

body: Decoding · appears on: Drafting Ladder: EAGLE-3 → Parallel Drafting (2026) - What: The number of tokens a drafter proposes per round. DFlash and DSpark evaluate at γ=7 offline; DeepSeek's V4 production deployment uses γ=5. - How it works: Larger γ raises the ceiling on tokens-per-round but lowers the probability that the whole block survives verification, and it consumes more batch capacity during verify. The optimum is workload- and load-dependent, which is precisely what DSpark's confidence scheduling adapts per request. - Why it matters: γ is the knob that trades acceptance against wasted verify work. Offline benchmarks tune it for AL; production tunes it for goodput under concurrency, which is why the production value is smaller. - Gotcha: Offline-optimal γ is not production-optimal — the γ=7 → γ=5 gap between DeepSeek's paper benchmarks and their live serving system is the illustration.
title: γ

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Pre-LLM Era: Serving Infrastructure 2017–2022 - What: Google's production model-serving system (open-sourced 2017) designed for TensorFlow SavedModel format, offering gRPC/REST endpoints and versioned model management. - How it works: Loads SavedModel artifacts from disk, exposes a typed gRPC Predict API, handles model versioning and hot-swapping, and supports static batching where requests are grouped into fixed-size batches before inference. Built for classification/regression models with fixed input/output tensor shapes. - Why it matters: TF Serving established the template for dedicated model-serving infrastructure (separate from training), which later informed the design of Triton, TorchServe, and BentoML. Understanding its limitations clarifies why LLM serving required a fundamentally new approach. - Gotcha: TF Serving's static batching introduces 200–500 ms extra latency because it waits for a batch to fill. For variable-length token generation, its fixed-length I/O assumption makes it fundamentally incompatible with autoregressive decoding — it cannot handle the growing KV cache or streaming token output.
title: TF Serving

body: Metric · appears on: Hardware Landscape 2026: Beyond H100 - What: A unit of compute throughput equal to 10^12 floating-point operations per second, used for individual chip performance figures at a given precision (e.g., Google TPU v7 = 4,614 TFLOPS FP8). - How it works: TFLOPS is the sub-PFLOPS measure: 1,000 TFLOPS = 1 PFLOPS. The TPU v7 Ironwood figure of 4,614 TFLOPS FP8 corresponds to 4.614 PFLOPS. Intel Gaudi 3 delivers 1,835 TFLOPS FP8. TFLOPS is typically used for chips where PFLOPS would require decimal fractions. - Why it matters: TFLOPS provides fine-grained comparison for chips that don't reach PFLOPS scale at standard precisions. However the same caveat applies as for PFLOPS: memory bandwidth is the actual bottleneck for LLM decode. - Gotcha: Vendors often quote sparsity-boosted TFLOPS (2x from 2:4 structured sparsity) alongside dense TFLOPS; always check whether a published figure is dense or sparse. B200's 9 PFLOPS FP4 is dense; the sparse figure is 18 PFLOPS.
title: TFLOPS

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Structured Generation (Tool & Reasoning Parsers) and Workflow defbox: reasoning parser extracts <think> to reasoning_content + content - What: A serving-layer mechanism where reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3, Kimi-K2) emit their chain-of-thought inside '<think>...</think>' XML tags, and the engine's reasoning parser extracts this into a separate 'reasoning_content' field in the API response, distinct from the final 'content' answer. - How it works: The '--reasoning-parser' flag (e.g., '--reasoning-parser deepseek-r1' or 'qwen3' or 'kimi_k2') registers a streaming parser that monitors the token stream for the '<think>' open tag, accumulates tokens into a reasoning buffer until '</think>', then routes subsequent tokens to the final content buffer. Both buffers are returned in the OpenAI-compat response as 'choices[0].message.reasoning_content' and 'choices[0].message.content'. Grammar constraints (via '--guided-decoding-backend') are applied only after the '</think>' closing tag. - Why it matters: Separating reasoning from output is critical for production: clients can display the final answer immediately, log reasoning traces separately for observability, and apply structured-output constraints only to the final answer without constraining the free-form CoT. It also enables token-budget enforcement by counting only content tokens against SLO. - Gotcha: Reasoning parser and tool-call parser can be combined ('--reasoning-parser deepseek-r1 --tool-call-parser kimi_k2') but the interaction is model-specific. If the model emits tool calls inside the thinking block (some Kimi-K2 variants do), the parser order matters. The '<think>' boundary is a model-specific convention, not a universal standard.

body: Metric · appears on: Semantic Caching: The Stack Is 3 Caches Deep - What: The minimum cosine similarity score between an incoming prompt's embedding and a cached prompt's embedding required to return the cached response rather than invoking the LLM. - How it works: After embedding the incoming prompt, the serving layer retrieves the nearest neighbor from the vector cache and computes their cosine similarity. If this score exceeds the threshold (e.g., 0.8), the cached response is returned. Threshold too low: incorrect responses returned for semantically different questions. Threshold too high: cache hit rate collapses to near-exact match only. - Why it matters: The threshold is the primary quality-vs-efficiency knob for semantic caching. Setting it correctly for the specific query distribution and response variance of a workload determines whether semantic caching provides net value or introduces accuracy regressions. - Gotcha: A single global threshold is suboptimal across diverse query types. vCache (ICLR 2026) demonstrates that per-prompt adaptive thresholds achieve 12.5x higher hit rate and 26x lower error rate than a fixed global threshold by accounting for per-prompt response variance.
title: Threshold

body: Metric · appears on: Latency Taxonomy: TTFT · TPOT · Goodput - What: The total number of tokens (or requests) processed per second by the serving system at saturation, without any SLO constraint applied. - How it works: Measured by running the system at maximum load until the GPU is fully utilized and counting output tokens per wall-clock second across all concurrent requests. Commonly reported as 'tokens/s' in benchmarks like vLLM's benchmark_serving.py. - Why it matters: Throughput determines raw cost efficiency: higher throughput means fewer GPUs needed to handle a given request rate. However, throughput benchmarks are often run at saturation where latency SLOs are violated, making them misleading for production planning without pairing with goodput. - Gotcha: Throughput at saturation is NOT the same as goodput at SLO. A system can achieve 1,800 tok/s throughput but only 1,200 tok/s goodput if 33% of requests violate TTFT/TPOT SLOs. Reporting only throughput without SLO context is misleading — always pair with goodput in production analyses.
title: Throughput

body: Metric · appears on: SLA Dashboard: Key Metrics - What: The number of output tokens generated per second per GPU, measured under a sustained load. The dashboard example shows 1,800 tok/s per GPU on an H100 running Llama-3-70B at batch 32. - How it works: Measured by a load testing tool (locust or k6) driving concurrent requests at a target concurrency level and recording total output tokens divided by elapsed wall time. Engine-reported metrics (vllm:gpu_cache_usage_perc, SGLang /metrics) complement external load-test measurements. - Why it matters: Throughput determines cost-per-token: higher tok/s per GPU means more revenue per dollar of compute. But raw throughput is only meaningful when bounded by an SLO — the deck emphasizes Goodput@SLO as the true production metric. - Gotcha: Throughput at saturation (scheduler fully loaded, high queue depth) is always higher than Goodput@SLO. Reporting peak throughput without SLO context is misleading in production. Use locust/k6 to benchmark at realistic concurrency before deploying.
title: Throughput

body: Attention / KV · appears on: FlashAttention: IO-Aware Attention (FA1→FA4) - What: The FlashAttention technique of partitioning the Q, K, V matrices into blocks (tiles) that fit in GPU SRAM so that the full attention computation is performed block-by-block without spilling intermediate results to HBM. - How it works: Q is tiled along the sequence dimension into blocks of size Br; K and V are tiled into blocks of size Bc, chosen so that 4×Br×Bc×d_head bytes fit in SRAM. The outer loop iterates over Q blocks; the inner loop iterates over K/V blocks, accumulating running softmax statistics (m and ℓ) to maintain numerical stability without materializing the full N×N score matrix. - Why it matters: Tiling is the core mechanism that converts O(N²) HBM operations to O(N) HBM operations. Without tiling, any attention kernel for N>16K sequences would either OOM or require multiple HBM passes. - Gotcha: Tile sizes must be tuned to SRAM capacity; too large a tile risks register spilling; too small wastes tensor-core efficiency. FA versions differ partly in how they automate or optimize this tile size selection.
title: Tiling

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Production SLA: Best Practices - What: A client- or proxy-side maximum wait time before abandoning a request and returning an error. The deck recommends 10–60 seconds for LLM generation. - How it works: Set at the HTTP client, API gateway, or reverse proxy (nginx, Envoy). For streaming responses (SSE), the timeout must apply to time-between-tokens (TPOT), not total response time. If no token arrives within the inter-token timeout window, the client terminates the connection and the server should abort generation to free KV cache slots. - Why it matters: Without timeouts, slow requests queue indefinitely, consuming KV cache memory and blocking other requests, turning a transient slowdown into a cascading failure. Timeouts are especially critical under overload because they bound queue depth. - Gotcha: LLM generation latency is variable (TTFT + TPOT x N_output_tokens). A fixed 30s timeout is too short for 4096-token outputs at 50 ms/token (would need 204 s) but too long for a P99 SLO of 1 s. Set separate TTFT timeout and per-token streaming timeout, not a single wall-clock timeout.
title: Timeout

body: Hardware · appears on: FlashAttention: IO-Aware Attention (FA1→FA4) - What: A dedicated hardware unit on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs that asynchronously loads multi-dimensional tensor tiles from HBM to shared memory (SRAM), decoupling data movement from compute and enabling pipeline overlap. - How it works: TMA issues non-blocking bulk transfer commands for N-dimensional tensor tiles (specified by descriptor objects). While TMA is transferring data for the next tile, tensor cores compute on the current tile already in SRAM. This producer-consumer pipeline allows near-100% tensor-core utilization on Hopper. - Why it matters: TMA is one of the key hardware features enabling FA3's ~1.3× speedup over FA2 on H100. Without TMA, the GPU must use synchronous `ldmatrix` instructions that stall compute while waiting for data, leaving tensor cores idle. - Gotcha: TMA requires Hopper (H100/H200) or later. A100 and earlier GPUs do not have TMA; code using TMA descriptors will fail to compile or run on Ampere. On Blackwell, TMA is present but FA4 uses an enhanced 2-CTA variant.
title: TMA

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Pre-LLM Era: Serving Infrastructure 2017–2022 - What: A serving mode where output tokens are sent to the client incrementally as they are generated, rather than buffering the entire response and sending it at the end. - How it works: The server uses HTTP Server-Sent Events (SSE) or a streaming gRPC call to push each generated token (or small chunks of tokens) to the client as soon as they become available. The OpenAI /v1/chat/completions API uses `stream: true` to enable this. On the server side, the engine passes each decode-step output through a streaming callback to the network layer. - Why it matters: Token streaming transforms user experience from a long blank wait followed by an instant full response to a progressive display where text appears word-by-word. This is why TTFT and TPOT are the relevant metrics for streaming interactions, not just E2E latency. - Gotcha: Pre-LLM serving frameworks (TF Serving, TorchServe) had no native streaming response concept because their models were single-pass. Adding streaming to these frameworks required ad-hoc websocket or polling solutions. Token streaming also requires the client to handle partial payloads correctly; malformed streaming parsers cause truncated or doubled output.
title: Token Streaming

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Speculative Decoding & Continuous Batching - What: Sending each generated token to the client immediately as it is produced rather than buffering the full response, so users perceive output beginning within milliseconds of the first generated token. - How it works: Typically implemented via Server-Sent Events (SSE) or WebSockets. The server flushes each token (or a small chunk) to the HTTP response buffer after each decode step. TTFT (Time To First Token) captures this user-visible latency; subsequent tokens arrive at the decode throughput rate (TPOT). - Why it matters: For interactive chat, perceived responsiveness depends almost entirely on TTFT + token rate, not total generation time. Streaming makes a 5-second response feel interactive because the user sees content begin within ~100–300 ms. - Gotcha: Token streaming and speculative decoding interact: speculative decoding accepts multiple tokens in one verification pass, so the token stream may arrive in bursts (4–8 tokens at once) rather than one-by-one. Some clients display bursts as a 'jumpy' stream.
title: Token Streaming

body: Metric · appears on: Tokens-per-Joule & The Power Wall - What: An energy efficiency metric for LLM inference that measures how many output tokens a system generates per joule of energy consumed; a first-class metric in MLPerf Power v5.1 (Sep 2025) benchmarking. - How it works: Measured by counting generated tokens against energy drawn from the wall (or estimated from GPU TDP and utilization) during a benchmark run. MLPerf Power v5.1 standardized the measurement methodology. The metric captures the combined effect of hardware efficiency, quantization, and model architecture on energy consumption per unit of useful output. - Why it matters: Power, not FLOPS, is the binding constraint for scaling AI serving in 2026: GB200 NVL72 racks consume 120–132 kW, and IEA projects datacenter electricity usage doubling from 485 to 950 TWh by 2030. Tokens-per-joule drives hardware selection, quantization choices, and routing decisions. - Gotcha: The median realistic energy per query is ~0.31 Wh — prior estimates overstated this by 4–20x. But reasoning models that generate 15x more tokens raise this to ~3.91 Wh/query (13x multiplier), making reasoning-model routing a primary energy lever, not just a cost lever.
title: Tokens-per-Joule

body: Metric · appears on: Hardware Landscape 2026: Beyond H100 - What: An energy efficiency metric for LLM serving that measures how many output tokens are generated per joule of energy consumed, adopted as a first-class metric at MLPerf Power v5.1. - How it works: Tokens-per-joule is computed as total tokens generated divided by total energy in joules (watt-seconds) consumed by the inference hardware and cooling infrastructure. FP8 quantization provides approximately 30% energy reduction at batch size ≥64 vs FP16 on the same hardware. Reasoning models with 15x more output tokens raise median energy from 0.31 to 3.91 Wh/query (13x increase). - Why it matters: As LLM inference dominates data center power budgets and electricity costs, tokens-per-joule directly translates to cost-per-token and carbon footprint. GB200 NVL72 at 120–132 kW/rack makes power a first-order operational concern. - Gotcha: Tokens-per-joule conflates prefill and decode energy; prefill is compute-bound and scales differently. Reasoning model inference (o3-style, extended thinking) is disproportionately energy-expensive because token count multiplies faster than quality gain — routing easy queries away from reasoning models is the primary energy lever.
title: Tokens-per-joule

body: Energy unit economics (median Gemini prompt ~0.24 Wh); reasoning queries cost 74–86× more energy than a small-model query.

body: CLI / flag · appears on: Structured Generation: XGrammar, Tool & Reasoning Parsers - What: A vLLM CLI flag that enables model-specific tool-call parsing, extracting function-call invocations from model output and exposing them as structured `tool_calls` in the API response. - How it works: When set (e.g., --tool-call-parser llama4 or --tool-call-parser kimi_k2), vLLM intercepts the raw text generation and applies a model-specific parser that recognizes the model's native tool-call syntax (e.g., <tool_call>...</tool_call> tags for some models, JSON blocks for others). Parsing happens incrementally, streaming args token-by-token as they arrive. Supports 15+ model families as of mid-2026. - Why it matters: Without this flag, tool calls appear as raw text strings; clients must implement model-specific parsing themselves, which is fragile and breaks on schema changes. The flag provides a unified `tool_calls` array in the OpenAI response regardless of model. - Gotcha: The parser is model-family specific — using the wrong parser (e.g., --tool-call-parser llama4 on a Qwen model) produces incorrect or missing tool_calls. Check the vLLM docs for the correct parser name for your model. Combine with --reasoning-parser when using reasoning models that output tool calls after a <think> block.

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Model Compilation: torch.compile + CUDA Graphs + TensorRT - What: PyTorch 2.0+ compiler that traces a Python model's computation graph via `torch.fx`, applies graph-level optimizations, and emits optimized Triton or CUDA kernels through the TorchInductor backend. - How it works: On the first call, `torch.compile` traces the computation, applies operator fusion and layout optimizations in TorchInductor, and generates Triton or C++/CUDA kernel code that is compiled and cached. Subsequent calls replay the compiled kernel. `mode='max-autotune'` explores multiple kernel configs (slow compile, fastest runtime); `mode='reduce-overhead'` focuses on eliminating Python dispatch overhead; `dynamic=True` handles variable-shaped inputs without recompilation. - Why it matters: Delivers 1.1–1.5× speedup on LLM decode phase from Python overhead elimination and kernel fusion, with minimal code changes (single decorator). Unlike TensorRT, does not require ONNX export or a 5–30 minute compile step. - Gotcha: Compilation happens lazily on the first call with each new input shape; `dynamic=False` (default) recompiles for every new shape, causing cold-start latency spikes. Production LLM engines guard against this by padding to fixed shapes or using `dynamic=True`. The compile cache may need warming on cold deploys.
title: torch.compile

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Model Compilation: torch.compile + CUDA Graphs + TensorRT - What: PyTorch's symbolic tracing and graph transformation framework, used by `torch.compile` to capture the computation graph of a Python model as a DAG of operations before passing it to TorchInductor for code generation. - How it works: torch.fx symbolically traces a model by running it with proxy inputs that record every ATen operation and its dependencies. The result is a `torch.fx.Graph` (DAG) that can be inspected, transformed (fusion passes, shape analysis), and lowered to Triton/C++ kernels by TorchInductor. - Why it matters: torch.fx is the intermediate representation layer that makes `torch.compile` composable with custom passes. Understanding it explains why `torch.compile` cannot trace through Python control flow that depends on tensor values (dynamic shapes) without `dynamic=True`. - Gotcha: torch.fx trace-based compilation breaks on models with Python-level control flow that branches on tensor values (e.g., `if tensor.item() > 0`). Such models require `torch.compile(dynamic=True)` or manual graph breaks, which reduce optimization scope.
title: torch.fx

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Model Compilation: torch.compile + CUDA Graphs + TensorRT - What: The default code-generation backend for `torch.compile` that lowers PyTorch ATen operations to optimized Triton GPU kernels (or C++/OpenMP for CPU) with automatic fusion and layout selection. - How it works: TorchInductor receives the FX graph from `torch.compile`'s tracing phase, applies fusion passes (combining element-wise operations into one kernel, horizontal and vertical fusion), selects memory layouts (channels-first vs contiguous), and emits Triton source code that is JIT-compiled to PTX and then to GPU machine code. - Why it matters: TorchInductor is what actually produces the speedup; `torch.compile` is the entry point. Understanding the pipeline (FX graph → Inductor fusion → Triton kernels → PTX) explains both the warmup cost and why `max-autotune` is slower to compile but faster at runtime. - Gotcha: TorchInductor does not produce kernels as fast as hand-tuned CUTLASS or FlashAttention kernels for the attention operation itself; it excels at fusing surrounding element-wise ops (rotary embeddings, layer norms, residuals). Major engines still call FlashAttention directly rather than relying on Inductor for the attention core.
title: TorchInductor

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Pre-LLM Era: Serving Infrastructure 2017–2022 - What: Facebook/Meta's PyTorch-native model-serving framework (2020) that packages models as MAR (Model ARchive) files and exposes a REST API with multi-model support. - How it works: A MAR file bundles the model weights, handler code, and dependencies into a single archive. TorchServe loads these archives, manages GPU allocation across multiple models, and handles REST requests with configurable batching. Handler code defines custom pre/post processing. - Why it matters: TorchServe provided a Pythonic, PyTorch-first alternative to TF Serving and Triton. It is still used for serving non-LLM PyTorch models (classification, detection, NLP encoders) in production. - Gotcha: Like TF Serving, TorchServe has no native support for KV-cache management, token streaming, or continuous batching — the LLM-serving essentials. Its MAR packaging model makes rapid iteration and hot-patching slower than Python-native frameworks like BentoML or vLLM.
title: TorchServe

body: Metric · appears on: Latency Taxonomy: TTFT · TPOT · Goodput - What: The average inter-token delay during the autoregressive decode phase — equivalently called ITL (Inter-Token Latency). It measures how quickly successive output tokens stream to the client. - How it works: Each decode step runs a KV-cache-assisted forward pass over only the new token (not the whole prompt), making it memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound. TPOT = (E2E latency − TTFT) / (N − 1) where N is the number of output tokens. Under batched serving, sharing compute across requests amortizes cost but increases TPOT (more requests = each waits for the batch to complete each decode step). - Why it matters: TPOT governs perceived streaming speed. Humans read at roughly 150–250 WPM, so a TPOT above ~40–80 ms makes text appear to trickle. For agentic/tool-call workloads, long reasoning chains (tens of thousands of tokens) multiply TPOT by N, making even 25 ms/token problematic for real-time pipelines. - Gotcha: TPOT and ITL (Inter-Token Latency) are used interchangeably in the literature; both refer to the same per-step decode interval. Speculative decoding improves TPOT for memory-bound, low-batch scenarios but can become net-negative (e.g., EAGLE-2 drops to 0.93x at batch ≥ 24) because the verify step consumes compute that could serve other requests.
title: TPOT

body: Metric · appears on: Production Tuning: Memory, Scheduling & Observability - What: The reciprocal of decode throughput: the time between consecutive generated tokens in a response, measuring the smoothness of streaming output for a single request. - How it works: TPOT = 1 / (tokens_per_second per request) for a single request during decode. Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound: TPOT ≈ (KV_cache_size + weights_size) / HBM_bandwidth. For H100 (3.35 TB/s HBM3), a 70B BF16 model (~140 GB weights + KV) at batch=1 gives ~25–40 ms/token. Increasing batch size amortizes the fixed weight-read cost, reducing TPOT until memory bandwidth saturates. - Why it matters: The SLO for streaming UX: TPOT > 100ms makes responses feel choppy (below human reading speed of ~5 tok/s); TPOT 25–50ms (20–40 tok/s) is comfortable for most use cases. Also determines maximum output throughput at a given concurrency. - Gotcha: TPOT increases linearly with batch size in the memory-bandwidth-bound regime — serving 128 concurrent users with the same TPOT as 1 user requires 128x more memory bandwidth (i.e., a bigger GPU or EP). TPOT and TTFT cannot be simultaneously optimized — disaggregation separates their optimization paths.
title: TPOT

body: Tokens/giây khi sinh (time-per-output-token là nghịch đảo). Flagship ~80–110 tok/s.

body: Attention / KV · appears on: Attention Backend Selection: FA3 / FA4 / FlashInfer / FlashMLA - What: A cross-platform attention kernel implemented in OpenAI Triton (GPU meta-language), used as the universal fallback backend for non-NVIDIA hardware (ROCm, Ascend NPU, CPU) in vLLM. - How it works: The Triton backend implements paged attention and standard MHA/GQA in Triton's Python-JIT DSL, which compiles to PTX (NVIDIA), GCN (AMD ROCm), or other targets. It is ~2.7x slower than FA4 on B200 but runs on any Triton-supported hardware. Activated via --attention-backend triton or auto-selected when no native kernel fits the detected hardware. - Why it matters: Enables vLLM to run on AMD ROCm, Huawei Ascend, and Intel hardware without requiring vendor-specific CUDA extensions; critical for heterogeneous cloud deployments and national-cloud hardware. - Gotcha: Triton backend performance varies significantly by GPU vendor and Triton version — expect 2–5x lower throughput than FA3/FlashInfer on equivalent NVIDIA hardware. Always benchmark with the native kernel before accepting Triton performance as the baseline.
title: Triton attention backend

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Pre-LLM Era: Serving Infrastructure 2017–2022 - What: NVIDIA's multi-framework inference server (2019), supporting TensorFlow, PyTorch, ONNX, TensorRT, and custom backends with per-model dynamic batching and a model repository concept. - How it works: Runs as a gRPC/HTTP server that loads models from a repository, applies per-model dynamic batching (collecting requests within a latency budget before sending to GPU), and exposes metrics via Prometheus. Supports concurrent model execution and multiple model instances per GPU. NVIDIA Dynamo 1.0 (2026) supersedes Triton as the recommended layer for LLM serving. - Why it matters: Triton was the standard multi-model GPU inference server for CNNs, embedding models, and pre-LLM NLP through 2022. Its dynamic batching is still relevant for embedding/reranker serving (prefill-only, no decode loop), and it remains the backend for traditional CV/speech tasks. - Gotcha: Triton's 'dynamic batching' is per-model and latency-budget-based — fundamentally different from LLM continuous batching. Triton has no concept of KV caches, autoregressive steps, or variable-length token generation. Do not confuse Triton Inference Server with the Triton GPU programming language (OpenAI's triton kernel language), which is a separate project.
title: Triton Inference Server

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Model Compilation: torch.compile + CUDA Graphs + TensorRT - What: GPU compute kernels written in OpenAI's Triton language — a Python-like DSL that compiles to PTX/CUBIN — providing most of FlashAttention's performance with less code than hand-written CUDA. - How it works: Triton programs are written as blocked/tiled Python-like code; the Triton compiler handles thread/block scheduling, shared memory allocation, and memory coalescing automatically. The resulting PTX is equivalent to hand-tuned CUDA for many memory-bound patterns. TorchInductor emits Triton; FlexAttention compiles mask functions to Triton; FlashAttention-3/4 use Triton for some sub-kernels. - Why it matters: Lowers the barrier to custom GPU kernel development from CUDA expertise to Python-level knowledge. Enables researchers and engine developers to write fast attention variants, quantization routines, and fused operations without a CUDA background. - Gotcha: Triton performs well for memory-bound tiled kernels but falls behind hand-tuned CUTLASS for compute-bound GEMM operations (FA4 on Blackwell is 2.7× faster than Triton for attention). For production-critical paths (main attention, large GEMM), CUTLASS or CUDA may still be preferred.
title: Triton Kernels

body: Metric · appears on: Latency Taxonomy: TTFT · TPOT · Goodput - What: The wall-clock elapsed time from when a client sends a request until the server emits the very first output token. - How it works: Dominated by two components: (1) queue wait — how long the request sits in the prefill queue before a worker picks it up, and (2) prefill compute — one full forward pass over the entire prompt, which is compute-intensive and scales O(n) in sequence length (O(n²) for full attention, but FlashAttention makes it more practical). No KV cache exists at the start, so every prompt token must be processed fresh. - Why it matters: TTFT is the primary perceived latency for interactive applications: users see nothing until the first token arrives. SLOs (P95/P99 TTFT targets) gate whether a deployment is production-acceptable for chat/copilot use cases. Prefill–decode disaggregation exists specifically to reduce TTFT by dedicating separate, compute-optimized hardware to the prefill phase. - Gotcha: TTFT includes both queue wait and compute; under load, queue wait can dominate. Reporting only the compute portion (single-request microbenchmark) massively understates real-world TTFT. Also, image-heavy VLM requests spike TTFT severely because visual tokens (thousands per image) extend the prefill phase — TTFT becomes a function of image count, not output length.
title: TTFT

body: Metric · appears on: Inference Engine Evolution: 2020 → 2025; Disaggregated Prefill/Decode Serving; Production Tuning: Memory, Scheduling & Observability - What: The latency from request submission to the arrival of the first generated token — the primary user-perceived latency metric for interactive LLM applications. - How it works: TTFT = time for the prefill phase (processing all input tokens in parallel) + scheduling queue wait time + any KV transfer latency (in disaggregated serving). Prefill is O(L²) in attention for length L (or O(L) with linearized variants), making TTFT grow quadratically with prompt length for standard attention. Prefix caching reduces TTFT by up to 70% on shared prefixes. Target: <500ms for interactive applications, <2s for complex RAG queries. - Why it matters: The SLO that disaggregated serving, prefix caching, and chunked prefill all optimize for; users perceive TTFT as application 'responsiveness' — a TTFT >2s causes significant user abandonment. - Gotcha: TTFT is dominated by prefill time for long prompts but by queue wait time at high load — monitoring only TTFT without separating queue wait from prefill time obscures the root cause of latency spikes. Use both num_queue_reqs and TTFT histograms together for diagnosis.
title: TTFT

body: Metric · appears on: Scaling Strategies (via research companion §12 KEDA pattern) - What: The elapsed wall-clock time from when a client sends an inference request to when the first output token is received; the primary latency metric for interactive LLM serving. - How it works: Measured at the client by recording the timestamp of the HTTP request and the timestamp of the first SSE/streaming token chunk. In the serving engine, TTFT is dominated by prefill compute time (processing all input tokens in one forward pass). KEDA can be configured to scale on a PromQL expression that computes P99 TTFT from Prometheus histograms. - Why it matters: TTFT is the metric users feel first — it determines perceived responsiveness. It is one of the two primary SLO dimensions for LLM serving (the other being TPOT/TBT). The 2025–26 KEDA pattern scales on TTFT (via PromQL) in addition to queue depth to enforce user-facing SLOs directly. - Gotcha: TTFT and TPOT trade off against each other in scheduling. Chunked prefill and decode-first scheduling reduce TPOT variance but inflate TTFT for new requests. Scaling on TTFT alone may cause over-scaling during reasoning-model runs where very long decode sequences dominate the queue.
title: TTFT

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Serving Stack 2026: 8 Engines table — LMDeploy's 'TurboMind engine' - What: LMDeploy's high-performance C++/CUDA inference engine that serves as the backend for GPU-accelerated LLM deployment, achieving high throughput on NVIDIA hardware including support for MXFP4 on V100+ GPUs. - How it works: TurboMind implements continuous batching, paged KV cache, and fused CUDA kernels for attention and FFN layers. In LMDeploy v0.13.0 (Jun 2026, CUDA 12.8, RTX 50-series support), it adds MXFP4 quantization support and achieves approximately 1.5x the throughput of vLLM on H800 for GPT-OSS-class models. It also supports prefill/decode disaggregation via DLSlime/Mooncake integration. - Why it matters: TurboMind is the reason LMDeploy is competitive with vLLM/SGLang on NVIDIA hardware — without it, LMDeploy would be a Python orchestration layer with no kernel advantage. It enables the 'high throughput' niche in the serving table: useful when maximising raw throughput on NVIDIA fleets is the primary objective. - Gotcha: TurboMind is NVIDIA-specific; LMDeploy's portability to other hardware (Ascend, etc.) uses a different backend path. The '1.5x over vLLM on H800' figure is for GPT-OSS-20B specifically and may not generalise to all model families.
title: TurboMind

body: Quantization · appears on: FP4 2026: MXFP4 vs NVFP4 & KV Cache Quantization - What: A data-oblivious vector-quantization algorithm from Google (arXiv 2504.19874, Zandieh/Daliri/Hadian/Mirrokni) used to compress the KV cache to roughly 3.5 bits per channel with no measurable quality loss. - How it works: Input vectors are randomly rotated, which induces a concentrated Beta distribution on the coordinates; because distinct coordinates are then near-independent in high dimension, an optimal scalar quantizer can be applied per coordinate. Since an MSE-optimal quantizer biases inner-product estimates, a second stage applies a 1-bit Quantized Johnson–Lindenstrauss (QJL) transform to the residual, yielding an unbiased inner-product estimator. - Why it matters: KV-cache memory scales with context × concurrency, so it is a bigger lever than weight quantization at long context. TurboQuant needs no training and no calibration data, so it can be applied online to any model. - Gotcha: Beware the inflated version circulating online. Aggregator posts claim “3-bit, zero loss, 6× memory reduction, 8× faster attention”. The paper says 3.5 bits/channel for absolute quality neutrality and 2.5 bits for marginal degradation, within ≈2.7× of the proven information-theoretic bound. It is also an Apr-2025 vector-quantization paper, not a 2026 KV-cache product.
title: TurboQuant

body: Metric · appears on: Tokens-per-Joule frame (The Power Wall): datacenter electricity '~485 → 950 TWh' - What: A unit of electrical energy equal to one trillion watt-hours (10^12 Wh) or one billion kilowatt-hours (10^9 kWh), used in the deck to quantify global data centre annual electricity consumption. - How it works: 1 TWh = 1,000 GWh = 1,000,000 MWh. Global data centre consumption of ~485 TWh/year is equivalent to approximately 55 GW of continuous average power draw — roughly the combined generating capacity of France and the UK. GB200 NVL72 racks at 132 kW each: 485 TWh / 132 kW / 8760 h/year ≈ 420,000 NVL72 racks running continuously to account for just data centre AI compute. At the per-query level, 0.31 Wh/query × (485 TWh / 0.31 Wh) ≈ 1.6 trillion queries/year served by the world's data centres. - Why it matters: Using TWh rather than smaller units (GWh, MWh) frames the power wall at a scale that connects to national energy policy and the electrical grid. It makes the energy consequence of architectural decisions (FP8 saves ~30% energy at batch≥64) tangible: 30% of 485 TWh = ~145 TWh saved, comparable to the annual electricity consumption of several countries. - Gotcha: TWh is an energy unit (power × time), not a power unit. A data centre consuming 485 TWh/year consumes ~55 GW on average, but individual facilities may have peak demand 2–3x their average. The IEA forecast uses calendar-year consumption as the comparand unit; comparing it to instantaneous GPU power (kW) requires multiplying by operating hours.
title: TWh

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Expert Parallelism: MoE Scaling - What: A scheduling technique that interleaves All-to-All communication and GEMM computation from two concurrent micro-batches to hide the A2A latency in MoE prefill. - How it works: While micro-batch N's expert activations are being dispatched and received via A2A (idle GPU GEMM units), micro-batch N+1's GEMM computations execute simultaneously on those idle units. The GPU alternates between compute and communication phases across the two micro-batches, achieving near-full utilization. SGLang flag: `--enable-two-batch-overlap`; vLLM: `--enable-dbo`. - Why it matters: In large-scale EP, A2A takes 20–40% of total prefill time. TBO converts this idle time into productive GEMM work, yielding +27–35% prefill throughput and ~50% peak memory reduction (SGLang measurements). - Gotcha: TBO requires the model to be batched into exactly two micro-batches and adds implementation complexity. The gain is specific to prefill-heavy MoE workloads; TBO may be net-neutral or harmful for decode-only or dense model workloads.
title: Two-Batch Overlap

body: Attention / KV · appears on: PagedAttention: vLLM v0 → v1 Deep Dive - What: A V1-specific GPU memory design where KV cache and model activations share a single managed pool, rather than having separate fixed pre-allocated regions for each. - How it works: In V0, VRAM was partitioned into a fixed model-weights region + fixed KV-cache region (sized by --gpu-memory-utilization at startup). In V1, activations are also pooled, and the allocator dynamically assigns pages across the combined pool. This eliminates the waste of the old fixed KV-cache pre-allocation when activation memory peaks are low. - Why it matters: Allows V1 to serve larger batch sizes and longer sequences on the same hardware, contributing to its 1.7x throughput improvement over V0. - Gotcha: The unified pool means that runaway activation memory (e.g., very long chunked prefills) can reduce KV cache capacity dynamically — monitor with the Prometheus num_gpu_blocks metric. The --gpu-memory-utilization flag still controls the fraction of total VRAM used by the pool.
title: Unified memory pool

body: Metric · appears on: SLA Dashboard: Key Metrics - What: The fraction of time the service successfully handles requests, expressed as a percentage. The dashboard target is 99.9%, which equates to at most 8.7 hours of downtime per year. - How it works: Measured via health-check probes (HTTP /health endpoints on each replica) aggregated at the load balancer or monitoring layer. Multi-AZ deployment is the primary mechanism for achieving 99.9%: a single AZ outage does not take the whole service down. Rolling deploys and circuit breakers prevent version updates from causing full downtime. - Why it matters: For user-facing LLM products, even brief outages degrade trust and directly violate SLA terms. The 99.9% figure (three nines) is the baseline expectation for most commercial AI APIs; higher-tier contracts demand 99.95% or 99.99%. - Gotcha: 99.9% uptime still allows 8.7 h/year of downtime. Achieving 99.9% vs 99.99% requires fundamentally different architecture (multi-region active-active vs multi-AZ active-passive). LLM services with long GPU cold-start times (1-5 min) must pre-warm replicas to count downtime correctly.

body: Caching · appears on: Semantic Caching: The Stack Is 3 Caches Deep - What: A semantic caching system (ICLR 2026) that uses per-prompt adaptive similarity thresholds with formal error bounds, rather than a single global threshold. - How it works: vCache (arXiv:2502.03771) trains a lightweight predictor that estimates the acceptable similarity threshold for each individual prompt based on its expected response variance. High-variance prompts (creative, open-ended) get stricter thresholds; low-variance prompts (factual FAQ) get looser ones. This gives formal error bounds on cache hit quality. - Why it matters: A single global threshold is a blunt instrument: too loose risks incorrect cached responses on creative queries; too strict misses valid hits on stable factual queries. Per-prompt thresholds achieve up to 12.5x hit rate and 26x lower error vs fixed-threshold approaches. - Gotcha: vCache requires an additional trained threshold-predictor model, adding latency and complexity to the cache lookup path. It was presented at ICLR 2026 and is not yet in mainstream open-source serving stacks as of mid-2026.

body: Concept · appears on: Multimodal (VLM) Serving: Encode–Prefill–Decode - What: A transformer applied to image patches rather than text tokens, used as the visual encoder stage in VLMs to convert raw pixels into embedding vectors. - How it works: The image is divided into NxN patches; each patch is linearly projected into an embedding vector; a standard transformer processes this sequence. The encoder runs once per image and its output is concatenated with text embeddings before the LLM decode stack. - Why it matters: ViT is a major compute bottleneck in VLM serving; for multi-image requests it can consume more wall-clock time than the LLM prefill, motivating CPU-side or disaggregated encode paths. - Gotcha: ViT does not parallelize well via tensor parallelism — at TP=8 it becomes slower, not faster. Intel Xeon AMX can run ViT encode concurrently on CPU while the GPU handles prefill/decode.
title: ViT

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Pre-LLM Era: Serving Infrastructure 2017–2022 - What: An open-source LLM inference and serving engine (UC Berkeley, first released Jun 2023) that introduced PagedAttention and continuous batching, now the most widely deployed LLM serving framework. - How it works: vLLM's V1 engine (production default from v0.8.0, Mar 2025) implements: PagedAttention for non-contiguous KV allocation, continuous batching with a unified token budget scheduler, chunked prefill to prevent decode stalls, automatic prefix caching (APC) on by default, piecewise CUDA graphs for efficient decode, and a pluggable KV Connector API for prefill–decode disaggregation. Supports ROCm, Intel, TPU, Trainium, Gaudi, and CUDA. - Why it matters: vLLM demonstrated 24x throughput over naive HuggingFace Transformers serving at launch and remains the reference engine for LLM serving benchmarks. Its wide hardware support, OpenAI-compatible API, and large contributor base (~3x SGLang's) make it the most common production choice. - Gotcha: vLLM V0 (prior to v0.8.0) had significantly worse performance than V1. Papers benchmarking vLLM before Mar 2025 may be comparing against V0. Also: HuggingFace TGI is archived (Mar 2026); the open-source serving landscape is now vLLM + SGLang as a duopoly, with TRT-LLM for maximum peak throughput.
title: vLLM

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Serving Stack 2026: 8 Engines That Matter; PagedAttention: vLLM v0 → v1 Deep Dive; Prefix Caching: RadixAttention, APC, HiCache & Pricing; Production Tuning: Memory, Scheduling & Observability; Disaggregated Prefill/Decode Serving - What: The dominant open-source LLM serving engine for production GPU deployments, offering OpenAI-compatible API, PagedAttention, and Automatic Prefix Caching. - How it works: vLLM serves models by managing GPU KV cache memory via PagedAttention (virtual-memory paging), scheduling requests with continuous batching, and exposing an OpenAI-compatible REST endpoint. V1 (default since v0.8.0, Mar 2025) adds a unified memory pool for KV + activations, prefix-aware scheduling, piecewise CUDA graphs, and APC on-by-default, delivering ~1.7x over V0 throughput. - Why it matters: Widest hardware support (NVIDIA/ROCm/Intel/TPU/Trainium/Gaudi), largest contributor community, and the reference implementation that virtually every other system benchmarks against; the default choice for production GPU deployments outside NVIDIA-native stacks. - Gotcha: vLLM V1 became the default engine in v0.8.0 (Mar 18, 2025), not January 2025 — the Jan 2025 V1 was an opt-in alpha. HF TGI is now archived (Mar 2026), making vLLM and SGLang the de-facto duopoly.
title: vLLM

body: High-throughput serving (Day-20 Track-2 territory). PagedAttention manages KV cache like OS paging.

body: Engine / Tool · appears on: Scaling Strategies (via research companion, §12) - What: An official Helm chart and supporting tooling (vllm-stack) that packages vLLM with a prefix-aware router, Prometheus metrics, and KEDA autoscaling into a production-ready Kubernetes deployment. - How it works: vllm-stack-0.1.11 (May 7 2026) deploys vLLM replicas behind a prefix-aware router that maps requests to replicas by KV-cache prefix, exposed via Prometheus scrape targets. KEDA is configured to scale on `vllm:num_requests_waiting`. Grafana dashboards are included. Reports 3–10x lower TTFT vs round-robin. - Why it matters: Closes the gap between running vLLM standalone and running it reliably at production scale: adds the routing, scaling, and observability glue that vLLM's core engine does not provide. - Gotcha: The prefix-aware router requires sticky or semi-sticky routing to be effective for KV-cache reuse — requests with the same prefix must reach the same replica. This can conflict with pure least-busy routing if not carefully balanced.
title: vLLM Production-Stack

body: Concept · appears on: Multimodal (VLM) Serving: Encode–Prefill–Decode - What: A neural model that jointly processes visual inputs (images, video frames) and text tokens, typically via a vision encoder coupled to a language decoder. - How it works: Images are processed by a Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder into patch embeddings, then projected into the LLM's token space; the concatenated visual+text token sequence is fed through normal prefill and autoregressive decode. Modern variants (e.g., Llama 4 early fusion) embed vision features directly without a separate encoder stage. - Why it matters: VLMs are now dominant inference traffic; their image-token inflation (hundreds to thousands of tokens per image) fundamentally changes TTFT scaling and batching strategies compared to text-only LLMs. - Gotcha: The ViT encoder does NOT benefit from tensor parallelism (TP); at TP=8 it actually slows down, requiring separate encoder disaggregation rather than standard TP scaling.
title: VLM

title: Vòng lặp agent

body: Concept · appears on: Embedding & Reranker Serving warningbox: 'Self-host break-even ... so với API (OpenAI/Voyage)' - What: Voyage AI, a specialised embedding model provider (founded by former Stanford NLP researchers) that offers embedding and reranker APIs competitive with OpenAI's text-embedding-3 models, cited in the deck as the commercial API baseline for embedding self-host break-even analysis. - How it works: Voyage provides embedding APIs (voyage-3, voyage-3-large, voyage-code-3) and reranker APIs (rerank-2) with per-token pricing comparable to OpenAI's embedding endpoints. The deck's break-even analysis compares self-hosted embedding inference costs (GPU/CPU hardware amortisation + electricity + ops) against Voyage and OpenAI API per-token costs, finding self-hosting becomes cost-effective above approximately 50–100M tokens/month. - Why it matters: The Voyage reference in the warningbox establishes that API alternatives exist for embedding/reranking and that the self-host vs API decision is quantifiable. For students designing RAG systems, this frames embedding serving not as 'always self-host' but as a cost-optimization decision dependent on query volume. - Gotcha: The 50–100M token/month break-even figure is a rough estimate dependent on GPU type, utilisation rate, and current API pricing — all of which change frequently. Voyage and OpenAI have both reduced embedding API pricing significantly in 2025–26. Self-hosting also includes operational overhead (model updates, reliability, latency SLAs) not captured in a pure per-token cost comparison.
title: Voyage

body: Hardware · appears on: Quantization: Precision vs Performance; Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ - What: The on-chip high-bandwidth memory on a GPU, used to store model weights, KV cache, activations, and intermediate computation buffers during inference. - How it works: GPU kernels can only operate on data resident in VRAM. For serving, the peak VRAM consumption is approximately: model_params × bytes_per_param + KV_cache_size + activation_buffer. For an 8B model at FP16 (2 bytes/param): 8B × 2 = 16 GB before KV cache. Any quantization that reduces bytes_per_param directly enables longer contexts or larger batch sizes. - Why it matters: VRAM is the primary constraint that quantization addresses. Most production decisions (which format to use, whether to shard across GPUs) flow from VRAM budget. The deck's comparison chart explicitly maps each format to VRAM consumption for 8B and 70B models. - Gotcha: VRAM usage during inference is not just model weights: KV cache for long contexts can dwarf the model weights. A 70B model at AWQ 4-bit uses ~40 GB weights, but a 32K context at FP16 KV adds another ~20–40 GB depending on architecture. Use FP8 or NVFP4 KV cache to reclaim that budget.
title: VRAM

body: Research · appears on: Request Scheduling: Ai Được Chạy Trước? - What: The reference fair-scheduling algorithm for LLM serving, from “Fairness in Serving Large Language Models” (Sheng et al., OSDI '24, arXiv 2401.00588). - How it works: Fairness is defined over a cost function counting input and output tokens processed per client. VTC tracks a virtual token counter per client as a proxy for service received and schedules to equalise it, on top of continuous batching. The paper proves a 2× tight upper bound on the service difference between two backlogged clients. - Why it matters: Rate limits — the usual fairness mechanism — under-utilise the server whenever there is spare capacity and still deliver poor experience. VTC is fairness without that waste. - Gotcha: No serving engine ships VTC. It belongs in the research column of any honest slide. Related work worth knowing: ELIS (arXiv 2505.09142) predicts output length for SJF-style ordering, and ProServe (arXiv 2512.12928) targets multi-priority scheduling.
title: VTC

body: Hardware · appears on: Edge Deployment Flow - What: A low-level, cross-platform GPU programming API (Khronos Group) supported by llama.cpp as a GPU backend on Linux, Windows, and Android, enabling GPU-accelerated inference without CUDA or Metal on non-NVIDIA, non-Apple GPUs. - How it works: llama.cpp's Vulkan backend (enabled via cmake -DGGML_VULKAN=ON) dispatches matrix multiply and attention operations as Vulkan compute shaders. It supports AMD GPUs (via ROCm Vulkan driver), Intel GPUs (ARC), and mobile GPUs (Qualcomm Adreno, ARM Mali) on Android. Performance is lower than CUDA or Metal due to Vulkan's higher driver abstraction overhead. - Why it matters: Vulkan provides GPU acceleration for llama.cpp on the long tail of hardware not covered by CUDA (NVIDIA) or Metal (Apple): AMD Linux GPUs, Intel ARC, Android mobile GPUs. It is the primary backend for Android GPU inference in llama.cpp. - Gotcha: Vulkan performance is significantly lower than CUDA on NVIDIA hardware and lower than ROCm for compute-heavy workloads; use CUDA or ROCm on NVIDIA/AMD for production. On Android, thermal throttling typically limits sustained GPU performance more than the Vulkan overhead.
title: Vulkan

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ (research companion) - What: A quantization configuration where model weights are stored and computed in 4-bit integer precision, but activations remain in FP16 (or BF16). The dominant GPU inference quantization regime for 4-bit. - How it works: At inference, weights are dequantized from INT4 to FP16 on the fly just before each matrix multiplication. The actual GEMM runs in FP16. This avoids accumulation errors from INT4 arithmetic but adds a small dequantization overhead. AWQ and GPTQ both default to W4A16. - Why it matters: W4A16 gives the memory reduction of 4-bit weights without the accuracy risks of 4-bit activation quantization. It is the standard for consumer-GPU 4-bit inference and is supported by all major serving frameworks. - Gotcha: W4A16 provides memory savings but limited compute throughput improvement because the GEMM itself still runs in FP16. For throughput gains, W4A8 (activations also quantized) is needed — but W4A8 has more accuracy risk. Research (arXiv:2505.22179) found W4A16 often cancels speculative decoding gains; use W8A8 + EAGLE instead.
title: W4A16

body: Quantization · appears on: Quantization for Memory: GGUF · NF4 · GPTQ · AWQ (research companion) - What: A quantization configuration where both model weights and activations are in 8-bit precision (either INT8 or FP8), enabling the use of 8-bit integer or FP8 tensor core acceleration. - How it works: In W8A8-FP (FP8), both weights and activations use E4M3 or E5M2. The GEMM runs natively in FP8 on Hopper+ tensor cores with FP32 accumulation. This is the format described as 'essentially lossless' (ACL 2025). In W8A8-INT8, TensorRT's integer path is used. - Why it matters: W8A8-FP8 is the recommended production format on Hopper hardware because it achieves both memory reduction (half vs FP16) and compute throughput gain (native FP8 tensor cores) with under 1% accuracy loss. It is also the safe pairing for speculative decoding (EAGLE). - Gotcha: W8A8-INT8 and W8A8-FP8 are different. FP8 has a floating-point scale per tensor/channel; INT8 uses a fixed integer scale. On Hopper, FP8 outperforms INT8 in both accuracy and throughput due to native hardware support.
title: W8A8

body: Ops / scaling · appears on: Scaling Strategies - What: A set of N pre-initialized GPU replicas kept idle (warmed up with model weights loaded) so that traffic spikes can be absorbed without incurring cold-start latency. - How it works: The operator configures a minimum replica floor (minReplicas > 0 in HPA/KEDA terms). These replicas sit loaded and healthy, accepting no traffic or very little, so they respond immediately when the load balancer routes requests to them. The autoscaler only adds replicas above the warm-pool floor when queue depth or utilization thresholds are crossed. - Why it matters: Eliminates cold-start latency for burst absorption while still allowing the pool to auto-scale beyond the warm floor. Essential for production tiers where P99 latency SLOs must be met even at traffic spikes. - Gotcha: Warm pools cost money continuously even with zero traffic — this is the direct trade-off against scale-to-zero. Optimal warm-pool sizing requires traffic forecasting; over-provisioning wastes GPU budget, under-provisioning defeats the purpose.
title: Warm Pool

body: Serving pattern · appears on: Serving Cho RL: Rollout Là Một Workload Riêng - What: vLLM's pluggable mechanism for pushing updated policy weights from a training process into a running inference engine. - How it works: After each optimisation step the trainer publishes new weights and the engine loads them, so subsequent rollouts sample from the current policy. When the engine is LoRA-aware, only adapter deltas are pushed rather than broadcasting every parameter — a sub-millisecond transfer. - Why it matters: In online RL the bottleneck is rarely token generation speed; it is the per-step weight synchronisation. Adapter-only sync is what makes colocated training and serving practical. - Gotcha: Weights must be in sync with the trajectories being scored — a stale engine silently produces off-policy data. Partial rollout (saving in-flight samples across a sync and continuing them next round) avoids idling the GPU while stragglers finish.
title: Weight transfer

body: RAG stores data in a deletable index; fine-tuning bakes it into weights. This is the core compliance asymmetry of the day.

body: Metric · appears on: Tokens-per-Joule frame: 'Median thực: ~0.31 Wh/query'; warningbox '3.91 Wh/query' - What: A per-query energy consumption metric that measures how much electrical energy (in watt-hours) a single LLM inference request consumes end-to-end, serving as the practical companion to 'tokens-per-joule' for cost and carbon accounting. - How it works: Wh/query is measured by instrumenting GPU power draw (via NVML or IPMI) during inference and dividing total energy consumed by number of queries processed. The research companion (Microsoft/Joule 2026, arXiv:2509.20241) measured a median of 0.31 Wh/query for standard chat tasks on production hardware, revising earlier estimates that overstated consumption by 4–20x. Reasoning model queries (with 15x more output tokens) raise this to ~3.91 Wh/query — a 13x increase cited in the deck's warningbox. - Why it matters: Wh/query converts the abstract 'tokens-per-joule' metric into a per-request cost that maps to billing (at $0.12/kWh: 0.31 Wh/query = $0.037/1000 queries in electricity alone) and carbon accounting (0.31 Wh × grid carbon intensity). It is the serving-layer energy SLO: routing easy queries to small models is justified when the Wh/query differential is large. - Gotcha: Wh/query is highly workload-dependent: a 2-token output query and a 2,000-token reasoning trace can differ by 100x in energy despite being the 'same request' at the API level. The 0.31/3.91 Wh comparison isolates the reasoning multiplier (more output tokens) from model size differences. Prior estimates (citing 1–10 Wh/query for GPT-4-class models) were measured under inefficient batch conditions or with idle GPU overhead included.
title: Wh/query
